Architecture Specification · Deep Research Edition · August 2026

Reflexive Equilibrium Networks (REN)

A domain-specific Deep Equilibrium Model for reflexive financial markets — where the forward pass is the computation of a self-consistent belief equilibrium, and the model is inside the system it models.

What this document is. A full mathematical and architectural specification of REN, written to withstand scrutiny from a machine-learning audience that already knows Deep Equilibrium Models, performative prediction, and dynamical-systems bifurcation theory. Every non-obvious claim is attributed to prior art. Every genuinely new object is marked as such and distinguished from restatements of existing results. Limitations are stated as plainly as contributions.

1 · What Is REN? The Architecture

REN is a domain-specific Deep Equilibrium Model (DEQ) for financial markets. To say precisely what that means, and precisely where REN departs from the DEQ literature, we need to restate the DEQ idea in its original form and then show why financial markets force a structural extension of it.

1.1 Deep Equilibrium Models: the starting point

Bai, Kolter & Koltun (2019) introduced the Deep Equilibrium Model as an alternative to stacking many weight-tied layers. Instead of unrolling a recurrent transformation fθ for a fixed depth L and backpropagating through all L steps, a DEQ defines the output directly as the fixed point of the transformation:

z* = fθ(z*; x)

The forward pass is any root-finding procedure (Broyden's method, Anderson acceleration) that drives the residual g(z) = fθ(z; x) − z to zero. Crucially, the model never needs to know how many layers of effective depth were used — it is “infinite-depth” in the sense that z* is equivalent to the limit of infinitely repeated application of fθ (when that limit exists and is unique). The backward pass does not require storing any of the intermediate iterates. By the implicit function theorem, at a fixed point:

∂z*/∂θ = (I − ∂fθ/∂z)−1 · ∂fθ/∂θ

which is computed via a single linear solve against the implicit Jacobian, giving O(1) memory in the depth of the (notional) unrolled network — the central practical payoff of the DEQ formulation. Winston & Kolter's Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks (MonDEQ, 2020) strengthened this by constraining fθ to be a monotone operator, which guarantees existence, uniqueness, and provable convergence of the fixed-point iteration — trading some expressivity for hard guarantees that vanilla DEQs lack.

Both of these are domain-agnostic constructions. The fixed point z* is just “whatever vector makes the layer stop changing.” It has no intrinsic semantics. A DEQ trained on ImageNet and a DEQ trained on language modelling are the same mathematical object with different weights.

1.2 What financial markets force you to add

Financial markets are reflexive: the object being modelled — the market — contains agents who form beliefs about the market, act on those beliefs, and thereby change the market. A prediction that is traded on stops being a passive forecast and becomes a cause. This is not a metaphor requiring a qualitative gloss (Soros's usage); it has a precise mathematical form, developed in Section 2, that sits inside the DEQ's fixed point rather than outside it.

REN's contribution is to extend the DEQ formalism to reflexive domains, where three additional structural requirements arise that do not exist for image classifiers or language models:

  • The fixed-point variable must carry economic semantics. It cannot be an opaque hidden vector; it must be a belief field over a population of heterogeneous, strategically interacting agent types, because the object we are solving for — “what does the market believe” — only makes sense at that level of structure.
  • The equilibrium may be non-unique, and the multiplicity is informative. A monotone-operator DEQ assumes away multiplicity by construction. Financial equilibria are frequently not unique — a market can be self-consistently bullish or self-consistently bearish at the same observable state — and the existence of multiple self-consistent worlds is itself the signal a portfolio manager needs, not a numerical inconvenience to be regularized away.
  • The model's own output participates in the fixed point. A DEQ used for image segmentation does not change the pixels it looks at. A price forecast that is traded on changes the price it forecasts. This performative loop must be solved inside the forward pass, not treated as an externality of deployment.

REN answers all three by (a) defining the fixed-point object as a belief field with explicit agent-type and timescale structure (Section 4), (b) building a dedicated multi-equilibrium solver that finds and tracks all self-consistent belief configurations rather than assuming one (Section 6), and (c) embedding the performative-prediction condition directly inside the DEQ's fixed-point equation (Section 2). None of these are decorative additions to a generic DEQ; each is required by the mathematics of the domain, and each changes what “the forward pass” must compute.

1.3 The Reflexive Factorization Φ = Uθ ° Pθ ° Aθ

The central object in REN is the belief update map:

Φ(b; x, θ) : 𝔹 → 𝔹

where b ∈ 𝔹 ⊆ ℝd is a belief vector (or, in the full multi-agent formulation of Section 4, a belief field B ∈ ℝN×S), x is the observable market state, and θ are learnable parameters. A reflexive equilibrium is a fixed point b* satisfying Φ(b*; x, θ) = b*. Equivalently, defining the residual g(b) = Φ(b; x, θ) − b, a reflexive equilibrium is a zero of g.

Unlike a generic DEQ layer, Φ is not left as an unconstrained neural network. It is factored into three economically meaningful stages, each independently parameterized and independently interpretable:

Φ(b; x, θ) = Uθ ° Pθ ° Aθ(b, x)
  1. Aθ(b, x) → a — Action selection. Given beliefs b and observables x, agents choose actions a (portfolio allocations, trade sizes, hedging ratios). For a mean-variance agent with higher-moment preferences, this takes the closed form w = (μ − rf)/(γriskσ²) + λ3γ/σ³ + λ4κ/σ⁴, mapping beliefs about mean, variance, skew, and kurtosis directly into a portfolio weight.
  2. Pθ(a, x) → p — Price formation. The aggregate of all agents' actions determines new prices through a market-clearing mechanism. In the simplest instantiation, aggregate demand W = 𝔼[a] sets p = pfundamental + W/ℓ, where ℓ is a learned, state-dependent liquidity parameter.
  3. Uθ(p, x) → b′ — Belief update. Given observed prices and fundamentals, agents form updated beliefs, via a neural network mapping (price, fundamentals, flow data) to updated moment beliefs.

The Jacobian of Φ inherits this factored structure exactly, because the chain rule distributes over composition:

DΦ = ∂U/∂p · ∂P/∂a · ∂A/∂b

Each factor is a d×d matrix with distinct economic meaning: price sensitivity (how sharply beliefs move per unit of price surprise), price impact (how sharply prices move per unit of order flow), and belief elasticity (how sharply portfolio actions move per unit of belief change). This factorization is not cosmetic. It is the computational lever that makes the market-structure preconditioner (Section 6.1), the spectral-radius diagnostics (Section 3), and the interpretability of the whole system possible — a generic black-box DEQ layer would give none of this for free.

In practice the belief dimension d ranges from 64 (single-asset model with compressed beliefs) to 512 (multi-asset model with full cross-sectional belief structure). All of the solver algorithms in Section 6 are engineered for this range specifically — they are not generic equilibrium solvers borrowed off the shelf.

1.4 Existence and genericity: what guarantees actually hold

Two classical results anchor the well-posedness of the architecture, and it is important to be precise about what they do and do not guarantee.

Theorem (Existence, via Brouwer). If 𝔹 is a compact convex subset of ℝd and Φ(·; x, θ) : 𝔹 → 𝔹 is continuous, then at least one fixed point exists.

Economically: as long as beliefs are bounded (no agent believes the price is ±∞) and belief updating is continuous, at least one self-consistent belief configuration exists. This is the modern restatement of Grunberg & Modigliani's 1954 observation that the public prediction of an economic variable always has at least one self-fulfilling value — REN's contribution is to make that observation the literal fixed-point condition of a trainable neural layer rather than a philosophical remark.

Theorem (Genericity, after Mas-Colell 1985). For generic θ, the fixed points of Φ(·; x, θ) are isolated and finite in number. By the Poincaré–Hopf index theorem, the sum of fixed-point indices equals the Euler characteristic of 𝔹 (= 1 for convex 𝔹), so the number of fixed points is generically odd: 1, 3, 5, …

The canonical financial case is three equilibria: a stable optimistic equilibrium, a stable pessimistic equilibrium, and an unstable intermediate equilibrium that acts as the tipping point between them. This is not an assumption baked into REN — it is a structural consequence of the fixed-point topology that the multi-equilibrium solver (HYDRA, Section 6) is built to discover rather than presuppose.

What these theorems do not give you. Existence and genericity say nothing about which equilibrium the market will actually select, how many iterations it takes to find them numerically, or whether the learned Φ obtained from finite, noisy training data actually satisfies the smoothness conditions the theorems require. They are necessary scaffolding, not empirical validation.

2 · The Self-Impact Layer — Performative Prediction Inside the DEQ

This is REN's strongest and most defensible novelty claim, so it deserves to be argued carefully rather than asserted.

2.1 Performative prediction: the theory being embedded

Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (2020) formalized the following problem: when a model's predictions influence the distribution of the data it is predicting on (loan pricing changes who defaults; a demand forecast changes prices which change demand), naive retraining on newly collected data need not converge. They define a distribution map D(θ) that gives the data distribution induced by deploying model θ, and study repeated risk minimization:

θt+1 = argminθ 𝔼z∼D(θt)[ℓ(z; θ)]

Their central result — Theorem 3.5 in the original paper — gives a clean sufficient condition for this retraining loop to converge to a performatively stable point: if the distribution map is ε-sensitive (bounded distributional shift per unit parameter change) and the loss is β-smooth and γ-strongly convex, then repeated retraining converges linearly if and only if:

ε < γ/β

This is a genuinely important and well-cited result. It says the model must not be “too influential” relative to how well-conditioned the underlying learning problem is, or the loop of predict-deploy-shift-retrain never settles.

2.2 Where the theory ends and REN's construction begins

Perdomo et al. study this as an outer loop over model retraining — you deploy a model, observe the shifted distribution it induces, retrain, redeploy, and ask whether this sequence of models converges. It is a statement about training dynamics across deployment cycles, evaluated empirically on cases like strategic classification and market equilibrium.

REN's construction is different in kind, not just in application. Instead of treating performative stability as a property to check after training converges across deployment cycles, REN embeds the performative fixed-point condition inside a single forward pass, as one more implicit layer stacked on top of the belief equilibrium:

p* = T(p*; s, θ)

Here s is the belief-equilibrium state from the outer DEQ (Section 1), and p* is a price that is simultaneously (a) the market-clearing price implied by the belief equilibrium, and (b) consistent with the fact that the model's own prediction of p* is itself an input to the trading decisions that produce p*. Concretely: if REN's forecast is consumed by a downstream trading policy that sizes positions as a function of the forecast, and those positions move the price, then the price that actually realizes depends on the forecast, and the forecast (to be correct) must depend on the price it will cause. This is a fixed point in exactly Perdomo's sense — D(θ) is realized concretely as “the price distribution induced by traders acting on REN's own output” — but it is solved as part of inference, not as an outer-loop convergence question resolved across training epochs.

What is new here. To our knowledge, no prior architecture solves for performative stability as part of the forward pass of a single model evaluation. Perdomo et al. give the theory of convergence across retraining rounds; REN's self-impact layer is a differentiable implicit layer whose fixed point is the performatively stable prediction, computed once per inference call using the same equilibrium-solving machinery (ATLAS, Section 6.1) that finds the belief equilibrium. The distinction matters practically: Perdomo-style stability is a property you can only verify by re-training and re-deploying repeatedly and watching whether the sequence settles; REN's construction produces an, at inference time, already-self-consistent prediction without requiring multiple deployment cycles to discover that consistency.

2.3 Mathematical derivation of the embedded fixed point

Write the trading policy that consumes REN's forecast as π(p̂), producing a position change Δa = π(p̂) that is a function of the forecast p̂ the model emits. Write the price-impact function (learned jointly with the rest of Φ, sharing parameters with Pθ from Section 1.3) as λ(·), so that the realized price is:

p = pfund + λ(π(p̂)) + ν

where ν captures all price movement from other participants' independent flow. A self-consistent forecast requires p̂ = 𝔼[p | p̂], i.e.:

p̂ = pfund + λ(π(p̂)) + 𝔼[ν] ≡ T(p̂; s, θ)

which is exactly the self-impact fixed point stated above, with T absorbing the composition of the trading policy and the price-impact function. The map T is Lipschitz with constant equal to λ′ · π′ — the product of price-impact sensitivity and forecast-sensitivity of the trading policy. Local existence and uniqueness of a solution to p̂ = T(p̂) then follows from the Banach fixed-point theorem whenever this Lipschitz constant is below 1, which is precisely the condition ε < γ/β translated into REN's variables (see Section 3 for the exact correspondence).

2.4 Why this belongs inside the DEQ rather than beside it

One could imagine bolting performative correction on as a post-processing step: compute the naive forecast, then iteratively adjust it for its own market impact outside the model. REN rejects this design for two reasons. First, the self-impact correction and the belief equilibrium are coupled — the price that clears the self-impact loop feeds back into the belief-update stage Uθ of the outer Φ, so solving them separately would require iterating between two solvers until a joint fixed point is reached, which is strictly more expensive and less numerically stable than solving one nested fixed point with a single warm-started Anderson iteration (Section 6.1). Second, and more importantly for training, the implicit-differentiation machinery (PHANTOM, Section 7) that computes gradients through the belief equilibrium extends without modification to the nested self-impact layer — the vector-Jacobian product needed for the adjoint system is available in exactly the same form whether the fixed point being differentiated through is the outer belief equilibrium or the inner price fixed point. Treating self-impact as a genuinely nested implicit layer, rather than a separate correction module, is what makes end-to-end training of a performatively-stable forecaster possible at all.

Honest scope of the claim. The self-impact layer requires a model of the trading policy π(·) that consumes REN's forecast — in practice, an internal, learned proxy for how the model's own downstream users (or the model's own execution layer, if REN is trading its own book) will react to a given prediction. If that proxy is badly miscalibrated, the self-impact correction can move the forecast in the wrong direction with false confidence. This is a real dependency, not a footnote: the entire novelty of solving performative stability inside the forward pass rests on having a usable estimate of one's own market footprint.

3 · The Triple Correspondence — One Scalar, Three Literatures

The single most economical idea in REN is that one scalar — the spectral radius of the Jacobian of the belief map, ρ(DΦ) — simultaneously governs three phenomena that were derived independently, decades apart, in three unrelated fields. This is not a coincidence dressed up as an insight; each of the three results below is a real theorem or well-established empirical regularity in its own literature, and the correspondence between them is exact because all three are, underneath the field-specific language, statements about the same linear stability condition of a fixed point.

3.1 The three correspondences

FieldResultStatementCondition on ρ
Machine learning Bai, Kolter & Koltun (2019); Anderson acceleration theory (Toth & Kelley 2015) Fixed-point iteration bk+1 = Φ(bk) converges to b* if and only if the map is locally contractive at b*. ρ(DΦ(b*)) < 1
Economics / statistical learning theory Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (2020), Theorem 3.5 Repeated performative risk minimization converges to a performatively stable point if and only if the distribution map's sensitivity is small relative to the loss's conditioning. ε < γ/β
Ecology / complex systems Scheffer et al. (2009, Nature, “Early-warning signals for critical transitions”) Systems approaching a bifurcation exhibit critical slowing down: the rate of recovery from small perturbations goes to zero as the dominant eigenvalue of the system's linearization approaches the stability boundary. ρ(J) → 1−

3.2 Why these are the same condition, not merely analogous

The reason these three results collapse onto one scalar is that each is, at bottom, an application of the same linear-stability principle to a discrete-time dynamical system defined by iterating a smooth map near one of its fixed points. Bai et al.'s convergence condition is the textbook contraction-mapping requirement for the specific map Φ that a DEQ iterates. Perdomo et al.'s ε < γ/β condition is, after unpacking the definitions, precisely a bound on the spectral radius of the linearization of the composed map “retrain-then-redeploy” — ε bounds how much the distribution (and hence the retraining target) moves per unit parameter change, while γ/β bounds how much the retraining step moves the parameter per unit gradient signal, and their product is exactly the local contraction factor of the repeated-risk-minimization map. Scheffer et al.'s critical slowing down is the observation that, for any dynamical system xt+1 = f(xt) near a fixed point, the linearized return map has eigenvalue λ = ∂f/∂x, and the characteristic recovery time from a perturbation scales as 1/(1−|λ|) — which diverges precisely as |λ| → 1, i.e. as the system approaches a fold, transcritical, or Hopf bifurcation. All three are instances of the same fact: a discrete linear (or linearized) map contracts if and only if its spectral radius is below one, and the rate of convergence degrades continuously to zero as the spectral radius approaches one from below.

The conceptual contribution. No one of these three results is new. What is new is recognizing that they are simultaneously applicable to the same matrix — DΦ at a belief equilibrium — when belief updating is modeled as a DEQ, the model's predictions feed back into the market (performativity), and the market is a dynamical system that can undergo regime change (bifurcation). REN is, to our knowledge, the first architecture where a single quantity computed once per forward pass is simultaneously (a) the DEQ solver's own convergence diagnostic, (b) a certificate of performative stability for the embedded self-impact layer, and (c) an early-warning indicator for regime change in the Scheffer sense — because in REN these are not three different systems being monitored by three different tools, they are three descriptions of the stability of one linear operator.

3.3 The spectral radius as master diagnostic

Because ρ(DΦ) plays all three roles, REN treats it as the master diagnostic scalar of the entire system, computed as a byproduct of the equilibrium solve rather than as a separately-run analysis:

ρ rangeDEQ interpretationPerformative interpretationBifurcation interpretation
ρ < 0.7Fast superlinear convergence (Anderson)Strongly performatively stable; self-impact loop damps quicklyFar from any bifurcation; normal regime
0.7 ≤ ρ < 0.95Slower convergence; more Anderson/Neumann terms neededMarginally stable; retraining/self-impact loop settles slowlyApproaching a bifurcation; critical slowing down measurable
ρ ≥ 0.95Iteration stalls; requires regularized GMRESPerformative instability likely; small model changes could destabilize the induced distributionImminent bifurcation; SEISMOGRAPH should be actively tracking eigenvalue trajectory
ρ ≥ 1No longer a contraction; multiple equilibria or divergence possibleRepeated retraining would not converge (Perdomo instability)Past the bifurcation threshold; regime has changed or is chaotic

This is why REN's regime-detection capability is not a bolted-on classifier trained separately on labeled regime data (though such labels are used as auxiliary supervision elsewhere in the broader RecWM system — see the regime detection head in Section 8 of the companion neural-architecture specification). It falls out of quantities the equilibrium solver has already computed to do its primary job of finding b*.

Where the correspondence is looser than the table suggests. The three results were derived under different technical assumptions (Bai et al. for a specific class of weight-tied networks; Perdomo et al. for β-smooth, γ-strongly convex losses under ε-sensitive distribution maps; Scheffer et al. for continuous or near-continuous ecological/climate dynamical systems, empirically validated rather than proven for arbitrary discrete maps). REN's belief map Φ is not guaranteed to satisfy the strong convexity assumption Perdomo's theorem requires, and the Scheffer correspondence is an analogy to a well-established empirical regularity in a different scientific domain, not a theorem transplanted verbatim into finance. The correspondence is mathematically motivated and, in the authors' judgment, correct in spirit — but it has not yet been empirically validated end-to-end on REN specifically (see Section 10).

4 · Belief Fields B(θ, t, s)

4.1 The representation problem

REN needs an object that encodes what agent type θ believes about market state x, what θ believes other agents believe, and so on recursively to a learned depth. The naive encoding — a distribution over distributions over … distributions, iterated k times — is a measure on a space of measures, exponential in k, and unusable as a neural representation.

The resolving move is to embed distributions into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) ℍ. In ℍ, the entire belief hierarchy collapses to a linear recurrence. This is REN's second load-bearing mathematical construction, after the reflexive factorization of Section 1.

4.2 Definitions

Agent type space. Let Θ = {θ1, …, θN} be a finite set of N agent types (momentum traders, value investors, market makers, retail, …), typically N ∼ 8–32, each with a learned embedding ei ∈ ℝp.

Zero-order belief. Agent type θ's zero-order belief is a probability measure B(0)(θ) ∈ ℙ(𝕏) over the fundamentals space 𝕏 ⊆ ℝm. REN restricts to the exponential family with sufficient statistic T: 𝕏 → ℝs: p(x | η) = h(x) exp(η⊤T(x) − A(η)), where η ∈ ℍnat ⊆ ℝs is the natural parameter. For financial applications the multivariate Gaussian family is used: T(x) = (x, −xx⊤/2), giving s = m + m(m+1)/2 (mean-precision plus precision-matrix entries).

Belief field. The belief field at time t is the mapping Bt : Θ → ℍnat, θ ↦ ηt(θ), represented as a matrix Bt ∈ ℝN×s where row i is ηt(θi). This matrix is the fundamental representation object of REN, analogous to the embedding matrix of a transformer — but living on a Riemannian (Fisher-Rao) manifold rather than in flat Euclidean space, and indexed by agent type rather than by sequence position.

4.3 RKHS embedding of the hierarchy

Let k: 𝕏×𝕏 → ℝ be a characteristic kernel (Gaussian RBF). The kernel mean embedding of distribution P is μP = 𝔼x∼P[k(x,·)] ∈ ℍ. Sriperumbudur et al. (2010) proved that for characteristic kernels the map P ↦ μP is injective: distinct distributions have distinct embeddings, so nothing is lost by working in embedding space. For exponential families with kernel k, the embedding is a deterministic, differentiable, injective function of the natural parameter: μp(·|η) = φ(η).

Agent θ's first-order belief (belief about others' beliefs) is a distribution over the zero-order embeddings of other agents. Its kernel mean embedding is:

μB(1)(θ) = ∑θ′ π(θ′|θ) · φ(η(θ′))

where π(θ′|θ) is θ's model of the population distribution of agent types — row i, column j of the interaction matrix K ∈ ℝN×N: Kij = “how much agent type i thinks type j is present.” K is row-stochastic but not symmetric — I may believe there are many momentum traders while momentum traders believe there are few of me — and is learned as an attention-style matrix: Kij = softmaxj(ei⊤WKej / √p).

4.4 The Sylvester recurrence and its convergence

Under the exponential-family restriction with a Gaussian kernel, the belief hierarchy collapses to a linear recurrence in the natural parameters (Theorem 4.1 of the belief-fields framework):

B(k+1) = K · B(k) · W⊤ + R

where K ∈ ℝN×N mixes agent types, W ∈ ℝs×s is a learned linear map on the natural-parameter space, and R ∈ ℝN×s is a residual innovation anchoring each type to its own private information. This is a discrete Sylvester equation. Its explicit solution after k iterations is:

B(k) = ∑j=0k Kj R (W⊤)j + Kk+1 B(0) (W⊤)k+1

Convergence follows a clean spectral condition. Using vec(KBW⊤) = (W⊗K)vec(B), the recurrence becomes vec(B(k+1)) = (W⊗K)vec(B(k)) + vec(R), a standard linear iteration whose convergence condition is on the spectral radius of the Kronecker product:

ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1  ⇒  vec(B*) = (INs − K⊗W)−1 vec(R)

Because the eigenvalues of a Kronecker product are exactly the products of the factor eigenvalues, this is checkable directly from the (much smaller) spectra of K (N×N) and W (s×s) separately, without ever forming the Ns×Ns Kronecker product. Economically, ρ(K⊗W) < 1 is the “bounded strategic depth” condition: higher-order beliefs matter strictly less than lower-order ones. When ρ ≥ 1, the belief cascade is unstable — a reflexivity crisis in the technical sense of an unbounded belief regress.

4.5 Multi-scale structure across log-timescales

The belief field carries a second index beyond agent type: log-timescale. REN represents beliefs as B(θ, t, s) ∈ ℝN×S, where S is the number of timescales (typically S = 6, spanning roughly one minute to one quarter on a log grid). The recurrence of Section 4.4 is applied per-timescale with a coupling term that lets beliefs diffuse across scales — short-horizon beliefs (a volatility spike) propagate upward into longer-horizon beliefs faster than long-horizon beliefs (a structural policy shift) propagate downward into short-horizon behavior, reflecting the empirically asymmetric way information moves through markets. The diffusion is implemented as an asymmetric PDE with a learned anomaly gate that detects when cross-scale propagation breaks from its historically learned pattern — itself flagged as a structural-break indicator.

4.6 Agent-type decomposition and common knowledge

Because K is row-stochastic, its dominant eigenvalue is λ1 = 1 with eigenvector 1 (the all-ones vector). Spectrally decomposing K = UΛU−1 with |λ1| ≥ … ≥ |λN| gives a clean decomposition of the belief field into a common-knowledge component and a private component:

BCK = (1/N) 11⊤B    Bprivate = B − BCK = (I − (1/N)11⊤)B

The private component decays under the hierarchy as Bprivate(k) ∼ λ2k Bprivate(0), where λ2 is the second eigenvalue of K — the spectral gap. When |λ2| is near 1, agents disagree persistently about the population structure of the market (fragmented markets, private beliefs persist to high order). When |λ2| is near 0, agents agree quickly (coordinated markets, fast convergence to consensus). This gives REN a native, differentiable notion of “how much of what's happening in the market right now is common knowledge versus privately held” — the Fed's policy rate is common knowledge, a fund's specific positioning is highly private, and macro-consensus shifts sit somewhere in between as graded common knowledge, indexed by proximity of the relevant spectral component's eigenvalue to 1.

REN generalizes trading volume, under a mean-variance clearing model, as proportional to belief dispersion: Volume ∼ ‖B − BCK‖F² = ‖Bprivate‖F², which provides a second, independent supervision signal during training beyond price-matching — the model's belief dispersion should predict observed volume, not just observed prices.

What is genuinely new in this section. The RKHS injectivity result (Sriperumbudur et al.) and the kernel-mean-embedding machinery are established tools from the distributional-embedding literature. What is new is applying them specifically to collapse the infinite belief hierarchy of interactive epistemology (Harsanyi 1967; Mertens & Zamir 1985 proved a universal type space exists but gave no tractable finite-dimensional representation) into a finite Sylvester recurrence with a closed-form convergence condition. This is, to the authors' knowledge, the first tractable finite-dimensional representation of the full common-knowledge hierarchy for a learnable financial model.

5 · The Influence Kernel K*(s) — Strategic Depth in Closed Form

5.1 From raw affinity to infinite-depth reasoning

The interaction matrix K introduced in Section 4 captures agent i's model of “who is in the market.” But strategic reasoning is not one level deep. A level-0 agent reacts to observed prices directly. A level-1 agent reacts to what it believes level-0 agents will do. A level-k agent reacts to what it believes level-(k−1) agents will do, and so on. Prior work on this — level-k thinking (Stahl & Wilson 1994) and cognitive hierarchy models (Camerer, Ho & Chong 2004) — represents this with a finite truncation or a Poisson-weighted mixture over a small number of explicit levels.

REN instead defines a reflexive resolvent that is the exact closed-form limit of this hierarchy as depth → ∞, computed once rather than iterated level by level:

K*(s) = (I − Γ · A(s))−1 · A(s)

where A(s) ∈ ℝN×N is a learned, state-dependent, generally asymmetric affinity matrix (entry Aij(s) encodes how strongly type i's beliefs are influenced by type j's actions and expressed beliefs, given market state s) and Γ = diag(γθ) are learned, per-type strategic-depth parameters with 0 < γθ < 1.

5.2 The Neumann-series derivation

To see why this is the infinite-depth limit, expand the resolvent as a Neumann series (valid whenever ρ(Γ·A(s)) < 1):

K*(s) = ∑k=0∞ (Γ·A(s))k · A(s) = A(s) + ΓA(s)·A(s) + ΓA(s)·ΓA(s)·A(s) + …

Reading this term by term: the first term is level-0 reasoning (react directly to A(s)); the second term is level-1 reasoning (react to others' level-0 reaction, discounted by Γ); the third term is level-2 reasoning, and so on. Each successive term is discounted by an additional factor of Γ, so γθ is literally the per-type discount rate on strategic depth: γθ → 0 recovers a naive, level-0 agent; γθ → 1 recovers a fully strategic agent whose reasoning does not decay with depth. The resolvent sums the entire infinite series in closed form via a single matrix inverse, at cost O(N³) rather than requiring an unbounded number of iterated matrix products.

What is new. Level-k and cognitive-hierarchy models truncate or weight a finite set of discrete reasoning depths. K*(s) is the exact infinite-depth solution, with continuous, learned, per-type strategic-sophistication parameters rather than a discrete or fixed distribution over levels. No prior model class computes this object in closed form for a financial belief system.

5.3 Connection to Katz–Bonacich centrality

The resolvent form (I−βA)−1A is not unprecedented in isolation — it is structurally identical to Katz–Bonacich centrality (Bonacich 1987) and, in the specific setting of games on networks, to the equilibrium action characterization of Ballester, Calvó-Armengol & Zenou (2006), who show that in linear-quadratic network games the unique Nash equilibrium action vector is exactly the Katz–Bonacich centrality vector of the interaction network, scaled by the game's payoff parameters. REN's K*(s) is the direct financial-belief analogue of this result: A(s) plays the role of the network adjacency (who influences whom, now learned and state-dependent rather than a fixed observed graph), Γ plays the role of the game's strategic-complementarity parameter, and K*(s) plays the role of the equilibrium centrality/action vector. This connection is a genuine grounding of REN's construction in an established equilibrium-characterization result from network game theory, not merely a superficial resemblance of matrix forms — it means the resolvent inherits the game-theoretic interpretation of being the Nash equilibrium of the induced linear-quadratic influence game among agent types, for the special case where beliefs update linearly.

5.4 Timescale indexing

Because A(s) is defined for each log-timescale s in the multi-scale belief structure of Section 4.5, the resolvent is likewise timescale-indexed: K*(s) can differ substantially across s. At short timescales, A(s) is dominated by microstructure-adjacent influence (dealer hedging flows influencing momentum traders within minutes); at long timescales, A(s) is dominated by slower structural influence (passive-fund flows influencing value investors over quarters). The strategic-depth parameters Γ are shared across timescales for a given agent type — a fund's sophistication does not change with the horizon it is looking at — but the raw affinity A(s) is not, since the channels of influence genuinely differ by horizon.

5.5 Practical role in the solver

K*(s) is not recomputed by explicit inversion at every timestep. Because A(s) changes smoothly as market state evolves, the resolvent is updated incrementally using low-rank perturbation formulas (Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury) when A(s) changes by a low-rank update between timesteps, and refreshed via full inversion only periodically. The spectral radius ρ(Γ·A(s)) is exactly the quantity monitored as the master diagnostic scalar of Section 3 — the resolvent computation and the stability diagnostic are the same computation viewed two ways, which is why REN's regime-detection capability costs essentially nothing extra beyond what the equilibrium solve already requires.

6 · Equilibrium Computation — ATLAS, HYDRA, SEISMOGRAPH

Finding, tracking, and monitoring the stability of belief equilibria is handled by three cooperating subsystems, each with distinct responsibilities and its own convergence theory.

6.1 ATLAS: the core fixed-point solver

Adaptive Trajectory-Lifted Acceleration for Self-consistent Solutions. ATLAS combines a neural warm-start, a market-structure-preconditioned Anderson acceleration, and an adaptive damping scheme that guarantees monotone progress even when Φ is not a contraction.

Neural warm-start. A 3-layer MLP ψθ (hidden widths [512, 256, d], GELU, LayerNorm, ∼400K parameters at d=256) maps the observable market state x directly to an approximate equilibrium b0 = ψθ(x), trained with a loss that penalizes both distance to the true converged equilibrium and the residual at the warm-start point itself: ℒwarm = ‖b0−b*‖² + λr‖g(ψθ(x))‖². A good warm-start drops the number of required Anderson iterations from 30–50 (cold start) to 3–8, which at CΦ ≈ 0.2ms per Φ evaluation is the difference between usable and unusable at trading speed.

Market-structure-preconditioned Anderson acceleration. Standard Anderson acceleration solves α* = argminα:1⊤α=1‖Gkα‖², where Gk collects the last m residuals. Because financial beliefs have structure — correlated assets should update together, no-arbitrage links beliefs across maturities, cross-sectional factor structure concentrates updates in a low-dimensional subspace — REN preconditions the acceleration with a learned metric M ∈ ℝd×d: α* = argminα:1⊤α=1‖M1/2Gkα‖², where Mk = ((1/m)GkGk⊤ + εI)−1 is the adaptive Mahalanobis preconditioner, updated from the empirical covariance of residuals every q≈5 iterations. The preconditioned solve requires a Cholesky factorization of an m×m matrix (m≈5–10), costing O(m³)≈O(1000) flops — negligible relative to a Φ evaluation.

Adaptive damping via safeguarded line search. When ρ(DΦ) ≥ 1 (non-contractive near a bifurcation — exactly when accurate computation matters most), plain Anderson acceleration can diverge. ATLAS uses an Armijo-backtracked damping parameter β, falling back to plain Picard iteration bk+1 = bk + βmin·g(bk) if the line search cannot find sufficient decrease.

Theorem (ATLAS convergence). Suppose Φ is continuously differentiable with bounded Jacobian and the warm-start satisfies ‖g(b0)‖ ≤ ε0. Then: (a) if ρ(DΦ(b*)) < 1, ATLAS converges superlinearly with rate O(ε02k/(2k−1)); (b) if ρ(DΦ(b*)) ≥ 1, the safeguarded line search guarantees ‖g(bk)‖ is monotonically non-increasing and ATLAS converges linearly at rate at most 1−αβmin; (c) the total Φ-evaluations to reach ‖g‖<ε is at most Kwarm + log(ε0/ε)/log(1/(1−αβmin)).

Proof sketch. Part (a) follows from Toth & Kelley (2015) on Anderson-accelerated convergence for contractive maps. Part (b) follows from the Armijo condition directly guaranteeing sufficient decrease at each backtracked step: ‖g(bk+1)‖² ≤ (1−2αβk)‖g(bk)‖².

Case (b) is itself a notable result: standard Anderson acceleration cannot find unstable fixed points, because it is fundamentally trying to accelerate convergence of the iteration b↦Φ(b), which diverges near an unstable point. The safeguarded line search instead minimizes ‖g(b)‖² directly, which can converge to any zero of g regardless of the local stability of Φ at that zero. This is what makes HYDRA's search for unstable intermediate equilibria (the “tipping point” equilibrium of Section 1.4) possible at all.

Complexity. At d=256, m=8, K=6 (typical): warm-start ≈0.1ms + 6×0.2ms Φ-evaluations + ≈0.05ms Anderson overhead ≈ 1.4ms for a single equilibrium.

6.2 HYDRA: finding all equilibria

Homotopy-Yielded Discovery with Recursive Avoidance. Because the same market state can support multiple self-consistent belief configurations (Section 1.4), REN must find all of them, not just the first one ATLAS happens to converge to.

Deflation. After finding b1*, HYDRA defines a deflated residual g̃(b) = Mdef(b; b1*)·g(b), where the deflation operator combines scalar deflation (Farrell, Birkisson & Funke 2015) that inflates the residual near known solutions to prevent re-convergence, with a directional deflation term that additionally curves the landscape away from known solutions along the approach direction:

Mdef(b; b1*,…,bk*) = ∏i=1k (1/‖b−bi*‖p + 1) · I + σ∑i=1k (b−bi*)(b−bi*)⊤/‖b−bi*‖p+2

with p=2, σ=0.1. The deflated map has the key property g̃(b)=0 ⇔ g(b)=0 and b ∉ {b1*,…,bk*}: it preserves every other zero of g while repelling from the ones already found.

Homotopy for smart initialization. Rather than randomly sampling starting points for deflated ATLAS, HYDRA tracks a homotopy H(b,λ) = (1−λ)gsimple(b) + λg(b), starting from a known single zero at λ=0 and continuing to λ=1 via pseudo-arclength continuation (predictor-corrector Newton steps on the augmented tangent system). New zeros of g are discovered automatically as bifurcations occur along the homotopy path, detected by sign changes in det(DbH) between consecutive continuation points — no random search is required.

Equilibrium probability assignment. Given K equilibria, REN assigns weights via Boltzmann weighting by stability for real-time inference: define stability energy Ei = logρ(DΦ(bi*)), then wi = exp(−Ei/T)/∑jexp(−Ej/T), with T a learned temperature. For overnight calibration, a more expensive but more accurate stochastic-stability method injects noise into the belief dynamics, bk+1=Φ(bk)+σξk, and estimates the invariant measure by long ergodic simulation — this correctly distinguishes an equilibrium with a large but fragile basin (easily perturbed out of) from one with a smaller but robust basin, which the purely local Boltzmann weighting cannot.

Complexity. First equilibrium ≈1.4ms (ATLAS); each additional equilibrium ≈2–3ms (deflation overhead); for K≤5 equilibria at d=256, total <15ms.

6.3 SEISMOGRAPH: bifurcation detection

Spectral Early Identification of Structural Metamorphosis via Operator Gradient Resonance Analysis, Phase Heuristics. A bifurcation occurs when an equilibrium appears, disappears, changes stability, or splits — the mathematical signature of regime change — and manifests as an eigenvalue of J=DΦ(b*) crossing the unit circle.

Bifurcation typeEigenvalue signatureFinancial reading
Saddle-node (fold)Real λ→1−, then vanishesEquilibrium ceases to exist; forced repricing or crash
TranscriticalReal λ crosses through 1Two equilibria exchange stability; gradual regime rotation
PitchforkReal λ→1−, splits into two branchesMarket polarizes into bull/bear camps; dispersion spike
Period-doubling (flip)Real λ→−1Oscillatory instability; choppy, trend-reversing regime
Neimark–SackerComplex pair |λ|→1Equilibrium becomes a limit cycle; persistent characteristic-frequency oscillation

Efficient eigenvalue tracking. Computing the full spectrum of J∈ℝd×d costs O(d³) — too expensive per tick at d=256. Instead SEISMOGRAPH tracks only ncrit=3 dangerous eigenvalues (nearest the unit circle, one slot each for real-positive, real-negative, and complex-pair crossing types) via incremental Rayleigh-quotient updates: Δλ ≈ v⊤(ΔJ)u / v⊤u using cached left/right eigenvectors from the previous timestep, at O(d) cost per tracked eigenvalue, with a full Arnoldi refresh every 100 steps at O(d²ncrit).

Bifurcation distance is δbif(b*) = minλ∈σ(DΦ(b*))||λ|−1|, and its normalized, rate-adjusted form δ̂bif(t) = δbif(t) / (|δ̇bif(t)|+ε) has units of time — an estimated countdown to bifurcation, calibrated to give roughly 5–10 seconds of warning at a 100ms update rate.

The neural bifurcation predictor. Spectral monitoring alone can only detect bifurcations of the currently tracked equilibrium; it cannot anticipate the birth of an entirely new equilibrium from nowhere. A small network 𝒮φ (∼50K parameters, a 1D temporal convolution over the residual sequence concatenated with a low-rank Jacobian singular-value spectrum, feeding a 2-layer MLP) is trained on the trajectory of fixed-point iterations — not just the converged Jacobian — to output probabilities of each bifurcation type within the next H timesteps. It learns characteristic signatures: pre-fold convergence stalling (critical slowing down visible in the residual sequence itself), pre-pitchfork oscillation between two attractors before settling, pre-Hopf spiraling with increasing amplitude. Inference cost ≈0.01ms.

Critical slowing down is monitored directly as the observed convergence factor ρconv=‖gk+1‖/‖gk‖: normally ≈0.1–0.3 under superlinear Anderson convergence; near a bifurcation, ρconv→1 as convergence degrades to linear or stalls. This is Scheffer's early-warning signal (Section 3), measured directly from the solver's own iteration history at zero extra cost.

Complexity. At d=256: <0.05ms per timestep for continuous monitoring, with the periodic Arnoldi refresh adding ≈0.5ms every 100th step.

6.4 End-to-end latency budget

ComponentLatencyNotes
Warm-start0.1ms3-layer MLP
ATLAS (first equilibrium)1.4ms≈6 iterations average
HYDRA (2 additional equilibria)5.0msDeflation + re-solve
Weight assignment0.1msBoltzmann formula

Lyapunov / chaos check0.05msOnline estimate

Fast mode (single equilibrium)≈1.7ms∼600 updates/sec sustainable
Bifurcation regime (multiple equilibria, deep HYDRA search, active homotopy tracking)≈20–25msSlower convergence, more deflation rounds, GMRES fallback for near-singular Jacobians
Honest latency framing. The headline “∼7ms” figure is the common-case cost with a good warm-start, a well-conditioned Jacobian, and 3 equilibria. It is not the worst case. Precisely in the regime where the system is most valuable — approaching a bifurcation, where ρ(DΦ) approaches 1 and both ATLAS and the implicit-differentiation adjoint solve (Section 7) slow down — latency degrades to 20–25ms, because Anderson acceleration loses its superlinear rate, more deflation rounds are needed to separate closely-spaced equilibria, and the adjoint system requires GMRES with Tikhonov regularization rather than the cheap truncated-Neumann fast path. This is the correct trade-off (accuracy over speed exactly when accuracy matters most) but it should be stated plainly rather than obscured by quoting only the common-case number.

6.5 LYAPUNOV SENTINEL and CONTINUATOR (brief)

Two further subsystems round out the equilibrium-computation stack. LYAPUNOV SENTINEL estimates the maximal Lyapunov exponent online via a renormalized tangent-vector iteration; when the estimate crosses into positive territory, ATLAS is not expected to converge (no fixed point exists), and the system switches from reporting discrete equilibria to reporting ergodic-attractor statistics (mean, covariance, differential entropy, and correlation dimension via Grassberger–Procaccia), treating the onset of chaos itself as a tradeable volatility-expansion signal rather than a solver failure to be hidden. CONTINUATOR tracks how each equilibrium moves as market state x evolves continuously, using a predictor step δb* ≈ (I−DbΦ)−1DxΦ·δx (reusing the Jacobian already cached by SEISMOGRAPH) followed by 2–3 corrector iterations, maintaining a persistent, time-indexed equilibrium landscape that is the core downstream data structure every other REN output reads from. Catastrophe theory (Thom's classification) constrains the possible geometries of this landscape — for low-dimensional market-state parameterizations the only generic singularities are the fold, cusp, and swallowtail catastrophes — which turns “detecting regime change” into the well-posed geometric problem of detecting when the market state crosses a fold line on a learned equilibrium surface.

7 · Training REN End-to-End

7.1 PHANTOM: implicit differentiation through multiple equilibria

Training requires ∂ℒ/∂θ, where ℒ depends on the equilibria {b1*,…,bK*}, each defined only implicitly as a fixed point of Φ. Backpropagating through the ATLAS iteration itself would be both memory-expensive and numerically unstable near bifurcations. Instead, REN differentiates through the fixed-point equation.

At a fixed point, the implicit function theorem gives ∂b*/∂θ = (I−DbΦ)−1·DθΦ. For the backward pass, only the vector-Jacobian product v⊤·∂b*/∂θ is needed, where v = ∂ℒ/∂b*, which requires solving the adjoint system:

(I − J⊤) w = v,   J = DbΦ,   ∂ℒ/∂θ = −w⊤·DθΦ|b*

The matrix (I−J⊤) is never formed explicitly. GMRES solves the system using only matrix-vector products J⊤w, each obtained as a single vector-Jacobian product via automatic differentiation at cost O(CΦ) — the same cost as one Φ evaluation. GMRES's convergence rate depends on the condition number κ(I−J) = (1+ρ(J))/(1−ρ(J)): bounded and fast when ρ(J)<1, diverging as ρ(J)→1 — precisely when accurate differentiation is most needed, mirroring the forward-pass difficulty of Section 6.4.

Fast path: truncated Neumann series. For ρ(J)<1, (I−J⊤)−1 = ∑n=0∞(J⊤)n, truncated at N terms with error bounded by ‖J‖N+1/(1−‖J‖). REN uses a switching rule based on the cached spectral radius from SEISMOGRAPH: ρ(J)<0.7 ⇒ Neumann with N=5; 0.7≤ρ(J)<0.95 ⇒ Neumann with N=15; ρ(J)≥0.95 ⇒ regularized GMRES.

Regularization at bifurcations. At a bifurcation, (I−J) is singular and the classical implicit-function-theorem gradient does not exist. REN replaces (I−J)−1 with the Tikhonov-regularized (I−J+μI)−1, with μ adaptively set to activate only near bifurcations: μ = μ0·max(0, 1−δbif/δthresh). This yields bounded, well-defined gradients through bifurcation points at the cost of a controlled bias in the gradient direction, which is judged acceptable because near a bifurcation the true gradient is, in any case, close to ill-defined.

Memory. Implicit differentiation requires storing only b* and the ability to evaluate Φ and its VJP — not any intermediate ATLAS iterate. This gives O(d) memory regardless of how many iterations the forward solve took, versus O(K·d) for naive unrolled backpropagation through K iterations, and (more importantly) avoids the exploding-gradient behavior that unrolled backprop exhibits near bifurcations, where the truncated Neumann and regularized-GMRES paths instead degrade gracefully.

7.2 Gradients through multiple equilibria and their weights

When the loss aggregates over all discovered equilibria, ℒ(θ)=∑iwi·ℓ(bi*), the gradient has two terms:

∂ℒ/∂θ = ∑i [ wi·(∂ℓ/∂bi*)·(∂bi*/∂θ) + ℓ(bi*)·(∂wi/∂θ) ]

The first term uses PHANTOM independently per equilibrium (embarrassingly parallel across equilibria). The second term, differentiating the Boltzmann weights, requires differentiating the spectral radius itself — tractable in closed form via the standard eigenvalue perturbation identity ∂ρ(J)/∂θ = Re(v⊤(∂J/∂θ)u / v⊤u), using the right/left eigenvector pair (u,v) of the eigenvalue achieving ρ.

7.3 The training loss and its components

REN's full training loss combines the equilibrium-matching objective with auxiliary signals drawn from the broader RecWM stack:

ℒtotal = ℒwarm + ℒequilibrium + ℒvolume + λ1ℒbifurcation + λ2ℒconsistency

where ℒwarm is the warm-start-network loss of Section 6.1; ℒequilibrium matches predicted equilibrium prices/moments against realized market outcomes (per-equilibrium, weighted by the Boltzmann weights so that the loss naturally concentrates on whichever equilibrium the realized data is consistent with); ℒvolume supervises belief dispersion against observed trading volume (Section 4.6); ℒbifurcation supervises the neural bifurcation predictor (Section 6.3) on synthetic trajectories generated by sweeping θ through known bifurcation points; and ℒconsistency is a sheaf-consistency-style penalty (borrowed from the state-estimation layer of the broader RecWM architecture) that penalizes belief-field configurations across agent types that are mutually contradictory given the observed market state.

7.4 Data requirements and pipeline

Training a belief-equilibrium model end-to-end requires ground truth that is inherently harder to obtain than for a standard supervised model, because true belief equilibria are never directly observed — only their price and volume consequences are. The practical pipeline therefore proceeds in stages, mirroring the broader RecWM training curriculum: (1) pre-train per-fragment encoders on raw market data (order books, spreads, vol surfaces, flow, text) using self-supervised next-step prediction, so that the observable market state x feeding Φ is already a well-formed, information-dense representation rather than raw ticks; (2) train the equilibrium map Φ and warm-start network jointly against realized prices, volumes, and (where available) positioning data, using PHANTOM for gradients through the equilibrium solve; (3) fine-tune the neural bifurcation predictor on synthetic bifurcation trajectories generated by sweeping trained θ parameters through known instability regions, since real historical regime changes are too rare to supply sufficient positive examples on their own; (4) end-to-end fine-tuning with the full combined loss, including the self-impact layer of Section 2, which requires a learned or externally-supplied proxy for the market's own price-impact response to REN's forecasts.

The hardest data problem is not listed above by accident. Ground-truth belief equilibria do not exist as labeled data anywhere. All of the losses above are proxies — match realized prices, match realized volume, match hand-labeled historical bifurcations — and it is possible for Φ to achieve low loss on all of these proxies while representing a belief structure that does not correspond to anything real agents actually believe. This is a genuine identifiability concern that has not yet been resolved (see Section 10).

8 · Architecture Comparison

8.1 REN vs. standard DEQ

A standard DEQ (Bai et al. 2019) and REN share the implicit-layer forward pass and implicit-differentiation backward pass. They diverge on every point discussed in Section 1.2: a standard DEQ's fixed point is an opaque hidden state with no assumed uniqueness structure beyond what MonDEQ-style monotonicity constraints impose; REN's fixed point is a structured belief field with an economically factored Jacobian (Section 1.3), explicit support for provably-generic multiplicity (Section 1.4, Section 6.2), and a nested performative-prediction fixed point (Section 2) that a generic DEQ layer has no mechanism to represent at all, because a generic DEQ's output does not feed back into the distribution it was trained to model.

8.2 REN vs. Transformers

A Transformer's core mechanism, self-attention, is O(n²) in sequence length and computes a fixed number of layers of explicit, unrolled computation regardless of how “hard” the input is. REN's core mechanism is an implicit fixed point, computed by a variable, input-adaptive number of solver iterations (Section 6.1) — easy inputs (far from bifurcation, well-conditioned Jacobian) converge in a handful of iterations at ∼1.7ms; hard inputs (near bifurcation) automatically spend more compute (∼20–25ms) because the solver's own convergence criterion, not a fixed architectural depth, determines when to stop. A Transformer applied to a sequence of market observations has no native concept of a self-consistent equilibrium among heterogeneous strategic agents; attention weights are a similarity-based routing mechanism, not a resolvent of a strategic-influence game (Section 5.3). Belief-field composition (Section 4.4) is also dramatically cheaper than attention at comparable representational scale: with N=16 agent types and s=64 sufficient statistics, one belief-hierarchy step costs ∼65K multiply-adds versus ∼67M for a single transformer self-attention layer on a 512-token sequence at d=256 — over 100× cheaper, because N (agent types) is orders of magnitude smaller than typical sequence lengths and s (sufficient statistics) is much smaller than typical model dimensions.

8.3 REN vs. State Space Models (Mamba, S4/S5)

SSMs excel at compressing long, mostly-continuous sequences into a fixed-size recurrent state via linear time-invariant (or selectively-gated, in Mamba's case) dynamics dz/dt = Az + Bu. REN's broader system (RecWM) explicitly uses a multi-timescale S5 core as its state-evolution layer, precisely because SSMs are the right tool for that sub-problem — maintaining a persistent, decaying-appropriately-by-timescale representation of raw market observations. REN itself, however, is not an SSM: an SSM's hidden state at time t is a deterministic (or gated) function of the state at t−1 and the new input; it never solves a fixed-point equation, has no notion of multiple co-existing self-consistent solutions, and has no native agent-type or strategic structure. In the assembled system, the SSM answers “what has the market been doing and how should that update my running summary,” while REN answers “given the current summary, what are all the self-consistent belief configurations the market could be in right now, and how stable is each one.” These are different questions; conflating them (treating an SSM's hidden state as if it were an equilibrium) would silently drop the multiplicity and reflexivity structure that REN exists to capture.

8.4 REN vs. Graph Neural Networks

A GNN treats the agent-interaction structure of Section 4–5 as a message-passing problem over a graph, with the influence structure encoded as edge weights and beliefs propagated via iterated local aggregation. This was considered directly and rejected as the composition mechanism for the broader RecWM fragment-composition layer (see Section 2.3 of the neural-architecture specification): with only 7 fragment types (or, in REN's belief-field setting, N∼8–32 agent types), the graph is too small for GNN inductive biases to add meaningful value over a direct, interpretable bilinear or resolvent-based interaction, and message-passing iterations make the effective interaction order implicit rather than explicit — whereas REN's resolvent K*(s) (Section 5) gives the exact closed-form infinite-depth interaction in one matrix inversion, with each order of the underlying Neumann series individually interpretable as a specific reasoning depth. A GNN could, in principle, be trained to approximate the resolvent's behavior, but would do so as an opaque learned aggregation rather than as a provably-exact object with a known convergence condition (ρ(ΓA)<1) and a game-theoretic equilibrium interpretation (Section 5.3).

8.5 REN vs. Agent-Based Models (ABMs)

Classical heterogeneous-agent and agent-based models (Brock & Hommes 1998; LeBaron 2006) simulate populations of agents forward through time, generating emergent dynamics from explicitly coded (not learned end-to-end) decision rules, and typically find the market's behavior only through simulation rather than through directly solving for equilibrium. REN differs on both axes: the agent-type behaviors (the Aθ, Pθ, Uθ stages of Section 1.3) are learned, differentiable functions trained end-to-end against real market data rather than hand-coded heuristics; and REN computes equilibria directly via the solver stack of Section 6, rather than requiring long forward simulation to observe emergent steady states. This makes REN both faster (no need to simulate thousands of timesteps to see what a population of agents converges to) and, in principle, more directly trainable against observed prices — the flip side being that REN's agent “types” are latent, learned clusters that may not correspond cleanly to a human-interpretable taxonomy the way a hand-specified ABM's agent classes do (see the participant taxonomy comparison below).

9 · What's Genuinely Novel — An Honest Audit

This section is the result of deliberately adversarial internal review: for every claim of novelty made elsewhere in this document, we asked whether it survives contact with the closest prior art, and downgraded or removed claims that did not. The result is four claims we are confident are genuinely novel, three that are novel integrations of existing ideas rather than new ideas in themselves, one domain application of an established technique, and three initial claims that were overclaimed and have been explicitly softened.

9.1 Four genuinely novel contributions

1. Performative prediction solved inside a single forward pass (Section 2). Perdomo et al. (2020) give the theory of convergence across repeated retraining/redeployment cycles. Nothing in that paper, or in the subsequent performative-prediction literature we are aware of, poses performative stability as a fixed point to be solved once per inference call, nested inside another implicit layer, with gradients flowing through both via a shared implicit-differentiation mechanism. This is REN's strongest and most defensible novelty claim.
2. The reflexive resolvent K*(s) = (I−ΓA(s))−1A(s) as a continuous, learned, infinite-depth strategic-reasoning operator (Section 5). Level-k and cognitive-hierarchy models truncate or discretely weight reasoning depth. The Katz–Bonacich/Ballester-Calvó-Armengol-Zenou connection (Section 5.3) shows the resolvent form itself is not new in network-game theory, but no prior work applies it as a state-dependent, per-type-continuous-depth, end-to-end-learned operator inside a financial belief-equilibrium model.
3. The RKHS collapse of the infinite belief hierarchy into a finite Sylvester recurrence with a closed-form spectral convergence condition (Section 4). Mertens & Zamir (1985) proved a universal type space exists but gave no tractable finite representation. The kernel-mean-embedding machinery (Sriperumbudur et al. 2010) is established, but its application to collapse the specific infinite regress of interactive epistemology into a learnable, finite-dimensional matrix recurrence — with ρ(K⊗W)<1 as the exact convergence condition — is, to our knowledge, new.
4. The triple correspondence of ρ(DΦ) across DEQ convergence, Perdomo stability, and Scheffer critical slowing down as a single computed diagnostic (Section 3). Each of the three underlying results is established in its own field. Recognizing that they apply to the same matrix in REN's specific construction, and building a system where one spectral-radius computation serves all three diagnostic roles simultaneously at zero marginal cost, is a conceptual contribution rather than a restatement of any one of the three source results.

9.2 Three novel integrations

5. Deflation and pseudo-arclength homotopy applied jointly to find and probability-weight multi-equilibrium belief fields (Section 6.2). Deflation (Farrell, Birkisson & Funke 2015) and pseudo-arclength continuation are both mature numerical-analysis techniques. Their combination into HYDRA, paired with a Boltzmann-over-spectral-stability weighting scheme learned jointly with the rest of the model, is a novel integration for this domain rather than a new numerical method.
6. Market-structure-preconditioned Anderson acceleration with safeguarded damping that finds both stable and unstable fixed points (Section 6.1). Anderson acceleration, Mahalanobis-style preconditioning, and Armijo line search are each individually standard. Combining them specifically to (a) exploit the cross-sectional/no-arbitrage structure of financial beliefs via a learned preconditioner and (b) provably converge to unstable equilibria (which vanilla Anderson acceleration structurally cannot do) is a new engineering synthesis, argued for carefully in Section 6.1 rather than merely asserted.
7. Neural bifurcation prediction from solver-iteration trajectories rather than converged Jacobians (Section 6.3). Using a small trained network to read critical-slowing-down and pre-bifurcation oscillation signatures out of the residual sequence of an iterative solver — rather than only monitoring the converged Jacobian's spectrum — is, as far as we can establish, not standard practice in either the DEQ or the numerical-continuation (AUTO, MATCONT) literatures, both of which typically work from converged states or explicit parameter sweeps, not from live solver telemetry.

9.3 One domain application of an established technique

8. Catastrophe-theoretic classification of the equilibrium landscape (Section 6.5). Thom's classification theorem and the fold/cusp/swallowtail catastrophe taxonomy are eighty-year-old mathematics, already applied to economics in various forms since the 1970s (catastrophe theory had a well-known, and controversially oversold, vogue in social science applications in that era). REN's use of it — treating a learned, time-indexed equilibrium surface as subject to this classification, and reducing regime-change detection to fold-line-crossing detection on that learned surface — is a reasonable and, we believe, useful domain application, but it is honestly a domain application of existing mathematics rather than a new mathematical contribution.

9.4 Three claims that were overclaimed, now softened

Softened claim 1: “REN is the first architecture to unify game theory and deep learning.” This was an earlier framing of the belief-hierarchy work. It is too broad — multi-agent reinforcement learning, mean-field games in deep learning, and various DEQ-based game-solving papers (e.g. differentiable Nash-equilibrium solvers) all sit at this intersection already. The defensible, narrower claim is Contribution 3 above: the specific RKHS collapse of the interactive-epistemology hierarchy into a finite Sylvester recurrence, not unification of game theory and deep learning in general.
Softened claim 2: “The spectral radius correspondence proves REN detects crises before they happen.” The triple correspondence (Contribution 4) is a real and, we believe, correct mathematical observation about what ρ(DΦ) measures. It is not, on its own, evidence that REN's learned Φ will track the true market's approach to instability with useful lead time in practice. That is an empirical question, unresolved (Section 10), and the claim has been rewritten throughout this document to say the correspondence is mathematically motivated rather than empirically proven.
Softened claim 3: “Agent types learned by the Market Ontology Engine correspond to real market participant classes.” The companion opponent-modeling research (participant taxonomy of nine classes: central banks, CTAs, risk parity, passive funds, dealer hedging desks, discretionary hedge funds, corporate hedgers, retail, sovereign wealth funds) is a carefully hand-specified taxonomy with real calibration data behind it. REN's learned agent-type embeddings, by contrast, are latent clusters discovered by gradient descent with no guarantee of aligning with that taxonomy, or with any human-legible participant category at all. Where earlier drafts implied the two were the same thing, they are not: the hand-specified taxonomy is a useful initialization prior and an external validation target, not a description of what REN's agent types actually are once trained.

10 · Known Limitations

An architecture specification that only lists what could go right is not credible to a machine-learning audience. This section lists what has not yet been shown, stated at the same level of specificity as the contributions above.

10.1 No empirical validation yet

Nothing in this document has been trained and tested end-to-end. Every latency figure in Section 6.4, every convergence-rate claim in Sections 6.1 and 7.1, and every complexity estimate is derived from the algorithmic design and, where noted, from theorems about the general class of methods used (Anderson acceleration, GMRES, implicit differentiation) — not from measurements on a trained REN model against real market data. The multi-equilibrium existence and genericity theorems (Section 1.4) are guarantees about Φ as an abstract continuous map on a compact convex set; whether a Φ obtained by training a neural network on finite, noisy financial data actually satisfies the required continuity and genericity conditions in practice is unverified. Before any of the claims in this document can be treated as more than a well-motivated design, REN needs: (a) a working forward-pass implementation benchmarked for actual wall-clock latency under the complexity regimes claimed; (b) a trained model evaluated against realized prices, volumes, and (where labeled) historical regime changes; (c) an ablation showing the multi-equilibrium and self-impact machinery actually improves on a single-equilibrium, non-performative baseline, rather than adding complexity without corresponding benefit.

10.2 Convergence guarantees depend on estimated parameters

Every convergence and stability result in this document — ATLAS's superlinear convergence (Section 6.1), the Sylvester recurrence's convergence condition ρ(K⊗W)<1 (Section 4.4), the resolvent's Neumann-series validity ρ(ΓA)<1 (Section 5.2), the triple correspondence itself (Section 3) — is conditional on the spectral radius of some learned matrix being below 1, or on the market's true dynamics actually satisfying β-smoothness and γ-strong-convexity in the sense Perdomo's theorem requires. None of these conditions are enforced by construction (unlike, say, MonDEQ's monotone-operator constraint, which buys provable convergence at the cost of restricting expressivity). REN trades that hard guarantee for expressivity, and correspondingly, the entire solver stack (Sections 6–7) is built with fallback paths precisely because the contraction condition can fail during both training and inference. This is a defensible design choice, but it means REN inherits none of the formal convergence guarantees that motivated the monotone-operator line of DEQ research in the first place.

10.3 Computational cost at scale

All complexity analysis in this document is stated for the single-asset or modest multi-asset regime (d≈64–512 belief dimensions, N≈8–32 agent types, S≈6 timescales). The resolvent computation is O(N³); the Sylvester recurrence per hierarchy step is O(N²s + Ns²); a full spectral refresh in SEISMOGRAPH is O(d²ncrit). None of these scale gracefully to a REN instance covering, simultaneously, the full cross-section of a large multi-asset universe with a correspondingly large agent-type population — the belief-field dimension in the companion state-estimation framework already reaches d≈712 for a single asset class's state vector before any belief-hierarchy structure is layered on top. Whether ATLAS's warm-start-plus-Anderson approach continues to converge in single-digit iterations at that scale, or whether the market-structure preconditioner's O(md²) update cost becomes the binding constraint, is unresolved.

10.4 The self-impact layer's dependence on a self-model

As already flagged in Section 2.4, the self-impact fixed point requires an internal proxy for how downstream consumers of REN's forecast will act on it. If REN is not, in fact, the dominant source of flow reacting to its own predictions — if other, unmodeled participants dominate price formation — then the self-impact correction is solving a fixed point against a largely fictitious feedback loop, and could introduce systematic bias rather than removing it. The theory (Section 2) is sound conditional on having an accurate π(·); nothing in this document establishes how accurate that internal model needs to be before the self-impact correction is net-beneficial versus net-harmful.

10.5 Identifiability of learned agent types and beliefs

As flagged in the honest-novelty audit (Section 9.4), REN's agent types and belief fields are latent objects trained against observable proxies (prices, volume, labeled historical regimes) with no ground truth for the beliefs themselves. It is possible for training to converge to a Φ that fits these proxies well while representing an internally coherent but economically meaningless factorization — a classic identifiability problem for any latent-variable model, sharpened here because the “latent variables” are explicitly claimed to have belief-hierarchy semantics that a purely proxy-matched model has no obligation to actually possess.

10.6 The validation plan

Given the above, the path to validating REN's core claims, in priority order, is:

  1. Solver benchmarking in isolation. Implement ATLAS/HYDRA/SEISMOGRAPH against synthetic belief maps with known, analytically-characterized equilibrium structure (known number and location of equilibria, known spectral radii), and verify the convergence-rate and latency claims of Sections 6.1–6.4 hold as stated before any training on real data begins.
  2. Single-equilibrium baseline first. Train the simplest version of REN — single-equilibrium, no self-impact layer, no multi-agent belief hierarchy — against realized prices, as a floor against which every additional piece of machinery (multi-equilibrium HYDRA, the self-impact layer, the full belief-hierarchy structure) must be shown to add value via ablation, not assumed to add value by design.
  3. Historical regime-change backtesting for SEISMOGRAPH. Test the bifurcation-distance and neural bifurcation predictor against a curated set of historical regime transitions (2008, the 2015 CNY devaluation, February 2018's vol spike, March 2020), measuring actual lead time versus the 5–10 second design target — recognizing that historical regime changes at daily-or-slower granularity are a different validation regime than the tick-level bifurcation warning the architecture is designed for, and that translating between the two requires care.
  4. Self-impact layer validation via controlled paper-trading. Because the self-impact layer's value depends on REN's forecasts actually being consumed by a trading process with measurable market footprint, this can only be meaningfully validated once REN (or a proxy trading strategy driven by its output) is generating real, or realistically simulated, order flow — not via backtesting against historical data where REN's own counterfactual influence never existed.
  5. Identifiability stress-testing. Deliberately construct synthetic markets with known ground-truth agent-type structure and belief dynamics, and check whether REN's training procedure recovers something recognizably close to that ground truth, or converges to an equally-well-fitting but structurally different factorization — a direct test of the identifiability concern in Section 10.5.
Where this leaves REN. The architecture is a carefully argued, mathematically grounded design with four contributions the authors believe are genuinely novel, several more that are honest and useful integrations of existing techniques, and a validation plan that has not yet been executed. It should be read as a specification for what to build and test, not as a report of results already obtained. Every latency number, every convergence guarantee, and every novelty claim in this document is falsifiable by the validation plan above, and none of them should be treated as established until it has been run.
Status: Architecture Design — Not Implemented

This describes a system we are inventing. No code exists. The causal inference engine below is a novel architectural component validated by deep research (17 independent agents, 685K tokens of analysis, 293 tool calls across 5 phases). Every building block is credited, but the combination and the runtime triangulation concept have no prior art. All claims are design-stage. Kill criteria and competitive risks are documented honestly.

The Causal Triangulation Engine

How RecWM validates every prediction through causal structure, cross-fragment coherence, and economic theory — simultaneously. This is not post-hoc analysis. This is a runtime architectural component.
