Section 19

Citation Strategy — What to Build On, What to Avoid

The research compendium that seeded this project draws on several exotic theoretical frameworks. Some are load-bearing and safe. Others carry active pseudoscience accusations that would follow our papers into review. This section is the filter. It exists so nobody spends a month building on a foundation that a referee can dismiss in one sentence.

Tier 1 — Build on these

FrameworkAnchor citationWhy it's safe
Performative predictionPerdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt, ICML 2020Top-tier, uncontested, and it is our formal core. Lead with it.
Dynamical independenceBarnett & Seth, Phys. Rev. E 108:014304 (2023)Built on Granger causality / transfer entropy. No arbitrary intervention distribution. Transformation-invariant. MATLAB code ships. The cleanest thing in the emergence field.
Exact CE, linear systemsLiu, Yuan & Zhang, Entropy 26(8):618 (2024)Closed form on exactly the model class economics uses. Our computational workhorse.
ΦID emergence criteriaRosas et al., PLOS Comp Biol 16:e1008289 (2020); Mediano et al., PNAS 122 (2025)Tests a macro variable you nominate rather than searching for one — sidesteps the combinatorics. PNAS gives citation armor.
Growth optimalityKelly (1956), Breiman (1961)The actual mathematics behind ergodicity economics, 70 years old and uncontroversial.
Path signaturesStandard rough-path literature; pysiglib for implementationMature, mathematically settled.

Tier 2 — Cite carefully, position deliberately

Ergodicity economics

Cite the mathematics and Peters & Adamou's transformation-equals-utility correspondence. Lead with Baumann et al. (TMLR 2025) — peer-reviewed, ships code, Peters is a co-author. Do not adopt the movement's rhetoric about economics being fundamentally in error. There is a live dispute on the record in Nature Physics (Doctor, Wakker & Wang 2020, with a reply from Peters), and one of our referees may be a disputant. Also note Peters' 2019 Nature Physics piece is a Perspective, not a research article — do not cite it as if it proves something.

Hoel's causal emergence

Cite the 2013 PNAS paper as the origin of the question — reviewers will expect it — but cite the critiques in the same sentence. Two peer-reviewed objections stand largely unanswered: Dewhurst (Thought, 2021) argues it supports only epistemic emergence, and Eberhardt & Lee (Philosophies, 2022) show the uniform intervention distribution is extraneous and that marginalization and abstraction do not commute. Pre-empting this signals sophistication instead of naivety.

Tier 3 — Do not build on, do not cite prominently

Assembly theory — avoid. The compendium proposed a "Copresheaf Assembly Constructor" architecture built on it. Do not pursue that. Zenil et al. argue the assembly index is reproducible by LZ-family compression, making it equivalent to a Shannon-entropy statistical measure rather than a new theory of selection; there is a critical review in BioSystems (2024); and the dispute is unsettled as of 2026 with named critics including Tour, Benner, Hazen and Jaeger. There is no quality economics application. It imports a live pseudoscience accusation in exchange for nothing formal.

Use instead, for "how much construction history is in this object": Bennett's logical depth, or Crutchfield & Young statistical complexity / ε-machines. The latter has real algorithms (CSSR), was designed for time series, and carries 40 years of standing with zero controversy. It does the same conceptual work.

IIT and Φ — do not cite. 124 signatories called it pseudoscience in 2023; that document became a Nature Neuroscience paper in April 2025 with 132+ named authors including Yoshua Bengio. Bengio's signature is precisely what makes this a problem in an ML venue — reviewers there treat him as an authority and will not adjudicate the consciousness debate. Φ is also computationally hopeless: O(n5·3n), practical limit around 10–12 nodes. We gain nothing and pay a real cost.

Note the entanglement: Hoel is a co-author on the IIT defense paper, and effective information is lifted from IIT machinery. That is a reason to prefer Barnett & Seth as our emergence anchor — same job, no inherited fight. ΦID is fine despite the name: it is a PNAS-published general information-theoretic decomposition, and the Φ is inheritance, not endorsement.

Constructor theory — low risk, near-zero payoff. Real venues (Deutsch, Synthese 2013; Deutsch & Marletto, Proc. R. Soc. A 2015), not fringe. But ~13 years in, uptake outside the originating circle is minimal and there is no economics application at all. A reviewer will ask what it buys us formally, and the honest answer today is "framing." It costs a paragraph and earns nothing. The possible/impossible transformation framing is genuinely useful to us as internal vocabulary for the constraint field — just don't hang the paper on it.

Direct substitutions — same idea, canonical instead of contested

Every exotic framework in the compendium has a mainstream equivalent that does the same conceptual work with an order of magnitude more citations and no baggage. Use the right column.

Instead of…Use…Citations
Assembly theory — "possibility space of what can be built next"Tria, Loreto, Servedio & Strogatz, Sci. Rep. 4:5890 (2014), "The dynamics of correlated novelties" — the formal Pólya-urn treatment of the adjacent possible~152
Assembly theory — economic version of the sameHidalgo & Hausmann, PNAS 106:10570 (2009); Hidalgo et al., Science 317:482 (2007)~2,388 / ~2,169
Assembly index — "construction history embodied in an object"Bennett, "Logical Depth and Physical Complexity" (1988) — the actual intellectual ancestor, 37 years unchallengedundercounted
Assembly index as a computable measureCrutchfield & Young, PRL 63:105 (1989); Shalizi & Crutchfield, J. Stat. Phys. 104:817 (2001) — statistical complexity / ε-machines, with real algorithms, built for time series~741 / ~328
Constructor theory — "a model that takes interventions"Barnett & Crutchfield, J. Stat. Phys. 161:404 (2015) — ε-transducers, the closest well-founded formal object to an intervention-capable world model~54
IIT / ΦTransfer entropy — Marschinski & Kantz, Eur. Phys. J. B 30:275 (2002). Already mainstream econophysics; nobody will blink.~395
The trade in one line: this substitution loses nothing conceptual and swaps ~150-citation contested work for 700–2,400-citation canon. The ε-transducer row is the one to look at hardest — it is a better formal fit for what we are actually building than constructor theory ever was.
Two things not to do, learned the expensive way. First: the constructor-theory thermodynamics paper (arXiv:1608.02625) has sat on arXiv for ten years across five versions with no journal reference — it is the paper you would want to lean on for entropy/irreversibility, and it has never passed peer review. Second: there is one preprint connecting both constructor theory and assembly theory to macroeconomic forecasting (arXiv:2603.24559, marked "draft"). It is not a citable precedent. If our paper becomes the second item in that reference class, that is the company we keep.

One attribution error to fix everywhere

Our internal notes record the convergence condition ε < γ/β as due to Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (2025). That is wrong. It is Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt, ICML 2020, Theorem 3.5. Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (Statistical Science, 2025) is the survey. A referee in this area will catch the misattribution immediately, and it would cost us credibility across the whole related-work section. Fix it in every document before anything ships.

The three thresholds — keep them straight

ConditionWhat it guaranteesSource
ε < γ/βRepeated risk minimization contracts; a unique performatively stable point exists and is reachablePerdomo Thm 3.5
ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)]Repeated gradient descent converges — strictly tighterPerdomo Thm 3.8
ε ≤ γ/(2β)Performative risk is convex, so the optimum is findableMiller, Perdomo & Zrnic, ICML 2021, Thm 3.1
The gap worth naming. Between γ/(2β) and γ/β there is a regime where you can find the reflexive fixed point but the performative risk is non-convex — stable but not optimizable. That regime is unnamed in the literature, and it is plausibly where any interesting economy actually lives. Characterizing it is cheap, honest novelty and it is sitting there unclaimed.

Where genuine extension is available, ranked by defensibility

  1. Endogenous ε — the strongest slot. In Perdomo, ε is a fixed environmental constant. In a real economy sensitivity is state- and regime-dependent. A model where εt is learned and endogenous, so the system crosses γ/β dynamically, converts a static condition into a crisis mechanism. Nobody has done this, and it is exactly what our Reflexive Instability signal measures.
  2. The differentiable equilibrium layer, made rigorous. Implicit-function-theorem differentiation through a fixed point requires (I − ∂G/∂θ) invertible — which is the contraction condition. So ε < γ/β becomes the well-posedness criterion for a differentiable performative-equilibrium layer. That reframes a borrowed condition as load-bearing in a new construction: legitimate, clean, and publishable. The DEQ machinery is mature and the performative-equilibrium definition is settled; searching the intersection returns the two literatures separately, with no paper joining them.
  3. Reflexive causal emergence. Per §4 — every emergence framework assumes a fixed generative process. Ours does not. Extending Barnett & Seth to a setting where the coarse-graining feeds back into the dynamics is a real open problem.
  4. Formal counterperformativity. Named by MacKenzie & Bamford in 2018, still qualitative in the 2025 meta-review, and the performative-prediction survey explicitly lists MacKenzie-style performativity as out of scope. Confirmed vacant by the field's own survey.
Section 20

Evaluation Protocol & Baselines — The Week-7 Bar

Our Fragment VAE is a structured latent-variable model with typed sub-states. That places it in a specific, well-benchmarked literature with published numbers. This section is the bar. Everything here is a real reported score from a real paper — these are not targets we invented.

The single most important fact in this literature. On the Turing Change Point Dataset — 37 real series, each annotated by 5 humans — a baseline called zero, which predicts no change points at all, outperforms 9 of the 13 published algorithms in the default-hyperparameter setting (covering 0.583, F1 0.669). The authors' reading: most methods return a flood of false positives.

Include a do-nothing baseline in week 7. If we don't, a reviewer will, and it will be in the rebuttal rather than the paper.

Direct competitors — structured switching models

RED-SDS and SNLDS are the closest published architectures to what we are building, and they are the only literature that evaluates regime decomposition against known ground truth with ARI/NMI. Frame-wise accuracy after Hungarian label matching:

MetricModelBouncing ball3-mode systemDancing bees (K=3)
AccuracySNLDS0.970.820.44
RED-SDS0.970.980.73
NMISNLDS0.830.630.10
RED-SDS0.810.910.48
ARISNLDS0.900.670.10
RED-SDS0.880.950.53

Two things to take from this literature. First, ARI / NMI / Hungarian-matched accuracy is the honest metric set for an unsupervised state decomposition — adopt it. Second, RED-SDS's entire advantage over SNLDS is explicit duration modelling (0.73 vs 0.44 on dancing bees). Our fragments have characteristic timescales τj by construction, which is the same idea. That is an argument we can make and test.

A warning from the same literature: in the SNLDS paper, a naive Gumbel-Softmax relaxation of the discrete variable collapses to F1 5.0 where proper forward-backward marginalization reaches 78.1. If any part of our architecture discretizes, marginalize it properly — do not reach for a straight-through relaxation.

Signature-MMD — a strong published competitor, not a freebie

§14 flagged signature kernels as a cheap extra baseline. The literature is more demanding than that. Issa & Horvath's non-parametric online detector reports, over 100 runs on regime-switching paths:

DetectorTotal accuracyROC AUCRuntime
Truncated signature (N=5)72.7%0.8755.1s
SIG-CON (Cochrane et al.)82.2%0.83545.0s
Untruncated sig-MMD93.6%0.9923.9s

Note that the untruncated signature kernel beats the truncated one decisively (93.6% vs 72.7%) and runs faster. If we use signature MMD, use the kernel — not truncated signature features fed to a distance.

Where to pick the fight

This is the most strategically useful finding in the whole literature review. Classical methods dominate mean-shift detection — BinSeg (1974) wins the TCPD default benchmark outright, and a 1970s generalized likelihood ratio test beats the celebrated deep KL-CPD method, whose average AUC of 0.48 is below chance. Learned methods only earn their keep on two things: covariance-structure change (neural 0.90–0.93 F1 vs classical 0.62–0.85) and long-range duration structure (RED-SDS 0.73 vs SNLDS 0.44).

Economic regimes are exactly covariance-structure and duration phenomena. Frame the contribution there and we are arguing on favourable ground. Frame it as general-purpose change detection and we lose to an algorithm from 1974.

Macro baselines — the numbers to beat

Real-time turning-point detection delay (months; negative = anticipates the NBER call). Barigozzi & Massacci's Markov-switching factor model on FRED-MD is best-in-class:

Turning pointChauvet & Piger (2008)Barigozzi–Massacci (2024)
Recession Feb-8061
Expansion Nov-826−7
Recession Jan-08139
Expansion Jul-097−4
Recession Mar-2001

Concordance with NBER: DoC 0.7718 on FRED-MD macro series, 0.8048 on stock returns. Chauvet–Piger's smoothed recession probabilities are live on FRED as RECPROUSM156N — a free, continuously updated real-time baseline with no excuse for omitting it.

Use PR AUC, not ROC AUC. The US recession base rate is ~0.086, so that is the random-guess floor for PR AUC. In the best current recession-prediction paper, ROC AUC compresses every model into 0.75–0.95 and hides real differences, while PR AUC spreads the same models across 0.17–0.72. A ROC AUC of 0.9 here is unremarkable; a PR AUC of 0.5 is genuinely strong. Reporting ROC AUC on a 9%-base-rate problem reads as either naive or evasive.

The corner-solution trap

A 2024 deep regime-detection paper on SPD manifolds reports 98.90% out-of-sample accuracy. It is a corner solution — the model classifies almost everything as "normal" — and a plain mean-variance benchmark still beat all their models on cumulative return. Their own conclusion: "using a singular performance metric is misleading."

Elsewhere in the same literature, a model posts accuracy 0.876 with F1 exactly 0.000 — it never predicts a recession at all. Report confusion matrices, always. And report downstream task performance separately, without claiming it validates the segmentation: the one paper that measured both found them decoupled.

The week-7 checklist

  1. Synthetic regime-switching data with known labels → ARI + NMI + Hungarian-matched accuracy, against: Gaussian HMM, HSMM, SNLDS, RED-SDS, Wasserstein k-means, BinSeg, PELT, BOCPD, sig-MMD, and zero.
  2. Confusion matrices for everything, to prove we have not found a corner solution.
  3. FRED-MD → NBER concordance + false-positive/false-negative rates + per-turning-point signed detection delay.
  4. PR AUC and F2 (a missed regime shift costs more than a false alarm), not accuracy and not ROC AUC alone.
  5. Default and tuned hyperparameters for every baseline. One kernel method on TCPD swings from 0.062 to 0.626 on tuning alone — reporting only one setting is not a result.
  6. Sensitivity to K (number of fragments) and to random seed. HMM initialization sensitivity is real and papers disclose it.
The opening this creates. The field's most-cited unsupervised regime-clustering paper reports no comparative accuracy table at all — its "vastly outperforms all competitors" claim is backed by two figures and a qualitative reading of three crises. Meanwhile the ML segmentation community has clean ARI/NMI protocols that nobody in finance has imported. Bringing RED-SDS-grade evaluation rigor to FRED-MD would be a contribution on evaluation methodology alone, independent of whether our architecture wins. That is a second, cheaper claim to novelty sitting inside work we are already committed to doing.

One calibration point on ambition. On real macro-financial regime shifts scored against a verified 26-event monetary-policy anchor list, pure data-only detectors max out at F1 = 0.68. The methods that reach 0.82 do it by adding unstructured text (FOMC minutes via an LLM). That is the honest ceiling for what fragments alone can achieve on real data — worth knowing before we set week-7 success criteria, and worth remembering as evidence that our narrative fragment type is not decoration.

Section 21

Identifiability — Whether "Interpretable Fragments" Survives Review

Paper 1's central claim is that world fragments are interpretable. There is a large, sharp literature on exactly when that claim is provable and when it is empty. This section determines the architecture. Read it before writing the VAE.

The impossibility theorem — this kills the original design. Locatello et al. (ICML 2019 best paper) prove that for any latent with a factorized density, there exists an infinite family of bijections f such that every output coordinate depends on every input coordinate (completely entangled) and the distribution is identical. Both give the same likelihood. Therefore no amount of unsupervised training on p(x) can distinguish disentangled from entangled solutions.

A total-correlation penalty does not fix this. β-TCVAE, FactorVAE, and DIP-VAE all penalize TC, and all are subject to the theorem. Their 12,600-model study found ~41% of disentanglement-score variance is explained by the random seed, and that unsupervised model selection remains unsolved. Our earlier loss used a TC term as the disentanglement mechanism. That has been removed from §12.

The threat specific to us — correlated factors. Träuble et al. (ICML 2021), Proposition 1: when the ground-truth factors are correlated but the model prior factorizes, a generative model that matches the true marginal likelihood cannot be disentangled. The objective actively prefers entangled solutions — it encodes the correlation's major and minor axes instead of the factors.

Macro factors are never independent. Liquidity, credit, and volatility co-move by construction. And the standard metrics — DCI, MIG, SAP, FactorVAE score — show no clear degradation trend when this happens. We would not detect the failure from our own numbers. This is the single biggest threat to the program and it must be designed against, not tested for.

What actually buys identifiability

There are roughly seven known symmetry-breakers. Interventions are unavailable to us. Of the rest, two fit typed fragments almost perfectly.

1. Structural sparsity of the measurement map START HERE

Zheng, Ng & Zhang, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2206.07751) Let ℱ = supp(Jf(s)) be the support of the decoder Jacobian. Structural Sparsity assumption: ∀k ∈ {1..n}, ∃ a set 𝒞k such that ⋂i∈𝒞k ℱi,: = {k} In words: for each latent source, there exists a set of observed variables whose ONLY common latent influence is that source. ⇒ Theorem 1: identifiable up to permutation + component-wise invertible transformation. // Critically: NO auxiliary variable. No regime count requirement. // The paper explicitly removes "common restrictions on required // auxiliary variables, such as number of distinct values."

Why this is our argument. In macro this holds by construction of the measurement model: credit spreads load only on the credit fragment, CPI components only on prices, the term structure only on policy. We do not have to discover this sparsity — we design the data-to-fragment map to have it, and then the identifiability follows. Same idea in Bayesian form: SparseVAE's anchor-feature assumption (≥2 observed features depending only on each factor), which notably still recovers ground-truth factors at factor correlation ρ ≤ 0.4 where a standard VAE fails.

2. Mechanism sparsity of the fragment transition graph

Lachapelle et al., CLeaR 2022 (arXiv:2107.10098) Graphical criterion: for each latent p, ∃ index sets I, J, L with (⋂i∈I Pazi) ∩ (⋂j∈J Chzj) ∩ (⋂ℓ∈L Chaℓ) = {p} ⇒ permutation-equivalence (full disentanglement). Proposition 2.6 — the checkable design rule: The criterion holds if all nodes have SELF-LOOPS (Gzii = 1) and there are NO 2-CYCLES in Gz. // Directly actionable: give every fragment its own persistence term, // and forbid mutual instantaneous feedback between fragment pairs. // That is an architecture constraint we can simply impose.

The 2024 nonparametric follow-up (arXiv:2401.04890) gives us the entanglement graph — the dependency graph of the entanglement map. This is the honest vocabulary for a partial result: "fragments 1, 2 and 5 are individually identified; fragments 3 and 4 are identified only as a block." That is a publishable, defensible claim shape, and far better than an overclaim a reviewer breaks.

The bar we should not pretend to clear

iVAE's condition is out of reach and we should say so. The auxiliary-variable route (Khemakhem et al., AISTATS 2020) requires nk+1 distinct values of the auxiliary variable, with an nk×nk difference matrix invertible. A conditional Gaussian with regime-varying mean and variance is k=2, so for n=20 fragments that is 41 distinct, sufficiently-varied regimes. Monthly macro data with recession/expansion labels gives us two. Do not build the identifiability argument on this route, and do not let it appear in the paper as though we cleared it — this is where most applied claims quietly break.

Two more design constraints from the theory

  • Gaussian-AR latents are not identifiable from temporal dependence alone. PCL requires non-Gaussianity; GCL's Theorem 2 shows the variability assumption cannot hold for an order-k=1 exponential family. If our fragment dynamics are linear-Gaussian — which is the natural first implementation — identifiability must come from sparsity or regimes, not from the temporal structure.
  • Contemporaneous effects break the standard temporal results. TDRL assumes no instantaneous causal influence between latents. Macro fragments plainly interact within-period (rates → FX inside a month). The assumption set that handles this without interventions is IDOL (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2405.15325), which pays for it with a sparsity condition on the instantaneous graph. Use that framing.

What we can honestly claim

"Fragment axes are identified up to permutation and a component-wise invertible reparameterization, under structural sparsity of the measurement map and sparsity of the fragment transition graph. Fragment magnitudes are not identified; fragment identity and conditional-independence structure are."

Anything stronger is not supported by any theorem in this literature. In particular, nothing gives us "fragment 3 = credit conditions in natural units" — scale and monotone reparameterization are fundamentally unidentifiable in nonlinear ICA. Plan every interpretability claim around which axis, never around what value.

Validation protocol

  1. Synthetic DGP matching our assumed structure → report strong (Hungarian-matched) Spearman MCC, and say explicitly which MCC you mean. Weak MCC (recovery up to an invertible linear map, scored by joint linear fit) and strong MCC are different numbers and are not comparable. Target > 0.95 — that is what matched-structure methods actually achieve.
  2. Run the TDRL-style ablation. In their paper: plain β-VAE reaches MCC ~0.45, adding the causal-process prior takes it to ~0.73, the nonstationary flow to ~0.94, the full model to ~0.98. Almost all the gain comes from the structural prior, not from the VAE. Our ablation should show the same decomposition, because it is the evidence that the fragment structure is doing the work.
  3. Report DCI-ES Explicitness, not just D and C. Eastwood et al. (ICLR 2023) show D/C and explicitness are largely orthogonal — a deliberately linearly-mixed ground truth scores D=0, C=0 yet E=1.0 under an MLP probe. Our fragments are meant to be usable, not axis-pure. E is the metric that measures that.
  4. Held-out-regime transfer as the real-data proxy. There is no ground truth for economic fragments, and no MCC has ever been reported on real data in this literature. Do not invent one.
  5. Keep a small labeled anchor set. Träuble's fix for correlated factors is a post-hoc substitution function needing as few as 100 labels (<0.02% of their dataset), cutting entanglement from 0.38 to 0.17. Cheap insurance against the failure mode our metrics cannot see.
Where this leaves Paper 1. The identifiability exposure flagged in §17 is real but addressable — and the fix is a better architecture, not a softer claim. Building on structural sparsity rather than a TC penalty gives us a theorem to cite instead of a metric to defend. It also sharpens the novelty: no identifiability-claiming causal-representation paper on macroeconomic time series surfaced in the literature search. We would be first, which means we will also be the first to have to defend one properly.
Section 22

What We're Measured Against — Foundation Models & the Honest Bar

There is now a crowded field of time-series foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, Toto-2.0, Moirai-2.0, TiRex). Before positioning against them, one fact reorganizes everything: on the data we care about, they barely work.

The single most important number for our positioning. In the only vintage-consistent, leakage-free real-time FRED-MD evaluation published (MACROCAST, June 2026, arXiv:2606.28670), the best purpose-built macro foundation model improves on a plain AR(1) by a median of 2.9% RMSFE at h=1 and 0.5% at h=12. Chronos-2 zero-shot manages 4.8% at nowcast horizon and converges to AR(1) by h=3. Moirai-2.0 tracks AR(1) at ~1.00 essentially everywhere.

On macro data, the entire foundation-model advantage collapses. This is not a gap in the models — it is a property of low-frequency, short-history, regime-switching economic data. It is also our opening: if scale barely helps, structure can.

Where the TSFM advantage actually lives — and doesn't

On the GIFT-Eval leaderboard, foundation models cut error ~35% below seasonal naive at secondly/minutely/hourly frequency. At monthly, AutoARIMA ties the best foundation model. At yearly, plain AutoETS and AutoTheta beat every foundation model. On fev-bench's FRED-MD/FRED-QD tasks, a classical statistical ensemble (AutoARIMA + AutoETS + AutoCES + DynamicOptimizedTheta) has geometric-mean MASE 1.000 versus Chronos-2's 1.039 and TimesFM-2.5's 1.101 — the ensemble beats two of the three leading foundation models.

Do not benchmark against seasonal naive on macro data. Every leaderboard headline uses it, and on macro it sits at ~1.84× a statistical ensemble — so anything reported relative to seasonal naive is inflated by roughly 45%. A model that "beats seasonal naive by 40%" on macro has demonstrated nothing. This is the single easiest way to produce a result that looks strong and means nothing, and a reviewer will see through it instantly.

Contamination — why financial TSFM numbers are especially untrustworthy

A January-2026 audit of 22 foundation models (Meyer et al., arXiv:2510.13654) found only 6% of evaluation datasets have never been used in some model's pretraining. The financial experiment is the one to remember: models with access to temporally overlapping correlated indices scored up to 37% better on S&P 500 prediction during the COVID shock — from an overlap of just 1.5% of training observations. Cross-sectional correlation leaks even when the target series itself is absent. Naive financial TSFM evaluation is worthless, and we should say so when positioning against anyone who reports one.

The baselines we must actually beat

BaselineWhy it's on the list
AR(p), per series, per vintageThe real macro bar. MACROCAST beats AR(1) by only 3–5% median. This is what "good" looks like.
Statistical ensembleAutoARIMA + AutoETS + AutoCES + DynamicOptimizedTheta (StatsForecast). Beats most foundation models on macro.
Bayesian VAR + Dynamic Factor ModelThe econometric standard. Note both fail badly on policy-rate series and during shocks — a place to win.
LightGBM / CatBoost on lagsCompetitive on macro, and the honest gradient-boosting baseline.
Chronos-2, TiRex-2 (zero-shot)The foundation-model representatives. Apache-2.0, so usable. TiRex-2 is the one that actually leads on the Econ slice.
Licensing, if any of this ships in the product. Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, Toto-2.0, Sundial, TabPFN-TS are Apache-2.0. Moirai (1.x and 2.0) is CC-BY-NC-4.0 — non-commercial, so it can be a research baseline but not a production dependency. TiRex is a bespoke NX-AI community license. TimeGPT is closed API-only. Do not let a non-commercial model become load-bearing in anything customer-facing.

Three places a structured latent-state model can genuinely win

These are not accuracy claims — they are capabilities the incumbents structurally lack. Positioning should lead with these, not with point-forecast MASE.

  1. Coherent joint trajectories. Two-thirds of foundation models emit only marginal point or quantile forecasts (arXiv:2510.19345). Marginals cannot answer path-dependent questions — "probability of a drawdown sequence," "joint stress across sectors." A latent-state generative model produces coherent sampled paths natively. This is exactly the reflexive/constructive question, and it is a capability gap, not a benchmark margin.
  2. Shock and regime robustness. Every macro evaluation finds foundation models degrade during shocks and structural breaks. MACROCAST's edge over AR(1) is specifically robustness — a near-absent right tail of error ratios — not peak accuracy. Our reflexive machinery is aimed precisely at regime transitions.
  3. Cross-channel causal structure. Deep models only beat tuned Ridge regression where genuine cross-variate structure exists (Electricity 321 channels, Traffic 862). If our fragments encode real economic co-movement, the benchmark to target is the 123-series FRED-MD panel and cross-sectional causal tasks — not ETT/Weather/Exchange, which cannot distinguish a good model from linear regression.
Scale is not the moat, and that is good news. Moirai-2.0 is 11.4M parameters and near the top of the general leaderboards; MACROCAST is ~1M parameters, pretrained synthetic-only in one GPU-day, and beats 120M Chronos-2 on macro by fine-tuning per-vintage on Bayesian VARs and DFMs. Domain structure beats scale on this data. A well-structured latent model with an economically-grounded prior is competing on exactly the axis where the giants have no advantage — nobody will out-compute us into irrelevance here.

The evaluation protocol this forces

This reinforces §10 and §17: the way to be taken seriously on macro forecasting is now well-defined, and cutting any corner here is how a result gets dismissed.

  • Real-time vintages (ALFRED), never the current FRED snapshot. US GDP first releases carry mean absolute revisions exceeding one percentage point annualized. A revised-data evaluation will be dismissed as unrealistic — the model got to see numbers no real-time forecaster had.
  • AR(1) and the statistical ensemble as the reference, reported as RMSFE ratios. Not seasonal naive.
  • Diebold–Mariano with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold small-sample correction, one-sided, multiplicity acknowledged. The financial-returns literature shows what happens without it: 8-of-10 raw "wins" collapsed to 2-of-9 statistically significant against a random walk.
  • Do not accept a returns benchmark. Financial returns are near-unpredictable and the 2026 literature says so with proper tests — nothing reliably beats a zero-return random walk. If we target economic state (volatility, regime, joint-path coherence, density calibration), we must refuse to be pushed onto a returns leaderboard where the honest baseline is unbeatable by anyone.
How this lands on the Paper 1 decision (§17). This is more evidence for the interventional-benchmark option. The forecasting-accuracy field is saturated, contaminated, and — on macro — barely ahead of AR(1); one more point-forecast model walks into all of that. An interventional benchmark scored on causal response to policy shocks sidesteps the entire contaminated-leaderboard game, and MACROCAST has already handed us the vintage-consistent real-time protocol to build it on.
Section 23

Multi-Timescale Architecture & Causal Emergence — The Research-Grounded Design

This section was written after a 220K-token deep literature review (50 papers verified against live repos, 15+ architectures benchmarked). Every recommendation names a working codebase. Every "avoid" names a specific failure mode. The review identified the unoccupied intersection that defines RecWM's contribution space — four things simultaneously true that nobody has combined.

The Unoccupied Intersection

Four facts that are simultaneously true and define our opening:

  1. Causal emergence has never been applied to economics. The theory now has a closed-form treatment for exactly the model class economists use (VAR), with working code — but nobody has taken the step.
  2. The SSM timescale mechanism (Δ) is well-understood and trivially controllable, but in every published model it is set by random log-uniform sampling, never by semantic typing.
  3. The structured-VAE-over-SSM architecture (LS4, ICML 2023) exists, works, and has been abandoned since 2023 — never combined with selective Δ, typed latent blocks, or modern pretraining.
  4. Economics/finance is the worst-served domain in every time-series benchmark — and the hardest for every architecture.

Every ingredient is published, permissively licensed, and runs on one GPU. What is missing is the integration.

Causal Emergence for VARs — The Closed-Form Baseline

For a VAR(1) system xt+1 = a0 + A xt + ε (the model class macroeconomists use daily), Liu, Yuan & Zhang (Entropy 26(8):618, 2024; extended to Phys. Rev. E 2025) prove causal emergence has a closed-form solution from the singular values of AT Σ−1 A.

SVD-Based Causal Emergence (Liu/Yuan/Zhang) Given x(t+1) = a₀ + A·x(t) + ε, ε ~ N(0, Σ) Compute: M = Aᵀ Σ⁻¹ A SVD: M = U S Uᵀ (S = diag of singular values) Clear CE: ΔJ_clear = (1/2q) Σᵢ₌₁ᵍ log(sᵢ) − (1/2p) Σⱼ₌₁ᵖ log(sⱼ) where q < p is the macro dimension and s₁ ≥ … ≥ sₚ // The optimal coarse-graining map is the top-q eigenvectors // of M — i.e. the PRINCIPAL DIRECTIONS of the dynamics, // weighted by noise precision. No training required. Effective rank r_ε = min q such that ΔJ(q) > 0 → a principled answer to "how many fragments?"

Code: kilovoltage/SVD-based_CE_Gaussian on GitHub. Functions clear_causal_emergence(A, Σ) and vague_causal_emergence(A, Σ). Inputs are just the VAR coefficient matrix and noise covariance — no neural network, no training.

Why this is the first experiment (week 1). It answers three questions for free: (1) how many effective fragments does the economy have? (2) what is the optimal linear coarse-graining? (3) what causal-emergence score must any learned encoder beat? If ΔJ ≤ 0, causal emergence is absent in the VAR approximation and we need nonlinear methods to find it. That is a "know now" result.

The S5 Typed-Δ Backbone

In structured state spaces (S4, S4D, S5, Mamba), the step size Δ controls which timescale each channel attends to. Gu et al. (2023) prove 1/Δ equals the dependency length — the distance into the past each channel can "see." In every published model, Δ is initialized from a random log-uniform distribution and then learned freely. Our contribution is to type the partition:

Typed Δ Partition Standard S5: log_step ~ Uniform(log(Δ_min), log(Δ_max)) // random Our modification: For fragment k with timescale band [τ_k^min, τ_k^max]: log_step_k ~ Uniform(log(1/τ_k^max), log(1/τ_k^min)) optionally: clamp log_step_k to stay in-band during training // ~20 lines of change to ssm_init.py // Converts S5's incidental timescale spread into // our architectural typed decomposition

The timescale bands come from the mrCOSTS experiment in week 1, not from assertion.

Non-Negotiable Design Constraints from the Literature

ConstraintSourceConsequence if Violated
Timescale ratios ≥ 10×MTRNN: τ=70/5≈14×, degrades at smaller ratios. CW-VAE: k=6 per level. MTS3: H≈30Ratios of 2–3× do not separate; fragments bleed into each other
Slow → fast parameterization (MTS3 coupling)Shaj et al. NeurIPS 2023 (spotlight)For economics: regime modulates transition operator. This is the only coupling with an economic interpretation
Within-trajectory negativesGulati & Nemenman (2026)Without them, latent predictive methods confuse slowly-varying noise with dynamical signal
Mori–Zwanzig memory budgetMZMD: ~1% overhead per 10 kernelsEconomic aggregates are non-Markovian by construction. Ignoring memory creates systematic error in the slow manifold
Temporal buffer trickRSMI (Koch-Janusz & Ringel, Nat. Phys. 2018)Predict t+Δt while masking (t, t+Δt). Without it, fragments become autoregressive echoes, not structural variables
Avoid Mamba-2/SSDGu & Dao, ICML 2024Timescale resolution collapsed 1000×: 32,768 distinct decay rates (Mamba-1) → 32 (Mamba-2). A regression for typed timescales

GateL0RD — The Fragment Update Rule

GateL0RD (Gumbsch, Butz & Martius, NeurIPS 2021) provides exact-zero gating via a hard-concrete relaxation of the L0 norm. Each fragment's state update is:

GateL0RD Update g_t = HardConcrete(σ(W_g · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_g)) h_t = g_t ⊙ ReTanh(W_h · [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_h) + (1 − g_t) ⊙ h_{t-1} L_gate = λ_k · E[g_t ≠ 0] // L₀ penalty, per-fragment λ // Slow structural fragments: high λ → gate rarely opens → state persists // Fast transient fragments: low λ → gate opens freely → state tracks market // The gate literally encodes "when did this fragment's world change?"

Drop-in single-file PyTorch. ReTanh = ReLU(tanh(x)) ensures updates are non-negative, preventing cancellation oscillations.

SPIB — The Per-Fragment Objective

State Predictive Information Bottleneck (Wang & Tiwary, J. Chem. Phys. 2021; Wang et al. JCTC 2024) gives each fragment its own coarse-graining objective:

SPIB Objective (Per Fragment) For fragment k with time delay Δt_k: max I(z_k ; state_{t+Δt_k}) − β · I(z_k ; X_t) The first term: z_k must predict the FUTURE state at its timescale The second term: z_k must compress away irrelevant detail β controls the resolution/compression tradeoff // Δt_k IS the coarse-graining knob — set from mrCOSTS bands // Learnable VampPrior mixture: K_mix components, self-consistent // label refinement → fragment cardinality self-determines

SPIB was developed for molecular dynamics (identifying metastable states from MD trajectories) and has never been applied to economic state estimation. The analogy is exact: metastable molecular states = economic regimes; conformational transitions = regime switches; the slow manifold = structural macro state.

Closest Prior Art — LS4 (ICML 2023)

LS4 (Zhou, Poli, Xu, Massaroli & Ermon) is a latent-state VAE with an S4 sequence model inside the ELBO. It works, achieves proper density estimation, and has been abandoned since 2023 — last commit, last citation trail, no follow-up. Our architecture is LS4 + three additions that are each independently justified:

  1. Typed Δ partition (replacing random log-uniform → semantic timescale bands)
  2. GateL0RD per fragment (replacing smooth gating → exact-zero state persistence)
  3. SPIB per fragment (replacing standard ELBO → predictive-IB with timescale-typed Δt)

Monitoring: Causal Emergence as Training Diagnostic

Wire approx_ei from the NIS+ repo (Matthew-ymz/Code-for-Finding-emergence-in-data-5.2, Apache-2.0) as a training callback. It takes any callable and computes dimension-averaged effective information. Track ΔJ per fragment at each epoch:

  • ΔJk > 0: fragment k captures genuine causal structure at its timescale
  • ΔJk ≤ 0: fragment k is not doing useful coarse-graining — consider merging it or changing its Δt
  • Σk ΔJk must beat the closed-form SVD-CE baseline from week 1 — if the neural encoder can't outperform a linear projection, the nonlinearity is wasted

What to Avoid

  • Mamba-2/SSD — timescale resolution collapsed 1000×; the shared scalar decay makes typed timescales impossible
  • Building on mamba-ssm CUDA kernels early — Linux/CUDA only, rules out Mac development and CI
  • ms-Mamba repo — no released code despite the paper; reimplement from the paper if needed
  • "Harmonic" SSM — no code, claims unverified
  • Chasing GIFT-Eval SOTA — top 9 entries are within 0.03 skill of each other, all 100M–2.5B params on proprietary corpora. Not our game
  • NIS+ for our data — needs enormous trajectories (~800K steps in published experiments), assumes Markov at micro-level. Use the SVD closed form instead, and NIS+ diagnostic functions as monitoring only

Section 25

ML Early Warning Systems — The AUROC Audit

A 260K-token audit of every published ML early-warning-system AUROC for banking crises, reading primary PDFs from Bank of England, Bundesbank, ECB, BIS, NBER, and Bank of Finland. Every number below was read from the source paper's tables. This section is the honest bar for anyone claiming to predict crises.

The single most important finding. The credit-to-GDP gap — a single indicator with zero hyperparameters — scores 0.80–0.86 AUROC at every horizon from 4 to 20 quarters (Drehmann & Juselius, BIS WP 421, Table A2). That is the real benchmark. ML's demonstrated edge over a well-specified logit on the same data is roughly 0.02–0.05 AUC and is not statistically significant on any existing sample (Bluwstein et al. report no DeLong test rejects at 5%).

Three regularities. (i) The gap scales with model flexibility — parametric/regularised models degrade 0.00–0.12; tree ensembles and k-NN degrade 0.25–0.63. (ii) The gap scales inversely with horizon — the slow-moving credit/asset-price signal at 3yr is more robust than the coincident signal at 1yr. (iii) CV design alone moves the answer as much as the choice of model — Bluwstein's 0.91→0.77 from fold constraints is bigger than the entire ML-over-logit margin.

The Small-Sample Reality

The effective sample size for an AUROC is the number of distinct crisis episodes, not the number of country-quarters:

ChronologyCountriesCrisis countPost-1945 crises
Jordà–Schularick–Taylor1790 crisis country-years24 (10 of which are 2008)
Drehmann & Juselius2619 systemic crises—
Holopainen & Sarlin1515 crisis events—
Beutel et al.1522 episodes11 pre-2008
Fouliard et al.7~2 per country1 per online sample
Laeven & Valencia (2026 update)~160151 systemic crises1970–2025

AUROC differences below ~0.10 on samples of 15–50 events are usually not statistically distinguishable. The post-war advanced-economy sample is desperately thin: 24 of the 90 JST crisis country-years are post-1945, and 10 of those are 2008.

The Goodhart / Lucas Gap

An unformalised open problem. A crisis successfully averted by policy is recorded as a false positive and lowers the model's measured AUROC. As macroprudential regimes tightened post-2010, the measurement gets systematically worse even if the model gets better. The audit found no paper that formalises Goodhart's law specifically for EWS.

The closest existing treatment is Fouliard, Howell & Rey's online-learning framework (NBER WP 28302): rather than modelling the feedback, they dispense with the stationarity assumption and adopt a no-regret criterion guaranteed against any outcome sequence including an adversarial one. That is what online learning buys and what logit/random-forest EWS do not.

The canonical Lucas-critique-for-risk-models argument is Daniélsson (2002, JBF): risk models estimated on historical data break down when adopted for regulatory purposes because the behaviour generating the data is endogenous to the model. This is exactly the performativity problem in §9 under a different name. The connection — Perdomo's performative prediction applied to macroprudential EWS — is wide open.

What This Means for Us

  1. Architecture matters more than model class. The only method that maintains its edge under strict sequential validation across all horizons is the recurrent network (Tölö, BoF 2019) — because it encodes temporal structure. Tree ensembles degrade most. Our S5+GateL0RD architecture is a recurrent model by construction.
  2. The credit-to-GDP gap is the bar, not logit. Report against that, not a 12-variable logit. It delivers 0.84 at 12 quarters with zero hyperparameters.
  3. Report PR AUC, not ROC AUC, on imbalanced crisis data (§20). The base rate is ~4–9%. A ROC AUC of 0.9 is unremarkable; a PR AUC of 0.5 is genuinely strong.
  4. Always report the number of distinct crisis episodes alongside any AUROC.
  5. The performativity-of-EWS is an open problem we can claim. Connecting Perdomo's ε < γ/β to the EWS Goodhart effect would be a genuine contribution, and it falls directly out of our reflexive framework (§9, §15).
  6. Greenwood et al.'s conditional probabilities are more policy-legible than any AUROC. Their R-zone framing (45% crisis probability within 3 years when both credit and asset prices are elevated, vs 4% unconditional) communicates more to a fund manager or regulator than any AUROC in this literature. Consider reporting our signals in this format.
Key papers for our bibliography. Bluwstein et al. (BoE WP 848 / JIE 2023) for the ML horse race and Shapley-value interpretability; Tölö (BoF RDP 14/2019 / JFS 2020) for the cleanest CV→OOS degradation measurement; Beutel, List & von Schweinitz (Bundesbank DP 48/2018 / JFS 2019) for the skeptical result; Drehmann & Juselius (BIS WP 421 / IJF 2014) for the credit-gap and DSR benchmarks; Greenwood, Hanson, Shleifer & Sørensen (JF 2022) for conditional crisis probabilities; Fouliard, Howell, Rey & Stavrakeva (NBER WP 28302) for online learning under adversarial feedback.

The Taxonomy: Stock vs. Flow, Not Index vs. Index

Everything leading by >1 year is a quantity (credit, leverage, debt service). Everything coincident is a price (spreads, implied vols). Any new index built by aggregating market prices lands in the coincident bucket regardless of aggregation sophistication.

Three Crisis Case Studies — What Actually Led

2008: the signal was there for six years. US credit-to-GDP gap exceeded +6pp in 2001-Q3 — 84 months before Lehman. The 2s10s inverted Dec 2005 (33 months). Bank equity peaked Jan 2007 (20 months). TED broke out 9 Aug 2007 — the first coincident signal. LIBOR-OIS and corporate spreads didn't move until 21 months after bank equity had already started declining.
2020: nothing financial led it. STLFSI2 printed its calmest value of the cycle on 14 Feb, five days before the S&P peak. NFCI didn't cross zero until 13 March (23 days after peak). The only leading signals were epidemiological and public: WHO PHEIC on 30 Jan (+20 days). The market made an all-time high 20 days after a WHO global health emergency. Across 120 years and 1,100+ daily jumps, not one was attributed to infectious disease. This is a hypothesis-space failure, not a signal-extraction failure — precisely the gap an endogenous causal architecture must argue it closes.
SVB 2023: the signal sat in a free public API for 14 months. FDIC BankFind (no key, CERT 24735) showed SVB at 94.7% uninsured deposits, 60.1% securities/assets on 31 Dec 2021 — filed end of January 2022. Not one published index fired. NFCI was at −0.312 on 3 Feb = loosest of the cycle. OFR FSI turned positive on the day of the run. VIX was near 52-week lows. Sell-side: 12 Buy / 11 Hold / 1 Sell. The 2× outlier status on uninsured deposits was visible to anyone with a browser, for over a year.

What Is Genuinely Hard to Get — The Data Moat

1Dealer-vs-customer options OI classificationProprietary Cboe dataset not sold. Every GEX rests on unverifiable ±call/put prior (15× spread)Highest — inference moat on free data

Five Operational Rules

  1. Start the daily snapshot cron today — unbuyable later, free now (see callout above)
  2. Vintage-correctness is the binding constraint. ALFRED is the only free source for real-time macro vintages. NFCI and STLFSI re-estimate their entire history every release, inflating apparent in-sample performance. Publish vintages from day one
  3. Prefer bulk over API: SEC zips over 800k REST calls; BIS bulk over SDMX; FRED v2 release-observations over v1 loops; GDELT masterfilelist over DOC API
  4. Audit for silently-stale URLs. These all return HTTP 200 with dead data: ticdata.treasury.gov (Jan 2023), Cboe *pc.csv (frozen 2019-10-04), NY Fed primary dealer statistics page (not-found shell)
  5. Only two sources publish an exact rate limit (SEC 10/s, BigQuery 1 TiB/mo). Build a shared token-bucket, not hardcoded constants

Licensing Tripwires

JST Macrohistory is NonCommercial. BIS speeches are noncommercial-only. Finnhub is personal-use at every tier including $3,500/mo. Massive individual plans are non-professional. Yahoo is personal-use. Some FRED series are individually copyrighted. Databento has by far the cleanest licensing — self-serve, pass-through exchange fees, no license fees on $199 tier.

Where the Defensible Position Is

The raw data is not the moat. Almost everything that matters — the credit gap that beats every ML model, the call reports that showed SVB's 94.7% uninsured deposits 13 months early, the daily options chain with exchange-computed greeks — is free behind unauthenticated endpoints.

  1. Attribution, not accuracy. The credit gap says that risk is building, never where or through what channel. That is the open surface.
  2. The distributional benchmark, where the incumbent is broken. Growth-at-Risk is entrenched (AER 2019 → IMF surveillance) and refuted OOS twice. The actual bar is GARCH(1,1) under the Brownlees–Souza protocol.
  3. Reflexivity, which nobody has formalised. The CCyB is mechanically tied to the credit gap in Basel III itself — every post-2016 OOS evaluation is contaminated by the signal triggering its own invalidation.
  4. Hypothesis-space coverage. COVID wasn't a signal failure — no statistical model had a slot for infectious disease. Fouliard et al.: "unable to predict any crisis of a type that has never happened in history." This is the argument for a structural causal architecture, made by the incumbent literature about itself.
Section 27

Mathematical Proof of Concept — Complete Formal Specification

This section is the full mathematical architecture in one place. Every equation is implementation-ready. Every prior section's math is unified here into a single, self-consistent system. Hand this to an engineer and they can write code. Hand it to a reviewer and they can verify correctness.

27.1 — The State Space and Notation

Definitions and Conventions Observable space: x(t) ∈ ℝD D-dimensional economic observation at time t. Concatenation of all raw data: yields, spreads, prices, volumes, text embeddings, constraint indicators. Latent fragment space: z(t) = (z1(t), ..., zK(t)) zk(t) ∈ ℝdk, k = 1, ..., K K typed world fragments, each with its own dimensionality dk. Total latent dimension: d = Σk dk Fragment types and timescales: Each fragment k has: σk ∈ {micro, meso, macro} // scale level τk ∈ ℝ+ // characteristic timescale (days) Δtk = τk // SPIB prediction horizon = timescale Hidden state (S5 backbone): h(t) ∈ ℂN N-dimensional complex-valued SSM hidden state, partitioned: h(t) = (h1(t), ..., hK(t)), hk(t) ∈ ℂNk where N = Σk Nk Convention: t indexes discrete observations at the fastest available frequency (daily). Fragment k's effective update frequency is controlled by Δk in the S5 discretization AND by the GateL0RD gate gk(t).

27.2 — The S5 Typed-Δ Backbone (Layer 0)

Continuous-Time State Space (before discretization) For each fragment block k: dhk/dt = Ak hk(t) + Bk u(t) yk(t) = Re( Ck hk(t) ) + Dk u(t) where: Ak ∈ ℂNk×Nk is diagonal (S5's key structural choice) Bk ∈ ℂNk×D Ck ∈ ℂdk×Nk Dk ∈ ℝdk×D u(t) is the input (raw data or signature features)
ZOH Discretization with Typed Step Sizes The Zero-Order Hold discretization with step size Δk: Āk = exp(Ak Δk) // diagonal, so element-wise exp &Bmacr;k = Ak−1(Āk − I) Bk // also diagonal A, so cheap Discrete recurrence: hk(t) = Āk hk(t−1) + &Bmacr;k u(t) The typed Δ partition (our contribution): Standard S5: log Δ ~ Uniform(log Δmin, log Δmax) // random Ours: For fragment k with timescale band [τkmin, τkmax]: log Δk,n ~ Uniform(log(1/τkmax), log(1/τkmin)) for n = 1, ..., Nk Optionally clamp during training: Δk,n ∈ [1/τkmax, 1/τkmin] ∀ n, ∀ training steps Because Ak is diagonal, the dependency length of state n is: Ln = 1/Δk,n so the band constraint forces each fragment to attend to its designated timescale window.
Why diagonal Ak matters for everything downstream. (1) Āk = exp(AkΔk) is element-wise, so the parallel scan runs in O(T log T) rather than O(T Nk3). (2) The Jacobian ∂hk(t)/∂hk(t−1) = diag(Āk) — a diagonal matrix — making RTRL cost O(Nk) per step instead of O(Nk3). This is the foundation of the continual learning story in §28.

27.3 — GateL0RD Fragment Update (Layer 1)

GateL0RD Update Rule per Fragment For each fragment k at each timestep t, given S5 output yk(t): Gate logit: ℓk(t) = Wg,k · [zk(t−1), yk(t)] + bg,k Hard-Concrete sampling (Louizos et al. 2018): u ~ Uniform(0,1) s = σ((log u − log(1−u) + ℓk(t)) / β) // β = temperature s̄ = s · (ζ − γ) + γ // stretch to (γ, ζ) = (−0.1, 1.1) gk(t) = clamp(s̄, 0, 1) // hard clamp → exact zeros State update: z̃k(t) = ReTanh(Wh,k · [zk(t−1), yk(t)] + bh,k) zk(t) = gk(t) ⊙ z̃k(t) + (1 − gk(t)) ⊙ zk(t−1) where ReTanh(x) = max(0, tanh(x)) — the rectified activation from the original GateL0RD paper. L0 gate penalty: Lgate,k = λk · (1/T) Σt P(gk(t) ≠ 0) P(gk(t) ≠ 0) = clamp(σ(ℓk(t) − β log(−γ/ζ)), 0, 1) This is the CDF of the Hard-Concrete evaluated at zero — the probability that the gate is non-zero, differentiable w.r.t. ℓ. Per-fragment λ schedule: λk ∝ τk / τmax Slow structural fragments (high τ): high λ → gate rarely opens Fast transient fragments (low τ): low λ → gate opens freely

27.4 — SPIB Per-Fragment Objective (Layer 2)

State Predictive Information Bottleneck For each fragment k, the SPIB objective (Wang et al. J. Chem. Phys. 2021): maxθ I(zk; statet+Δtk) − βk I(zk; Xt) Variational lower bound on the first term: I(zk; statet+Δtk) ≥ Ezk~q[log pφ(statet+Δtk | zk)] + H(statet+Δtk) Variational upper bound on the second term: I(zk; Xt) ≤ EXt[ KL( qθ(zk|Xt) || r(zk) ) ] where r(zk) is a learnable VampPrior: r(zk) = (1/M) Σm=1M qθ(zk | υm) with pseudo-inputs υm learned jointly. Practical SPIB loss per fragment: LSPIB,k = −Ex∼data[ Ezk~q[log pφ(statet+Δtk | zk)] − βk KL(qθ(zk|xt) || r(zk)) ] The time delay Δtk IS the coarse-graining knob: Small Δtk (fast fragments): zk must predict near-future → retains fast dynamics Large Δtk (slow fragments): zk must predict far-future → compresses out noise Self-consistent label refinement: The "labels" for SPIB are future states z(t+Δtk), which depend on the encoder. Run iteratively: train encoder → re-embed future states → re-train until convergence. 2–3 rounds suffice (Wang et al.).

27.5 — The Complete RecWM Loss Function

End-to-End Training Objective Ltotal = Lrecon + Σk=1K LSPIB,k + α Lsparsity + Σk=1K Lgate,k + μ LMZ + ν Lcoupling Term 1 — Reconstruction: Lrecon = ||x(t) − x̂(t)||22 where x̂(t) = Σk gk(zk(t)) (K independent decoders, summed) Term 2 — SPIB per fragment (§27.4): LSPIB,k = −E[log pφ(statet+Δtk | zk)] + βk KL(q(zk|x) || r(zk)) Term 3 — Structural sparsity (what buys identifiability, §21): Lsparsity = ||supp(Jdecoder)||0 + ||Gz||0 In practice: L1 relaxation on the decoder Jacobian rows + L1 on the learned causal graph adjacency Gz. This is the iVAE-compatible identifiability mechanism. Term 4 — Gate L0 (§27.3): Lgate,k = λk · E[P(gk(t) ≠ 0)] Term 5 — Mori–Zwanzig memory (~1% overhead per 10 kernels): LMZ = ||zslow(t) − fMZ(zslow(t−1), ..., zslow(t−P))||22 A residual autoregressive correction on the slow manifold only. P = 10 memory terms. Budget: ~1% parameter overhead. Term 6 — Cross-fragment coupling (MTS3 design): Lcoupling = ||Afast(t) − fcouple(zslow(t))||22 where Afast(t) is the fast-fragment transition operator at time t, and fcouple maps slow regime fragments to the parameters of the fast transition. Slow parameterizes fast, not the reverse. What is NOT in this loss: − No total correlation (TC) penalty (Locatello impossibility, §21) − No Gaussian slowness penalty (use Laplace/heavy-tail prior instead) − No E[log(loss)] (wrong three ways, §13)

27.6 — Encoder Architecture

Encoder: Data → Fragment Latents Input pipeline: 1. Raw data x(t) ∈ ℝD 2. Time-augment: x̃(t) = [t/T, x(t)] 3. Lead-lag transform (for path signatures): xLL ∈ ℝ2D+1 4. Log-signature at depth 3 over hierarchical dyadic windows: s(t) = LogSig≤3(xLL[t−L:t]) S5 backbone: Feed s(t) through the typed-Δ S5 (§27.2): y(t) = S5_typed(s(t)) ∈ ℝΣk dk K projection heads: For each fragment k: μk(t) = Wμ,k yk(t) + bμ,k ∈ ℝdk log σk(t) = Wσ,k yk(t) + bσ,k ∈ ℝdk Sampling with reparameterization: zk(t) = μk(t) + σk(t) ⊙ ε, ε ~ N(0, I) GateL0RD update: zk(t) ← GateL0RD(zk(t−1), zk(t)) (§27.3) Transition prior (SlowVAE): p(zk(t) | zk(t−1)) = Laplace(μprior,k(zk(t−1)), bk) where μprior,k is a learned nonlinear function. The heavy tail of the Laplace prior concentrates probability mass at z(t) ≈ z(t−1), giving provable nonlinear disentanglement (Klindt et al. ICLR 2021, "Towards Nonlinear Disentanglement in Natural Data with Temporal Sparse Coding").

27.7 — Decoder Architecture

Decoder: Fragment Latents → Observation K independent decoder heads, one per fragment type: x̂k(t) = gk(zk(t)) where gk: ℝdk → ℝD x̂(t) = Σk=1K x̂k(t) Structural sparsity on the decoder Jacobian: Jk = ∂gk/∂zk ∈ ℝD × dk Each decoder maps its fragment to a sparse subset of the observation dimensions. Enforce via L1 on Jk rows. Fragment "liquidity" should reconstruct spreads and volumes but NOT equity prices — the sparsity discovers this. Why independent decoders: The composition x̂ = Σ x̂k with sparse Jacobians is exactly the "mechanism sparsity" condition of Lachapelle et al. (ICML 2022, "Disentanglement via Mechanism Sparsity Regularization"). Combined with the temporal structure (conditional prior + SPIB), this provides identifiability guarantees WITHOUT any TC penalty.

27.8 — Causal Emergence Bounds

When Fragments Beat the Micro-Description A world model is worth building (vs. just forecasting raw data) if and only if the macro description has positive causal emergence. Formal definition (Liu/Yuan/Zhang, Phys Rev E 2025): For a linear stochastic iteration system x(t+1) = A x(t) + ε, ε ~ N(0, Σ) Define: M = AT Σ−1 A Let s1 ≥ ... ≥ sp be the eigenvalues of M. Clear causal emergence at macro dimension q < p: ΔJclear(q) = (1/2q) Σi=1q log si − (1/2p) Σj=1p log sj ΔJ > 0 iff the top-q eigenvalues carry more information-per-dimension than the full set. The optimal linear coarse-graining map is the matrix of top-q eigenvectors of M. Effective rank (our answer to "how many fragments?"): rε = argminq { ΔJ(q) > 0 } The bound our learned encoder must beat: ΔJlearned(z) ≥ ΔJSVD(rε) If our nonlinear encoder does not exceed the closed-form SVD baseline, the architecture is not earning its complexity. Online monitoring via approx_ei: During training, compute ΔJk = ½ log det(Σzk) − ½ log det(Σzk|zk(t−1)) per fragment per epoch. This is the determinism of fragment k's dynamics — higher means more causal emergence. Plot ΔJk trajectories to verify fragments are learning real structure.

27.9 — Performative Stability Analysis

When the Model's Predictions Change the World Setup (Perdomo et al. ICML 2020): The model deploys predictions θ. The data distribution shifts: D(θ) ≠ D(θ'). The distribution map D is ε-sensitive: W1(D(θ), D(θ')) ≤ ε ||θ − θ'|| The loss is γ-strongly convex and β-smooth. Theorem 3.5 (Perdomo): If ε < γ/β, then Repeated Risk Minimization converges to a unique performatively stable point θPS at rate: ||θt+1 − θPS|| ≤ (εβ/γ)t ||θ0 − θPS|| For RecWM: θ = the model parameters (encoder + decoder + S5) D(θ) = the economic data distribution AFTER market participants observe and act on our model's outputs ε = the reflexivity coefficient: how much do our predictions move the market? The three thresholds (§19): (a) ε < γ/β ⇒ RRM converges (Perdomo Thm 3.5) (b) ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)] ⇒ RGD converges (Thm 3.8) (c) ε ≤ γ/(2β) ⇒ performative risk is convex (Miller+ ICML 2021) Our contribution — endogenous ε: In the literature, ε is a fixed constant. In reality, the reflexivity of the economy is STATE-DEPENDENT. We model εt = ε(θ, W(t)) as a learned function: εt = ||∂D(θ)/∂θ|| · ||∂θ/∂D|| The first factor is the model's market impact (how much our predictions change the distribution). The second is the model's sensitivity to the distribution (how much we retrain when data changes). Crisis mechanism: When εt crosses γ/β: • Below: model and market co-converge (stable equilibrium) • Above: self-amplifying spiral (bubble/crash dynamics) • At the boundary: critical transition This dynamic crossing IS the Reflexive Instability signal (§9). Practical monitoring: Estimate εt empirically via finite differences: ε̂t = ||W(t+1) − W(t)|| / ||θt − θt−1|| when the model is updated and the world responds.

27.10 — Convergence Guarantees

Formal Convergence of the RecWM Evolution Theorem (Reflexive Convergence): The RecWM evolution W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) converges to a fixed point W* if: (i) The constructive operator C is LC-Lipschitz: ||C(W, a, φ) − C(W', a, φ)|| ≤ LC ||W − W'|| (ii) The belief-to-action map A ˆ B is ε-sensitive: ||A(B(W)) − A(B(W'))|| ≤ ε ||W − W'|| (iii) The contraction condition holds: LC (1 + ε) < 1 equivalently: ε < 1/LC − 1 Proof (Banach fixed-point theorem): Define F(W) = C(W, A(B(W)), Φ) Then: ||F(W) − F(W')|| = ||C(W, A(B(W)), Φ) − C(W', A(B(W')), Φ)|| ≤ LC ||(W, A(B(W))) − (W', A(B(W')))|| ≤ LC (||W − W'|| + ||A(B(W)) − A(B(W'))||) ≤ LC (1 + ε) ||W − W'|| By condition (iii), the contraction factor c = LC(1+ε) < 1. By Banach, there exists a unique fixed point W* and: ||W(t) − W*|| ≤ ct ||W(0) − W*|| ▮ Connection to Perdomo: This IS Perdomo's Theorem 3.5 in our notation. Their ε-sensitivity = our ε. Their γ-strong-convexity over β-smoothness = our 1/LC. We do NOT claim novelty on the convergence result itself. The novel claim (for Paper 3): Conjecture: LC is MONOTONICALLY DECREASING in constraint-field tightness. Tighter constraints ⇒ fewer feasible actions ⇒ less distributional movement per step ⇒ smaller LC. If this holds: constraints buy stability, and the Constructibility Index becomes a direct read on the convergence margin 1/LC − 1.

27.11 — The Ergodicity-Correct Evaluation

Growth-Optimal Objective for Portfolio Applications For any downstream application involving compounding: Optimize the time-average growth rate: max E[Δ log x(t)] where x is the compounding quantity NOT E[log L] (wrong sign, wrong object, wrong transform — §13). When the dynamics are unknown, learn the transformation: 1. Estimate the variance function v(x) via LOESS regression of log((R(tk+1) − R(tk))2) on R(tk) 2. Set h(x) = ∫0x 1/√v(u) du 3. Optimize increments of h(R) (Baumann et al. TMLR 2025) For the prediction losses in the RecWM training loop: Leave them as standard MSE/NLL. The ergodicity correction applies to the EVALUATION of signals and portfolio decisions, not to the gradient of the encoder.

27.12 — The Four Derived Signals

From Fragments to Actionable Signals Signal 1 — Constructibility Index (CI): CI(t) = μaction[ Φ(t, a) = feasible ] / |A| Monte Carlo: sample 10K construction operators, evaluate feasibility through the constraint field. CI = fraction feasible. CI ↓ means the economy's action space is shrinking. Signal 2 — Reflexive Instability (RI): RI(t) = ε(t) · χ(t) where ε(t) is the reflexivity coefficient (§27.9) and χ(t) is belief coherence (cosine similarity of institutional positions from 13F data). RI ↑ means reflexive amplification is increasing. Signal 3 — Composition Fragility (CF): CF(t) = 1 − mini,j ρ(WFi(t), WFj(t)) where ρ is the composition compatibility score. CF ↑ means fragment compositions are becoming unstable. Signal 4 — Path Lock-In Risk (PLR): PLR(t) = 1 − VarMC[W(t+H) | W(t)] / Varprior[W(t+H)] Monte Carlo forward simulation with 1K perturbations, horizon H. PLR ↑ means the current path is hard to escape from.

27.13 — Computational Complexity

Per-Step Costs S5 parallel scan: O(T log T · N) // N = total state dim GateL0RD update: O(K · max(dk)2) // K fragments SPIB objective: O(K · dk · D) // per fragment Log-signature: O(T · d3) // depth 3, d channels Reconstruction: O(K · D · dk) // K decoders Total training step: O(T log T · N + T d3 + K D max(dk)) Dominated by the parallel scan and signature computation. Concrete numbers (typical macro-financial setting): D = 50 (raw features), K = 5 fragments, dk = 8 each, N = 64 (SSM state), T = 250 (1 year daily): Log-sig: d=6 (after PCA), depth 3 → 35 features. O(T · 216). S5 scan: O(250 · 8 · 64) ≈ 128K ops. Fits on a single GPU with batch size 32.
Section 28

Continual Learning Architecture — How the Model Stays Alive

This section was written after a 500K+ token literature review across 20+ research agents. Every claim is grounded in verified papers and code. The RecWM must continually learn because: (1) economic regimes shift, (2) the model's own predictions affect the data (performativity), (3) data sources appear and die, (4) the L6 "sim-to-real twin with continuous online correction" is the target. No current time-series foundation model natively supports online learning — this is our architectural vacancy.

28.1 — Which CL Scenario Applies to Us

Van de Ven & Tolias (Nature Machine Intelligence 4:1185, 2022) define three scenarios. Our setting maps to Domain-Incremental Learning (Domain-IL) — the prediction task stays the same (forecast the next economic state), but the input distribution shifts under regime changes. However, there is an important nuance:

Our CL Scenario: Domain-IL + Performative Shift Standard Domain-IL: Task T is fixed. Distribution Dt changes exogenously. At time t: observe x ~ Dt, predict y. No task oracle at test time. Our setting adds two complications: 1. Performative shift: Dt+1 depends on our prediction θt: Dt+1 = Dt+1(θt) This is not standard Domain-IL — the distribution shift is ENDOGENOUS, caused by the model itself. 2. Gradual + abrupt + recurring drift: Economic regimes exhibit all three drift types simultaneously: - Gradual: slow structural change (demographics, technology) - Abrupt: policy shocks, crises (regime switches) - Recurring: business cycles, seasonal patterns The correct framing is "online continual learning under performative distribution shift" — a setting that has NO established benchmark or methodology in the CL literature. This is an open research problem, and our architecture's answer to it is a genuine contribution.

28.2 — The Five-Layer CL Strategy

We compose five mechanisms, each operating at a different timescale. No single mechanism handles all three drift types — the composition is the design.

LayerMechanismTimescaleHandles
0GateL0RD implicit stabilityEvery stepNatural resistance to forgetting — gates that rarely open = weights that rarely change
1O(N) RTRL on S5Every stepStreaming gradient updates — no BPTT truncation artifacts
2Per-fragment EWCPer regimeElastic protection of fragment-specific knowledge across regime changes
3BOCPD regime detection + replayEvent-drivenDetects regime shifts, triggers adaptation protocol, selectively replays
4Slow-fast weight bifurcationStructuralStructural fragments adapt on a geological timescale; transient fragments track the market

28.3 — GateL0RD as Natural Continual Learning (Layer 0)

Implicit Regularization from Exact-Zero Gates The GateL0RD update (§27.3) already provides continual learning properties for free: When gk(t) = 0 (gate is closed): zk(t) = zk(t−1) // state is UNCHANGED ∂L/∂Wh,k = 0 // NO gradient flows through the update ∂L/∂Wg,k ≠ 0 // gradient still flows to the GATE decision Consequence: High-λk fragments (slow/structural) have gates that are almost always closed. Their state persists across long periods, and their weights receive sparse gradient updates. This is EXACTLY the selective plasticity that CL methods try to achieve — but it emerges from the architecture naturally. Formal connection to EWC: EWC penalizes Σi Fi(θi − θi*)2 where Fi = Fisher information. GateL0RD achieves the same effect through a different route: parameters of rarely-opening gates have LOW effective learning rate (few gradient steps per unit time), which is mathematically equivalent to high Fi in EWC under the natural gradient interpretation (Amari 1998). Quantitative prediction: A fragment with gate-open rate p receives ~p·T gradient updates over T steps. Its effective learning rate is ηeff = p · η. For a slow fragment with λ set so p ≈ 0.02 (opens ~5 days/year), the weight change per year is 50× smaller than a fast fragment with p ≈ 1.

28.4 — O(N) RTRL for Streaming Updates (Layer 1)

Real-Time Recurrent Learning on Diagonal SSMs The key insight (Irie et al. ICLR 2024; Elelimy et al. NeurIPS 2024): For a recurrence with diagonal transition matrix (which S5 has): h(t) = diag(ā) · h(t−1) + &bmacr; · u(t) the RTRL Jacobian decomposes: ∂h(t)/∂θ = diag(ā) · ∂h(t−1)/∂θ + ∂[local terms]/∂θ This is O(N) per step instead of O(N3) for general RTRL, because diag(ā) is element-wise multiplication, not matrix-matrix. Streaming S5 training: For each new observation x(t): 1. Forward pass through S5: h(t), y(t) 2. Compute loss L(t) on y(t) vs actual 3. Compute gradient via RTRL: O(N) per step 4. Update parameters: θ ← θ − η ∇L(t) No need for BPTT. No truncation artifacts. No storing activations. Pure streaming. Code: Irie et al. provide PyTorch RTRL in their ICLR 2024 repo. Elelimy et al. (NeurIPS 2024) provide Recurrent Trace Units (RTUs) specifically designed for RTRL-based online RL. For RecWM: Use RTRL for the S5 backbone weights (A, B, C, D, Δ). Use standard backprop for the GateL0RD and decoder weights on mini-batches from the replay buffer. This gives the S5 STREAMING adaptation while the fragment-level parameters update on a slower schedule.
The streaming training contribution. Lemmel et al. (IEEE SMC 2025, arXiv:2508.00804) is the first paper applying RTRL to SSMs outside RL — for online fine-tuning of carbon emission predictions. But nobody has done it for selective/typed-Δ SSMs or for multi-timescale economic world models. This is a genuine, publishable gap: "Real-Time Recurrent Learning for Typed State Space Models" — streaming S5 updates where the per-fragment Δ typing constrains which gradients flow where.

28.5 — Per-Fragment EWC (Layer 2)

Elastic Weight Consolidation, Fragment-Specific Standard EWC (Kirkpatrick et al. PNAS 2017): LEWC = Lcurrent + (Ω/2) Σi Fi (θi − θi*)2 where Fi = diagonal Fisher information for parameter i and θi* = parameter value at end of previous regime. Our modification — per-fragment Fisher: Instead of one global Fisher, compute K block-diagonal Fishers: Fk = (1/Tregime) Σt ∈ regime (∇θk log p(x(t)|θ))2 where θk = parameters of fragment k only (encoder head k, decoder head k, GateL0RD weights for fragment k). LEWC = Lcurrent + Σk (Ωk/2) Σi ∈ θk Fk,i (θk,i − θk,i*)2 Per-fragment Ω schedule: Ωk ∝ τk / τmax (same schedule as λk) Slow fragments: high Ω ⇒ strong protection against forgetting Fast fragments: low Ω ⇒ free to adapt quickly Online EWC (Schwarz et al. "Progress & Compress" 2018): Instead of storing a separate Fisher for each regime, maintain a running EMA of the Fisher: Fk ← α Fk + (1−α) Fk,new This avoids quadratic memory growth in the number of regimes. Computational cost: The per-fragment Fisher is block-diagonal by construction (fragments share no parameters). Computing K diagonal Fishers of size |θk| each costs O(Σk |θk| · T) — same as global Fisher, but structured.

28.6 — BOCPD Regime Detection + Replay (Layer 3)

Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection Adams & MacKay (2007): Maintain a distribution over the run length rt (time since last changepoint): P(rt | x1:t) ∝ Σrt−1 P(xt | rt, x(r)) × P(rt | rt−1) × P(rt−1 | x1:t−1) where P(rt | rt−1) is the hazard function: rt = 0 with probability H(rt−1+1) (changepoint) rt = rt−1+1 otherwise (growth) Code: hildensia/bayesian_changepoint_detection (Python) or the bocpd package. Integration with RecWM: Run BOCPD on the fragment representation z(t), not the raw data. When P(rt = 0 | x1:t) exceeds threshold δ: 1. Snapshot current model parameters θ* 2. Compute Fisher Fk for all fragments on the ending regime 3. Store exemplars from the ending regime in per-fragment replay buffers (reservoir sampling, buffer size Bk) 4. Activate EWC with the computed Fisher 5. Reset fast-fragment GateL0RD states (force gk = 1 for transient fragments to allow rapid re-learning) 6. Keep slow-fragment states unchanged (structural knowledge persists across regimes)

28.7 — Per-Fragment Replay Buffers

Fragment-Specific Experience Replay Each fragment k maintains its own replay buffer Rk: Buffer structure: Rk = { (xt, zk(t), zk(t+Δtk), logitsk(t)) } Storing logits (dark knowledge) alongside inputs enables DER++ style replay (Buzzega et al. NeurIPS 2020): Lreplay,k = α ||fθ(xt) − logitsk(t)||22 // logit matching + β LSPIB,k(xt, zk(t+Δtk)) // task loss on replay Reservoir sampling (Vitter 1985): Buffer size Bk. For the n-th sample, include it with probability Bk/n; if included, replace a random existing element. Guarantees each sample has equal probability Bk/n of being in the buffer — unbiased across the data stream. Temporal coherence: Economic data has temporal structure — replaying isolated time steps destroys sequential information. Store SEQUENCES of length Lk = min(2τk, 60) rather than individual samples. Reservoir sampling operates on sequence starts, not individual timesteps. Fragment-specific buffer sizes: Bk ∝ dk · τk Slow structural fragments need larger buffers (more to remember, less often updated). Fast transient fragments need small buffers (recent data is most relevant).

28.8 — Slow-Fast Weight Bifurcation (Layer 4)

Complementary Learning Systems for World Models Inspired by CLS theory (McClelland et al. 1995) and CLS-ER (Arani et al. NeurIPS 2022): Maintain two copies of the model: θfast — the actively trained model θslow — an EMA of the fast model EMA update: θslow ← ρ θslow + (1 − ρ) θfast Per-fragment ρ: ρk = ρbaseτk/τref Slow structural fragments: high τ → ρ near 1 → EMA barely moves Fast transient fragments: low τ → ρ near ρbase → EMA tracks fast model Deployment inference: Use θslow for stable predictions (default). Use θfast when BOCPD detects a regime shift (the fast model adapts immediately; the slow model catches up). Blend: ŷ = (1−wshift) · yslow + wshift · yfast where wshift = P(rt = 0 | data) from BOCPD.

28.9 — The Performativity-CL Connection

When the Model Changes What It Predicts The core tension: CL assumes exogenous distribution shift. Performative prediction shows the shift can be ENDOGENOUS — caused by the model itself. In RecWM, BOTH happen simultaneously. How CL mechanisms interact with performativity: Consider the model retraining step under performative prediction: θt+1 = argminθ Ex~D(θt)[L(x, θ)] With EWC, this becomes: θt+1 = argminθ Ex~D(θt)[L(x, θ)] + (Ω/2) Σ Fi(θi − θi*)2 The EWC penalty REDUCES the effective sensitivity: ||θt+1 − θt|| ≤ ||θt+1unconstrained − θt|| Therefore: EWC reduces the effective ε. Higher Ω ⇒ smaller parameter change per retraining ⇒ smaller distributional shift ⇒ more likely to satisfy ε < γ/β. Theorem (informal — to formalize for Paper 3): Under EWC with penalty Ω, the effective sensitivity is: εeff ≤ ε / (1 + Ω · λmin(F)) where λmin(F) is the smallest Fisher eigenvalue. EWC makes performative convergence easier to achieve. Replay further stabilizes by anchoring the loss surface. The practical prescription: When ε̂t approaches γ/β: 1. Increase Ωk for all fragments (more conservative updates) 2. Increase replay ratio (more past data in each mini-batch) 3. Slow the EMA momentum (slower slow model) This is an adaptive CL schedule driven by the reflexivity signal.

28.10 — TTT-Style Self-Supervised Adaptation

Test-Time Training for the S5 Backbone TTT (Sun et al. ICML 2025, arXiv:2407.04620) and Titans (Behrouz et al. arXiv:2501.00663) show that self-supervised gradient descent during the forward pass is a viable recurrence mechanism. For RecWM, the opportunity (unpublished): Apply TTT-style self-supervised updates to the S5 Δ parameters at test time — enabling the model to adapt its temporal resolution online without full retraining. At each new observation x(t): 1. Compute self-supervised loss on the input: Lself = ||x(t) − reconstruct(encode(x(t)))||2 2. Take one gradient step on Δk only: Δk ← Δk − ηTTT ∇Δk Lself 3. Clamp Δk to stay in its typed band This allows the model to shift temporal attention within each fragment's band WITHOUT retraining the full model. Connection to Test-Time Regression (Wang et al. arXiv:2501.12352): This paper proves that linear attention, SSMs, fast-weight programmers, and online learners are all special cases of test-time regression — differing only in weights, function class, and optimization algorithm. SSMs are formally within this framework.

28.12 — CL Evaluation Protocol

How to Measure Whether Continual Learning Works Backward Transfer (BWT): BWT = (1/R) Σr=1R (accr,after − accr,before) where accr,* is the accuracy on regime r's test data before and after training on subsequent regimes. BWT < 0 means forgetting. Adapt for regression: BWT = (1/R) Σr (RMSEr,before − RMSEr,after) / RMSEr,before Forward Transfer (FWT): FWT = (1/R) Σr=2R (accr,0 − accrandom,r) where accr,0 is zero-shot accuracy on regime r (before any training on r's data), and accrandom is a randomly initialized model. FWT > 0 means prior learning helps with new regimes. Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation: For each new window of data: 1. Test on it (measure prediction quality) 2. Train on it (update model) This interleaved protocol prevents look-ahead bias and is standard in online learning evaluation. Online regret: Regret(T) = Σt=1T L(xt, θt) − minθ Σt L(xt, θ) Sublinear regret (o(T)) means the model is learning. For adaptive regret, compare against the best fixed model per regime, not globally. Concrete test: Train on 2000–2007 (pre-crisis calm). Evaluate on 2008–2009 (GFC). Continue training on 2008–2009. Re-evaluate on 2000–2007 (does it forget calm-regime dynamics?). Continue to 2020 (COVID — a completely different crisis type). Measure: BWT on GFC data, FWT on COVID data.
