Section 7

Critical Analysis: Multivariate Continuous Data

Core Problem None of the five "classic" detectors (ADWIN, Page-Hinkley, DDM, EDDM, KSWIN) natively handles multivariate continuous distributions. DDM and EDDM require a binary error stream. ADWIN and Page-Hinkley detect mean shifts in a scalar. KSWIN uses the KS test, which is inherently univariate. For economic world models with dozens or hundreds of interacting continuous variables, these methods are insufficient without adaptation.

Taxonomy of Approaches

Approach Multivariate? Continuous? Detects Complexity
ADWIN per featureMarginal onlyYesMean shift per dimO(d log n)
ADWIN on projectionVia PCA/randomYesMean shift in projected spaceO(log n)
KSWIN per featureMarginal onlyYesDistribution per dimO(d n log n)
MMD two-sampleTrue multivariateYesAny distributional changeO(n²)
LSDDTrue multivariateYesDensity-level changesO(n²)
Classifier two-sampleTrue multivariateYesAny change learnable by classifierO(train cost)
Energy distanceTrue multivariateYesAny distributional changeO(n²)

MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)

"A Kernel Two-Sample Test" Arthur Gretton, Karsten M. Borgwardt, Malte J. Rasch, Bernhard Scholkopf, and Alexander Smola
Journal of Machine Learning Research, 13:723–773, 2012.
JMLR Paper ID: gretton12a

The foundational paper. An earlier conference version appeared at NIPS 2006:

"A Kernel Method for the Two-Sample Problem" Arthur Gretton, Karsten M. Borgwardt, Malte J. Rasch, Bernhard Scholkopf, and Alexander Smola
Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 19 (NIPS 2006), 2007.

Mathematical Definition

Given two distributions P and Q and a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) H with kernel k, the MMD is:

MMD(P, Q; H) = supf ∈ H, ||f||_H ≤ 1 | EP[f(X)] - EQ[f(Y)] |

Equivalently, using the kernel mean embedding:

MMD²(P, Q) = EX,X'~P[k(X,X')] - 2 EX~P, Y~Q[k(X,Y)] + EY,Y'~Q[k(Y,Y')]

The unbiased empirical estimator given samples {x_1,...,x_n} ~ P and {y_1,...,y_m} ~ Q:

MMD²u = 1/(n(n-1)) ∑i≠j k(x_i,x_j) - 2/(nm) ∑i,j k(x_i,y_j) + 1/(m(m-1)) ∑i≠j k(y_i,y_j)
Theorem (Gretton et al. 2012, Theorem 12)

If k is a characteristic kernel (e.g., the Gaussian RBF kernel k(x,y) = exp(-||x-y||² / 2σ²)), then MMD(P,Q) = 0 if and only if P = Q. Under H_0 (P=Q), the distribution of n · MMD²u converges to a weighted sum of chi-squared random variables. Under H_1 (P ≠ Q), MMD²u converges to MMD²(P,Q) > 0 at rate O(1/sqrt(n)).

For Streaming: Online MMD

The batch MMD test requires O(n²) computation. For streaming, Caron et al. (2023, alibi-detect) implement a sequential variant based on:

"Sequential Kernelized Independence Testing" Arthur Gretton and others (various formulations)
Various venues including ICML and AISTATS

The online detector maintains a running test statistic and uses a configurable expected run length (ERT) under H_0 to control false positives.

Relevance to Economic World Models

MMD is the strongest candidate for multivariate economic data. It detects any change in the joint distribution (not just marginals). The kernel choice controls what changes are detectable: the Gaussian RBF kernel with median heuristic bandwidth works well in practice. The O(n²) cost can be managed via random Fourier features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007), giving O(n · D) where D is the number of random features.

LSDD (Least-Squares Density Difference)

"A Least-Squares Approach to Direct Importance Estimation" Masashi Sugiyama, Taiji Suzuki, and Takafumi Kanamori
Journal of Machine Learning Research, 9:1391–1438, 2008.
"Density Difference Estimation" Masashi Sugiyama, Taiji Suzuki, Takafumi Kanamori, et al.
Neural Computation, 25(10):2734–2775, 2013.
DOI: 10.1162/NECO_a_00492

Mathematical Formulation

Instead of comparing CDFs (KS) or kernel embeddings (MMD), LSDD directly estimates the density difference p(x) - q(x) and uses its L2 norm as a divergence measure:

L²(p, q) = ∫ (p(x) - q(x))² dx

This is estimated via a kernel model. The key insight is that L²(p, q) can be computed without ever estimating p or q individually — only the difference matters, and this can be computed in closed form via a regularized least-squares problem in the RKHS.

The permutation test on the estimated L² statistic yields a p-value. This method is fully multivariate and handles continuous data natively.

Relevance

LSDD has similar power to MMD (both detect changes in joint distributions) but uses a different statistical framework. The alibi-detect implementation provides both batch and online versions. For economic data, LSDD is slightly more interpretable than MMD because the density difference has a direct probabilistic meaning.

Classifier Two-Sample Test

"Revisiting Classifier Two-Sample Tests" David Lopez-Paz and Maxime Oquab
International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2017), 2017.
arXiv: 1610.06545

The idea: train a classifier to distinguish between a reference sample and a test sample. If the classifier achieves significantly better than 50% accuracy (via cross-validation), the distributions differ. This is fully multivariate and can leverage any powerful classifier (gradient-boosted trees, neural networks) to detect subtle, nonlinear distributional changes.

Available in alibi-detect as ClassifierDrift.

Other Multivariate Methods

Energy Distance

"Testing for Equal Distributions in High Dimension" Gabor J. Szekely and Maria L. Rizzo
InterStat, 5, 2004. Also: Annals of Statistics, 41(1):168–194, 2013.
DOI: 10.1214/12-AOS1076

The energy distance is a multivariate distance between distributions based on pairwise Euclidean distances. It is characteristic (like MMD with a specific kernel) and has a simple U-statistic estimator. Computationally O(n²).

Multivariate KS Generalizations

Fasano, G. and Franceschini, A.
"A multidimensional version of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test"
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 225:155–170, 1987.

Extends KS to 2D (Peacock 1983) and higher dimensions, but with O(n²) cost and no clean distribution-free critical values. Rarely used in practice for d > 3.

PCA-ADWIN and Projection Methods

A practical compromise: project multivariate data onto the top principal components (or random projections), then apply a univariate detector (ADWIN, KSWIN) to each projected dimension. Multiple testing corrections (Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg) control the overall false discovery rate. This sacrifices power for computational efficiency.

Recommendations for Economic World Models

Practical Guidance

For a multivariate continuous economic data stream where you need to detect changes in the joint distribution (not just marginals), the recommended stack is:

Primary detector: alibi_detect.cd.MMDDriftOnline with a Gaussian RBF kernel (bandwidth set via median heuristic on a calibration window). This is the most principled choice with strong theoretical guarantees and true multivariate sensitivity.

Fast filter: river.drift.ADWIN applied to a scalar summary (e.g., the model's predictive log-likelihood or a rolling loss). This catches obvious shifts cheaply.

Feature-level diagnostics: alibi_detect.cd.KSDrift with Bonferroni correction to identify which features are drifting after the multivariate test fires.

Deep changes: alibi_detect.cd.LearnedKernelDrift or ClassifierDrift for detecting complex nonlinear shifts that a fixed kernel might miss — important for structural breaks in economic regimes.

Key Papers on Multivariate Concept Drift

"Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift" Stephan Rabanser, Stephan Gunnemann, and Zachary Lipton
Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019), 2019.
arXiv: 1810.11953

Comprehensive empirical comparison of multivariate two-sample tests for dataset shift. Found that the classifier two-sample test and MMD (with appropriate kernel) are the most powerful, while univariate KS per feature with Bonferroni correction is a surprisingly strong baseline.

"A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation" Joao Gama, Indre Zliobaite, Albert Bifet, Mykola Pechenizkiy, and Abdelhamid Bouchachia
ACM Computing Surveys, 46(4):44:1–44:37, 2014.
DOI: 10.1145/2523813

The standard survey on concept drift. Covers drift types (sudden, gradual, incremental, recurring), detection methods, and adaptation strategies.

"Learning under Concept Drift: A Review" Jie Lu, Anjin Liu, Fan Dong, Feng Gu, Joao Gama, and Guangquan Zhang
IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 31(12):2346–2363, 2019.
DOI: 10.1109/TKDE.2018.2876857

A more recent survey that includes multivariate and deep-learning-based approaches.

Architecture-Based Continual Learning Methods for Multi-Timescale Economic World Models

MoE routing, modular networks, supermask superposition, iterative pruning, and SSM-expert hybrids — surveyed for applicability to structured latent-variable models with S5 SSMs, GateL0RD, and SPIB objectives.

August 2026 · Compiled for the RecWM research programme
Contents
  1. Mixture-of-Experts with Routing for Continual Learning
  2. Expert Gate — Aljundi et al. 2017
  3. Modular & Compositional Networks for CL
  4. Supermasks in Superposition (SupSup) — Wortsman et al. 2020
  5. PackNet — Mallya & Lazebnik 2018

Section 1

Mixture-of-Experts with Routing for Continual Learning

The core idea is simple: if each expert specialises on a subset of tasks or regimes, and the router learns to dispatch inputs to the right expert, then old knowledge is naturally preserved in experts that are not updated during new-task training. The challenge is making the router stable enough to preserve old assignments while remaining plastic enough to integrate new ones.

1.1   Theoretical Foundations: MoE in CL

Hongbo Li, Sen Lin, Lingjie Duan, Yingbin Liang, Ness B. Shroff. "Theory on Mixture-of-Experts in Continual Learning." ICLR 2025 (Spotlight). arXiv:2406.16437

This is the first paper to provide formal guarantees for MoE in continual learning. The analysis uses overparameterised linear regression with sequential task arrival as a tractable model. The key results are:

Theorem: Expert Specialisation & Router Convergence

The MoE model diversifies its experts to specialise in different tasks, while its router learns to select the right expert for each task and balance loads across all experts. Crucially, the authors prove that the gating network update must be terminated after sufficient training rounds to attain system convergence — a requirement absent from standard MoE theory that ignores continual task arrival.

Forgetting & Generalisation Bounds

The paper provides explicit closed-form expressions for expected forgetting and overall generalisation error. A counterintuitive finding: adding more experts requires additional convergence rounds and may not improve learning performance, since the router needs more data to learn correct assignments when the expert pool is larger.

MoE Gating Function (Standard Formulation)

G(x) = Softmax(W_g · x) ∈ ℝ^K y = ∑_{k=1}^{K} G(x)_k · E_k(x) where E_k is the k-th expert network, K is expert count, and G selects (Top-1 or Top-2) which experts are active.

1.2   CP-MoE: Consistency-Preserving MoE

Yang Liu, Toan Nguyen, Flora D. Salim. "CP-MoE: Consistency-Preserving Mixture-of-Experts for Continual Learning." CoLLAs 2026. arXiv:2605.20247

CP-MoE addresses the core tension in LoRA-based MoE methods: isolating experts too aggressively limits transfer, but allowing free updates causes forgetting. The solution introduces two coupled mechanisms:

Transient Expert Parameter Protection

A transient expert (TE) is trained alongside stable experts (SE) on each new task. It captures task-specific adaptation signals and estimates parameter importance via path-integral accumulation:

ω_{t,k} = ∑_{s=0}^{S-1} -g_{t,s,k} · Δφ_{t,s,k}^{TE} (Eq. 6) Ω_{t,k} = ω_{t,k} / ((φ_{t,S,k}^{TE} - φ_{t,0,k}^{TE})² + ξ) (Eq. 7) where g is the gradient, Δφ is the parameter change during TE training, and ξ is a small constant for numerical stability.

Consistency-Preserving Routing via CKA

The routing logits are biased by representation consistency between the transient expert and each stable expert, measured by Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA):

h_i^{CP} = CKA(Z^{TE}, Z_i^{SE}) (Eq. 9) s̃_{i,t} = s_{i,t} + α · h_i^{CP} (Eq. 10) where s_{i,t} = x_t^T W_i is the standard routing logit.

Selective Regularisation

L_{reg} = ∑_i (⟨Ω^{(i)}_{A,total}, (A_i - A_i^{old})^{⊙2}⟩ + ⟨Ω^{(i)}_{B,total}, (B_i - B_i^{old})^{⊙2}⟩) (Eq. 14) L_{total}^t = L_{task}^t + λ L_{reg}^t + γ L_{aux}^t (Eq. 15)

Spectral Filtering Interpretation (Theorem 1)

The transient expert trajectory induces multi-step adaptation via a spectral filtering operator:

φ_{t,S}^{TE} - φ_{t,0}^{TE} = -q_S(H_t) · g_t (Eq. 8) where q_S performs spectral filtering favouring flat loss landscape directions — favouring parameters that generalise.

1.3   Stable Routing for MoE in Class-Incremental Learning

Zirui Guo, Quan Cheng, Da-Wei Zhou, Lijun Zhang. "Stable Routing for Mixture-of-Experts in Class-Incremental Learning." arXiv preprint, 2026. arXiv:2605.17571

Constrains the routing function to maintain consistency across tasks, penalising significant deviations in router output distributions. Prevents expert drift by stabilising which experts handle specific task distributions, ensuring earlier-learned expert assignments remain unchanged when learning new classes.

1.4   Expert Routing with Synthetic Data (G2D)

Yeongbin Byun, Sachin V. Mehta, Saurabh Garg, Emma Strubell, Michael Oberst, Bryan Wilder, Zachary C. Lipton. "Expert Routing with Synthetic Data for Continual Learning." arXiv preprint, 2025. arXiv:2412.17009

Generate-to-Discriminate (G2D): rather than training classifiers on synthetic data, the method trains a domain-discriminator on synthetic data to route incoming samples to the correct domain-specific expert at inference time. This is more effective than using synthetic samples directly for classifier training.

1.5   Task-Agnostic Experts Composition

Luigi Quarantiello, Andrea Cossu, Vincenzo Lomonaco. "Task-Agnostic Experts Composition for Continual Learning." arXiv preprint, 2025. arXiv:2506.15566

Eliminates the requirement for task identity at inference time. Dynamic composition weights are learned during training that blend expert outputs based on input characteristics alone, enabling the model to compose existing expert knowledge for new scenarios without explicit task boundaries.

Application to RecWM

For the multi-timescale economic world model: MoE routing is the most natural CL strategy. Each expert could specialise in an economic regime (expansion, contraction, crisis, structural break). The S5 SSM backbone processes temporal dynamics, while a learned router dispatches observation windows to regime-specific expert SSMs. The key insight from Li et al. (ICLR 2025) — that the gating network must be frozen after convergence — maps directly to the RecWM setting: once regime identification is stable, freeze the router to prevent catastrophic reassignment when a new regime appears. CP-MoE's CKA-based routing bias is particularly relevant: when a new economic regime emerges, its transient expert can measure representation similarity to existing regime experts, steering routing toward the most structurally similar predecessor while protecting previously learned regime dynamics.

Section 2

Expert Gate — Aljundi et al. 2017

Rahaf Aljundi, Punarjay Chakravarty, Tinne Tuytelaars. "Expert Gate: Lifelong Learning with a Network of Experts." CVPR 2017, pp. 7120–7129. IEEE.
DOI: 10.1109/CVPR.2017.753

2.1   Architecture Overview

Expert Gate maintains a pool of expert networks {E1, ..., ET}, one per task learned so far. Each expert Et has an associated autoencoder At trained on the same data distribution as the expert. At test time, a new input x is forwarded through all autoencoders, and the expert whose autoencoder achieves the lowest reconstruction error is selected:

t* = argmin_{t ∈ {1,...,T}} ||x - A_t(x)||² (Gate selection) ŷ = E_{t*}(x)

2.2   Autoencoder-Based Task Relatedness

The autoencoders serve a dual purpose. Beyond gating, they measure task relatedness for knowledge transfer: when learning a new task T+1, the system evaluates all existing autoencoders on the new task's training data. The expert whose autoencoder best reconstructs the new data serves as the initialisation point for the new expert:

E_{T+1} ← initialise from E_{t_best} where t_best = argmin_t 𝔼_{x ~ D_{T+1}} [||x - A_t(x)||²]

This provides a principled measure of which prior task's learned representations are most relevant to the new problem, enabling positive transfer without manual task relationship specification.

2.3   Strengths and Limitations

  • No forgetting by construction: each expert is frozen after training; old knowledge cannot be overwritten.
  • O(T) memory: linear in number of tasks — one full network per task plus one autoencoder per task.
  • Single expert loaded at inference: only the selected expert needs to be in memory, making the approach practical for deployment.
  • Limitation: the autoencoder gate tests all T autoencoders at inference, creating O(T) computational cost for routing. This is addressed by the Hierarchically Gated Experts extension (below).

2.4   Hierarchically Gated Experts (HGE)

Khanh Luong, Michael Thielscher. "Hierarchically Gated Experts for Efficient Online Continual Learning." arXiv preprint, 2024. arXiv:2412.17188

HGE organises experts into a tree structure. During inference, the algorithm traverses the tree by following the child with the lowest autoencoding loss at each step, reducing expert queries from O(T) to O(log T). The online variant (GE) introduces task-switch detection via exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of training losses combined with a statistical Z-test:

Upper loss bound: μ + εσ Z-score: ZS = |μ_2 - μ_1| / SE, SE = σ / √n A task switch is detected when ZS exceeds the threshold, distinguishing genuine regime changes from training noise.
Application to RecWM

Expert Gate's autoencoder gating maps naturally to economic regime detection. Train an autoencoder per regime on the latent state trajectories produced by S5. At inference, the autoencoder with lowest reconstruction error on the current observation window identifies the active regime. HGE's tree structure is particularly relevant for hierarchical economic regimes (e.g., first distinguish expansion vs. contraction, then distinguish within expansion: early-cycle vs. late-cycle). The EWMA-based task-switch detection is essentially a regime-change detector, directly analogous to Hamilton's regime-switching model but learned rather than prescribed.

Section 3

Modular & Compositional Networks for CL

3.1   PathNet

Chrisantha Fernando, Dylan Banarse, Charles Blundell, Yori Zwols, David Ha, Andrei A. Rusu, Alexander Pritzel, Daan Wierstra. "PathNet: Evolution Channels Gradient Descent in Super Neural Networks." arXiv preprint, 2017. arXiv:1701.08734

Architecture

PathNet is a deep neural network with L layers, each containing M modules. A "path" through the network selects at most N modules (typically N = 3 or 4) per layer. Each module is a standard neural network component (e.g., a convolutional block or fully-connected layer). The key constraint: at most N out of M modules can be active in any layer at any time.

Path Discovery

The paper describes two algorithms for discovering paths:

  1. Tournament genetic algorithm: maintain a population of path genotypes; evaluate fitness on the current task; select, replicate, and mutate the best paths.
  2. A3C reinforcement learning: an RL agent learns to select paths that maximise task performance.

Continual Learning Mechanism

PathNet CL Procedure
1. For task t, discover optimal path P_t through genetic/RL search 2. Train modules along P_t via gradient descent 3. Freeze all modules on P_t (parameters become read-only) 4. For task t+1, search over remaining unfrozen modules — Frozen modules CAN be used in new paths (read-only) — Only unfrozen modules receive gradient updates 5. Repeat

This enables positive transfer: new tasks can reuse frozen modules from old tasks without modifying them. The evolutionary path selection is key — it determines which subset of the network to use before any gradient-based training begins.

3.2   PICLE: Probabilistic Framework for Modular CL

Lazar Valkov, Akash Srivastava, Swarat Chaudhuri, Charles Sutton. "A Probabilistic Framework for Modular Continual Learning." ICLR 2024.

PICLE addresses the combinatorial challenge of module composition. Given a library of K modules and the need to compose a subset for each new task, the number of possible compositions grows exponentially. PICLE uses a probabilistic model to cheaply compute the fitness of each composition, integrating prior knowledge about good module compositions with dataset-specific information. This avoids training every candidate composition to assess viability. The framework enables perceptual, few-shot, and latent transfer across task sequences.

3.3   MoCL: Rehearsal-Free Modular Compositional CL

(Authors from NAACL 2024 proceedings.) "Rehearsal-Free Modular and Compositional Continual Learning." NAACL 2024 (Short Papers).

MoCL continually adds new modules to language models and composes existing and new modules based on task matching weights. When a new task arrives, the framework determines which existing modules are relevant (via learned matching weights) and adds a new module if existing compositions are insufficient. This is rehearsal-free: no replay buffer of old data is needed.

3.4   Recent Modular CL Directions (2025–2026)

Recent work explores how modular networks support compositional organisation of representational subspaces, with the goal of similarity-dependent geometry: overlapping representations when tasks share structure, stronger separation when they diverge. The "Continual Compositionality and Orchestration" (CCO) paradigm, emerging in 2025–2026, moves from monolithic models to dynamic, decentralised ecosystems of specialised modules.

Application to RecWM

Modular CL fits the RecWM's multi-timescale architecture naturally. Each S5 SSM layer (fast business-cycle, medium structural, slow institutional) can be treated as a module library. PathNet-style path discovery could learn which combinations of fast/medium/slow modules best capture a given regime. PICLE's probabilistic composition is particularly attractive: when a new economic shock arrives (pandemic, financial crisis), the system can cheaply evaluate which module compositions best explain the new dynamics before committing to full training. The compositional approach also maps to the SPIB objective: each module's information bottleneck can be tuned independently, with module composition determining which fragments of the economic state are relevant for each timescale.

Section 4

Supermasks in Superposition (SupSup) — Wortsman et al. 2020

Mitchell Wortsman, Vivek Ramanujan, Rosanne Liu, Aniruddha Kembhavi, Mohammad Rastegari, Jason Yosinski, Ali Farhadi. "Supermasks in Superposition." NeurIPS 2020.
arXiv:2006.14769
Code: github.com/RAIVNLab/supsup

4.1   Core Idea

A randomly initialised, fixed-weight base network W is shared across all tasks. For each task k, the method learns a binary mask M(k) ∈ {0,1}|W| (a "supermask") that selects a subnetwork achieving good performance on that task. The weights W are never trained — only the masks change.

4.2   Edge-Popup Algorithm

The edge-popup (EP) algorithm discovers supermasks within the random base network. It assigns a real-valued score si to each weight (edge) in the network:

Forward pass: M = h(s) where h is the Heaviside step function f(x) = W ⊙ h(s) applied to input x h(s_i) = 1 if s_i ∈ top-k% of all scores, else 0 Backward pass: ∇_{s_i} L is computed using a straight-through estimator (STE) s_i ← s_i - η · ∇_{s_i} L The STE treats h as the identity in the backward pass, allowing gradients to flow through the discrete mask. Key property: Only scores are learned; weights W remain at random init. The mask M selects WHICH edges to keep, not their values.

4.3   Task Inference via Entropy Minimisation

When task identity is unknown at inference, SupSup optimises a linear superposition of learned masks. Given k learned supermasks {M(1), ..., M(k)}, each is associated with a coefficient αi:

Superposed mask: M(α) = ∑_{i=1}^{k} α_i · M^{(i)} Objective: minimise output entropy α* = argmin_α H(f(x; W ⊙ M(α))) where H(p) = -∑_j p_j log p_j is Shannon entropy Initialisation: α_i = 1/k for all i (uniform belief over tasks) Optimisation: A single gradient step on α with respect to the entropy is often sufficient to identify the correct mask, even among 2,500 tasks.

4.4   Hopfield Network Mask Storage

As the number of tasks grows, storing all binary masks becomes expensive. SupSup stores the growing set of supermasks as attractors in a fixed-size Hopfield network, creating a constant-sized reservoir regardless of task count. At retrieval time, the Hopfield network's dynamics converge to the nearest stored mask from a query pattern.

4.5   Scenarios and Scalability

Scenario Task ID at Train Task ID at Test Mask Selection
GG (Given-Given)YesYesDirect lookup
GNs (Given-Not, shared output)YesNoEntropy minimisation (1 grad step)
GNu (Given-Not, unique output)YesNoEntropy minimisation + Hopfield
NNs (Not-Not)NoNoUncertainty-based new mask allocation

The NNs scenario is most relevant for real-world deployment: the system can detect when inputs are unlike any learned task (via output entropy) and autonomously allocate a new supermask.

4.6   ExSSNeT: Exclusive Supermask Extension

Prateek Yadav, Mohit Bansal. "Exclusive Supermask Subnetwork Training for Continual Learning." ACL Findings 2023. arXiv:2210.10209

ExSSNeT addresses SupSup's limitation that weights remain frozen at random init. It introduces exclusive, non-overlapping subnetwork weight training: each task operates on a distinct weight region and can actually update those weights. A KNN-based Knowledge Transfer (KKT) module enables transfer between tasks. Result: 8.3% average improvement over SupSup on sparse masks activating 2–10% of parameters.

Application to RecWM

SupSup's mask superposition maps elegantly to the RecWM's regime-switching requirement. The S5 SSM weight matrices (A, B, C, D) form the base network W, initialised once and frozen. Each economic regime learns a binary mask over these SSM parameters, selecting which state-transition dynamics are active. The entropy-minimisation inference is a natural regime detector: given a new observation window, one gradient step on the mask coefficients identifies which regime(s) are active. For mixed regimes (transition periods between expansion and contraction), the superposed mask M(α) with non-binary α provides soft blending of regime dynamics. The Hopfield storage enables constant-memory regime catalogues as the model encounters more economic episodes over decades of data. ExSSNeT's exclusive masks + weight training would allow regime-specific S5 parameter adaptation within non-overlapping subnetworks.

Section 5

PackNet — Mallya & Lazebnik 2018

Arun Mallya, Svetlana Lazebnik. "PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning." CVPR 2018, pp. 7765–7773. IEEE.
arXiv:1711.05769
Code: github.com/arunmallya/packnet

5.1   Iterative Pruning Procedure

PackNet Algorithm
Phase 1 — Initial Task (e.g., ImageNet): 1. Train full network to convergence 2. Prune: sort weights by |w_i|, remove bottom p% (e.g., 50%) 3. Generate binary mask: M_1(i) = 1 if |w_i| ≥ threshold, else 0 4. Retrain surviving weights for ~10 epochs to recover accuracy 5. Freeze M_1 — these parameters are permanently assigned to Task 1 Phase K — Subsequent Task k: 1. Identify free parameters: F_k = {i : M_j(i) = 0 ∀ j < k} 2. Initialise free parameters (from prior pruning) 3. Train ONLY free parameters on Task k data (~20 epochs) 4. Prune free parameters: remove bottom q% (e.g., 75%) M_k(i) = 1 if i ∈ F_k AND |w_i| ≥ threshold 5. Retrain Task k parameters for ~10 epochs (lr = 1e-4) 6. Freeze M_k permanently Inference for Task k: Apply mask: W_effective = W ⊙ (∪_{j=1}^{k} M_j) All parameters from Tasks 1..k are superimposed.

5.2   Pruning Criterion

For each layer l with weights W_l: Compute absolute magnitudes: {|w_i| : i ∈ F_k ∩ layer_l} Sort in ascending order Prune bottom p% (one-shot magnitude pruning) M_k^l(i) = ℐ(|w_i| ≥ quantile(1-p))

5.3   Capacity Allocation

With 50% initial pruning of a VGG-16 (134M parameters total):

TaskAvailable ParamsPruning RateAssigned ParamsRemaining Free
Task 1 (ImageNet)134M50%~67M~67M
Task 2~67M75%~17M~50M
Task 3~50M75%~13M~37M

5.4   Mask Storage Efficiency

For T tasks, each parameter needs at most log_2(T+1) bits to encode its task assignment, rather than T bits (1 per task). VGG-16 overhead: 1 additional task: ~17 MB (vs. 537 MB base model) 3 additional tasks: ~34 MB (1/16 model size increase)

5.5   Key Properties

  • Zero forgetting: frozen masks guarantee old task parameters are never modified.
  • No computational overhead: inference cost is identical to a single model (just mask application).
  • Always optimises for current task: unlike regularisation methods, the loss is purely the current task's objective.
  • Limitation: no multi-task inference — responses of a filter change depending on sparsity level and are not separable after nonlinearities like ReLU.
  • Limitation: fixed capacity — eventually the network runs out of free parameters.
Application to RecWM

PackNet's iterative pruning provides the most parameter-efficient CL strategy for the RecWM. The S5 state matrices (A, B, C) are overparameterised for any single regime. PackNet can prune regime-1 parameters to 50%, freeing capacity for subsequent regimes. Each regime's dynamics are permanently frozen after learning, guaranteeing zero forgetting of calibrated transition matrices. The log2(T+1)-bit mask storage is attractive for long-horizon economic models that accumulate many regimes over decades. However, the fixed-capacity limitation is a concern: if the number of distinct economic regimes grows without bound, PackNet will exhaust its parameter budget. This could be mitigated by combining PackNet with network growth (adding new S5 layers when free parameters drop below a threshold).

Section 6

MoE Combined with State Space Models

6.1   MoE-Mamba

Maciej Pióro, Kamil Ciebiera, Krzysztof Król, Jan Ludziejewski, Marek Krutul, Jakub Krajewski, Szymon Antoniak, Piotr Miłoś, Marek Cygan, Sebastian Jaszczur. "MoE-Mamba: Efficient Selective State Space Models with Mixture of Experts." arXiv preprint, 2024. arXiv:2401.04081
Code: github.com/kyegomez/MoE-Mamba (community impl., WIP)

Architecture

MoE-Mamba interleaves standard Mamba SSM layers with MoE feed-forward layers using a Switch Transformer routing mechanism (top-1 expert selection). The architecture alternates:

Layer sequence: [Mamba] → [MoE-FFN] → [Mamba] → [MoE-FFN] → ... Each MoE-FFN layer uses Switch routing: G(x) = Softmax(W_r · x) i* = argmax_i G(x)_i (top-1 selection) y = G(x)_{i*} · FFN_{i*}(x) (selected expert output) The Mamba layers handle temporal/sequential state dynamics. The MoE-FFN layers handle conditional computation & scaling.

Key Result

MoE-Mamba reaches the same performance as dense Mamba in 2.35x fewer training steps while preserving Mamba's inference speed advantages over Transformers. This demonstrates that SSMs and MoE are complementary: SSMs provide efficient sequence modelling, MoE provides efficient conditional computation.

6.2   Routing Mamba (RoM)

Zheng Zhan, Liliang Ren, Shuohang Wang, Liyuan Liu, Yang Liu, Yeyun Gong, Yanzhi Wang, Yelong Shen. "Routing Mamba: Scaling State Space Models with Mixture-of-Experts Projection." arXiv preprint, 2025. arXiv:2506.18145

Routing Mamba (RoM) identifies a key limitation of MoE-Mamba: independent routers for each Mamba projection layer create fragmented expert pathways. RoM implements a shared routing mechanism across Conv, Gate, and Output projection layers within each Mamba block, ensuring coherent token-wise specialisation.

Mathematical Formulation

Shared router: P(X_t) = Softmax(X_t · W_r) R_i(X_t) = P(X_t) · ℐ(i ∈ TopK(P)) Conv projection (expert): H_t = ∑_{i=1}^{N} ℐ(i ∈ TopK(P_G)) · X_t W_{in,i} Gate projection (expert): G = SiLU(∑_{i=1}^{N} ℐ(i ∈ TopK(...)) · X_t W_{g,i}) Output projection (expert): E_i(Y_t, X_t) = Y_t ⊙ G · W_{out,i} Final RoM output: O_t = ∑_{i=1}^{N} R_i(X_t) · E_i(Y_t, X_t) Smaller components (x_proj, dt_proj, 1D conv) remain shared across all experts to reduce parameter overhead.

Performance

ArchitectureActive ParamsTotal ParamsPPL @4K
Mamba (dense)353M353M11.18
RoM353M2.5B10.00
Samba (hybrid)421M421M10.05
Samba + RoM421M1.0B9.77

At 1.3B active parameters (10B total), RoM achieves equivalent performance to dense Mamba requiring over 2.3x more active parameters, with 23% FLOPS reduction when applied to hybrid Samba architectures.

6.3   Jamba (AI21 Labs)

Jamba mixes Transformer attention layers and Mamba SSM layers, with MoE blocks on top, achieving very long context windows (hundreds of thousands of tokens). The architecture is: Mamba → Attention → MoE-FFN, repeated, demonstrating that hybrid SSM-attention-MoE architectures can scale effectively.

6.4   EEGMamba: SSM + MoE for Multi-Task Classification

(Authors from EEGMamba, 2024.) "EEGMamba: Bidirectional State Space Model with Mixture of Experts for EEG Multi-task Classification." arXiv preprint, 2024. arXiv:2407.20254

Uses a bidirectional SSM backbone with MoE for multi-task EEG classification. Relevant because it demonstrates SSM+MoE applied to multi-task learning on physiological time series — the closest existing work to economic time series in terms of signal characteristics (non-stationary, multi-scale, regime-switching).

Application to RecWM

This is the most directly applicable section for the RecWM architecture. The proposed design:

  • Base architecture: S5 SSM backbone (replacing Mamba's selective SSM with S5's MIMO formulation and parallel scan).
  • Expert routing for regime switching: Following RoM's shared-router design, a single router dispatches across the S5 projection matrices (A, B, C, D), ensuring coherent regime assignment. Each expert contains a distinct set of (Ai, Bi, Ci, Di) matrices encoding regime-specific state dynamics.
  • Continual learning: When a new economic regime is detected (via Expert Gate's autoencoder loss or SupSup's entropy signal), a new expert is allocated. The router is retrained with CP-MoE's CKA-consistency bias to preserve existing regime assignments.
  • Multi-timescale integration: Separate MoE-S5 stacks for fast (business cycle), medium (structural), and slow (institutional) timescales, with GateL0RD update rules controlling information flow between timescales.
  • SPIB objective per expert: Each regime expert has its own information bottleneck (SPIB per-fragment objective), ensuring that the model learns maximally informative representations of regime-specific dynamics without retaining noise.

The RoM finding that shared routing across projection layers outperforms independent routing is critical: in the RecWM, the state transition matrix A and observation matrix C must be routed together (you cannot have expansion-regime transitions with contraction-regime observations). RoM's coherent routing enforces this consistency.

Synthesis

Recommended Hybrid Architecture

The strongest approach for the RecWM combines three complementary mechanisms:

  1. RoM-style shared routing over S5 experts as the primary architecture, with each expert holding regime-specific state-space parameters.
  2. SupSup entropy-based regime detection as the task-identity inference mechanism, enabling automatic regime identification without labelled regime data.
  3. CP-MoE's CKA-consistency routing bias as the CL regulariser, ensuring that router updates when new regimes appear do not reassign existing regimes to wrong experts.

This combination yields: automatic regime detection (no task labels), zero forgetting of learned regime dynamics (expert isolation), constant-memory regime storage (Hopfield network), coherent SSM parameter routing (shared router), and principled new-regime allocation (CKA similarity to existing experts).

C.1 TTT -- Test-Time Training with Self-Supervision

Yu Sun, Xiaolong Wang, Zhuang Liu, John Miller, Alexei A. Efros, Moritz Hardt
"Test-Time Training with Self-Supervision for Generalization under Distribution Shifts"
ICML 2020 arXiv: 1909.13231 GitHub (160 stars)

Key Idea

At test time, update the model using a self-supervised auxiliary task (rotation prediction) on each unlabeled test input. The model has a shared feature extractor that is updated at test time by optimizing the auxiliary loss, while the main task head remains fixed.

Architecture

The model decomposes into three parameter groups:

  • θe -- shared feature extractor (updated at both train and test time)
  • θm -- main task head (classification; frozen at test time)
  • θs -- self-supervised task head (rotation prediction; frozen at test time)

Mathematical Formulation

Joint Training Objective (Eq. 2):

min_{θ_e, θ_m, θ_s} (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} [ l_m(x_i, y_i; θ_m, θ_e) + l_s(x_i; θ_s, θ_e) ]

where lm is the main task loss (cross-entropy for classification) and ls is the self-supervised loss (rotation prediction as 4-way classification over {0, 90, 180, 270} degrees).

Test-Time Update (Eq. 3):

min_{θ_e} l_s(x; θ_s, θ_e)

At test time, only θe is updated by minimizing the self-supervised loss on the single test sample x. The prediction is then made using the updated extractor: θ(x) = (θe*, θm).

Theorem 1 (Gradient Correlation Condition):

⟨ ∇ l_m(x,y; θ), ∇ l_s(x; θ) ⟩ > ε

TTT improves performance when the gradient of the main task loss and the self-supervised loss are positively correlated. Under this condition, a single gradient step θ(x) = θ - η ∇ ls(x; θ) reduces the main task loss.

EWM Relevance: The core insight -- that an auxiliary self-supervised task can provide a gradient signal correlated with the main task at test time -- directly applies to economic models. An economic world model could use reconstruction of masked economic indicators as the auxiliary task, updating the shared representation when the economic regime shifts from training conditions.

C.2 TENT -- Fully Test-Time Adaptation by Entropy Minimization

Dequan Wang, Evan Shelhamer, Shaoteng Liu, Bruno Olshausen, Trevor Darrell
"Tent: Fully Test-Time Adaptation by Entropy Minimization"
ICLR 2021 (Spotlight) arXiv: 2006.10726 GitHub (472 stars, MIT)

Key Idea

Adapt batch normalization (BN) affine parameters (γ and β) at test time by minimizing the entropy of the model's predictions. No labels needed, no source data needed, updates less than 1% of parameters.

Mathematical Formulation

Entropy Minimization Objective:

min_{γ, β} H(ŷ) = -Σ_c p(ŷ_c) log p(ŷ_c) where ŷ = f_θ(x^t) are predictions on test data x^t

Parameters Updated: Only the BN affine parameters {γl,k, βl,k} for each layer l and channel k. All other parameters remain fixed. This constitutes less than 1% of model parameters.

Feature Modulation (two steps per BN layer):

Normalization: x̄ = (x - μ) / σ (μ, σ estimated from test batch) Transformation: x' = γ x̄ + β (γ, β updated via ∇H(ŷ))
TENT Algorithm: 1. Initialize: collect {γ, β} from source model; discard source BN statistics 2. For each test batch: a. Forward pass: estimate μ, σ from test batch (replace source statistics) b. Compute predictions ŷ = f_θ(x^t) c. Compute entropy loss H(ŷ) d. Backward pass: update {γ, β} via gradient descent on H(ŷ) 3. Online: single pass per batch; Offline: multiple epochs possible
EWM Relevance: TENT's entropy minimization is the simplest possible TTA signal -- no auxiliary task design required. When predictions become uncertain (high-entropy) under regime shift, TENT-style updates to normalization layers recalibrate the model's internal statistics. The limitation: entropy minimization alone can reinforce confident-but-wrong predictions, which is dangerous in economic settings where miscalibration has real costs.

C.3 CoTTA -- Continual Test-Time Domain Adaptation

Qin Wang, Olga Fink, Luc Van Gool, Dengxin Dai
"Continual Test-Time Domain Adaptation"
CVPR 2022 arXiv: 2203.13591 GitHub (325 stars)

Key Idea

Addresses error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting in continual TTA where the target domain keeps changing. Two mechanisms: (a) weight-averaged teacher with augmentation-averaged pseudo-labels for more reliable supervision; (b) stochastic restoration of weights to source-pretrained values to prevent drift.

Mathematical Formulation

Student Loss (Eq. 1) -- Cross-entropy with teacher pseudo-labels:

L_{θ_t}(x_t^T) = -Σ_c ŷ'^T_{tc} log ŷ^T_{tc} where teacher pseudo-labels: ŷ'^T_t = f_{θ'_t}(x_t^T) student predictions: ŷ^T_t = f_{θ_t}(x_t^T)

Teacher EMA Update (Eq. 2):

θ'_{t+1} = α θ'_t + (1 - α) θ_{t+1}

Augmentation-Averaged Pseudo-Labels (Eq. 3):

ỹ'^T_t = (1/N) Σ_{i=0}^{N-1} f_{θ'_t}(aug_i(x_t^T))

Confidence-Based Selection (Eq. 4):

y'^T_t = { ŷ'^T_t, if conf(f_{θ_0}(x_t^T)) ≥ p_th (source confident) { ỹ'^T_t, otherwise (use augmented avg)

Stochastic Restoration (Eqs. 7-8):

M ~ Bernoulli(p) W_{t+1} = M ⊙ W_0 + (1 - M) ⊙ W_{t+1}

Each weight has probability p of being restored to its source-pretrained value W0. This prevents catastrophic forgetting by maintaining proximity to the source model.

EWM Relevance: The continual adaptation setting is precisely the economic scenario -- regimes shift continuously. Stochastic restoration is a "memory anchor" preventing the model from forgetting fundamental economic relationships while adapting to current conditions. The augmentation averaging over economic scenarios could improve pseudo-label quality during turbulent periods.

C.4 TTT-MAE -- Test-Time Training with Masked Autoencoders

Yossi Gandelsman, Yu Sun, Xinlei Chen, Alexei A. Efros
"Test-Time Training with Masked Autoencoders"
NeurIPS 2022 arXiv: 2209.07522 GitHub (96 stars)

Key Idea

Replaces rotation prediction from original TTT with masked autoencoder (MAE) reconstruction. Critically, the encoder is frozen during supervised training (ViT probing) -- only the lightweight head is trained. At test time, the encoder is fine-tuned via the MAE reconstruction objective on each test sample.

Mathematical Formulation

Training Phase (ViT Probing):

h_0 = arg min_h (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n l_m(h ˆ f_0(x_i), y_i)

where f0 is the frozen pre-trained MAE encoder and h0 is the trainable main task head (a ViT-Base, not just a linear layer).

Test-Time Training Objective (MAE reconstruction):

f_x, g_x = arg min_{f,g} l_s(g ˆ f(mask(x)), x)

where ls is pixel-wise MSE between reconstructed and original patches, mask() randomly masks 75% of image patches, f is the encoder, g is the decoder. Prediction: h0 ˆ fx(x).

Theoretical Analysis (Bias-Variance Trade-off):

M(α) = (1 - α) Σ + α x̃ x̃^T α = 0 : fully biased (standard fixed model, no TTT) α = 1 : high variance (train exclusively on single test sample) optimal α: balances both Prediction: ŷ = w · v_1^T x̃ (v_1 = top eigenvector of M(α))

Main Theorem: Under linear assumptions with k=1 PCA component and specific eigenvalue conditions, there exists α > 0 where TTT strictly dominates the fixed baseline (α=0) in prediction risk E[|ŷ - y|].

TTT-MAE Hyperparameters: Masking ratio: 75% TTT steps: 20 (SGD, not AdamW) Learning rate: 5e-3 Momentum: 0.9 Weight decay: 0.2 Reset f, g to f_0, g_0 after each test sample
EWM Relevance: MAE reconstruction as the auxiliary task is directly applicable -- an economic world model could mask economic indicators and reconstruct them as the self-supervised signal. The bias-variance analysis formalizes the trade-off between staying close to training knowledge and adapting to the new sample. The "ViT probing" approach (frozen encoder during training) prevents the encoder from specializing to labeled examples, preserving its reconstruction capability for test-time adaptation.

C.5 EATA -- Efficient Test-Time Model Adaptation without Forgetting

Shuaicheng Niu, Jiaxiang Wu, Yifan Zhang, Yaofo Chen, Shijian Zheng, Peilin Zhao, Mingkui Tan
"Efficient Test-Time Model Adaptation without Forgetting"
ICML 2022 arXiv: 2204.02610 GitHub (143 stars)

Key Idea

Two problems with naive TTA: (1) updating on every sample is wasteful and noisy; (2) continual updates cause catastrophic forgetting. EATA solves both via (a) active sample selection -- only adapt on reliable, non-redundant samples -- and (b) Fisher information regularization to prevent important parameters from changing too much.

Mathematical Formulation

Entropy-Based Reliability Weight (Eq. 3):

S^{ent}(x) = [1 / exp(E(x;Θ) - E_0)] · I_{E(x;Θ) < E_0}(x)

Only samples with entropy below threshold E0 are selected. Their weight decreases exponentially as entropy approaches E0.

Diversity-Based Weight (Eq. 7):

S^{div}(x) = I_{cos(f_Θ(x), m^{t-1}) < ε}(x) m^t = α ȳ^t + (1-α) m^{t-1} (EMA of predictions)

Combined Selection & Overall Objective (Eqs. 8, 10):

S(x) = S^{ent}(x) · S^{div}(x) min_{Θ̃} S(x) E(x;Θ) + β R(Θ̃, Θ̃^o)

Fisher Information Regularization (Eq. 9):

R(Θ̃, Θ̃^o) = Σ_{θ_i ∈ Θ̃} ω(θ_i)(θ_i - θ_i^o)^2 ω(θ_i) = (1/Q) Σ_{x_q ∈ D_F} [∂/∂θ_i^o L_CE(f_{Θ^o}(x_q), ŷ_q)]^2
EWM Relevance: The sample selection mechanism is critical for economic data -- not every time step should trigger adaptation. Only periods of genuine regime shift (low-entropy, informative samples) should drive updates. Fisher regularization prevents the model from forgetting stable economic relationships when adapting to new ones. This is a principled version of "adapt only when confident the shift is real, and preserve fundamentals."

C.6 SAR -- Towards Stable Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Wild World

Shuaicheng Niu, Jiaxiang Wu, Yifan Zhang, Zhiquan Wen, Yaofo Chen, Peilin Zhao, Mingkui Tan
"Towards Stable Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Wild World"
ICLR 2023 (Oral, top 5%) arXiv: 2302.12400 GitHub (213 stars, BSD-3)

Key Idea

Identifies three realistic challenges that break existing TTA methods: (1) mixed distribution shifts (multiple corruption types simultaneously); (2) small batch sizes (even single samples); (3) online imbalanced label distributions. Proposes SAR: sharpness-aware and reliable entropy minimization.

Mathematical Formulation

Reliable Entropy Minimization (sample filtering):

min_Θ S(x) E(x;Θ), where S(x) = I_{E(x;Θ) < E_0}(x)

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (flat minima):

min_Θ E^{SA}(x;Θ), where E^{SA}(x;Θ) = max_{||ε||_2 ≤ ρ} E(x; Θ + ε) Optimal perturbation (first-order): ε̂(Θ) = ρ · sign(∇_Θ E(x;Θ)) |∇_Θ E(x;Θ)| / ||∇_Θ E(x;Θ)||_2 Gradient: ∇_Θ E^{SA}(x;Θ) ≈ ∇_Θ E(x;Θ)|_{Θ + ε̂(Θ)}

Combined SAR Objective:

min_{Θ̃} S(x) E^{SA}(x;Θ) (Θ̃ ⊂ Θ = normalization affine params)

BN Analysis: SAR identifies that BN statistics estimated from limited test samples under mixed shifts produce biased estimates. It advocates batch-agnostic normalization (Group Norm, Layer Norm) computing statistics per sample or channel-wise.

Recovery: Track moving average entropy em; if em < e0 (model collapse), reset parameters to source pretrained values.

SAR Algorithm: For each test sample x_j: 1. Compute entropy E_j = E(x_j; Θ) 2. If E_j > E_0: skip update (unreliable sample) 3. Compute ∇_{Θ̃} E(x_j; Θ) 4. Calculate perturbation ε̂(Θ̃) 5. Update Θ̃ ← Θ̃ - η g, g = ∇_{Θ̃} E(x_j; Θ)|_{Θ + ε̂} 6. Track e_m; recover if e_m < e_0
EWM Relevance: SAR's three challenges map perfectly to economics: (1) mixed distribution shifts = simultaneous economic shocks (inflation + supply chain + geopolitics); (2) small batch sizes = limited real-time economic data; (3) imbalanced labels = rare events (crises). Sharpness-aware optimization seeks flat minima generalizing across shift types -- precisely what an economic model needs under heterogeneous perturbations. The recovery mechanism prevents collapse during unprecedented events.

C.7 Connection to Economic Regime Shifts

The Core Analogy

Test time = deployment time when the economic environment has shifted from training conditions. The model was trained on historical economic data (source domain), but at deployment it encounters a new regime (target domain) -- post-pandemic recovery, high-inflation environment, or geopolitical disruption.

Papers Applying TTA to Financial/Economic Data

Yurui Wu, Qingying Deng, Wonou Chung, Mairui Li
"Test-Time Adaptation for Non-stationary Time Series: From Synthetic Regime Shifts to Financial Markets"
arXiv: 2602.00073 2026

Freezes model backbone, updates only normalization parameters using recent unlabeled data. For classification: entropy minimization + temporal consistency. For forecasting: reduces prediction variance via weak augmentations + optional teacher distillation. Stability via quadratic drift penalty and uncertainty-triggered fallback logic. Evaluated on equity (SPY, QQQ) and forex (EUR/USD) during pandemic, high-inflation, and recovery periods. Critical finding: simple BN updates outperform more aggressive adaptation in real financial settings, despite stronger results on synthetic drift.

Indar Kumar, Akanksha Tiwari, Sai Krishna Jasti, Ankit Hemant Lade
"RG-TTA: Regime-Guided Meta-Control for Test-Time Adaptation in Streaming Time Series"
arXiv: 2603.27814 2026

Meta-controller that continuously modulates adaptation intensity based on distributional similarity to previously seen regimes. Uses an ensemble of statistical metrics (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Wasserstein-1, feature-distance, variance-ratio) for similarity scores. Two controls: (1) learning rate scaling -- aggressive for novel distributions, conservative for familiar ones; (2) loss-driven early stopping instead of fixed budgets. Manages a regime memory, reloading specialist models at 30%+ loss improvement. Across 672 experiments, regime-guided policies achieved lowest error in ~70% of cases (5.7-14.1% improvement).

Critical Implication for RCE: These 2026 papers confirm TTA for economic time series is an active, validated direction. Key insight from Wu et al.: conservative adaptation (BN-only) outperforms aggressive adaptation in real markets -- structural economic relationships are more stable than surface statistics. RG-TTA's regime-guided approach is an automatic "how much should I adapt?" controller, precisely what an economic world model needs during regime transitions.

C.8 TTA vs. Online Fine-Tuning

DimensionTest-Time AdaptationOnline Fine-Tuning
Labels at test timeNone (unsupervised)Typically available (delayed)
Update signalEntropy, self-supervised loss, pseudo-labelsTrue labels (possibly delayed)
Parameters updatedMinimal (BN affine, <1%)All or large subsets
Forgetting riskHigh (no replay, no labels)Moderate (labels anchor learning)
Computational cost1 backward pass per batchMultiple epochs possible
StabilityFragile without safeguardsMore stable with labels
LatencyImmediate (per-sample/batch)Delayed (wait for labels)

Key Survey

Jian Liang, Ran He, Tieniu Tan
"A Comprehensive Survey on Test-Time Adaptation under Distribution Shifts"
IJCV 2024 arXiv: 2303.15361 738+ citations

Organizes TTA into three categories: (1) test-time domain adaptation (access to full test set), (2) test-time batch adaptation (adapt per batch), (3) online test-time adaptation (single-pass, streaming). The key constraint distinguishing TTA from online fine-tuning: TTA operates without labels and must maintain stability without catastrophic forgetting safeguards that labels provide.

EWM Relevance: Economic data occupies a middle ground -- labels (outcomes) arrive with delay (GDP quarters later, employment monthly, markets daily). TTA fills the gap between when the regime shifts and when labeled outcomes confirm the shift. The optimal strategy is likely hybrid: TTA for immediate adaptation when distribution shift is detected, followed by online fine-tuning once delayed labels arrive to correct any TTA drift.

D.9 Error Accumulation in Continual TTA

The Problem

When TTA is applied continuously (not just a single domain shift), errors compound. The model updates based on its own predictions (pseudo-labels or entropy), and errors propagate into the weights, producing progressive degradation -- confirmation bias.

Mechanisms of Error Accumulation

  1. Pseudo-label noise: Under distribution shift, model predictions are unreliable. Using these as supervision introduces label noise that compounds.
  2. Entropy collapse: Minimizing entropy without constraints can produce degenerate solutions (predicting a single class with high confidence).
  3. Distribution shift stacking: Each adaptation step changes the model, which changes the distribution of future pseudo-labels, creating a feedback loop.
  4. Catastrophic forgetting: Adapting to domain Dt erases knowledge needed for domain Dt+1.

Key Papers Analyzing Error Accumulation

  • CoTTA (Wang et al., CVPR 2022) -- First to formally identify and address error accumulation in continual TTA via stochastic restoration and augmentation-averaged pseudo-labels.
  • Wang et al. (CVPR 2024) -- "Continual Test-Time Domain Adaptation via Dynamic Sample Selection." Mitigates error accumulation through selective adaptation.
  • Dobler, Marsden, Yang (CVPR 2023) -- "Robust Mean Teacher for Continual and Gradual Test-Time Adaptation." Analyzes error accumulation in sequential scenarios.
  • Hoang & Vo (NeurIPS 2024) -- "Persistent Test-Time Adaptation in Recurring Testing Scenarios." Theoretical analysis of the error accumulation phenomenon.
  • Ye et al. (Pattern Recognition 2025) -- "Domain Consistency Learning for Continual Test-Time Adaptation in Image Semantic Segmentation."
EWM Relevance: Error accumulation is the central risk for economic TTA. Economic regimes can persist for years -- continual adaptation without anchoring will cause arbitrary drift. The solutions (stochastic restoration, sample selection, Fisher regularization) are all forms of "remembering fundamentals while adapting to specifics." For economic models, "source weights" encode structural economic relationships (supply-demand, monetary transmission), which must be preserved while adapting surface statistics to the current regime.

D.10 NOTE -- Robust Continual Test-Time Adaptation Against Temporal Correlation

Taesik Gong, Jongheon Jeong, Taewon Kim, Yewon Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sung-Ju Lee
"NOTE: Robust Continual Test-time Adaptation Against Temporal Correlation"
NeurIPS 2022 arXiv: 2208.05117 GitHub (50 stars, MIT)

Key Idea

Most TTA methods assume i.i.d. test data, but real data is temporally correlated. NOTE addresses this with: (1) Instance-Aware Batch Normalization (IABN) that corrects per-instance statistics; (2) Prediction-Balanced Reservoir Sampling (PBRS) that creates balanced mini-batches from correlated streams.

Mathematical Formulation

IABN Corrected Statistics (soft-shrinkage function ψ):

μ^{IABN}_{b,c} = μ̄_c + ψ(μ̃_{b,c} - μ̄_c; α s_{μ̃,c}) (σ^{IABN}_{b,c})^2 = σ̄^2_c + ψ(σ̃^2_{b,c} - σ̄^2_c; α s_{σ̃^2,c}) ψ(x; λ) = { x - λ, if x > λ { x + λ, if x < -λ { 0, otherwise

Instance-specific corrections are applied only when they deviate significantly from running statistics, controlled by α=4 (standard deviations).

Instance-wise Statistics:

μ̃_{b,c} = (1/L) Σ_l f_{b,c,l} σ̃^2_{b,c} = (1/L) Σ_l (f_{b,c,l} - μ̃_{b,c})^2
PBRS Algorithm: Maintain memory bank M of capacity N For each incoming sample x_t with predicted label ŷ_t: If |M| < N: add (x_t, ŷ_t) Else if ŷ_t NOT in majority class(es): Replace random majority-class sample with (x_t, ŷ_t) Else: Reservoir sampling with probability p < m[ŷ_t]/n[ŷ_t]

BN Statistics Update (EMA):

μ_t = (1-m) μ_{t-1} + m (N/(N-1)) μ̂_t σ^2_t = (1-m) σ^2_{t-1} + m (N/(N-1)) σ̂^2_t Hyperparameters: α=4, m=0.01, lr=0.0001 (Adam), N=64
EWM Relevance: NOTE's handling of temporal correlation is essential for economics -- economic data is inherently non-i.i.d. and strongly autocorrelated. IABN detects per-instance distribution shifts (analogous to detecting that today's market data comes from a different regime), while PBRS ensures the adaptation signal isn't dominated by the most recent regime. This is the "balanced memory" needed for an economic model that must remember both crisis and normal periods.

D.11 RoTTA -- Robust Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Scenarios

Longhui Yuan, Binhui Xie, Shuang Li
"Robust Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Scenarios"
CVPR 2023 arXiv: 2303.13899 GitHub (71 stars, MIT)

Key Idea

Addresses "Practical Test-Time Adaptation" (PTTA) with three components: (1) Robust Batch Normalization using global statistics from a memory bank; (2) Category-balanced sampling with timeliness and uncertainty scoring; (3) Time-aware reweighting in a teacher-student framework.

Mathematical Formulation

Robust Batch Normalization (EMA of global statistics):

μ_g = (1 - α) μ_g + α μ α = 0.05 σ^2_g = (1 - α) σ^2_g + α σ^2

Category-Balanced Sampling (CSTU heuristic):

H = λ_t · 1/(1 + exp(-A/N)) + λ_u · U/log(C) A = sample age, U = -Σ p(c|x)log p(c|x), λ_t = λ_u = 1.0

Higher score = more likely to be replaced. Old, uncertain samples go first.

Time-Aware Reweighting:

E(A_i) = exp(-A_i/N) / (1 + exp(-A_i/N))

Teacher-Student Loss & Overall Objective:

l(x'_i, x''_i) = -(1/C) Σ_c p_T(c|x'_i) log p_S(c|x''_i) x'_i = weakly augmented (teacher), x''_i = strongly augmented (student) Teacher EMA: θ^T_{t+1} = (1 - ν) θ^T_t + ν θ^S_{t+1} (ν = 0.001) L_r = (1/|M|) Σ E(A_i) · l(x'_i, x''_i)
EWM Relevance: RoTTA's time-aware reweighting is natural for economic data -- recent observations should matter more than stale ones. CSTU scoring (replace old, uncertain samples first) creates a memory retaining informative examples from each regime while discarding noisy, outdated observations. The teacher-student framework provides stability under constantly shifting economic distributions.

D.12 Continual TTA for Sequential/Time-Series Data

Challenges Beyond Image Classification

  • Temporal dependence: Consecutive samples are correlated; the i.i.d. assumption fails completely
  • Concept drift vs. covariate shift: In time series, both P(X) and P(Y|X) may shift
  • Gradual vs. abrupt shifts: Economic regimes can transition gradually or switch abruptly
  • Non-stationarity: The underlying data-generating process itself evolves

Key Papers (2024-2026)

HG Kim, S Kim, J Mok, S Yoon
"Battling the Non-Stationarity in Time Series Forecasting via Test-Time Adaptation"
AAAI 2025

Adaptation mechanisms specific to the temporal domain for distribution shifts in forecasting.

D Kim, S Park, J Choo
"When Model Meets New Normals: Test-Time Adaptation for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection"
AAAI 2024

Mitigates distribution shifts in anomaly detection -- relevant because anomaly detectors must adapt to new "normal" regimes without labels.

M Schirmer, D Zhang, E Nalisnick
"Temporal Test-Time Adaptation with State-Space Models"
arXiv 2024

Integrates state-space models (inherently modeling temporal dynamics) with TTA. The state-space formulation naturally accommodates sequential data.

YF Zhang, W Chen, Z Zhu, D Qin, L Sun
"Addressing Concept Shift in Online Time Series Forecasting: Detect-then-Adapt"
arXiv 2024

Two-phase approach: first detect concept shift, then adapt. Avoids unnecessary adaptation during stable periods.

H Sun, K Ammann, S Giannoulakis, O Fink
"Continuous Test-Time Domain Adaptation for Efficient Fault Detection"
arXiv 2024

Continual TTA for fault detection in operational systems -- relevant analogy to detecting economic anomalies under shifting conditions.

D Duan, R Xu, P Liu, F Wen
"Lifelong Test-Time Adaptation via Online Learning in Tracked Low-Dimensional Subspace"
NeurIPS 2026

Frames TTA as "essentially a local fine-tuning of a source pretrained model" and constrains adaptation to a low-dimensional subspace to prevent catastrophic forgetting over the model's lifetime.

Synthesis for Economic World Models: The time-series TTA landscape is maturing rapidly (2024-2026). The most promising directions for economic applications converge on a single principle: adapt the statistics, preserve the structure.

1. Regime-aware adaptation intensity (RG-TTA): Modulate based on how different the current regime is from training.

2. Conservative BN-only adaptation (Wu et al. 2026): In real markets, minimal adaptation outperforms aggressive methods -- structural relationships are stable, only surface statistics shift.

3. Detect-then-adapt (Zhang et al.): Only trigger adaptation when genuine regime change is detected.

4. Low-dimensional subspace adaptation (Duan et al.): Constrain what the model can change.

For an economic world model built on causal/structural foundations, this means adapting the distributional parameters of exogenous shocks while preserving the causal graph and structural equations.
