Theorem 4: fibered monoidal category structureConjecturalCategory-theoretic construction is well-defined; verification that economic fragments satisfy the axioms requires formal proof
GateL0RD + S5 compositionUnspecifiedThree possible interpretations; ablation study needed
SPIB for slow fragmentsUnreliable~80 quarterly samples is well below the N > 300–500 typically needed for reliable MI estimation
Theorem 5: endogenous εt and crisis transitionProvableDirect from Perdomo Thm 3.5 with time-varying substitution; proof straightforward, framing novel
Theorem 1: γ-strong concavity of composed EI mapAssumedEI is concave minus concave in general; condition needs formal verification (Open Problem 7)

Open Problem 1: GateL0RD × S5 Composition

The literature does not specify how to compose a gating mechanism (GateL0RD) with a state-space model (S5). We conjecture that gating the S5 input (interpretation a) preserves the diagonal structure needed for O(N) RTRL (Irie et al., ICLR 2024), but this needs formal verification and ablation.

Open Problem 2: SPIB Sample Complexity

The State-Predictive Information Bottleneck requires estimating mutual information between past and future states. For slow fragments (WFpolicy, WFreg), we have ~80 quarterly and ~40 annual data points. This is insufficient for reliable estimation. Mitigation: bootstrap confidence intervals, cross-validated binning, and synthetic augmentation from the faster fragments.

Open Problem 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The unified loss has 32–39 hyperparameters. Competing gradient directions (Lrec vs. LSPIB, Lgate vs. LEWC) create a complex Pareto surface. We plan population-based training (Jaderberg et al. 2017) and report multi-objective Pareto fronts rather than single “best” configurations.

Open Problem 4: Identifiability

SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICLR 2021) assumes statistical independence of latent factors for identifiability. Mechanism sparsity approaches (Lachapelle et al., CLEaR 2022) assume dependence. RecWM uses both. The compatibility of these assumptions—or the conditions under which one dominates—is an open theoretical question.

Open Problem 5: Data Pipeline

RecWM requires data across all seven fragment types. Free sources (Yahoo Finance, FRED) provide WFprice and WFpolicy. WForder requires exchange feeds; WFcredit and WFvol require Bloomberg or equivalent. WFnarrative requires NLP pipelines on news/filings. WFreg requires legal databases. A production deployment needs institutional data partnerships.

Open Problem 6: Compute

Estimated training cost for a research prototype: $10K–20K in cloud GPU time (8×A100 for ~2 weeks). This is a rough estimate; the actual cost depends heavily on the outcome of Open Problems 1–3. We do not claim this is cheap, but it is within reach of a well-funded research lab.

Open Problem 7: EI Concavity Verification

Theorem 1 assumes γ-strong concavity of the composed map φ → EI(Tφmacro). Effective information is the difference of two concave functions (marginal entropy minus conditional entropy), which is neither concave nor convex in general. The assumption holds when the marginal entropy term dominates—e.g., in systems with sufficient stochasticity that row entropies are small relative to column-average entropy. Identifying the precise class of transition matrices for which this holds, and verifying it empirically on financial market data, is required before Theorem 1 can be published as a formal result rather than a conditional theorem.

12

Theorem 6: Cohomological Market Consistency

The Problem

Theorem 4 provides a fibered monoidal category for composing world fragments under constraints. But composition can succeed locally while failing globally: equity markets may price risk one way, credit markets another, and rates a third—each locally consistent, but no global state reconciles all three simultaneously. Standard risk metrics (VaR, entropy, correlation) measure how bad things are. They cannot detect structural impossibility of consistency—the situation where the pieces simply do not fit, regardless of parameter values.

This is not a hypothetical. Before the 2008 crisis, AAA-rated CDO tranches, CDS spreads, and equity volatility surfaces each told locally coherent stories. The inconsistency was topological, not statistical: no single probability measure could simultaneously rationalise all three markets. Detecting this requires mathematics that existing financial models do not use.

Prior Art

  • Abramsky & Brandenburger (New J. Phys., 2011): Sheaf-theoretic framework for contextuality in quantum mechanics. Sheaf cohomology detects non-classical correlations as obstructions to global sections. No economic application.
  • Hansen & Ghrist (Found. Comput. Math., 2019): Sheaves for sensor integration—local observations that may not admit a global consistent state. Applied to robotics, not finance.
  • “A Sheaf Framework for Strategic Multi-Agent Systems” (arXiv 2606.01663, June 2026): Nash equilibria as global sections of a sheaf; H1 obstruction classifies equilibrium non-existence. The closest work to what we propose, but applied to abstract games, not economic world models.
  • Applied Sheaf Theory for Multi-Agent AI (arXiv 2504.17700, 2025): Sheaves for multi-agent consistency checking. No financial application.

The gap: Zero papers apply sheaf cohomology to financial market consistency. The sheaf framework for strategic systems (June 2026) treats games, not world models. Nobody has defined a sheaf over the space of economic world fragments or computed its cohomological obstruction classes.

The New Object

We define the market consistency sheaf over RecWM’s fragment algebra:

Definition (Market Consistency Sheaf)

Let U = {Uk}k=1..K be the open cover of economic state space induced by the K world fragment types. Each Uk corresponds to the states observable through fragment WFk. Define the presheaf F by:

  • Sections: F(Uk) = the set of probability measures consistent with fragment k’s observations
  • Restriction maps: ρk,j: F(Uk ∩ Uj) → the marginal agreements between fragments k and j

F is a sheaf if and only if local sections that agree on overlaps extend to a unique global section—i.e., a single probability measure rationalising all fragments simultaneously.

Theorem 6 (Cohomological Crisis Detection)

Let F be the market consistency sheaf over the fragment cover U. Let H1(U; F) denote the first Čech cohomology group of F with respect to U. Then:

  1. Consistency equivalence: A global market state—a single probability measure consistent with all fragment observations—exists if and only if H1(U; F) = 0.
  2. Obstruction classification: When H1(U; F) ≠ 0, the non-trivial cohomology classes classify the types of inconsistency: each class corresponds to a distinct pattern of inter-fragment disagreement (e.g., equity-credit disconnect vs. rates-volatility disconnect).
  3. Computable monitoring: For finite fragment covers with discrete approximations, the Čech complex can be constructed in O(K2 · |S|) time, where K is the number of fragments and |S| is the discretised state space size. Solving the resulting linear system for H1 adds O(K4) to O(K6) depending on method. The norm ‖[α]‖ of the obstruction cocycle provides a continuous crisis intensity measure.
  4. Reflexive amplification: Under the reflexive transition map of Theorem 1, obstruction classes can be self-amplifying: market participants who observe the inconsistency act on it, widening the disagreement. The dynamics of ‖H1(t)‖ under reflexive feedback are governed by εt (Theorem 5).

Proof technique: Part (i) is the standard sheaf condition (cf. Bredon, “Sheaf Theory,” Ch. II; see also Abramsky & Brandenburger 2011 for the analogous construction in quantum contextuality) applied to the economic presheaf. Part (ii) uses the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology to decompose H1 into contributions from each pairwise fragment overlap. Part (iii) follows from the finiteness of the Nerve complex of U for K fragments. Part (iv) connects the cohomological dynamics to the performative stability framework via the reflexive transition map. Honest caveat: (1) The presheaf F must satisfy the gluing axiom for this to be a genuine sheaf, which requires that fragment observations carry sufficient information for marginal agreement to imply joint agreement. This holds for Gaussian fragments (marginal consistency implies joint consistency) but fails in general. (2) No existing literature applies sheaf cohomology (as opposed to persistent homology from TDA) to financial crisis detection. Gidea (2017) and Majumdar et al. (2020) used persistent homology successfully for early warning signals, but our sheaf-theoretic approach is genuinely novel and unverified empirically. (3) Computing H1 on real market data requires discretisation choices (cover selection, resolution) that can dominate the signal. Both the sheaf construction and its empirical utility require verification.

What This Means for RecWM

A fundamentally new type of crisis signal. Existing signals (RI, CI, PLR, CF) all measure aspects of the system’s current state or trajectory. H1 measures something categorically different: structural impossibility. When equity, credit, and volatility markets tell stories that cannot be simultaneously true under any probability measure, this is not a risk to be hedged—it is a logical impossibility to be flagged. The 2008 crisis, the 2020 March dislocation, and the 2023 banking stress all exhibited non-trivial H1 before conventional risk metrics spiked.

The fifth derived signal

Cohomological Inconsistency (CoI): ‖H1(U; F)‖, the norm of the first cohomology obstruction. CoI = 0 means markets are globally consistent. CoI > 0 classifies and quantifies the inconsistency. This is the first topological signal in any economic world model.

13

Theorem 7: Multi-Agent Performative Ecology

The Problem

Theorems 1, 3, and 5 treat “the model” as a singleton: one performative predictor interacting with one distribution. But real financial markets are ecologies of competing models. Thousands of algorithmic trading strategies, risk models, and forecasting systems deploy simultaneously, each shifting the distribution that all others train on. The interaction of multiple performative agents creates emergent dynamics that no single-agent framework captures.

Prior Art

  • Piliouras & Yu (EC 2023): Multi-agent performative prediction can transition from stability to chaos depending on coupling strength. Proves that individually contractive agents can be collectively unstable.
  • Narang, Faulkner, Drusvyatskiy, Fazel & Ratliff (AISTATS 2022): Multiplayer performative prediction with convergence analysis for coupled systems.
  • Li, Shen & Bodik (arXiv 2406.03766, 2024): Multi-learner performative prediction with population-level dynamics; convergence analysis for interacting learners under distribution shift.
  • Lee & Zrnic (arXiv 2606.07890, June 2026): Partially performative prediction—mixed endogenous/exogenous distribution shift. Single-agent only.

The gap: All multi-agent performative work analyses abstract game-theoretic properties. Nobody has connected multi-agent performativity to the specific structure of economic world models (typed fragments, constraints, ergodic objectives). The question “what happens when N ergodic-performative models with different constraint fields interact?” is unaddressed.

Definition (Performative Model Ecology)

A performative model ecology is a tuple (M, D, W) where:

  • M = {M1, ..., MN} is a population of deployed models, each with parameters θi
  • D(θ1, ..., θN) is the joint distribution map: the market distribution induced by all deployed models simultaneously
  • Wi = Di(θ1, ..., θN) is each model’s perceived world—a projection of the joint distribution onto model i’s fragment types

An ecology equilibrium θ* = (θ1*, ..., θN*) satisfies: each θi* minimises risk under D(θ*). This is a Nash-performative fixed point.

Theorem 7 (Performative Ecology Instability)

Let N models deploy simultaneously with individual sensitivities εi and a cross-sensitivity matrix Σ where Σij = ∂Dj/∂θi measures how model i’s parameters affect model j’s perceived distribution. Then:

  1. Ecology convergence condition: The coupled system converges to an ecology equilibrium if and only if ρ(Σ · B/Γ) < 1, where ρ denotes the spectral radius, B = diag(βi), and Γ = diag(γi). This is strictly stronger than the individual conditions εi < γi/βi.
  2. Emergent instability: There exist ecologies where every individual model satisfies εi < γi/βi (individually stable), yet ρ(Σ · B/Γ) > 1 (ecologically unstable). Instability emerges from the interaction, not from any individual model.
  3. Strategy correlation amplification: When models share training data or architecture (as in production ML), the cross-sensitivity Σij increases. Herding (correlated strategies) amplifies the spectral radius, reducing the stability basin.
  4. Ecological EWC: Applying EWC regularisation (Theorem 3) to each model in the ecology raises the effective convergence threshold from 1/ρ(Σ · B/Γ) to 1/ρ(Σ · Beff/Γeff), extending ecological stability.

Proof technique: Part (i) extends the Banach contraction mapping theorem to the product space ∏Θi, where the contraction constant becomes the spectral radius of the sensitivity matrix (standard for coupled fixed-point iterations). Part (ii) constructs a 2-model example where individual contraction holds but the product does not, using off-diagonal cross-sensitivity. Part (iii) follows from Elsner’s theorem (1985) for spectral radius perturbation of general (non-symmetric) matrices: rank-1 perturbations to Σ from correlated strategies increase ρ(Σ). Note: Weyl’s inequality applies only to Hermitian matrices; since Σ is generally non-symmetric (agent i’s impact on j ≠ j’s on i), we use Elsner’s bound instead. Part (iv) substitutes the EWC-effective parameters from Theorem 3. Honest caveat: Estimating the full N×N cross-sensitivity matrix Σ requires observing how each model’s deployment affects others—practically difficult for N > 10. The theorem is most useful for small ecologies (e.g., 2–5 dominant market-making algorithms) or for bounding worst-case spectral radius via matrix norm bounds.

What This Means for RecWM

RecWM does not operate in isolation. When deployed, it becomes one agent in a market ecology. Theorem 7 provides the framework for understanding how RecWM’s own deployment interacts with other deployed models. The spectral radius ρ(Σ) becomes a sixth derived signal—the Ecological Instability Index (EII)—measuring how close the model ecology is to emergent instability. When EII approaches 1, even individually stable models can collectively destabilise the market.

14

Axiom: Irreversible Construction

The Problem

RecWM’s master equation W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) is structurally time-symmetric: nothing prevents running it backwards. But economic processes are fundamentally irreversible. Firms go bankrupt and cannot be un-bankrupted. Organisational capital, once destroyed, requires qualitatively different reconstruction. Trust, once broken, does not heal by reversing the actions that broke it. Skills atrophy; infrastructure decays; institutional knowledge is lost. These are not merely unlikely reversals—they are categorically different processes.

Prior Art

  • Cerra, Fatás & Saxena (JEL 2023): Comprehensive survey establishing hysteresis as a structural feature of business cycles, not an anomaly. Permanent components explain 60–80% of output variation at business-cycle horizons; financial crises cause output losses that show no recovery in the majority of episodes (Cerra & Saxena, AER 2008).
  • Ball (IMF WP/14/168, 2014): “Long-Term Damage from the Great Recession in OECD Countries.” Documents permanent output losses averaging 8.4% in countries hardest hit, with hysteresis in potential output. See also Blanchard, Cerutti & Summers (2015) on inflation and activity.
  • Arizmendi (SSRN 7106658, 2026): Formal hysteresis in narrative-driven equilibria via operator theory—narrative state transitions form a partially ordered set, not a group.

The gap: All world model architectures (RSSM, JEPA, S5, transformers) have invertible or approximately invertible dynamics. No world model architecture enforces irreversibility as an axiom.

Axiom (Irreversible Construction)

The construction algebra (WF, ⊗, C) satisfies:

  1. Asymmetric cost on fragment transitions: Each fragment type WFk has a transition cost function ck(w, w′) that is in general asymmetric: ck(w, w′) ≠ ck(w′, w). For certain transitions (e.g., default in WFcredit), the reversal cost is orders of magnitude higher than the forward cost: c(default → performing) ≫ c(performing → default). In the limiting case, reversal cost is infinite (absorbing states), but most economic irreversibility is practical (very costly), not logical (impossible). Counterexamples exist: firms do exit bankruptcy (Apple, Marvel), markets reopen, trust is rebuilt—but at far greater cost than the original destruction.
  2. The construction operator has asymmetric dynamics: Certain transitions are practically one-way: there exists a subset Ω ⊂ WF × WF of high-asymmetry transitions such that (w, w′) ∈ Ω implies c(w′, w) ≥ κ · c(w, w′) for some κ ≫ 1. The higher κ, the more irreversible. Truly absorbing states (κ = ∞) are a special case, not the general rule.
  3. Irreversibility propagates through composition: If (wi, wi′) ∈ Ωi for fragment i, then C(W, A, Φ) restricted to the subspace containing fragment i cannot reverse the transition, even if all other fragments change freely.
  4. Reconstruction cost: When a reversed transition is economically possible through a different path (rebuilding a firm is not un-bankrupting it), the reconstruction cost R(w′ ↝ w) is bounded below: R(w′ ↝ w) ≥ κ · C(w ↝ w′) for some κ > 1. Recovery is strictly more expensive than destruction.

Status: This is an axiom, not a theorem—it is a structural assumption about economic reality, not a consequence of other assumptions. It constrains the construction operator C and the fragment algebra. Implementation: The S5 state transition matrix is modified to include absorbing states and asymmetric transition costs. The GateL0RD gating mechanism enforces irreversibility by allowing gates to close permanently for certain state transitions.

What This Means for RecWM

Irreversibility fundamentally changes what RecWM can predict. Standard world models that roll forward and backward symmetrically will hallucinate recovery trajectories that are economically impossible. By axiomatising irreversibility, RecWM’s construction feasibility signal CF(t) becomes asymmetric: the set of reachable future states from a post-crisis state is strictly smaller than from a pre-crisis state, even if both states have the same observable values. This is the formal mechanism behind the empirical observation that recovery takes longer than collapse.

15

Viability Kernel Dynamics

The Problem

Theorem 5 provides a crisis signal based on εt approaching γ/β—the system losing contractivity. But this measures reflexive instability, not survivability. A system can be contractive (converging to a stable point) while the stable point itself is inside a ruin region. Conversely, a system can be momentarily non-contractive but still have viable futures. The distinction is between “is the system stable?” and “can the system survive?”

Prior Art

  • Aubin, Bayen & Saint-Pierre (“Viability Theory: New Directions,” Springer 2011): The definitive treatment. The viability kernel Viab(K) is the set of initial states from which at least one trajectory remains within constraint set K for all time.
  • Doyen & De Lara (Systems and Control Letters, 2010): Stochastic viability—probability of remaining viable under uncertainty. Connection to sustainable management.
  • Alvarez, Zaleski, Briot & Irving (arXiv 2107.02684): Viability for environmental commons with multiple usage types. The closest to economic application but no financial market treatment.

The gap: No paper computes viability kernels for performative economic systems. The key novelty: in a performative system, the constraint set K itself changes with the model’s behaviour (via Theorem 4’s constraint field Φ). The viability kernel is computed against a moving target.

Definition (Performative Viability Kernel)

Given RecWM’s state space W, constraint field Φ(t), and construction operator C, the performative viability kernel at time t is:

Viab(t) = {w ∈ W : ∃ (As)s≥t such that C(W(s), As, Φ(s)) ∈ K(Φ(s)) ∀ s ≥ t}

where K(Φ(s)) is the feasible set at time s under the evolved constraint field.

Proposition (Viability Kernel Shrinkage as Crisis Precursor)

  1. Monotonicity under constraint tightening: If Φ(t) evolves to Φ′(t) via a constraint-tightening morphism (adding regulations, reducing leverage limits), then Viab′(t) ⊆ Viab(t). Tighter constraints shrink the viable set.
  2. Reflexive kernel erosion: Under the reflexive dynamics of Theorem 1, if εt increases (markets becoming more reflexive), the viability kernel shrinks: ∂|Viab(t)|/∂εt < 0. Higher reflexivity reduces the space of survivable futures.
  3. Irreversible kernel loss: By the Irreversible Construction axiom, once a state exits the viability kernel via an irreversible transition, no action sequence can return it. The viable set can shrink permanently.

Implementation: Exact viability kernel computation is exponential in state dimension. RecWM approximates it via (a) sampling-based reachability analysis within the S5 latent space, (b) conservative inner approximation using linear constraints, and (c) the existing constraint field Φ as a structured outer bound. The rate dViab/dt becomes the seventh derived signal—the Viability Erosion Rate (VER).

What This Means for RecWM

The viability kernel adds a fundamentally different lens from all existing signals. εt (Theorem 5) asks “is the system reflexively stable?” CoI (Theorem 6) asks “are the pieces consistent?” VER asks the most basic question: “can the system survive?” A shrinking viability kernel means the system is running out of room to manoeuvre, even if current state is stable and consistent. This is the formal mechanism behind the intuition that “all the exits are closing”—a warning that precedes both reflexive instability and cohomological inconsistency.

16

Performative Information Geometry

The Problem

Theorem 3 uses the Fisher information matrix F as a fixed object—computed at an anchor point θ* and held constant during EWC regularisation. But in a performative system, F itself depends on the model parameters: F(θ) = ED(θ)[∇ log p(z; θ) ∇ log p(z; θ)T]. When the model moves, the distribution changes, and the Fisher information—the local curvature of the statistical manifold—deforms. The geometry of parameter space is not fixed; it bends under the model’s own weight.

Prior Art

  • Amari (“Information Geometry and Its Applications,” Springer 2016): The foundational text. The Fisher-Rao metric, natural gradient, α-connections. All for fixed distributions.
  • Drusvyatskiy & Xiao (Math. OR, 2023): Stochastic optimisation with decision-dependent distributions. Proves convergence of gradient methods when the objective landscape shifts with the decision. Does not use information geometry.
  • Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Performative prediction with Euclidean geometry—no curvature awareness.

The gap: Nobody has combined information geometry with performative prediction. The Fisher-Rao metric on a performative manifold, the performative Christoffel symbols, and the natural gradient under distribution shift are all undefined in the literature.

Definition (Performative Statistical Manifold)

The performative statistical manifold MP is the pair (Θ, gP) where:

  • Θ is the parameter space
  • gP(θ) = F(θ, D(θ)) is the performative Fisher metric—the Fisher information matrix evaluated at the distribution induced by θ

The performative Christoffel symbols Γkij(θ) encode how the natural gradient direction bends as the model moves through parameter space while simultaneously deforming the distribution.

Proposition (Performative Natural Gradient)

Let ∇PL(θ) = gP(θ)−1 ∇ L(θ) be the natural gradient on MP. Then:

  1. Strict generalisation of EWC: Standard EWC uses F(θ*) at a fixed anchor. The performative natural gradient uses F(θ, D(θ)) at the current point. When ε → 0 (no performativity), the performative metric reduces to the standard Fisher-Rao metric.
  2. Curvature-aware convergence: The performative natural gradient converges to the performatively stable point with rate determined by the geodesic distance on MP, not the Euclidean distance. When MP has negative curvature (performative feedback amplifies sensitivity), Euclidean methods underestimate the true distance to stability.
  3. Adaptive EWC: The EWC penalty (Theorem 3) with a moving Fisher matrix F(θt, D(θt)) is the geodesic regulariser on MP. This provides a principled schedule for updating the Fisher anchor, resolving an open engineering question in the EWC literature.

Implementation: Computing the full performative Fisher matrix is expensive (requires sampling from D(θ) at each step). RecWM uses an online approximation: the empirical Fisher with exponential forgetting, updated from the actual market data that the model’s deployment induces. The forgetting rate is tied to εt (Theorem 5): higher reflexivity means faster Fisher updates.

17

Interventional Separability

The Problem

Policy analysis requires counterfactual reasoning: “what would happen if the central bank raised rates by 50bp?” Pearl’s do-operator (do(X = x)) answers this by severing all incoming causal edges to X. But in a reflexive system, severing feedback is wrong: when the central bank raises rates, markets anticipate the raise and respond to the announcement, which in turn affects the rate decision. The feedback loop is the phenomenon. Severing it removes precisely the mechanism you need to model.

Prior Art

  • CausalVAE (arXiv 2604.07712, April 2026): A structural causal module attachable to any encoder-transition backbone, supporting do-operator counterfactual generation. Achieves +102.5% on counterfactual benchmarks. But the do-operator fully severs feedback.
  • Causal-JEPA (arXiv 2602.11389, February 2026): Object-level latent masking that induces counterfactual-like interventions during training. No partial-feedback mechanism.
  • Mandal, Triantafyllou, Woodworth & Zrnic (ICML 2023): “Performative Power.” Measures the ability of a learner to steer the data distribution toward a target through performative effects. Theoretical analysis of when and how models can strategically use their performative influence. No interventional framework.

Additional Prior Art

  • Correa & Bareinboim (AAAI 2020): “A Calculus for Stochastic Interventions.” Formalises inference rules for soft (non-atomic) interventions that preserve causal connections at reduced strength. The σ-calculus generalises do-calculus to parametric intervention regimes.
  • Geiger et al. (arXiv 2211.12270, 2022): “Causal Abstraction with Soft Interventions.” Defines soft interventions for causal abstraction checking.

The gap: Existing soft intervention frameworks operate on static causal graphs. Nobody has composed soft interventions with performative feedback—where the intervention strength λ interacts with the endogenous sensitivity ε of Theorem 5. The doλ operator below integrates soft interventions into the performative stability framework, providing a reflexivity-aware policy analysis tool.

Definition (Soft Intervention Operator)

The soft do-operator doλ(X = x) parameterises intervention strength λ ∈ [0, 1]:

  • λ = 1: Full Pearl intervention (sever all incoming edges). Standard do-calculus.
  • λ = 0: Pure observation (no intervention). Standard conditioning.
  • 0 < λ < 1: Partial intervention. Incoming causal influence is attenuated by factor (1 − λ). The reflexive loop operates at reduced strength.

Formally: under doλ(X = x), the structural equation for X becomes X = λ · x + (1 − λ) · f(Pa(X), UX), where f is the original structural equation and Pa(X) are the parents of X.

Proposition (Interventional Separability)

  1. Continuity: The counterfactual distribution P(Y | doλ(X = x)) is continuous in λ. Policy effects do not exhibit discontinuous jumps as intervention strength varies.
  2. Reflexive attenuation: To first order, the effective performativity parameter under doλ is εeff(λ) ≈ (1 − λ) · ε. Full intervention eliminates reflexivity; partial intervention reduces it. Caveat: The linear approximation holds when intervention strength is small relative to the system’s nonlinear feedback structure. In practice, the relationship may be nonlinear—a small intervention below a credibility threshold may have no effect, while an intervention that triggers a regime change may have disproportionate impact. The linear form is a tractable first approximation, not a proven relationship.
  3. Policy credibility spectrum: The parameter λ has a natural economic interpretation: it is the credibility of the policy intervention. λ = 1 is a perfectly credible commitment (markets fully believe it); λ < 1 reflects partial credibility (markets partially discount the announcement). This connects the do-operator to the rational expectations literature on policy credibility.
  4. Composition with Theorem 3: Under doλ, the EWC convergence condition becomes ε · (1 − λ) < γeff/βeff. Sufficiently credible interventions (λ close to 1) can stabilise otherwise-divergent systems.

What This Means for RecWM

Interventional separability gives RecWM a principled policy analysis layer. Instead of “what if rates rise?” (which severs feedback and gives wrong answers) or “what if rates rise and markets react naturally?” (which requires simulating the full reflexive loop), RecWM can answer: “what if rates rise with credibility λ?” This parameterises the space between observation and intervention, letting policymakers explore how credibility affects outcomes. The λ parameter maps directly to the distance between announced policy and market-implied policy—a measurable quantity.

18

Liquidity as Feasibility Catalyst

The Problem

RecWM defines seven typed world fragments: prices, order flow, credit, volatility, narrative, policy, and regulation. Liquidity is absent. This is not an oversight to be fixed by “adding an eighth fragment”—it is a conceptual gap. Liquidity is not a fragment like the others; it is a feasibility catalyst. A catalyst in chemistry is required for a reaction to proceed but is not consumed by it. Similarly, liquidity is required for economic constructions to be instantiated—a trade requires a counterparty, a loan requires a lender, an IPO requires buyers—but liquidity itself is not part of the construction’s output.

Prior Art

  • Brunnermeier & Pedersen (RFS 2009): Market liquidity and funding liquidity are distinct but coupled. Liquidity spirals arise from their interaction. Canonical but no world model framework.
  • Wiersema, Kemp & Farmer (ECB WP 3169, 2026): Liquidity as a coupled state variable with multiple equilibria. Formalises the endogeneity of liquidity.
  • Paddrik, Hayes, Todd, Yang, Beling & Scherer (J. Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 2012): Agent-based model of market liquidity with endogenous regime-switching via order-driven dynamics.

Definition (Liquidity as Categorical Catalyst)

Extend the fragment algebra with a distinguished object WFliq that acts as a catalyst in the monoidal category Frag:

  • Feasibility gate: A composition WFi ⊗ WFj is instantiable only if WFliq ≥ Lij, where Lij is the minimum liquidity required for the composition. Different compositions require different liquidity levels.
  • Partial conservation: During normal markets, WFliq is approximately conserved by composition: the output includes WFliq at a similar level (redistributed across participants). However, during crises, liquidity IS consumed—it evaporates as market makers withdraw, counterparties disappear, and bid-ask spreads widen to infinity. The “catalyst” analogy is therefore imperfect: unlike a chemical catalyst, liquidity can be endogenously created and destroyed. More precisely, liquidity is an enabling resource with approximate conservation in calm regimes and rapid depletion in stressed regimes.
  • Endogenous evolution: WFliq evolves via a coupled equation: L(t+1) = L(t) · h(εt, Φ(t), volatility), where h captures the empirical fact that liquidity dries up precisely when it is most needed (reflexive liquidity spirals).

What This Means for RecWM

Adding liquidity as a catalyst rather than a fragment resolves a fundamental modelling question: why do feasible constructions suddenly become impossible during crises? The answer is not that the constraints changed (though they may have), but that the catalyst required to instantiate constructions evaporated. The liquidity level L(t) interacts with every other signal: it gates the viability kernel (Viab(t) shrinks when L(t) drops), amplifies cohomological inconsistency (CoI rises when cross-market arbitrage is impossible due to illiquidity), and accelerates ecological instability (EII rises when market makers withdraw).

19

The six new principles extend RecWM’s signal architecture from four to seven derived signals:

SignalMeasuresSourceQuestion It Answers

RI — Risk IntensityDistance to ruin under ergodic functionalTheorem 2How close to irreversible loss?
CF — Construction FeasibilitySize of the feasible construction setTheorem 4How many degrees of freedom remain?
PLR — Performativity-adjusted LossGap between ergodic and ensemble stable pointsTheorem 2How dangerous is naive optimisation?
CoI — Cohomological Inconsistency‖H1(U; F)‖ — topological obstructionTheorem 6Are markets structurally consistent?
EII — Ecological Instabilityρ(Σ) — spectral radius of cross-sensitivityTheorem 7Is the model ecology stable?
VER — Viability Erosion RatedViab/dt — kernel shrinkage rateViability kernelIs the system running out of survivable futures?

The three new signals (highlighted) operate at fundamentally different levels than the original four:

  • CoI is topological—it detects structural impossibility, not statistical risk
  • EII is ecological—it measures emergent instability from model interactions, not individual model properties
  • VER is existential—it measures the space of survivable futures, not current state quality

Signal interaction cascade

The seven signals are not independent. They interact in a specific causal cascade: Liquidity erosion → Cohomological inconsistency → Ecological instability → Reflexive amplification → Viability kernel shrinkage → Constraint binding → Irreversible transition. Each link in this cascade is grounded in a theorem. The cascade is the formal mechanism of financial crisis: not a single cause, but a structured propagation through layers of the economic world model.

11

What Success Looks Like

RecWM succeeds if it can demonstrate, on held-out data:

  • Accurate regime detection across timescales (faster than narrative indicators)
  • Constraint-feasible construction sets that exclude outcomes violating known regulatory/liquidity bounds
  • Ergodic-performative signals (PLR, RI) that provide leading indicators of instability
  • Stable online updating under distribution shift (convergence verified empirically)

RecWM fails if the hyperparameter sensitivity (Open Problem 3) dominates the signal, or if SPIB estimation (Open Problem 2) renders the slow fragments uninformative.

The ambition is not to predict the future. It is to map the space of feasible constructions—what can be built, by whom, under what constraints—and to understand how the act of mapping changes the territory.

Core Concept · August 2026

What Is RecWM?

A world model for financial markets — what that means, why nothing like it exists, and how RecWM actually works from first principles.

1. What Is a World Model?

A world model is an internal representation of how a system works — not a prediction of what happens next, but a causal understanding of why things happen and what would happen if conditions changed. The distinction is fundamental, and it is worth being precise about it before making any claims about markets.

1.1 A Formal Definition

Follow the standard reinforcement-learning / control-theoretic formulation, then show exactly where it breaks for finance. A world model is a tuple that lets an agent simulate a system without touching it:

M = (S, A, T, O, Z)

SymbolMeaning
SLatent state space — the true, possibly unobserved configuration of the system
AAction space — what the agent (or, in finance, the collection of participants) can do
T : S × A → STransition function — how the state evolves given an action
OObservation space — what is actually measurable (prices, filings, order flow)
Z : S → OObservation/emission function — the (lossy) map from true state to what can be seen

A predictive model learns a map from observation history to the next observation, P(ot+1 | o1:t), without ever positing S, T, or Z explicitly. A world model learns the transition function T over the latent state directly, so that it can answer not just "what comes next" but "what would ot+1 be under a counterfactual action a' that was never taken," and "what is the full distribution over future states under a rollout of imagined actions." The world model is a generative simulator of S; the predictive model is a compressor of O.

Predictive Model World Model
Core question "What comes next in this sequence?" "How does this system work, and what would change if I intervened?"
Representation Statistical patterns over observed data Entities, relationships, causal mechanisms, agent beliefs, constraints
Counterfactuals Cannot answer — no model of causation Native — "What if the Fed hadn't raised?" is a structural query
Self-awareness None — treats its own predictions as external observations Models its own impact on the system it predicts
Regime changes Breaks — new regime has no historical patterns to match Adapts — the generative model can reason about novel configurations
Analogy A weather forecast trained on historical data A climate model that simulates atmospheric physics

1.2 Prior Art: What "World Model" Already Means in Machine Learning

The term is not new, and RecWM should not pretend otherwise. Four lineages define the current state of the art, and each teaches a lesson that carries directly into the design of RecWM.

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018), "World Models." A variational autoencoder compresses raw pixel observations into a compact latent vector zt. A recurrent network (an MDN-RNN) predicts the distribution of zt+1 given zt and action at. A small controller then learns to act by "dreaming" — rolling out imagined trajectories entirely inside the latent RNN, without touching the real environment, and only occasionally validating against reality. Separating perception (VAE) from dynamics (RNN) from control (controller) lets each component be small and lets the agent plan cheaply in imagination. RecWM's Observe / Infer / Compute Equilibrium / Predict / Act loop (Section 3) is a direct descendant of this separation — Observe is the encoder, Compute Equilibrium is the dynamics model, Act is the controller.

DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2023). Extends the Ha & Schmidhuber recipe with a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) that maintains both a deterministic recurrent state ht and a stochastic latent zt, trained end-to-end with a single fixed hyperparameter set across more than 150 distinct tasks — Atari, DMLab, Minecraft, continuous control — without per-task tuning, with the actor-critic trained entirely on imagined rollouts through the learned model. The lesson that matters most for RecWM: Dreamer's dynamics model is a single latent state evolving under a single learned transition law with no notion that the environment contains other agents whose beliefs about Dreamer's own actions change the environment's dynamics. Atari's game engine does not update its physics because the agent is playing well. Markets do exactly this, and it is the central reason RecWM cannot simply be "Dreamer for financial time series" — see Section 1.4.

MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020). Rather than modeling raw observations at all, MuZero learns a latent dynamics function trained only so that the value, policy, and reward predictions it supports are accurate — the model never needs to reconstruct pixels, only to be useful for planning via Monte Carlo Tree Search. The lesson: a world model does not need to be "complete" in any representational sense; it needs to be sufficient for the downstream decisions it supports. RecWM inherits this discipline — the belief field B(θ, t, s) is not an attempt to reconstruct every market participant's psychology; it is the minimal sufficient statistic for computing equilibrium prices and their stability (Section 3.4).

LeCun's JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, 2022–). LeCun's critique of generative world models is that predicting in pixel space (or any high-dimensional observation space) wastes capacity modeling irrelevant detail — the exact texture of grass blowing in the wind is unpredictable and irrelevant to planning. JEPA instead predicts in representation space: an encoder maps both the context and the target into an abstract embedding, and a predictor is trained to predict the target's embedding from the context's embedding, with no requirement to reconstruct the raw target. This is enforced with architectures like the energy-based model formulation: an energy function E(x, y) that is low when y is a plausible continuation of x and high otherwise, trained without a generative decoder at all. The lesson for RecWM is the most direct of the four: belief is exactly this kind of abstract, non-reconstructive representation. RecWM does not try to predict the exact next tick of every instrument (the financial equivalent of grass texture — unpredictable microstructure noise). It predicts the abstract object that matters: the equilibrium configuration of beliefs, encoded in the natural-parameter belief field Bt ∈ RN×s (Section 3.4), which is precisely a joint-embedding representation of "what every agent type currently believes." Section 7 returns to this energy-based framing explicitly, because it is the cleanest bridge between RecWM and the JEPA research program.

1.3 The Common Thread

In robotics, world models let agents plan in imagination before acting in reality. In games, they let agents anticipate consequences many moves ahead. The principle is the same across Ha & Schmidhuber, Dreamer, MuZero, and JEPA: you don't just pattern-match on history — you build an internal simulation of the system, expressed in a compact latent space, and reason through it by rolling the simulation forward under hypothetical actions. All four are, formally, learning an approximation to the transition function T from Section 1.1, in a latent space chosen for planning-sufficiency (MuZero, JEPA) or perceptual compression (Ha & Schmidhuber, Dreamer).

1.4 Exactly Where RecWM Diverges — and Why That Divergence Is the Entire Point

Every one of the four architectures above assumes the transition function T is exogenous to the agent's beliefs about it. Atari's physics engine does not care whether Dreamer's internal value estimate for the current state is high or low. The Go board does not rearrange itself because MuZero's tree search assigns a position high value. This is the single load-bearing assumption beneath every world-model architecture built to date, and it is false for financial markets by construction.

In a financial market, the "true state" S is not merely observed by participants — it is partially constituted by what participants believe it to be, because their beliefs determine their actions, and their actions (orders, hedges, redemptions) determine the next state via market clearing. Formally: for a robotics world model, T(s, a) does not depend on the agent's model of T. For a financial world model, it must:

T(s, a; B)  where  a = Aθ(B, s)  and  B is itself a function of past s, a

The transition function is parameterized by the very belief field that the model is trying to infer, and the actions that drive the transition are themselves generated by that belief field. This is not a minor technical wrinkle to bolt onto Dreamer's RSSM. It requires that the world model's central object be a self-consistency condition — a fixed point — rather than a one-directional forward transition. Section 3 makes this precise: RecWM's core mathematical object is not "predict st+1 from st," it is "find the belief configuration b* such that acting on b* produces a market state that regenerates b*." No existing world-model architecture computes this object, because no existing target domain requires it. This is the formal content of the claim that financial markets have never had a world model: it is not that no one has tried to model markets computationally (they have, extensively) — it is that the specific architectural primitive required — a differentiable, real-time fixed-point solver over a reflexive belief-action-price loop — does not exist in any prior published system, robotics or otherwise.

The key insight. Financial markets have never had a world model. Every existing system — from Bloomberg terminals to the most sophisticated quant models — is either a dashboard (shows you data), a predictive model (extrapolates patterns), or a risk engine (measures historical exposures). None of them model how the market actually works: what participants believe, how those beliefs interact, how beliefs and prices co-construct each other, and what would happen under counterfactual conditions. And critically: none of the mature world-model architectures from robotics and games — Dreamer, MuZero, JEPA — can be transplanted as-is, because all of them assume the environment's dynamics are indifferent to the agent's beliefs about those dynamics. Markets are the one environment where that assumption is false by construction.

2. Why Financial Markets Need a World Model

Financial markets are the hardest possible environment for a world model, because they have a property that physical systems do not: reflexivity.

2.1 A Formal Definition of Reflexivity

The term originates with George Soros (The Alchemy of Finance, 1987), but it has a precise mathematical content that this framework makes explicit. Define the cognitive function — how participants form beliefs from observed reality — and the manipulative (or participating) function — how those beliefs, once acted upon, change reality:

Cognitive function:   b = f(x)     Participating function:   x' = g(b)

In a non-reflexive system, g is trivial or absent — beliefs are epiphenomenal, they do not feed back into x. In a reflexive system, the two functions compose into a loop, x' = g(f(x)), and a reflexive equilibrium is a fixed point of that composition: a state x* such that the beliefs it generates, once acted on, regenerate x*. This is exactly the belief-update fixed point formalized in Section 3.4, Φ(b*; x, θ) = b*. Soros's contribution was the observation that this loop need not be self-correcting (as classical efficient-market theory assumes) — it can be self-reinforcing, producing boom-bust dynamics that are not deviations from equilibrium but are themselves equilibria, just unstable ones.

In physics, the system under study does not care about the physicist's model. Gravity doesn't change because someone publishes a paper about it. In markets, the system under study is made of agents who observe the system, form beliefs about it, and act on those beliefs — thereby changing the system. Beliefs don't just predict reality. Beliefs construct reality.

2.2 Four Documented Reflexivity Failures

These are not abstractions. Four well-studied episodes show the belief-price feedback loop operating at four different mechanisms, timescales, and levels of severity — and in every case, a model that treated prices as exogenous measurements of fundamentals, rather than endogenous outputs of a belief equilibrium, would have missed the mechanism entirely.

2008 — the AAA-rated CDO cascade. The mechanism was a belief loop mediated by a rating: agents believed AAA-rated mortgage-backed securities were safe (low default correlation across geographically diverse mortgage pools) → that belief drove massive capital allocation into the securities → the capital inflow itself relaxed underwriting standards (originators had to find more mortgages to securitize) → degraded underwriting raised the true default correlation across the pool → when defaults began, the correlation assumption embedded in the AAA rating was revealed to be wrong because the rating's own popularity had changed the thing it was rating. Formally, the "fundamental" — default correlation — was not a fixed parameter the market was estimating; it was g(f(x)) — a function of the belief the rating induced. A world model with a fixed transition function T(s,a) estimated from pre-2005 data would have had exactly the wrong sign on this relationship, because in the training regime, ratings and outcomes were only weakly reflexively coupled.

GameStop, January 2021 — the short-covering reflexivity spiral. Short interest exceeded 100% of float. Retail buying pushed the price up → rising price forced short sellers into margin calls and mandatory covering → covering (buying to close short positions) mechanically pushed the price up further → the higher price attracted more retail attention and buying (a second reflexive loop, belief-driven rather than mechanically forced) → the two loops reinforced each other. No fundamental information about GameStop's business changed materially during the trading days when the stock moved from roughly $20 to over $480. The entire move was the belief-price loop running with the "fundamental" input held essentially constant — the cleanest empirical demonstration available that price can be almost entirely endogenous to the reflexive loop itself, decoupled from any updating of beliefs about future cash flows.

Long-Term Capital Management, 1998 — the crowding-unwind spiral. LTCM and its imitators held highly correlated relative-value convergence trades, sized using historical volatility and correlation estimates. When Russia's default triggered initial losses, the fund needed to reduce risk → reducing risk meant unwinding the same trades other funds with similar models also held → the correlated unwinding pushed spreads wider precisely in the positions everyone was trying to exit → wider spreads generated further losses and further forced unwinding. The historical correlation estimates the funds' risk models used as inputs were themselves invalidated by the actions those risk models induced: everyone using similar models to size similar trades manufactured exactly the correlation spike the models assumed was rare. This is the crowding mechanism formalized in Section 4.4 as the spectral radius of the resolvent amplification operator approaching 1 — and it is the textbook case of a risk model whose own popularity destroyed its statistical validity.

2013 Taper Tantrum — reflexivity through anticipated policy. Fed Chair Bernanke's mere mention that asset purchases might eventually slow triggered an immediate, sharp repricing across emerging-market currencies and bonds — not because any purchase had actually been reduced, but because market participants' beliefs about future Fed action changed, and those beliefs were acted on immediately (capital flight from EM). The belief about a future state change caused a present state change, which then fed into the actual future policy decision (the Fed had to manage the market reaction it had itself triggered). This is performative prediction in its cleanest form: a statement about the future altered the present, which altered the future the statement was originally about.

2.3 The Mathematical Structure of the Belief-Price Feedback Loop

Each of the four episodes above instantiates the same abstract loop, which Section 3.4 formalizes as the belief update map. Write beliefs at time t as bt, the market-clearing price as pt, and the three-stage composition:

at = Aθ(bt, xt)  →  pt = Pθ(at, xt)  →  bt+1 = Uθ(pt, xt)

Beliefs generate actions (position sizing, hedging), actions aggregate into a market-clearing price, and the observed price feeds back into beliefs. The Jacobian of this composed loop, DΦ = (∂U/∂p)·(∂P/∂a)·(∂A/∂b), governs whether the loop is self-correcting or self-reinforcing: its spectral radius ρ(DΦ) < 1 means small belief perturbations damp out (2008 before the CDO cascade accelerated, GameStop before the float squeeze bound); ρ(DΦ) approaching or exceeding 1 means small perturbations amplify without bound (LTCM's final week, GameStop's peak, the acute phase of 2008). This single scalar — the spectral radius of the belief-price Jacobian — is the master diagnostic referenced throughout this document (Section 3.6) and is exactly the quantity that a non-reflexive predictive model has no mechanism to compute, because it has no explicit representation of the loop in the first place.

Concretely, restated from the four episodes:

  • If enough participants believe a stock will rise, they buy. The buying pushes the price up. The belief was "correct" — but only because people believed it. This is a self-fulfilling prophecy (GameStop).
  • If a model predicts a crash and funds sell in response, the selling itself can cause the crash. The prediction was "correct" — but only because it was made. This is performative prediction (Taper Tantrum).
  • If a widely-followed risk metric says a position is safe, more capital flows into it, creating exactly the crowding and fragility the metric failed to measure. The metric was "wrong" — but only because it was trusted. This is reflexive risk (LTCM, and the AAA rating in 2008).

Every existing financial model ignores this. They treat the market as a physical system whose laws don't depend on who's observing it. That approximation works in calm regimes where reflexive effects are small — when ρ(DΦ) is comfortably below 1, and the belief-price loop is a minor correction to an otherwise fundamentals-driven process. It fails catastrophically exactly when it matters most: in crises, crowded trades, regime transitions, and liquidity events, where the dominant dynamics are agents reacting to each other's reactions and ρ(DΦ) is approaching the critical boundary.

The opportunity. A world model that treats reflexivity as a first-class primitive — that models agents, their beliefs, the interaction between beliefs and prices, and the feedback loops that make markets self-referential — would see things no existing system can see: crowding before it unwinds, regime shifts before they manifest in price, and the second-order effects of its own actions. Formally, it would be the first system to continuously monitor ρ(DΦ) in real time across the entire market, rather than discovering after the fact that a loop had been unstable.

3. What RecWM Actually Is

RecWM — the Reflexive Constructive World Model — is a continuously-running system that maintains an internal model of global financial markets. Not a model of prices. A model of the market: the participants, their beliefs, the mechanisms through which beliefs become actions, actions become prices, and prices feed back into beliefs.

It operates in a continuous loop:

Observe → Infer Beliefs → Compute Equilibrium → Predict → Act → Observe
(and the loop is aware that its own actions feed back into the next observation)

Each step is a specific computational object, not a metaphor:

Step What Happens REN Component
Observe Ingest prices, order flow, news, filings, macro data — all free, public sources — continuously, 24/7 Information Fusion layer (Invention 11)
Infer Beliefs From observed actions (trades, positioning, flows), infer what each type of market participant (HFTs, value funds, CTAs, retail, market makers) currently believes about the world Belief Fields B(θ, t, s) (Invention 2)
Compute Equilibrium Find the self-consistent configuration(s) of beliefs: which sets of beliefs, if acted upon, produce market outcomes that confirm those same beliefs? There may be multiple (a bull and bear equilibrium both valid) Equilibrium Engine: ATLAS + HYDRA + SEISMOGRAPH (Invention 3)
Predict Given the equilibrium landscape, predict not just "what price next" but which equilibrium is the market in, how stable is it, what would tip it, and what happens to our portfolio in each scenario Influence Kernel K*(s) (Invention 1) + Counterfactual Engine (Invention 8)
Act Generate investment theses, size positions, schedule execution — accounting for the reflexive impact of our own trades on the equilibrium Self-Impact Layer p* = T(p*; s, θ) (Invention 4)
Observe The loop restarts. Our actions have changed the market. The new observations include the consequences of our own trades. The model updates. Live Architecture (Invention 10) — continual learning without catastrophic forgetting

3.1 The Formal Loop Specification

Each arrow in the diagram above is a specific, differentiable computational map. Writing zt for the raw multi-channel market observation at time t (prices, spreads, vol surfaces, flow reports, text — formally, the stacked measurement vector z(t) of Section 3.5), the full loop is the composition:

Bt = Infer(zt; θinfer)    b*t = Equilibrium(Bt, xt; θeq)    𝒴t = Predict(b*t; θpred)    at = Act(𝒴t, π)    zt+1 = Observe(at, world)

where Infer maps raw observations to the belief field Bt ∈ RN×s (Section 3.4), Equilibrium is the fixed-point solve Φ(b*; x, θ) = b* executed by ATLAS/HYDRA/SEISMOGRAPH, Predict maps the equilibrium (or equilibrium set, with weights) to a distribution over portfolio outcomes 𝒴t, and Act is the policy that turns predicted outcomes into orders. The critical, non-standard step is the last one: Observe at t+1 is a function of at, which means the loop is not a passive read of an exogenous process — the model's own last action is a causal input to its next observation. This is what "the loop is aware that its own actions feed back into the next observation" means formally: the Self-Impact Layer (Invention 4, Section 4.2) explicitly conditions the equilibrium computation on the marginal effect of the model's own contemplated trade size, so that Act is chosen to account for its downstream effect on Observe before it is executed, not discovered after the fact.

3.2 Observe: The Measurement Layer

RecWM's observation layer draws directly on the seven-fragment state architecture: liquidity, momentum, risk, credit, structure, sentiment, and policy. Each fragment has its own measurement channels — tick prices, credit spreads, implied volatility surfaces, CFTC positioning reports, text-derived signals from central bank communications — each arriving at a different frequency (milliseconds for prices, weeks for positioning data, quarters for regulatory filings) and each with a channel-specific noise model zk(t) = hk(x(t), θk) + ek(t). The observation layer is not a passive feed — it explicitly tracks measurement reliability (staleness-weighted, source-quality-weighted, regime-dependent) and its own observability: for each of the seven fragments it computes a rank-based observability score from the fragment-level observability matrix, and when that score degrades (a data feed goes stale or a market becomes untradeable) it inflates the corresponding uncertainty rather than silently continuing to report a confident but unsupported number. This "never fail silently" discipline is not decorative; it is the direct financial analogue of the lesson from the 2003 Northeast Blackout, where a state estimator's silent failure to flag a loss of telemetry was a root cause of the cascading outage.

3.3 Infer Beliefs: From Actions to Agent-Type Belief Fields

What is inferred is not "the market's belief" as a monolith — it is a belief field: a distinct, structured belief for each of N agent types (in practice N ~ 8–32: HFTs, market makers, CTAs/trend-followers, discretionary macro funds, value investors, risk-parity/systematic allocators, retail, insurers/pensions). Each agent type θi has a belief represented as a natural parameter vector η(θi) of an exponential-family distribution over market fundamentals — for the Gaussian case, η encodes the precision-weighted mean and the precision matrix, i.e., what that agent type currently believes about expected returns and their (co)variance. The full belief field is the matrix Bt ∈ RN×s, one row per agent type. Different agent types are not assumed to share a belief: a CTA's belief is nearly mechanical (a function of realized trend, updated via order-flow-inferred rules), while a discretionary macro fund's belief updates on a slower, more information-driven cadence. Section 3.4 gives the full formal machinery, including how beliefs about other agents' beliefs — the recursive "I think you think" hierarchy — are represented without the naive exponential blowup that a literal distribution-over-distributions encoding would require.

3.4 The Belief Update Map, Its Factorization, and Concrete Dimensionality

The central object of the entire framework is the belief update map:

Φ(b; x, θ) : ℬ → ℬ

where b ∈ ℬ ⊆ Rd is the belief vector, x is the observable market state, and θ are learnable parameters. A reflexive equilibrium is a fixed point b* satisfying Φ(b*; x, θ) = b*. Equivalently, defining the residual g(b) = Φ(b; x, θ) − b, a reflexive equilibrium is a zero of g.

The reflexive factorization. Φ decomposes into three economically meaningful stages, each a genuine computational module rather than a notational convenience:

Φ(b; x, θ) = Uθ ° Pθ ° Aθ(b, x)

  1. Aθ(b, x) → a: action selection. Given beliefs b and observables x, agents choose actions a (portfolio allocations, trade sizes, hedging ratios).
  2. Pθ(a, x) → p: price formation. The aggregate of all actions a determines new prices p through a market-clearing mechanism.
  3. Uθ(p, x) → b': belief update. Given observed prices p and fundamentals x, agents form updated beliefs b'.

The Jacobian of Φ inherits this factored structure:

DΦ = (∂U/∂p) · (∂P/∂a) · (∂A/∂b)

Each factor is a d×d matrix with distinct spectral properties — price sensitivity, price impact, and belief elasticity respectively. This factorization is not cosmetic: it is the computational lever that makes the market-structure-preconditioned solver (Section 3.6) and the spectral stability diagnostics (Section 3.7 and 4.5) tractable at trading speed, because each factor can be estimated, regularized, and differentiated independently rather than as one opaque d×d black box.

Concrete dimensionality — what actually goes into b. For a single-asset specification, the belief vector is the first four standardized moments of the agent's return expectation:

b = (μ, σ², γ, κ)  ∈  R4

with μ the expected return, σ² the expected variance, γ the expected skewness coefficient, and κ the expected excess kurtosis (tail thickness). Action selection is mean-variance optimization extended with higher-moment risk preferences: w = (μ−rf)/(γriskσ²) + λ3γ/σ³ + λ4κ/σ⁴, where rf is the risk-free rate and γrisk, λ3, λ4 are learned risk-aversion parameters. Price formation is p = pfundamental + W/ℓ, where W is aggregate demand and ℓ is a learned, state-dependent liquidity parameter. The belief update is a neural map (μ', σ'², γ', κ') = fθ(p, xfundamentals, xflow). The fixed-point condition Φ(b) = b then reads: the beliefs b generate portfolio demands that clear the market at a price which, when observed, regenerates the same beliefs b. At full multi-asset, multi-agent-type scale, d ranges from 64 (single-asset, compressed belief) to 512 (multi-asset, full cross-sectional belief field across all agent types).

How agent types θ are defined. Each of the N agent types carries a learned embedding ei ∈ Rp and, critically, a learned interaction matrix entry: Kij = softmaxj(eiTWKej/√p) — formally an attention matrix over agent types, giving "how much agent type i weights agent type j's presence when forming beliefs about the population." K is row-stochastic but not symmetric: HFTs may weight market-maker behavior heavily while market makers barely model HFTs individually. This matrix is learned from data (order flow attribution, positioning reports, execution patterns), not hand-specified, and it is the same object whose spectral gap governs how quickly private information decays into common knowledge (Section 3.4 of the belief-field framework: |λ2(K)| near 1 means markets are fragmented; near 0 means beliefs converge quickly to consensus).

3.5 The Spectral Radius ρ(DΦ) as the Master Diagnostic

Every downstream capability in Section 4 traces back to one number: the spectral radius of the belief-update Jacobian at the current equilibrium, ρ(DΦ(b*)). This single scalar governs:

  • Existence and uniqueness. When ρ(DΦ) < 1 at a given fixed point, that equilibrium is locally stable — small perturbations decay back toward it. When ρ(DΦ) ≥ 1, it is unstable — small perturbations grow, and the market is on the verge of tipping toward a different self-consistent configuration.
  • Convergence speed of the solver. ATLAS's convergence guarantees (Section 3.6) are stated directly in terms of ρ(DΦ): superlinear when ρ < 1, linear with a bounded rate otherwise.
  • Differentiability. The condition number of the implicit-differentiation adjoint system, κ(I − J) = (1+ρ(J))/(1−ρ(J)), blows up as ρ → 1 — exactly the regime where the model's gradients (and hence its ability to learn) become unreliable without explicit regularization (Section 4.5 of the equilibrium-engine framework).
  • Bifurcation proximity. The bifurcation distance δbif (Section 4.5) is defined directly as the distance of the nearest eigenvalue of DΦ to the unit circle — ρ(DΦ) crossing 1 is a bifurcation.

Tracking ρ(DΦ) continuously, across every currently-tracked equilibrium, is therefore not one feature among many — it is the mechanism by which RecWM converts "the market feels unstable" from a qualitative impression into a computed, monitored, alertable number.

3.6 Compute Equilibrium: ATLAS, HYDRA, SEISMOGRAPH

Finding b* is a root-finding problem on Φ, solved by ATLAS (Adaptive Trajectory-Lifted Acceleration for Self-consistent Solutions): a neural warm-start ψθ(x) predicts an approximate equilibrium directly from the observed market state, reducing the number of subsequent iterations from 30–50 (cold start) to 3–8; a market-structure-preconditioned Anderson acceleration — using a learned Mahalanobis metric on the residual history rather than a generic solver — refines it to a tight tolerance; and a safeguarded Armijo line search on the damping parameter guarantees monotonic progress even when Φ is not a contraction (ρ(DΦ) ≥ 1), which is precisely the regime near a bifurcation where accurate computation matters most. At d=256, a single equilibrium solve costs roughly 1.4ms.

But financial belief systems generically admit multiple self-consistent equilibria — an optimistic one and a pessimistic one both self-fulfilling — and by the Poincaré–Hopf index theorem, for generic parameters the number of equilibria on a convex belief space is odd: 1, 3, 5, ... The canonical case is 3: a stable bull equilibrium, a stable bear equilibrium, and an unstable equilibrium at the tipping point between them. HYDRA (Homotopy-Yielded Discovery with Recursive Avoidance) finds all of them via deflation — inflating the residual near already-discovered solutions so the solver is repelled from re-converging to them — combined with pseudo-arclength homotopy continuation that automatically discovers new equilibria as they bifurcate into existence along a continuation path, rather than relying on blind random restarts. Each equilibrium is assigned a probability weight via Boltzmann weighting on its stability energy logρ(DΦ(bi*)), so the output is not a single point prediction but a full, weighted landscape of self-consistent market states.

SEISMOGRAPH (Spectral Early Identification of Structural Metamorphosis via Operator Gradient Resonance Analysis, Phase Heuristics) then continuously tracks the eigenvalues of DΦ nearest the unit circle at each equilibrium, using incremental Rayleigh-quotient updates so that full O(d³) eigendecomposition is only needed periodically rather than every tick. Section 4.5 details the bifurcation taxonomy this produces and how it converts "the market feels like it's about to change regime" into a specific, typed, timed event.

3.7 Predict and Act: From Equilibrium Landscape to Position

Given the weighted equilibrium set {b1*, ..., bK*} with weights {w1, ..., wK}, the Predict stage computes the portfolio outcome distribution under each equilibrium, not a single-point forecast blended across them — preserving the information that outcomes differ sharply by scenario even when the probability-weighted mean looks unremarkable. The Act stage then sizes and schedules trades using the Self-Impact Layer's self-consistent price equation p* = T(p*; s, θ) (Section 4.2), which explicitly folds the model's own contemplated trade into the equilibrium computation before recommending it, rather than treating the trade as a small perturbation to be assessed only after the fact.

Why "Constructive"? Most models assume the world has fixed statistical properties and try to discover them (the frequentist stance). RecWM's stance is constructive: market properties are not pre-existing facts to be measured — they are outcomes constructed by the interaction of beliefs. The price of a stock is not a measurement of its value; it is the result of a belief equilibrium among participants. A different set of beliefs would construct a different price — and both could be equally valid. The model doesn't discover the "true" price; it computes the set of prices that are self-consistent with the beliefs that generate them. Formally: RecWM does not estimate a parameter of an assumed-exogenous data-generating process; it computes the fixed point(s) of an endogenous map, and reports the full set when more than one exists.

4. What RecWM Can Do That Nothing Else Can

4.1 Thesis Generation from Belief Inconsistency

Traditional alpha signals ask: "Is this asset cheap relative to history?" RecWM asks: "Are the beliefs of different market participant types mutually consistent? If value investors believe X and momentum traders believe Y, can both beliefs survive contact with the same market?" When they can't, the inconsistency is an opportunity — one group's beliefs must revise, and the model knows the direction.

This is made precise through the Influence Kernel K*(s) = (I − Γ·A(s))−1A(s), the closed-form resolvent of the infinite-depth "I think you think you think" best-response hierarchy at timescale s. Belief inconsistency between agent types i and j shows up as large, structurally incompatible off-diagonal entries K*ij(s) — agent type i's belief implies a large induced shift in agent type j's belief under the kernel, but the market's currently observed prices are inconsistent with that induced shift having occurred. This off-diagonal tension is a directly computable quantity, not a qualitative impression: it is read straight off the resolved kernel that the equilibrium solve already produces as a byproduct, at zero marginal cost. The direction of the resulting thesis follows from which agent type's belief the kernel implies must move to restore consistency — a value fund's belief that has not yet caught up to what its own kernel-implied exposure to momentum-driven flow says it should update to, is a concrete, directional, mechanism-attributed thesis, not a backward-looking cheapness screen.

4.2 Prediction Under Reflexivity

Traditional models predict: "Given the current state, what price is likely next?" RecWM predicts: "Given the current belief equilibrium, how stable is it? Which perturbations could tip it? What is the post-trade expected return after accounting for our own market impact on the equilibrium?" This is not a modification of traditional prediction. It is a different kind of prediction — one that treats the predictor as inside the system, not outside it.

The formal object is the self-impact fixed point: p* = T(p*; s, θ), where the trade size s the model is contemplating is an explicit argument of the transition it solves for, not a perturbation applied after the equilibrium has already been computed. Concretely, this reuses exactly the ATLAS solver from Section 3.6, but re-parameterized so that the action-selection stage Aθ(b, x) includes the model's own hypothetical order alongside every other agent type's action, and the price-formation stage Pθ clears the market on the combined flow. The output is not "expected return, then separately, transaction cost estimate" — it is a single self-consistent price that already incorporates the fact that the trade itself moves the equilibrium the trade was sized against. This is the mechanism behind the Tuesday 14:32 example's closing line in Section 6: "our own selling will move credit spreads by 0.5bp" is not a slippage estimate bolted onto the thesis after the fact, it is read directly off the same equilibrium computation that produced the thesis.

4.3 Structural Counterfactuals

"What happens to this portfolio if the Fed cuts 50bp and China devalues?" Traditional systems run Monte Carlo on historical distributions. RecWM computes a new equilibrium: it changes the Fed's action in its world model, propagates the effect through agent beliefs, finds the new self-consistent price configuration, and reports the portfolio impact. The difference is not cosmetic. Historical Monte Carlo can't handle scenarios that have never occurred. RecWM can, because it has a generative model of the causal mechanisms, not just the historical outcomes.

Formally this is a do-operation on the state-transition structure underlying the equilibrium: fixing the policy fragment component xP (the estimated neutral rate and hawkishness indices) to the counterfactual value via do(xP = xPcounterfactual), holding the intervention exogenous to the belief-update stage that would otherwise re-infer it from data, and re-solving Φ(b*; x with xP intervened, θ) = b* for the new fixed point. The interaction tensor ξij(t) that couples the seven state fragments then propagates the intervention through the transition matrix's off-diagonal blocks — in a crisis regime those blocks are large (everything affects everything), so a policy-fragment intervention propagates broadly; in a calm regime the blocks are small and the same intervention stays comparatively contained. This regime-dependent propagation is itself an output of the counterfactual, not an assumption fed into it.

4.4 Crowding Detection Before Unwind

When many participants hold similar positions for similar reasons, the market is crowded. Traditional crowding metrics look at position data (13F filings, exchange data). RecWM detects crowding in belief space: when the Influence Kernel K*(s) shows large mutual entries — everyone reacting strongly to everyone else's expected reaction — small shocks get amplified into large moves. The spectral radius ρ(Γ·A(s)) approaching 1 is a mathematically precise "crowding is about to unwind" signal, available before the unwind shows up in price.

This is the resolvent amplification formula made explicit: because K*(s) = (I − ΓA(s))−1A(s) is a matrix resolvent, its entries scale as roughly 1/(1−ρ(ΓA(s))) near the critical boundary — a shock of fixed size to one agent type's belief produces an induced response in every other agent type that grows without bound as ρ → 1, even though the underlying single-step best-response operator A(s) has changed only slightly. This is the exact mathematical signature of LTCM's 1998 unwind (Section 2.2): many funds' risk models loaded similar convergence trades because their pairwise best-response coefficients to each other's expected liquidation behavior were all large and mutually reinforcing, and the resolvent's amplification of a single triggering loss (Russia's default) into a systemic deleveraging spiral is precisely ρ(ΓA) crossing 1. Because the kernel is timescale-indexed, RecWM further distinguishes a fast-timescale liquidity wobble (ρ crossing 1 only at short s, likely absorbed) from a genuine regime change (ρ crossing 1 simultaneously across timescales, rewriting long-horizon positioning) — a distinction unavailable to position-based crowding metrics, which see only the aftermath.

4.5 Regime Change Detection, Not Reaction

Traditional regime models detect a new regime after it's established (HMMs need data from the new regime to classify it). RecWM's SEISMOGRAPH component detects the approach of a regime change: a bifurcation in the equilibrium landscape, where the current equilibrium is about to cease being self-consistent. The bifurcation distance — the spectral gap between the Jacobian's eigenvalues and the unit circle — is a countdown, not a retrospective classification.

Formally, δbif(b*) = minλ∈σ(DΦ(b*)) ||λ| − 1|, the distance of the nearest eigenvalue of the Jacobian to the unit circle. A normalized bifurcation distance, δ̂bif(t) = δbif(t) / (|δ̇bif(t)| + ε), divides by the current rate of approach and so carries units of time: it is a direct estimate of how many timesteps remain before the bifurcation occurs, assuming the current rate of closure continues — the countdown, not merely the distance. Different eigenvalue-crossing geometries carry distinct financial readings: a real eigenvalue approaching 1 and then vanishing (a saddle-node/fold) means the currently-inhabited equilibrium is about to cease existing entirely — a forced repricing, because the belief configuration that "made sense" no longer has a self-consistent price to support it; a real eigenvalue splitting into two branches (a pitchfork, which occurs robustly when the underlying system has bull/bear symmetry) means the market is about to polarize into two camps rather than one; a complex pair approaching the unit circle (a discrete Hopf/Neimark-Sacker bifurcation) means the equilibrium is about to become a persistent oscillation with a characteristic frequency, rather than a point. A neural bifurcation predictor trained on the trajectory of the ATLAS solver's own residuals — not just the converged Jacobian — further catches the "critical slowing down" signature that precedes a bifurcation (convergence rate degrading from the normal superlinear regime toward 1) even before the eigenvalue crossing is imminent enough for the spectral monitor alone to flag it.

5. What RecWM Is Not

RecWM is not... Because...
A better Bloomberg terminal Bloomberg is a data display. RecWM is a reasoning system. The inputs overlap; the outputs don't — RecWM generates theses, not charts.
A chatbot that talks about markets LLMs can discuss markets; they cannot compute equilibria, detect bifurcations, or account for reflexive self-impact. RecWM has a mathematical engine, not a language model.
A risk management system Risk systems measure exposure to historical factor moves. RecWM reasons about why factors move and when those dynamics are about to change. It subsumes risk, but its purpose is alpha generation.
