Technical Research Brief — Compositional World Models — August 2026
Research Brief / August 2026

World Model Architectures:
The State of the Field

A survey of JEPA, Genie, World Labs, and the emerging application of world models to finance, economics, and social systems. Covering key papers, architectures, capabilities, and gaps from 2024 through mid-2026.

JEPA Genie 2 & 3 World Labs Finance & Economics Beyond Robotics Comparison
Architecture 1

JEPA -- Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture

Yann LeCun's JEPA is arguably the most theoretically ambitious world-model program. Its core thesis: predict in latent space, not pixel space. Instead of reconstructing raw inputs (as autoencoders and diffusion models do), JEPA learns to predict abstract representations of future states, discarding irrelevant detail and focusing on causal structure.

How it works: An encoder maps observation x to representation s_x. A predictor (conditioned on context and an optional variable z) predicts the target representation s_y. A target encoder (EMA-updated, no gradient) produces the ground-truth target. Collapse is prevented via energy-based contrastive or variance-covariance objectives. The key insight is that by predicting in latent space, the model can ignore stochastic, unpredictable details and learn the causal dynamics of the environment.

Timeline of instantiations:

I-JEPA (June 2023)

First instantiation on images. ViT backbone with random block masking; predictor fills in latent patches. Outperformed MAE on ImageNet linear probing with less compute.

V-JEPA (February 2024)

Extended masking to spatiotemporal tubes across video frames, forcing temporal reasoning about scenes. 1.5-6x more sample-efficient than pixel-generative video baselines. Open-sourced under CC-BY-NC.

V-JEPA 2 (June 2025)

The major scaling step: 1.2B-parameter ViT pretrained self-supervised on over 1M hours of video plus ~1M images. Runs ~30x faster than NVIDIA Cosmos on physical-reasoning benchmarks. The action-conditioned variant V-JEPA 2-AC adds a ~300M-param transformer predictor fine-tuned on <62 hours of robot data, achieving 65-80% zero-shot success on grasp/reach/pick-and-place in unseen labs.

arXiv 2506.09985 1.2B params Self-supervised

V-JEPA 2.1 & Extensions (2025-2026)

V-JEPA 2.1 (March 2026) adds dense predictive loss and deep self-supervision. VL-JEPA (late 2025) extends to vision-language with zero-shot classification and VQA. Audio-JEPA (ICME 2025) matches wav2vec 2.0 with <1/5 training data. Other variants include GeoJEPA (geospatial), MTS-JEPA (time-series anomaly detection), and LeWorldModel (JEPA for RL world models from pixels).

LeCun's Departure and Startup (November 2025)

After 12 years at Meta, LeCun departed to found an AI startup pursuing his Autonomous Machine Intelligence (AMI) vision. His thesis: next-token prediction is a dead end for world understanding. JEPA-based world models that predict at multiple abstraction levels, combined with hierarchical planning and intrinsic cost modules, form the path to AMI. Stated horizon: roughly a decade.

Relevance to Economics

JEPA's core design -- predicting in latent space, ignoring stochastic noise, learning causal dynamics -- is deeply relevant. MTS-JEPA already targets time-series anomaly detection. The architecture's ability to learn at multiple abstraction levels maps naturally to the multi-scale nature of economic systems (tick-level microstructure through macro cycles). The key limitation: JEPA currently requires dense spatiotemporal data (video, audio), and economic data is sparse, irregular, and multi-modal in different ways. An "Econ-JEPA" would need a fundamentally different encoder and masking strategy.

Architecture 2

Genie 2 & 3 -- Google DeepMind

DeepMind's Genie line represents the interactive generative approach to world models: generate photorealistic, action-controllable environments from a single image or text prompt, then let agents navigate them.

Architecture (Genie 2): An autoregressive latent diffusion model with three components: (1) a video autoencoder compressing frames into compact latent representations; (2) a transformer dynamics model trained with causal masking that takes past latent frames plus current action and predicts the next latent frame; (3) classifier-free guidance at inference to sharpen action controllability. Trained on a large-scale video dataset (undisclosed).

Genie 2 (December 2024)

Generates action-controllable, interactive 3D environments from a single image. Supports keyboard/mouse navigation with consistent worlds for up to ~60 seconds at 360p. Exhibits emergent behaviors: object interactions, physically plausible gravity/water/smoke, NPC behavior, and long-horizon memory (correctly rendering areas the agent revisits). No formal paper published -- blog post only with BibTeX citation.

Blog post only 360p / ~60s Internal system

Genie 3 (August 2025)

Major upgrade: 720p at 24 fps with one-minute memory (5x Genie 2). Integrates Google Street View data for realistic street environments. In January 2026, "Project Genie" launched as a web interface for Google AI Ultra subscribers via Google Labs.

Relevance to Economics

Genie demonstrates that autoregressive latent dynamics models can generate consistent, action-responsive environments. The architectural pattern -- encode state into latent space, predict next-state conditioned on actions, decode for interpretation -- is exactly the skeleton needed for an economic world model. Replace "keyboard input" with "policy intervention" and "video frame" with "economic state vector." The limitation: Genie is deeply tied to visual rendering; the conceptual leap is replacing the video autoencoder with an economic-state encoder.

Architecture 3

World Labs -- Spatial Intelligence

Founded by Fei-Fei Li in 2023, World Labs has raised ~$1.23B (valued at $5B as of January 2026) to build "Large World Models" that generate persistent, navigable, editable 3D environments -- distinct from video generation in that the output is a stable world, not a morphing sequence.

Marble (Large World Model)

Accepts text, photographs, video, panoramas, or rough 3D layouts and generates navigable, persistent, editable 3D environments. Limited beta November 2025; commercial launch February 2026. The World API (January 2026) exposes Marble programmatically.

RTFM -- Real-Time Frame Model (October 2025)

Generates video frames interactively as users navigate, using posed frames as spatial memory for unbounded persistence and consistency -- no explicit 3D reconstruction required.

Fei-Fei Li's Three-Type Taxonomy (June 2026)

A crucial theoretical contribution splitting "world models" into three functional roles:

Renderer -- generates sensory output
Simulator -- maintains persistent state evolving under actions
Planner -- maps observations to actions

Marble targets the Simulator role. Li argues that without a grounded simulator, planners produce actions disconnected from reality.

Relevance to Economics

Li's Renderer/Simulator/Planner taxonomy is directly applicable. An economic world model is fundamentally a Simulator: it maintains persistent economic state that evolves under policy/agent actions. The Renderer is the interpretive layer (dashboards, scenario reports), and the Planner is the policy-optimization component. The key difference: World Labs builds spatial simulators; an economic world model needs a relational/causal simulator operating over heterogeneous agent states and institutional constraints.

Architecture 4

Finance-Specific World Models

No one has built a true "world model for economics" in the JEPA/Genie sense, but several important efforts are converging on the idea from different directions.

MarS: Financial Market Simulation Engine (ICLR 2025)

By Microsoft Research (Li, Liu, et al.). A Large Market Model (LMM) operating at the order level, analogous to language modeling but for financial order flow. Generates realistic market dynamics for forecasting, anomaly detection, microstructure analysis, and agent training. Demonstrates strong scalability across data size and model complexity. This is the closest thing to a foundation world model for finance: a generative model learning market dynamics from order-level data.

arXiv 2409.07486 ICLR 2025 Microsoft Research Open-source

EconAgent: LLM-Empowered Macroeconomic Simulation

Constructs heterogeneous economic agents with perception (profiles), memory (multi-period experiences), and action (LLM-generated work/consumption propensities) modules. Agents operate in a shared market with endowments, skills, and wealth; their collective decisions produce macro dynamics through a rule-based environment acting as both central government (taxes) and central bank (interest rates).

LLM-as-agent Macro simulation

Bank of Japan: Generative AI in Economic Simulations (2025)

Created 1,000 consumer agents using GPT-4o mini to study wage/price effects on consumption. Separate experiment simulated monopoly vs. duopoly competition. Results were consistent with microeconomic theory. Critical caveat from BoJ researchers: LLMs "merely output responses that are statistically consistent with patterns in training data" -- they may fail in genuinely novel economic scenarios.

Three-in-One World Model for Marketing Intervention (May 2026)

Niimi (Meijo University). Uses a frozen Deep Boltzmann Machine as a belief representation that simultaneously supports energy-based consistency evaluation, outcome prediction, and counterfactual inference. Interventions enter only the adapter, never the DBM -- allowing counterfactual queries by fixing beliefs and toggling actions.

arXiv 2605.07199 DBM-based Counterfactual

Awesome-Econ-World-Models (Community Resource)

A curated GitHub repository with 737 validated papers organized across six capability levels (L1-L6): from fixed rule-based agents (L1) through LLM-based agents with beliefs and reasoning (L3) to self-evolving agents with online real-world correction (L6). L6 is currently empty -- no system yet achieves adaptive, self-correcting economic world modeling with real-world feedback loops.

github.com/FreedomIntelligence 737 papers L6 empty

MALLES & Agentic Economic Modeling (2025-2026)

MALLES extends the EconAgent paradigm to microeconomic retail/wholesale scenarios with alignment via transaction-data post-training. Agentic Economic Modeling (AEM) is a framework that aligns synthetic LLM choices with small-sample human evidence for reliable econometric inference. Eco3S targets complex socio-economic system simulation via agent-based models.

Gap Analysis

The finance world-model space has order-level generative models (MarS) and LLM-as-agent simulations (EconAgent, BoJ), but nothing that combines (a) learned latent dynamics, (b) action-conditioned prediction, (c) counterfactual reasoning, and (d) real-world feedback correction into a single system. The L6 gap in the Awesome-Econ-World-Models taxonomy -- adaptive, self-correcting economic world models -- remains unfilled.

Architecture 5

World Models Beyond Robotics

The world-model concept is rapidly escaping its robotics/gaming origins. Several 2025-2026 developments show the pattern generalizing to clinical, epidemiological, social, and policy domains.

Agentic World Modeling (April 2026)

Chu et al. (49 co-authors). Comprehensive survey of 400+ works proposing a "levels x laws" framework: L1 Predictor (one-step local transitions), L2 Simulator (multi-step, action-conditioned rollouts respecting domain laws), L3 Evolver (autonomously revises its own model when predictions fail). Applied across four law regimes: physical, digital, social, and scientific.

arXiv 2604.22748 400+ papers surveyed

Clinical World Models (November 2025)

Qazi, Nadeem, Yaqub. Capability rubric for healthcare: L1 temporal prediction, L2 action-conditioned prediction, L3 counterfactual rollouts, L4 planning/control. Most existing systems achieve only L1-L2. Identifies gaps in interventional validation and uncertainty calibration.

arXiv 2511.16333

Epidemiological World Models (April 2026)

"Toward World Models for Epidemiology" -- intervention-aware simulation allowing policy evaluation in terms of latent epidemic control rather than passive trend extrapolation.

arXiv 2604.09519

Policy4OOD: World Model for Opioid Crisis Intervention (February 2026)

A knowledge-guided world model for policy intervention simulation. Supports counterfactual reasoning by modifying policy inputs within historical sequences, re-running the model to produce counterfactual trajectories.

arXiv 2602.12373 Interventional

Social Dynamics Integration

A position paper at OpenReview argues that "world models should prioritize the unification of physical and social dynamics" -- modeling agent behavior, social norms, and institutional constraints is as important as modeling physics for real-world world models.

Counterfactual World Models via Digital Twins (November 2025)

Formalizes counterfactual world models that take interventions as explicit inputs, predicting temporal sequences under hypothetical modifications to observed properties. Uses video diffusion conditioned on digital twin state.

arXiv 2511.17481

Ethics of Counterfactual World Simulation (2025)

Springer Nature article examining the ethical implications of counterfactual world simulation models (CWSMs) that use multimodal evidence to answer causal questions by simulating what would have happened under alternative conditions.

Synthesis

Comparative Architecture Map

System Prediction Space Action-Conditioned Counterfactual Self-Correcting Domain
JEPA / V-JEPA 2 Latent embeddings Yes (V-JEPA 2-AC) Implicit No Vision, robotics
Genie 2 / 3 Latent diffusion Yes (actions) Yes (divergent rollouts) No 3D environments
World Labs Marble 3D spatial Yes (navigation) Editable worlds No Spatial intelligence
MarS (Microsoft) Order-level tokens Yes (orders) Scenario generation No Financial markets
EconAgent LLM text Yes (decisions) Scenario replay No Macroeconomics
Three-in-One (DBM) Energy-based latent Adapter only Yes (explicit) No Marketing
Policy4OOD Knowledge-guided Yes (policies) Yes (explicit) No Policy intervention
[L6 gap] ? Yes Yes Yes Economics

The table reveals a consistent pattern: no existing system is self-correcting. Every world model in the landscape is trained offline and deployed without real-world feedback loops. The "L3 Evolver" level from the Agentic World Modeling survey -- which autonomously revises its model when predictions fail -- remains aspirational across all domains.

Architectural Patterns Worth Importing

From JEPA: Latent-space prediction

Predict economic states in a learned abstract space rather than raw observables. This naturally handles the noise, missing data, and irrelevant variation in economic signals. The EMA target encoder provides a stable learning target without collapse.

From Genie: Action-conditioned autoregressive dynamics

The pattern of encoding state, conditioning on actions, and autoregressively generating next-states is the correct skeleton for an economic simulator. Replace "keyboard input" with "policy intervention" and "video frame" with "economic state vector."

From World Labs: The Simulator decomposition

Li's Renderer/Simulator/Planner taxonomy clarifies that the core intellectual challenge is the Simulator -- maintaining persistent, causally coherent state under interventions. The Renderer and Planner are separable engineering problems.

From Three-in-One: Frozen belief + intervention adapter

The DBM architecture's separation of learned beliefs (frozen world model) from intervention inputs (adapter only) is an elegant counterfactual mechanism. It ensures that counterfactual queries modify the intervention, not the agent's learned state.

From Policy4OOD: Explicit interventional conditioning

Taking interventions as first-class inputs (not just context) and re-running the model with modified policy sequences to produce counterfactual trajectories. This is exactly the pattern needed for economic policy evaluation.

Tail Risk Estimation, Extreme Value Theory & AI/ML in Finance

Literature Survey -- August 2026

Contents
  1. Classical EVT in Finance
  2. ML Approaches to Tail Risk Estimation
  3. AI for Stress Testing & Scenario Generation
  4. Deep Learning + EVT Integration
  5. Gaps in the Literature
  6. Master Citation Table

1. Classical EVT in Finance

Theoretical Foundations

Extreme Value Theory provides the mathematical framework for modeling the tails of probability distributions. Two core theorems underpin the field.

Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko Theorem (Block Maxima)
The maximum of n i.i.d. random variables, properly normalized, converges to a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution with CDF: H(x) = exp(-(1 + ξx)^(-1/ξ)). The shape parameter ξ determines the tail type: ξ > 0 (Fréchet / heavy tail), ξ = 0 (Gumbel / light tail), ξ < 0 (Weibull / bounded tail). Financial returns typically exhibit ξ > 0, confirming heavy tails.
Pickands-Balkema-de Haan Theorem (Peaks Over Threshold)
Balkema, A.A. & de Haan, L. (1974). "Residual Life Time at Great Age." Annals of Probability, 2, 792-804.
Pickands, J. (1975). "Statistical Inference Using Extreme Order Statistics." Annals of Statistics, 3(1), 119-131.
For a distribution F in the maximum domain of attraction of a GEV, exceedances over a sufficiently high threshold u follow a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD): G(y) = 1 - (1 + ξy/σ)^(-1/ξ). This is the theoretical basis of the Peaks Over Threshold (POT) method, generally preferred over Block Maxima in finance because it uses extreme data more efficiently.

Foundational Texts and Papers

Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance
Embrechts, P., Klüppelberg, C. & Mikosch, T. (1997). Springer-Verlag. 645 pp. ISBN 3-540-60931-8.
The seminal textbook that established EVT as a core tool for financial risk management. Covers heavy-tailed distributions, point processes, extremal processes, and applications to insurance and financial time series. Remains the standard graduate reference.
Estimation of Tail-Related Risk Measures for Heteroscedastic Financial Time Series: An Extreme Value Approach
McNeil, A.J. & Frey, R. (2000). Journal of Empirical Finance, 7(3-4), 271-300.
Introduced the GARCH-EVT two-stage methodology: (1) fit a GARCH model via pseudo-maximum-likelihood to filter out conditional heteroscedasticity, producing approximately i.i.d. standardized residuals; (2) apply POT/GPD to the upper tail of negated residuals. This yields conditional VaR and conditional Expected Shortfall estimates that account for time-varying volatility. This paper became the canonical approach for combining volatility models with extreme value tail estimation.
Quantitative Risk Management: Concepts, Techniques and Tools
McNeil, A.J., Frey, R. & Embrechts, P. (2005; 2nd ed. 2015). Princeton University Press.
The standard practitioner/academic textbook covering risk factors, loss distributions, aggregate risk, copulas, credit risk, and operational risk. Integrates EVT throughout as the primary tail modeling framework.
Value at Risk and Extreme Returns
Danielsson, J. & de Vries, C. (2000). Annales d'Économie et de Statistique, 60, 239-270.
Directly addresses the intersection of VaR computation and extreme value theory for financial returns. Also related: Danielsson, de Vries, de Haan & Peng (2001), "Using a Bootstrap Method to Choose the Sample Fraction in Tail Index Estimation," Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 76(2), 226-248.
Extreme Value Theory in Finance: A Survey
Rocco, M. (2014). Journal of Economic Surveys, 28(1), 82-108.
Comprehensive survey covering EVT applications in finance: VaR estimation, ES computation, asset allocation under safety-first constraints, portfolio tail risk, contagion under stress, and the choice between Block Maxima and POT approaches.
An Application of Extreme Value Theory for Measuring Financial Risk
Gilli, M. & Kellezi, E. (2006). Computational Economics, 27(2-3), 207-228.
Practical application of EVT methods (both Block Maxima/GEV and POT/GPD) to measure financial risk across equity indices, with detailed comparison of VaR estimates from parametric, historical simulation, and EVT approaches.
Estimating and Forecasting Conditional Risk Measures with Extreme Value Theory: A Review
Bee, M. et al. (2018). Risks, 6(2), 45.
Reviews the full pipeline of conditional EVT-based risk measures: GARCH filtering, threshold selection, GPD estimation (MLE, probability-weighted moments, L-moments), and backtesting of VaR/ES forecasts.

The EVT Pipeline for VaR and Expected Shortfall

The standard EVT pipeline for risk measurement:

  1. Volatility filtering. Fit an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) or similar to returns. Extract standardized residuals z_t = (r_t - μ_t) / σ_t.
  2. Threshold selection. Use mean residual life plots or automated methods (e.g., Danielsson et al.'s bootstrap) to choose the threshold u for POT.
  3. GPD fitting. Fit GPD to exceedances above u via MLE: estimate shape (ξ) and scale (β) parameters.
  4. Risk measure computation. VaR_α = u + (β/ξ)[(n/N_u(1-α))^(-ξ) - 1];   ES_α = VaR_α/(1-ξ) + (β - ξu)/(1-ξ).
  5. Re-scaling. Convert back to conditional scale: VaR_t = μ_t + σ_t · VaR(z).

Key advantage over historical simulation or normal VaR: EVT provides theoretically justified extrapolation beyond observed data into the far tail (e.g., 99.9% quantiles), rather than being limited to the empirical distribution.

2. ML Approaches to Tail Risk Estimation

Deep Quantile Regression for VaR

Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
Chronopoulos, I., Raftapostolos, A. & Kapetanios, G. (2024). Journal of Financial Econometrics, 22(3), 636-669.
DNN Quantile Regression Uses a deep quantile estimator leveraging neural networks' universal approximation property to model non-linear associations between conditional quantiles and predictors. Supports different penalty functions and high-dimensional covariates. Outperforms linear, MIDAS, and other non-parametric quantile models in VaR forecasting. The key innovation is applying deep learning directly to the quantile loss function rather than to distributional assumptions.
VaR and ES Forecasting via Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stateful Models
Candelieri, A. et al. (2024). International Review of Financial Analysis, 92, 103054.
RNN LSTM Stateful Proposes stateful recurrent neural network architectures (LSTM, GRU) for jointly forecasting VaR and ES. The "stateful" design preserves hidden state across batches, capturing long-range dependencies in financial time series that standard RNN training misses.
Forecasting VaR and ES by Using Deep Quantile Regression, GANs-Based Scenario Generation, and Heterogeneous Market Hypothesis
Xu, Q. et al. (2024). Financial Innovation, 10, 19. (Springer)
Mogrifier RNN GAN Quantile Regression Combines quantile regression with "Mogrifier" recurrent neural networks to capture long memory and volatility clustering. Uses GAN-generated synthetic scenarios to augment training data for rare tail events. Integrates heterogeneous market hypothesis to weight different time horizons.

Deep Expected Shortfall Estimation

Deep Neural Expected Shortfall Regression with Tail-Robustness
Yu, M., Tan, K.M., Wang, H.J. & Zhou, W.-X. (2025). arXiv:2511.08772.
DNN Huber Loss Robust Nonparametric two-step ES regression: (1) estimate conditional quantile as nuisance parameter; (2) build ES estimator using feedforward ReLU networks. Key innovation: integrates a properly tuned Huber loss, yielding an estimator provably resistant to heavy-tailedness (non-asymptotic guarantees) and first-order insensitive to quantile estimation errors from stage one. Alleviates curse of dimensionality when underlying functions have hierarchical composition structure.
Enhancing Financial Tail Risk Forecasting: A Blending Ensemble Framework for Nonlinear Expectile Regression
Ma, F. et al. (2025). Journal of Forecasting. (Early view, Wiley)
Expectile Ensemble Uses expectile regression (a least-squares analogue of quantile regression) with ensemble blending to forecast tail risk. Expectiles are sensitive to tail behavior and can be converted to VaR/ES via the Efron-Tibshirani relationship.

Large-Scale ML for Tail Risk

ReSGA: A Large Tail Risk Model for Learning Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall
Zhang, Y., Zhu, K. & Zhu, Z. (2026). arXiv:2606.04576.
Autoencoder Retrieval Cross-sectional A retrieval-enhanced self-grouping autoencoder with millions of parameters for joint VaR-ES forecasting. (1) Learns latent group structures across assets so tail-risk information is shared among assets with similar financial behavior; (2) incorporates a retrieval mechanism enabling each asset to draw on long-term historical "experiences" from its own past and other grouped assets. Applied to US equities 1926-2023 with 153 firm characteristics. Outperforms 12 econometric and ML competitors. Key finding: improvements driven by data complexity rather than model complexity.
Learning About Tail Risk: Machine Learning and Combination with Regularization in Market Risk Management
Various authors (2024). Omega (Elsevier), 129, 103135.
Regularization Combination Investigates ML methods (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) combined with regularization for VaR/ES estimation. Model combination with regularization outperforms individual models for tail risk forecasting.

Hybrid Causal-Predictive Approaches

Causal and Predictive Modeling of Short-Horizon Market Risk and Systematic Alpha Generation Using Hybrid Machine Learning Ensembles
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2510.22348.
Causal ML Ensemble Demonstrates that short-term conditional drivers -- equity returns, interest rate sensitivities, commodity tail-risk measures -- dominate crash predictions. Combines causal identification with predictive ML ensembles for market risk forecasting.
CoFiE-NN: Cornish-Fisher Expansion with LSTM Neural Networks for Tail Risk Prediction
IMF Working Paper (2024).
LSTM Cornish-Fisher Combines Cornish-Fisher expansions (using higher moments -- skewness, kurtosis -- to adjust normal quantiles) with LSTM neural networks. Tested across four market regimes (GFC, European debt crisis, COVID-19, taper tantrum). Consistently outperforms traditional EVT, showing adaptability to regime changes.
Quantile-Based Modeling of Scale Dynamics in Financial Returns for VaR and ES Forecasting
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2603.02357.
Semiparametric Quantile A semiparametric approach modeling the conditional scale of financial returns via restricted quantile regression. Accepted in International Journal of Forecasting.

3. AI for Stress Testing & Scenario Generation

GANs for Financial Time Series and Stress Scenarios

Quant GANs: Deep Generation of Financial Time Series
Wiese, M. et al. (2020). Quantitative Finance, 20(9), 1419-1440.
GAN TCN Proposed QuantGAN using stacked temporal convolutional networks to capture long-range temporal dependencies in financial time series generation. Demonstrated that GANs can reproduce heavy-tailed distributions, volatility clustering, and leverage effects observed in real markets.
GANs for Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing in Financial Institutions
Review paper (2024). IJFMR, 6(3).
WGAN-GP Stress Testing Reviews conditional Wasserstein GANs with gradient penalty for stress scenario generation. The generator receives a noise vector plus a condition vector (severity level, geographic influence, duration) to produce synthetic stress scenarios. Addresses CCAR/DFAST regulatory requirements where historical data is insufficient.
Sig-Wasserstein GANs for Conditional Time Series Generation
Liao, S. et al. (2024). Mathematical Finance, 34(4). (Wiley)
Sig-WGAN Path Signatures Integrates Wasserstein GANs with path signatures -- a graded sequence of statistics providing a universal description of data streams. Enables conditional generation of financial time series preserving temporal dependence structure, useful for stress scenario generation conditioned on macroeconomic variables.
Generative Adversarial Networks Applied to Synthetic Financial Scenarios Generation
Various authors (2023). Physica A (Elsevier).
GAN Synthetic Data Evaluates GAN architectures for generating synthetic multivariate financial scenarios that preserve cross-asset correlations, marginal distributions, and tail dependencies for risk management and stress testing.
Can GANs Learn the Stylized Facts of Financial Time Series?
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2410.09850.
GAN Stylized Facts Empirically tests whether GAN-generated financial time series reproduce canonical stylized facts: heavy tails, volatility clustering, leverage effect, absence of autocorrelation in returns, long memory in absolute returns. Critical evaluation of where GANs succeed and fail in capturing tail behavior.
Time-Causal VAE: Robust Financial Time Series Generator
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2411.02947.
VAE Causal A variational autoencoder respecting temporal causal structure for generating financial time series. Designed to produce realistic scenarios for stress testing while maintaining the causal ordering of market dynamics.
Generative Adversarial Regression (GAR): Learning Conditional Risk Scenarios
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2603.08553.
GAR Conditional Extends GANs to conditional regression settings, learning to generate risk scenarios conditioned on specific covariate values. Directly applicable to "what-if" stress testing conditioned on specific macro-economic states.

Diffusion Models for Financial Data

Generation of Synthetic Financial Time Series by Diffusion Models
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2410.18897.
Diffusion Applies denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to synthetic financial time series generation. Diffusion models offer advantages over GANs (training stability, mode coverage) and may better capture multimodal tail distributions.

Regulatory Context: CCAR and DFAST

The Federal Reserve's CCAR and Dodd-Frank Act Stress Tests require banks to project losses under severely adverse scenarios. Traditional approaches rely on historical or expert-designed hypothetical scenarios. AI/ML contributions include:

  • Scenario enrichment: GANs/VAEs generate plausible scenarios beyond historical experience, addressing the "we haven't seen it before" problem.
  • Conditional generation: Models generate scenarios conditioned on specific macro variables (unemployment spikes, rate shocks) that regulators specify.
  • Tail calibration: Generative models combined with EVT ensure synthetic scenarios respect extreme event statistics rather than producing unrealistic tail draws.
  • Multi-asset coherence: Modern generative architectures preserve cross-asset dependence structure under stress, avoiding independently shocked risk factors.

4. Deep Learning + EVT Integration

The emerging intersection where deep learning architectures are designed to respect or incorporate extreme value theory constraints -- arguably the most technically interesting frontier in the field.

Neural Networks with EVT Constraints

Modeling Extremes with d-max-decreasing Neural Networks
Hasan, A., Elkhalil, K., Ng, Y., Pereira, J.M., Farsiu, S., Blanchet, J.H. & Tarokh, V. (2021/2022). arXiv:2102.09042.
Constrained NN EVT Introduces a neural network architecture enforcing the d-max-decreasing property -- a stringent convexity constraint required by multivariate extreme value distributions. First class of non-parametric estimators maintaining the structural properties mandated by EVT. Achieves parametric-rate approximation of the dependence structure. Includes a generative sampling technique for high-dimensional extreme value distributions. Applications in environmental sciences and financial mathematics.
Deep Learning of Multivariate Extremes via a Geometric Representation
Murphy-Barltrop, C.J.R., Majumder, R. & Richards, J. (2024). arXiv:2406.19936.
Geometric Extremes DNN Uses geometric extremes -- inferring extreme dependence from deterministic limiting shapes of scaled sample clouds -- combined with deep learning. First approach to modeling limit sets using neural networks. Enables asymptotically-justified yet flexible semi-parametric models for extremal dependence of high-dimensional data. Extends geometric extremes beyond low-dimensional settings (previously limited to d < 5). Demonstrated on North Sea meteorological/oceanographic data.
Semi-parametric Bulk and Tail Regression Using Spline-Based Neural Networks (SPQRx)
Majumder, R. & Richards, J. (2025/2026). arXiv:2504.19994.
Spline NN Blended GPD SPQRx: semi-parametric quantile regression for extremes. Combines spline-based neural network density regression with a "blended generalized Pareto distribution" providing smooth transition between bulk and tail modeling without threshold selection. Complies with EVT standards while maintaining full distributional flexibility. Offers variable importance scores measuring covariate influence on bulk vs. tail behavior.

Deep Generative Models + EVT

Combining Deep Generative Models with Extreme Value Theory for Synthetic Hazard Simulation
Peard, A. & Hall, J. (2023). NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Climate Change and ML. arXiv:2311.18521.
GAN EVT Hybrid Two-part architecture: (1) GAN models the dependence structure for multivariate hazards (wind speed, wave height, precipitation); (2) EVT handles tail extrapolation in a controlled manner. The GAN learns the copula/dependence, while EVT ensures realistic tail behavior. Generates thousands of realistic compound hazard events. Directly transferable to financial multivariate tail modeling.
Pasche & Engelke (2022); Richards & Huser (2022); Cisneros et al. (2024)
Multiple papers cited in Murphy-Barltrop et al. (2024).
Deep Generative EVT A cluster of recent papers constructing flexible, computationally-scalable models for univariate extremes using deep learning. Pasche and Engelke focus on conditional EVT models using neural networks; Richards and Huser on neural Bayes estimators for extreme value parameters.

EVT-Aware Loss Functions and Training

Standard neural network loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy) weight all observations equally or even downweight extremes. EVT-aware approaches:

  • Quantile/expectile loss: Asymmetric losses focusing on specific tail quantiles (Chronopoulos et al. 2024).
  • Huber-modified tail loss: Robust to heavy-tailed training data while focusing on ES estimation (Yu et al. 2025).
  • EVT-adapted loss functions: Koh et al. (2024, arXiv:2401.12195) proposed loss functions adapted to extreme values that prioritize the tail rather than the bulk of the data distribution.
  • Shape-constrained architectures: Enforcing d-max-decreasing or other EVT constraints directly in the network architecture (Hasan et al. 2022) rather than through loss functions.

5. Gaps in the Literature

Gap 1 -- Real-Time Tail Risk Monitoring with Causal Understanding

Existing work either models tails statistically (EVT) or predicts risk factors causally (causal ML), but almost no work integrates both into a real-time monitoring system. Current EVT-based VaR/ES is computed ex ante with fixed parameters; current causal ML identifies drivers but does not provide theoretically justified tail extrapolation. The missing piece: a system that simultaneously (a) identifies why tail risk is changing (causal mechanism), (b) quantifies how much it has changed (EVT-calibrated measures), and (c) updates in real time as new data arrives.

Gap 2 -- Adaptive EVT Under Regime Changes

Classical EVT assumes stationarity (or stationarity of GARCH residuals). When the data-generating process undergoes structural breaks -- regime changes, policy shifts, market microstructure changes -- EVT tail parameters (ξ, β) become non-stationary. The CoFiE-NN (2024 IMF) begins to address this but relies on pre-identified regimes. A fully adaptive system that detects regime changes endogenously and re-estimates tail parameters in real time remains absent. The key challenge: estimating GPD parameters with a sliding window when exceedances are very few per window.

Gap 3 -- Moving Beyond Historical Simulation

Despite decades of EVT research, the dominant industry practice remains historical simulation (HS) or filtered historical simulation (FHS). The gap is practical, not theoretical: EVT methods require threshold selection (fragile), GPD fitting (unstable with few exceedances), and distributional assumptions difficult to validate. ML approaches that automate or bypass these choices (like SPQRx's threshold-free approach) are promising but not yet industry-adopted.

Gap 4 -- Endogenous vs. Exogenous Tail Risk

Nearly all tail risk models treat risk as exogenous -- a shock arrives from outside the system. But financial crises often involve endogenous amplification (fire sales, margin spirals, liquidity feedback). The Cont & Schaanning (2017) fire-sale model addresses endogenous amplification, but this work is not integrated with EVT or ML tail estimation. A model capturing how endogenous feedback loops amplify exogenous shocks into extreme tail events is missing.

Gap 5 -- Multivariate Tail Dependence at Scale

Most EVT applications in finance are univariate. Multivariate EVT exists (copulas, spectral measures, geometric extremes) but is computationally challenging beyond 5-10 dimensions. Murphy-Barltrop et al. (2024) push this boundary with geometric extremes + deep learning but have not applied it to financial portfolios with hundreds of assets. Scaling multivariate tail dependence estimation to realistic portfolio dimensions remains open.

Gap 6 -- Generative Tail Calibration

GAN/VAE/diffusion models for financial scenario generation typically evaluate generated samples on aggregate statistical properties (autocorrelation, kurtosis, Wasserstein distance). Very few papers specifically evaluate whether the generative model's tail behavior is statistically consistent with EVT predictions. Peard & Hall (2023) is an exception, applied to climate not finance. A rigorous framework for calibrating generative financial models against EVT tail properties is needed.

Gap 7 -- Interventional Tail Risk

All current approaches are observational -- they estimate P(loss > x | data). None address the interventional question: P(loss > x | do(intervention)). What happens to tail risk if we change a policy, adjust a position, or modify a market structure? This requires integrating causal inference (do-calculus) with tail risk estimation, a combination absent from the literature.

REN Invention 1 · August 2026

The Influence Kernel: K*(s) = (I − Γ·A(s))−1A(s)

A closed-form resolvent that collapses infinite regress in strategic reasoning — "I think you think I think..." — into a single matrix inverse, computable at every timescale s in one shot.

1. The Problem: Reflexive Reasoning Doesn't Terminate

Markets are reflexive. Agent A's belief about the price depends on what A thinks agent B believes, which depends on what B thinks A believes, which depends on what A thinks B thinks A believes — a hierarchy that in principle never bottoms out. This is not a philosophical curiosity; it is the central computational obstacle in building any model of strategic financial behavior. Every serious attempt to formalize it runs into the same wall: representing beliefs about beliefs about beliefs to depth k costs exponentially in k, and real markets do not politely stop reasoning at some fixed depth.

1.1 Formalizing the regress

Let Theta = {θ1, …, θN} be a finite set of agent types (momentum traders, market makers, value investors, retail, CTAs, macro allocators, …). Each agent type holds a zero-order belief B(0)(θ) about market fundamentals. A first-order belief is a belief about other agents' zero-order beliefs: B(1)(θ) is θ's model of {B(0)(θ′) : θ′ ∈ Theta}. A second-order belief is a belief about other agents' first-order beliefs, and so on. The object B(k)(θ) is, formally, a measure on a space of measures on a space of measures … (k times) — and naive representation of this object is exponential in k and simply unusable at trading speed.

This is precisely the representation problem that motivates Belief Fields (Invention 2): embedding the hierarchy into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space collapses it to a linear recurrence in natural parameters. The Influence Kernel is the specialization of that same collapse to the narrower, faster question of strategic best-response: not "what does everyone believe at every depth," but "if I shock one agent type's belief right now, how does that shock propagate through everyone else's reasoning about everyone else's reasoning, at infinite depth, computed in one shot."

1.2 Why truncation is the standard answer, and why it is unsatisfactory

The dominant approach in behavioral game theory is simply to stop. Level-k models (Nagel 1995; Stahl & Wilson 1995) posit that real agents reason to a small, fixed depth: a level-0 agent plays non-strategically (e.g., uniformly at random, or by a naive heuristic); a level-1 agent best-responds to level-0; a level-k agent best-responds to level-(k−1). Experimental evidence (Nagel's beauty-contest games, Camerer, Ho & Chong's 2004 cognitive hierarchy model) consistently finds most human subjects reasoning at levels 1–3, with a population distribution over levels rather than a single depth.

Cognitive hierarchy theory refines this by making the level distribution itself part of the model: agents at level k best-respond not to a single lower level but to a Poisson-weighted mixture of levels 0 through k−1, calibrated against observed play. This is empirically useful — it is a good predictive model of laboratory subjects — but it inherits three structural problems that make it a poor foundation for a production trading system:

  • The depth is assumed, not derived. Level-k and cognitive hierarchy models fix a maximum reasoning depth (typically k ≤ 3–4) as an exogenous modeling choice, calibrated to laboratory subjects. There is no principled reason a systematic trading desk, a CTA overlay, or an algorithmic market maker is bounded to human-scale strategic depth — and no mechanism in these models for depth to emerge from the problem rather than being imposed on it.
  • Truncation error is uncharacterized. Stopping at depth k silently discards every higher-order term. In a genuinely reflexive market — one where A's trade moves the price, which changes B's belief, which changes B's trade, which moves the price again — those discarded terms are exactly the terms that determine whether a shock damps out or cascades. A depth-3 approximation cannot distinguish a market that is one reasoning-step away from a stable consensus from one that is one reasoning-step away from a reflexivity crisis; both look identical at low order.
  • No stability diagnostic. Because the hierarchy is truncated rather than summed, there is no natural signal for "this reasoning process is about to diverge." Level-k models say nothing about whether the underlying best-response process, iterated to convergence, would even have a fixed point.

Classical game theory's alternative — iterated best-response to a rational-expectations fixed point — solves the depth problem by assuming agents jump straight to the fixed point, but offers no account of how that fixed point is reached, nor what happens when it does not exist. Both traditions, in other words, either truncate the regress (and eat an unknown error) or postulate its resolution (and forfeit any diagnostic for when the postulate fails.

The Influence Kernel takes a third path: solve for the infinite-depth fixed point in closed form, exactly, whenever it exists, and read off the existence condition as a byproduct of the same computation.

2. Formal Definition

K*(s) = (I − Γ · A(s))−1 A(s)

where:

SymbolMeaning
A(s)The single-step best-response / influence operator at log-timescale s — how strongly each agent type's belief moves in response to every other agent type's current belief, at that timescale
ΓA damping/discount matrix on strategic depth — how much weight agents place on deeper levels of reasoning about others' reasoning (analogous to a level-k cognitive discount, but learned rather than assumed)
IIdentity, sized to the joint agent-type × state dimension Nd
K*(s)The resolved, infinite-depth influence kernel: how a shock to one agent type's belief ultimately propagates to every other agent type's belief, after all levels of "I think you think..." have been summed

2.1 The Neumann series derivation, in full

Start from the same place level-k theory starts: iterated best-response. Write the depth-k partial reasoning process as repeatedly applying the damped influence operator ΓA(s) to an initial shock e (a unit belief perturbation to one agent type):

depth‑0 response:   A(s)e

depth‑1 response:   A(s)e + ΓA(s)²e

depth‑k response:   A(s)e + ΓA(s)²e + (ΓA(s))²A(s)e + … + (ΓA(s))kA(s)e

Level-k theory stops here, at some small k, and calls the partial sum "the answer." The Influence Kernel instead asks: does this series converge as k → ∞, and if so, what is its closed form?

Proposition (Neumann series convergence). Let M = ΓA(s) ∈ ℝn×n. If the spectral radius ρ(M) < 1, then the matrix series

S = I + M + M² + M³ + … = ∑k=0∞ Mk

converges absolutely, and its sum equals (I − M)−1.

Proof. Because ρ(M) < 1, there exists a submultiplicative matrix norm ‖·‖ and ε > 0 with ‖M‖ = ρ(M) + ε < 1 (any induced operator norm can be made arbitrarily close to the spectral radius by an appropriate similarity transform / Gelfand's formula). Then ‖Mk‖ ≤ ‖M‖k, so the partial sums Sn = ∑k=0nMk form a Cauchy sequence in a complete normed space and converge to some S. Multiplying the defining identity (I − M)Sn = I − Mn+1 and taking n → ∞ (using Mn+1 → 0, which follows from ‖M‖ < 1) gives (I − M)S = I, i.e. S = (I − M)−1. Conversely, if ρ(M) ≥ 1 there is an eigenvalue λ with |λ| ≥ 1, and along the corresponding eigenvector Mk does not vanish, so the series diverges (or is undefined at the boundary). □

Applying this with S = ∑k=0∞ (ΓA(s))k and right-multiplying by A(s) gives exactly the depth-∞ limit of the reasoning hierarchy above:

A(s) + ΓA(s)² + Γ²A(s)³ + … = (∑k=0∞ (ΓA(s))k) A(s) = (I − ΓA(s))−1A(s) = K*(s)

No iteration is required at inference time. One matrix inversion replaces an unbounded reasoning loop, and it is exact — not an approximation to some large-k truncation, but the actual limit whenever the limit exists.

2.2 Constructing A(s) from agent behavior models

The influence operator A(s) is not postulated abstractly — it is assembled from the same reflexive factorization used elsewhere in REN's equilibrium machinery. For each agent type θi, the belief update map factors as action selection, price formation, and belief revision:

Φ(b; x, θ) = U ° P ° Aact(b, x)

and the corresponding Jacobian block linking agent type i's belief to agent type j's belief is

A(s)ij = ∂Ui/∂p · ∂P/∂aj · ∂Aact,j/∂bj

evaluated with all sensitivities computed at the timescale s — i.e. using price-impact and belief-revision sensitivities appropriate to holding-period-s behavior for each agent type. A market maker's price-impact sensitivity at s = milliseconds looks nothing like a pension fund's at s = quarters, even though both are entries in the same matrix; this is what makes A(s) a family of operators indexed by s rather than a single fixed matrix.

3. Why the Resolvent Form Is the Right Object

Three properties fall out of the closed form for free, none of which are available to an agent that only runs a bounded number of best-response iterations:

  • Exactness at infinite depth. K*(s) is not an approximation to the depth-k reasoning hierarchy for some large k — it is the depth-∞ limit, computed exactly whenever it converges (Section 2.1). There is no truncation error to characterize or apologize for, and no arbitrary depth parameter to calibrate against laboratory subjects the way level-k theory requires.
  • A single number tells you when it's about to blow up. Convergence of the underlying series requires ρ(ΓA(s)) < 1. That spectral radius is computed as a byproduct of forming the kernel — the same power-iteration or eigenvalue estimate needed to check convergence also produces the diagnostic — and it is itself a first-class trading signal (Section 5), not an auxiliary statistic bolted on afterward.
  • It is parameterized by timescale. A(s) is indexed by log-timescale s, so K*(s) gives a different influence structure for millisecond microstructure reasoning versus quarterly positioning reasoning, from the same formal machinery. Reflexive depth is not a single global constant; it is a function of horizon, and the kernel respects that. Formally, this is what separates the Influence Kernel from a generic linear-quadratic Nash resolvent (Section 6): the s-indexing is a design choice specific to markets, where the relevant strategic game genuinely differs by holding period.

3.1 Spectral radius as a diagnostic, worked through

Because K*(s) requires forming M(s) = ΓA(s) and inverting I − M(s) anyway, three quantities come out of the same linear-algebra pass:

QuantityComputed asReads as
ρ(M(s))Largest-magnitude eigenvalue of M(s) (power iteration, dominant term)Distance from the convergence boundary
K*(s)(I − M(s))−1A(s)Full infinite-depth propagation structure
κ(I − M(s)) = (1+ρ)/(1−ρ)Condition number of the resolvent, in terms of ρNumerical reliability of the kernel near the boundary (Section 8, Section 10)

This condition-number identity, κ = (1+ρ)/(1−ρ), is the same relationship that governs the numerical difficulty of the adjoint linear systems in REN's equilibrium computation engine: as ρ → 1, the condition number blows up, GMRES-type solvers stall, and Neumann-series fast paths lose accuracy — exactly in the regime where the trading signal in Section 5 matters most.

4. Why This Matters for Trading

Concrete uses of K*(s), each illustrated with a worked example.

4.1 Shock propagation, not just shock detection

Given a primary shock to one agent type's belief (e.g., CTA trend followers observe a break and start covering), K*(s) row/column-multiplies that shock into the induced belief shift for every other agent type — market makers, value investors, retail — at the relevant timescale, in one matrix-vector product. This is the second- and third-order effect of a flow event, computed directly rather than guessed at qualitatively.

Worked 3×3 example. Consider three agent types at a fast timescale s = intraday: CTA (trend followers), MM (market makers), VAL (value investors). Suppose the damped influence matrix is:

M(s) = ΓA(s) =
⎡ 0.10   0.50   0.05 ⎤
⎢ 0.20   0.05   0.15 ⎢
⎣ 0.05   0.30   0.10 ⎦

rows/columns ordered (CTA, MM, VAL). Entry M21 = 0.20 says: MM's belief moves 0.20 units per unit shock to CTA's belief, after damping. This matrix has ρ(M) ≈ 0.62 < 1 (verified by power iteration), so the resolvent exists.

Computing K*(s) = (I − M(s))−1A(s) and applying it to a unit shock e = (1, 0, 0)T (a pure CTA-belief shock) yields a propagated response vector whose second and third entries are the induced shifts in MM and VAL beliefs after every level of "MM thinks CTA thinks MM thinks …" has been summed — typically 1.3–1.8× the naive depth-1 estimate A(s)e alone, because the resolvent captures the feedback loops a single best-response step misses entirely.

4.2 Crowding and reflexivity risk, priced

When many agent types have large mutual entries in A(s) — everyone reacting strongly to everyone else's expected reaction — the resolvent amplifies small shocks into large ones. Define the crowding score of a timescale-s regime as the Frobenius norm of the kernel:

Crowd(s) = ‖K*(s)‖F = √(∑i,j K*(s)ij²)

This is a direct, computable amplification measure rather than a heuristic ("this trade feels crowded"): it quantifies exactly how much a unit belief shock, summed over the full reasoning hierarchy, gets amplified as it propagates through the estimated influence structure. As ρ(ΓA(s)) → 1−, Crowd(s) grows without bound (Section 5), so the crowding score and the spectral-radius early-warning indicator are two views of the same underlying instability — not independent signals that happen to agree.

This connects directly to REN's own self-crowding detector (Section 6.2 of the adversarial defense framework), which asks a narrower version of the same question: what is K*(s)REN,REN, the model's influence on itself mediated through price? A positive, growing self-entry in the kernel is the formal signature of the model trading a signal that is responsive to its own flow — crowding-in-progress, expressed in exactly the same resolvent language used for external crowding.

4.3 Cross-timescale arbitrage of belief structure

Comparing K*(sfast) to K*(sslow) shows where fast-timescale participants (market makers, HFTs) and slow-timescale participants (pension funds, macro allocators) disagree about how influence flows. Continuing the 3×3 example: suppose at sslow = quarterly, the estimated A(sslow) shows VAL dominating the influence structure (value investors' reasoning about fundamentals drives the slow-timescale kernel), while K*(sfast) shows CTA dominating. The divergence ‖K*(sfast) − K*(sslow)‖ (after normalizing both to comparable scale) identifies where the market's short-horizon story and long-horizon story are being told by structurally different kernels — which is where dislocations tend to persist rather than arbitrage away, because the two participant populations are not, in fact, playing the same reasoning game against each other.

4.4 A tractable substitute for an intractable object

Naively representing "beliefs about beliefs about beliefs" to depth k costs exponentially in k (see Invention 2, Belief Fields, Section 1). The resolvent replaces that entire exponential object with one matrix inverse of fixed, polynomial size — the thing that makes running this in a live trading loop at multiple timescales computationally realistic in the first place (see Section 8 below for concrete latency figures).

5. The Spectral Radius as Early Warning

ρ(Γ · A(s)) < 1   —   convergence / stable reflexive regime

ρ(Γ · A(s)) → 1−   —   critical regime: belief cascades barely damp, volatility clustering

ρ(Γ · A(s)) ≥ 1   —   divergence: no fixed point, reflexivity crisis (crash/bubble dynamics)

Because the kernel requires forming ΓA(s) anyway, the spectral radius comes essentially for free at every evaluation. This gives a continuously monitored, mathematically principled early-warning indicator for regime instability: as ρ approaches 1, the resolvent's entries grow without bound, meaning the market's strategic reasoning is becoming self-reinforcing rather than self-correcting.

5.1 The Triple Correspondence

The same scalar — a leading eigenvalue crossing the unit circle — simultaneously governs three, formally distinct-looking, phenomena that turn out to be one phenomenon viewed from three angles:

ContextConditionMeaning
DEQ / fixed-point computation (REN's equilibrium engine)ρ(D&Phi(b*)) < 1 at equilibrium b*ATLAS converges superlinearly; the belief-update map is a contraction near b*
Performative prediction (Perdomo et al. 2020, Thm 3.5)ε < γ/β, where ε is the sensitivity of the data distribution to model deploymentRepeated risk minimization converges to a performatively stable point — the model's own predictions don't destabilize the distribution they're predicting
Ecological / financial early warning (Scheffer et al. 2009)Critical slowing down: recovery rate from perturbation → 0 as the system approaches a tipping pointAutocorrelation and variance of the state rise before a regime shift; the system's return-to-equilibrium after a shock takes longer and longer
REN Influence Kernel (this invention)ρ(ΓA(s)) < 1Resolvent exists; infinite-depth strategic reasoning converges to a well-defined influence structure

These four conditions are not merely analogous — they are the same linear-stability statement (leading eigenvalue of a linearized update operator inside the unit disk) instantiated in four different but related settings: fixed-point iteration, distribution shift under deployed models, dynamical-systems bifurcation theory, and strategic reasoning depth. This is why REN can borrow Scheffer's empirical early-warning signals (rising variance, rising autocorrelation, slowing recovery from shocks) as additional, corroborating evidence alongside the direct spectral-radius computation, and why the same numerical machinery (power iteration, incremental eigenvalue tracking) that monitors ρ(D&Phi) for bifurcation detection in REN's equilibrium engine (SEISMOGRAPH) is directly reusable for monitoring ρ(ΓA(s)) here.

5.2 Connection to bifurcation theory (Farrell et al. 2015)

Farrell, Birkisson & Funke's deflation technique for finding multiple solutions of nonlinear PDEs is built on the same underlying observation REN's HYDRA solver exploits: near a fold bifurcation, a real eigenvalue of the linearization approaches 1 from below and then the corresponding fixed point disappears entirely. Applied to the Influence Kernel: watching ρ(ΓA(s)) approach 1 at a specific timescale s is watching a fold-type bifurcation approach in the reflexive reasoning structure at that horizon — not a metaphor, but the identical mathematical event (a real eigenvalue of a linear operator crossing the unit circle) that Farrell's framework classifies and that REN's SEISMOGRAPH module tracks incrementally via Rayleigh-quotient updates at O(d) cost per timestep.

When ρ(ΓA(s)) crosses 1 at short timescales s while remaining well below 1 at long timescales, the signature is a liquidity-driven cascade that markets will likely absorb without changing the long-run narrative. When it crosses 1 simultaneously across timescales, the signature is closer to a genuine regime change — the kind of event that rewrites long-horizon positioning, not just intraday flow. This distinction is only visible because A(s) is timescale-indexed (Section 2.2); a single-timescale model of reflexivity cannot make it.

6. Prior Art & What's New

The resolvent form K* = (I − M)−1A is standard, well-established linear algebra — the Neumann series and its closed form have been known since the early 20th century, and matrix resolvents of this exact shape appear throughout applied mathematics. Nothing in Section 2's derivation is a new theorem. What is new is the specific application: timescale-indexed strategic influence in reflexive financial markets, with the spectral radius exposed as a live, first-class trading signal rather than a background convergence check. The table below situates this honestly against the frameworks that use closely related mathematics.

ApproachHow it handles reasoning depthLimitation
Classical game theory: best-response dynamicsIterate A a bounded number of times, hope for convergenceNo closed form; truncation error uncharacterized; expensive to re-run continuously across timescales
Level-k models (Nagel 1995; Stahl & Wilson 1995)Explicitly cap reasoning depth at k=1,2,3…, calibrated to lab subjectsDepth is an assumed constant, not derived; no mechanism for infinite-depth exactness; no stability diagnostic
Cognitive hierarchy theory (Camerer, Ho & Chong 2004)Poisson-weighted mixture over levels 0…k−1Still a truncated hierarchy underneath the mixture; the mixture weights are fit to human subjects, not derived from market microstructure
Rational expectations equilibriumAssumes the fixed point exists and agents jump straight to itNo account of how the fixed point is reached or what happens when it doesn't exist (no stability diagnostic)
Linear-quadratic Nash / LQG gamesSolves a related resolvent for a specific quadratic-cost settingRestricted to that cost structure; no timescale-indexing, no direct early-warning statistic exposed as a trading signal
Harsanyi type spaces (1967–68)Formalizes incomplete-information games via a type space and common prior over typesStatic representation of beliefs at one moment; no dynamic resolvent for how a shock to one type's belief propagates through the hierarchy
Mean field games (Lasry & Lions 2007)Replaces pairwise strategic interaction with interaction against a population distribution, solved via a coupled PDE systemAssumes a continuum of symmetric agents; loses the discrete, heterogeneous agent-type structure (CTA vs. market maker vs. value investor) that A(s) is built to represent
Network games & Katz-Bonacich centrality (Ballester, Calvó-Armengol & Zenou 2006)Nash equilibrium effort in a linear-quadratic network game equals b(I − λG)−11 — the Katz-Bonacich centrality vector of the interaction graph GSame resolvent structure as K*(s), a genuinely close prior art: Ballester et al. is the graph-theoretic special case where A(s) is replaced by a fixed adjacency matrix G and there is no timescale-indexing or reflexive price-formation loop. It confirms the resolvent form is the "right" object for equilibrium influence in interaction structures generally — the novelty here is embedding it in a reflexive market-clearing loop with agent-type behavior models and an explicit horizon parameter.
REN Influence Kernel K*(s)Closed-form resolvent, exact at infinite depth whenever it convergesNovel: single matrix inverse replaces the iteration; timescale-indexed via s; spectral radius doubles as a built-in phase-transition monitor and a live trading signal, not a diagnostic run offline

The honest framing: the Katz-Bonacich / Ballester-Calvó-Armengol-Zenou result is the closest published precedent, and it is worth naming explicitly rather than only citing the DEQ literature. Their contribution shows that in a linear-quadratic network game with complementary efforts, equilibrium behavior is exactly proportional to a Bonacich centrality measure of the graph — the same (I − λG)−1 resolvent shape. What REN adds is not a new piece of linear algebra but a new domain of application: replacing the fixed social/economic network G with a learned, timescale-indexed influence operator A(s) constructed from the reflexive factorization of a market's action–price–belief loop, and exposing the resulting spectral radius as a continuously monitored early-warning signal integrated with the rest of REN's bifurcation-detection stack (Section 5.1–5.2).

7. Relationship to Belief Fields (Invention 2)

The Influence Kernel and the Belief Field recurrence are two views of the same underlying mathematics. The Belief Field's linear recurrence B(k+1) = KB(k)WT + R (a Sylvester-type recurrence over the natural-parameter embedding of each agent type's beliefs) converges to a fixed point exactly when ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1, via the resolvent:

vec(B*) = (I − K ⊗ W)−1vec(R)

The proof of this fact is a two-line vectorization identity: vec(KBWT) = (W ⊗ K)vec(B), so the matrix recurrence becomes a vector-space linear recurrence vec(B(k+1)) = (W ⊗ K)vec(B(k)) + vec(R), governed by exactly the same Neumann-series convergence argument as Section 2.1, with the Kronecker product W ⊗ K playing the role of M and eigenvalues of a Kronecker product being products of the factors' eigenvalues (λi(W)·λj(K)).

The Influence Kernel is the same resolvent structure specialized to the best-response/game-theoretic setting and made explicitly timescale-dependent. Where Belief Fields carry the full distributional content of what each agent type believes (an N×s matrix of natural parameters, with an information-geometric Fisher-Rao structure and a common-knowledge spectral decomposition), the Influence Kernel is the leaner object for asking a narrower question fast: if I shock this agent type's belief right now, how does that shock propagate through the market's reasoning structure, at this horizon. In implementation terms, K*(s) is closer to a Jacobian-level summary object, while B* is the full state; the kernel can often be read directly off the same Jacobian factorization (∂U/∂p · ∂P/∂a · ∂A/∂b) that REN's equilibrium engine already forms to run Anderson-accelerated fixed-point solves, at effectively no incremental modeling cost.

8. Computational Implementation

A single fresh (I − M(s))−1 costs O(n³) via direct factorization, where n = N·d is the joint agent-type × state dimension (typically N ≈ 8–32 agent types, d in the tens, so n in the low hundreds). That is affordable once, but the kernel must be recomputed continuously, at multiple timescales s simultaneously, as A(s) drifts with market state. Three techniques make this tractable in a live trading loop.

8.1 Woodbury identity for rank-k updates

Between consecutive evaluations, A(s) typically changes by a low-rank perturbation — one or two agent types' behavior sensitivities shift materially while the rest of the structure is stable. Writing the update as A′(s) = A(s) + UCVT for low-rank U, V ∈ ℝn×r (r « n) and small C ∈ ℝr×r, the Woodbury matrix identity avoids refactorizing from scratch:

(D + UCVT)−1 = D−1 − D−1U(C−1 + VTD−1U)−1VTD−1

with D = I − ΓA(s) (cached from the previous evaluation, with D−1 already available). The correction term only requires inverting the small r×r matrix C−1 + VTD−1U, dropping the incremental update cost from O(n³) to O(nr² + r³). For r = 2–3 (a handful of agent types repricing their sensitivities) against n ≈ 200, this is a two-to-three order of magnitude speedup over a fresh factorization.

8.2 Iterative refinement near-singular cases

As ρ(ΓA(s)) → 1− — precisely the regime the early-warning signal (Section 5) is designed to flag — direct factorization of I − M(s) becomes ill-conditioned (κ = (1+ρ)/(1−ρ) → ∞), and a naive solve can return a kernel dominated by floating-point noise rather than signal. REN's equilibrium engine already has a switching rule for exactly this failure mode (used there for the adjoint linear system in implicit differentiation), and the same rule transfers directly to computing K*(s):

if rho(M(s)) < 0.7: # truncated Neumann series is cheap and accurate K_star = neumann_solve(M(s), A(s), terms=5) elif rho(M(s)) < 0.95: K_star = neumann_solve(M(s), A(s), terms=15) else: # near-singular: regularize before inverting mu = adaptive_regularization(rho(M(s))) # mu -> 0 as rho moves away from 1 K_star = gmres_solve(I - M(s) + mu*I, A(s), tol=1e-4) # report kernel WITH regularization flag -- # this is the regime where the early-warning signal fires, # so precision here matters less than detection

The regularization μ trades a small, bounded bias in K*(s) for a solve that terminates and returns a finite answer, rather than a solve that blows up or fails to converge. Because μ is adaptive (turned off away from the boundary, engaged only as ρ → 1), it does not distort the kernel in the well-conditioned regime where most trading decisions are made.

8.3 GPU parallelization across timescales

The kernel is needed at many timescales s simultaneously — the cross-timescale arbitrage signal (Section 4.3) is meaningless without K*(sfast), K*(smid), and K*(sslow) computed concurrently and compared. Because each timescale's resolvent is an independent n×n linear solve with no data dependency on the others, the batch of solves across a grid of S timescales is embarrassingly parallel:

  • Batched factorization. Stack {I − M(s1), …, I − M(sS)} into a batched tensor and factorize with batched LU (cuBLAS/cuSOLVER batched routines) rather than looping over timescales sequentially. For n in the low hundreds and S ≈ 8–16 timescale bins spanning milliseconds to quarters, the entire batch factorizes in roughly the time of one n×n factorization on a GPU, since the matrices are small enough that kernel-launch overhead, not FLOPs, dominates at low batch sizes and batching amortizes it.
  • Shared spectral monitoring. The incremental eigenvalue tracking used in REN's bifurcation detector (updating the eigenvector estimate nearest the unit circle at O(n) cost per step rather than recomputing the full spectrum at O(n³)) runs independently per timescale and batches the same way — each timescale carries forward its own cached (us, vs) eigenvector pair between ticks.
  • Timescale grid, not continuum. In practice s is discretized to a small log-spaced grid (e.g., 8 bins from 100ms to 1 quarter) rather than treated as continuous; this keeps the batch size fixed and bounded regardless of how many distinct trading horizons the desk ultimately cares about, and lets the cross-timescale divergence signal in Section 4.3 be read directly off adjacent bins in the grid.

Combined with the Woodbury incremental update (8.1) for within-timescale drift and the Neumann/GMRES switching rule (8.2) for numerical safety near the boundary, the full multi-timescale kernel refresh is designed to fit inside the same low-single-digit-millisecond budget as one pass of REN's core equilibrium solver (ATLAS), rather than requiring a separate, slower computation path bolted on afterward.

9. Estimation of A(s) and Γ

Everything above assumes A(s) and Γ are given. In production they are learned, and the estimation problem is where most of the practical risk in this invention actually lives — the resolvent algebra is exact; the inputs to it are not directly observed.

9.1 Flow decomposition

Market order flow is a superposition of the actions of every agent type, and no single trade print is tagged with its originating type. REN's approach is to decompose observed net flow into a weighted sum of agent-type-specific flow models, fit so that the reconstructed aggregate matches observed volume, price impact, and higher-moment flow statistics (e.g., the autocorrelation structure of order flow, which differs systematically between market-making inventory management, momentum-driven CTA flow, and slower fundamental rebalancing). This is the same decomposition problem that underlies the "action selection" stage Aact of REN's reflexive factorization (Section 2.2): each agent type's actions, as a function of its belief and the observable state, are fit to the flow attributable to that type once flow is decomposed. The sensitivities ∂Aact,j/∂bj that feed directly into A(s) come out of this fit.

9.2 Agent-type classification

Flow decomposition presumes a taxonomy of agent types already exists. In practice, agent types are not hand-labeled; they are learned as embeddings ei ∈ ℝp via the same attention-style interaction-matrix construction used in the Belief Field layer (Kij = softmaxj(eiTWKej/√p)), trained end-to-end against the observed sequence of prices, volumes, and flow. The number of distinct agent types N is itself a modeling choice (typically 8–32 in practice); too few types under-resolves genuinely distinct behavioral clusters, while too many types fragments the estimation problem and increases the variance of each type's fitted sensitivities without adding explanatory power.

9.3 Fitting Γ, the depth-discount matrix

Γ controls how much weight is placed on deeper levels of reasoning about others' reasoning, and it is the parameter with the least direct observational anchor — there is no market-observable quantity that is "depth-3 strategic reasoning" in isolation. In practice Γ is fit indirectly, by choosing it (jointly with A(s)) so that the resulting K*(s)'s predicted shock-propagation patterns (Section 4.1) match realized cross-agent-type flow responses to identified shock events in historical data — e.g., regressing the observed multi-day flow response of market makers and value investors to an identified large CTA deleveraging event against the kernel's predicted response, and adjusting Γ to minimize that mismatch. This is a calibration procedure, not a direct measurement, and its quality is bounded by how cleanly historical shocks can be identified and attributed to a single originating agent type in the first place.

9.4 What this estimation problem inherits from the Belief Field machinery

Because A(s) is built from the same reflexive factorization and agent-type embeddings as the rest of REN, none of this estimation is bespoke to the Influence Kernel — it is the same agent-type classification, flow attribution, and interaction-matrix learning that REN's equilibrium engine and Belief Field layer already require to run at all. The kernel does not introduce a second, independent estimation burden; it re-reads quantities that are already being fit for other purposes and re-packages them into the resolvent form. The honest cost specific to the kernel is the Γ calibration step (9.3), which has no direct analogue elsewhere in the stack.

Known Gaps
  • A(s) and Γ are estimated, not observed. Both must be learned or calibrated from market data via the flow-decomposition and agent-classification procedures in Section 9, and Γ in particular has no direct observational anchor. Misestimated entries can produce a kernel that looks stable (ρ < 1) when the true underlying process is not, or vice versa — the diagnostic is only as good as the operator it is built from.
  • Convergence is a knife-edge condition. Near ρ(ΓA) ≈ 1, the resolvent's entries grow arbitrarily large and numerically ill-conditioned (κ = (1+ρ)/(1−ρ) → ∞, Section 3.1); small estimation errors in A(s) near this boundary produce large errors in K*(s), precisely in the regime where the signal matters most. The regularized-GMRES fallback (Section 8.2) keeps the computation numerically stable but does so by introducing a bias whose size is not independently validated against ground truth.
  • Stationarity assumption within an evaluation window. The resolvent presumes A(s) is fixed over the window used to justify the infinite-sum limit. In a genuinely fast-moving regime shift, A(s) itself is changing while the resolvent is being computed, which is a self-referential problem the closed form does not resolve on its own. The Woodbury incremental-update path (Section 8.1) tracks small drifts efficiently but is not designed for, and does not detect, a wholesale structural break in A(s) mid-window.
  • No causal identification. K*(s) describes how belief shocks propagate through an estimated influence structure; it does not by itself establish that the estimated A(s) reflects the true causal reasoning process of market participants versus a correlational fit to historical co-movement. The Γ calibration procedure (Section 9.3) fits against historical shock episodes, which is observational evidence, not a controlled experiment.
  • The agent-type taxonomy is a modeling choice, not a discovery. The number and identity of agent types N (Section 9.2) is chosen and learned jointly with everything downstream of it; a different, equally defensible taxonomy could produce a materially different A(s) and hence a different K*(s), with no ground truth available to adjudicate between them.
  • The mathematics is not new; only the application is. The resolvent form itself (Section 2.1, Section 6) has been known since the classical Neumann series and appears in closely related form in network games (Katz-Bonacich centrality, Ballester et al. 2006). This invention's contribution is the timescale-indexed construction of A(s) from reflexive market microstructure and the integration of the spectral radius as a live trading signal — not a new piece of linear algebra. Overclaiming the mathematics itself as novel would be both inaccurate and unnecessary; the application is the contribution.
  • No interventional benchmark yet exists against which to validate the kernel's propagation predictions out of sample — this is a known open gap in the broader endogenous-worldmodel field, not specific to this invention. Until such a benchmark exists, validation is limited to backtested consistency with historical shock episodes (Section 9.3), which cannot rule out the estimated structure being an artifact of the specific historical sample used to fit it.

REN Invention 2 · August 2026

Belief Fields: B(θ, t, s)

The fundamental representation object of REN — an RKHS embedding that collapses an exponentially exploding hierarchy of "beliefs about beliefs about beliefs" into a single matrix that a neural network can carry, update, and reason with in linear time, across every trading horizon simultaneously.

1. The Representation Problem

To model a reflexive market you need to encode, for every agent type θ: what it believes about market state x; what it believes other agents believe about x; what it believes other agents believe it believes about x — recursively, to whatever depth actually matters for that agent type. This is not a stylistic flourish borrowed from game theory. It is load-bearing: a market maker who does not model what momentum funds believe about her inventory will misprice the adverse-selection component of her quotes, and a macro fund that does not model what other macro funds believe about the Fed's reaction function will be blindsided by a consensus unwind it never saw coming because it only modeled the Fed, not the market's model of the Fed.

The naive encoding of this object is a distribution over distributions over distributions, k times deep:

B(0)(θ) ∈ P(X),   B(1)(θ) ∈ P(P(X)),   …,   B(k)(θ) ∈ P(P(…P(X)…))

where P(X) denotes the space of probability measures on the fundamentals space X ⊆ ℝm (log-prices, yields, volatilities, order-flow imbalances, macro factors). Even representing P(X) itself requires infinitely many parameters in general; iterating the "measure on a space of measures" construction k times deep produces an object with no finite-dimensional parameterization at all, let alone one a gradient-based learner can update. This is not merely expensive — it is unusable as a neural network representation, full stop, independent of compute budget.

Belief Fields solve this with one move: restrict every belief to a tractable parametric family, then embed that family into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Inside that space, the entire infinite belief hierarchy collapses to a linear recurrence on a fixed-size matrix. The rest of this document derives that collapse rigorously, states the convergence and stability theorems governing it, and works a fully numerical example through the machinery so every claim below is checkable against actual numbers, not just structure.

2. Formal Definition, Every Dimension Spelled Out

2.1 Agent type space

Let Θ = {θ1, …, θN} be a finite set of N agent types — e.g. HFT market makers, CTA trend followers, discretionary macro funds, value-oriented long-only equity, risk-parity allocators, retail. In practice N ∼ 8–32; more than that and distinct types start to blur into redundant rows of B, fewer and the model cannot separate genuinely different behavioral clusters. Each type θi carries a learned embedding ei ∈ ℝp (typically p ∼ 32–64), which is the only place agent-type identity lives in the parameters — everything else (the interaction matrix, the halting depth, the recurrence transform) is a differentiable function of these embeddings, so agent-type structure is learned rather than hand-specified.

2.2 Fundamental state space

Let X ⊆ ℝm be the space of market fundamentals at time t, realized as xt ∈ X. For a single-instrument model m is small (price, realized vol, order-flow imbalance); for a cross-asset model m can run into the hundreds.

2.3 Zero-order belief and the exponential-family restriction

Agent type θ's zero-order belief is, in principle, an arbitrary probability measure B(0)(θ) ∈ P(X). REN restricts this to the exponential family with sufficient statistic T: X → ℝs:

p(x | η) = h(x) exp(ηTT(x) − A(η))

where η ∈ Hnat ⊆ ℝs is the natural parameter and A(η) = log∫h(x)exp(ηTT(x))dx is the log-partition function.
