For financial applications the multivariate Gaussian family is used: T(x) = (x, −xxT/2), giving natural parameter η = (Σ−1μ, Σ−1), sufficient-statistic dimension s = m + m(m+1)/2 (mean-precision vector plus the upper triangle of the precision matrix), and log-partition A(η) = −½log det(η2) + ½η1Tη2−1η1 + (m/2)log(2π). This restriction is what makes the belief field finite-dimensional at all: it says every agent's belief, however sophisticated, is representable as a point in a fixed s-dimensional space rather than an arbitrary element of an infinite-dimensional function space.

2.4 The belief field, as a matrix

Bt : Θ → Hnat,   θ ↦ ηt(θ) ∈ ℝs

represented as a matrix   Bt ∈ ℝN×s,   row i = ηt(θi)

This N×s matrix is the fundamental representation object of REN, playing the same architectural role that the token embedding matrix plays in a transformer: everything downstream (predictions, regime signals, the Influence Kernel of Invention 1) is a differentiable function of Bt, and nothing about market beliefs is represented anywhere else in the model.

The subscript t denotes real time. The full object is written B(θ, t, s) with a third argument, log-timescale s (in the sense used by the Influence Kernel, Invention 1) — the horizon over which the belief is being reasoned about, from milliseconds (s ≈ −3 in log₁₀-seconds) to quarters (s ≈ 7). Section 6 makes precise how the belief field at one timescale relates to the belief field at another; until then, treat s as a fixed index and Bt = B(·, t, s) as the object of interest.

SymbolDimensionMeaning
Nscalar, ∼8–32number of agent types
mscalardimension of the fundamentals space X
sm + m(m+1)/2dimension of the natural-parameter / sufficient-statistic space
pscalar, ∼32–64dimension of agent-type embedding ei
BtℝN×sbelief field at time t: row i is agent type i's natural parameter
KℝN×Ninteraction matrix (Section 3.3)
Wℝs×slearned linear transform on the natural-parameter space (Section 4)

3. Why an RKHS Embedding, Specifically

3.1 The kernel mean embedding

Let k: X × X → ℝ be a characteristic kernel (e.g. Gaussian RBF). The kernel mean embedding of a distribution P is:

μP = 𝔼x~P[k(x,·)] ∈ H

Theorem 3.1 (Sriperumbudur et al. 2010, injectivity). For a characteristic kernel, the map P ↦ μP is injective: distinct distributions have distinct embeddings. No information is lost by moving from the space of measures to the RKHS.

This single fact is the reason the embedding is safe to use as the representation of a belief rather than a lossy compression of one. Combined with the exponential-family restriction of Section 2.3, it yields the second fact that does the real work: for exponential families, the kernel mean embedding is a deterministic, differentiable function of the natural parameter,

μp(·|η) = φ(η),   φ: Hnat → H differentiable and injective

i.e. the RKHS embedding of an exponential-family belief is fully determined by a finite-dimensional vector η. This is what licenses working entirely in ℝs instead of the (generally infinite-dimensional) RKHS H itself: the RKHS is the space in which the argument for tractability is made (injectivity, linearity of expectation), but the actual computation never has to leave Hnat.

3.2 Higher-order beliefs collapse to weighted sums of embeddings

Agent type θ's first-order belief — belief about the population of other agents' zero-order beliefs — is a distribution over the embeddings {μB(0)(θ') : θ' ∈ Θ}. Its own kernel mean embedding is, by linearity of expectation:

μB(1)(θ) = 𝔼θ'~π(·|θ)[μB(0)(θ')] = ∑θ' π(θ'|θ) φ(η(θ'))

where π(θ'|θ) is agent type θ's model of how prevalent type θ' is in the population. The critical move: this is now a finite linear combination of finitely many embeddings, not an integral over a space of measures. Iterating — belief about beliefs about beliefs — simply nests this weighted sum inside itself, and because expectation is linear, the nesting never re-introduces the exponential blowup of the naive encoding. That is the entire content of "the RKHS embedding is needed": it is the mechanism by which an operation (marginalizing over a distribution of distributions) that is a genuinely infinite-dimensional operation in measure space becomes a finite-dimensional linear operation in the embedding space.

3.3 The interaction matrix

Define the interaction matrix K ∈ ℝN×N with Kij = π(θj|θi) — "how much agent type i thinks agent type j is present in the market." K is row-stochastic (each row is a probability distribution over types) but is not symmetric: HFTs may believe CTAs dominate flow while CTAs' own model of the population under-weights HFTs. Rather than hand-specify K, REN learns it as an attention matrix over agent-type embeddings:

Kij = softmaxj(eiTWKej / √p),   WK ∈ ℝp×p learned

This is exactly the query-key attention computation of a transformer, specialized to a fixed, small vocabulary (agent types instead of tokens) and interpreted as a probability model over "who is in the market" rather than as an opaque attention weight.

4. The Sylvester Recurrence: Full Derivation

4.1 From the embedding-space sum to a natural-parameter recurrence

Section 3.2 gave the embedding of a first-order belief as a weighted sum of embeddings of zero-order beliefs. To make this a recurrence purely on natural parameters — the object REN actually stores and updates — posit that going from depth k to depth k+1 also applies a learned linear transform W ∈ ℝs×s and bias b ∈ ℝs to each contributing natural parameter before mixing, plus an agent-specific residual r(θi) ∈ ℝs anchoring the update to that agent's own private information:

η(k+1)(θi) = ∑j Kij[Wη(k)(θj) + b] + r(θi)

Writing B(k) ∈ ℝN×s for the matrix whose i-th row is η(k)(θi), the sum over j weighted by Kij is exactly the matrix product (KB(k)WT)i·, and the row-wise addition of b and r(θi) is exactly the matrix 1bT + R where 1 ∈ ℝN is the all-ones vector and R ∈ ℝN×s stacks the residuals. So:

B(k+1) = K[B(k)WT + 1bT] + R

Absorbing the bias term into R (define R' = K1bT + R, then drop the prime) gives the canonical form used throughout the rest of this document:

B(k+1) = KB(k)WT + R

This is a discrete-time Sylvester recurrence — each step applies a linear map on the left (mixing across agent types, via K) and a linear map on the right (transforming the natural-parameter coordinates, via WT), plus an additive forcing term R that is constant across depth k (it represents each agent's own information, which does not change as you reason about deeper levels of "what do others think"). It is named for its resemblance to the continuous Sylvester equation AX + XB = C from control theory, though here it is a recurrence rather than a single algebraic equation — the fixed point of the recurrence (Section 5) is the corresponding discrete Sylvester/Stein equation.

4.2 Unrolling the recurrence in closed form

Unrolling from B(0):

B(1) = KB(0)WT + R

B(2) = K(KB(0)WT + R)WT + R = K2B(0)(WT)2 + KRWT + R

⋮

B(k) = ∑j=0k−1 KjR(WT)j + KkB(0)(WT)k

By induction: assume the formula holds at step k; then B(k+1) = K·B(k)·WT + R = ∑j=0k−1Kj+1R(WT)j+1 + Kk+1B(0)(WT)k+1 + R, which re-indexes to the claimed formula at k+1 (the j=0 term of the new sum is exactly the added R). This closed form is what turns "run the recurrence k times" into an explicit finite sum — useful for reasoning about convergence, and for the depth-truncation argument of Theorem 10.4 below.

5. Convergence via ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1 — Full Proof

5.1 Vectorization and the Kronecker identity

The standard identity for matrix equations of the form AXB is vec(AXB) = (BT ⊗ A)vec(X), where vec stacks the columns of a matrix into a single vector and ⊗ is the Kronecker product. Applying this to KB(k)WT with A = K, X = B(k), B = WT (so BT = W) gives:

vec(KB(k)WT) = (W ⊗ K) vec(B(k))

so the recurrence B(k+1) = KB(k)WT + R becomes, after vectorizing both sides, an ordinary linear recurrence in ℝNs:

vec(B(k+1)) = (W ⊗ K) vec(B(k)) + vec(R)

5.2 When a linear recurrence converges

A linear recurrence v(k+1) = Mv(k) + c converges to a fixed point, for every initial condition v(0), if and only if every eigenvalue of M has modulus strictly less than 1 (spectral radius ρ(M) < 1). This is standard linear-systems theory: writing the error e(k) = v(k) − v* relative to any fixed point, e(k) = Mke(0), and Mk → 0 as k → ∞ iff ρ(M) < 1 (Jordan-form argument: each Jordan block's k-th power is bounded by a polynomial in k times λk, which vanishes iff |λ| < 1).

5.3 The eigenvalues of a Kronecker product

Lemma. If K has eigenvalues λ1,…,λN and W has eigenvalues μ1,…,μs, then W ⊗ K has eigenvalues {μaλb : a ∈ {1,…,s}, b ∈ {1,…,N}}. Proof. If Ku = λu and Wv = μv, then (W ⊗ K)(v ⊗ u) = (Wv) ⊗ (Ku) = μλ(v ⊗ u), using the mixed-product property (A ⊗ B)(C ⊗ D) = (AC) ⊗ (BD). So v ⊗ u is an eigenvector of W ⊗ K with eigenvalue μλ. There are Ns such products, matching the dimension of W ⊗ K, and (generically, when K and W are each diagonalizable) they exhaust the spectrum. □

It follows immediately that ρ(W ⊗ K) = ρ(K)·ρ(W), and since K is row-stochastic, ρ(K) = 1 exactly (Perron–Frobenius: the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1, and no eigenvalue of a row-stochastic matrix exceeds 1 in modulus). So the entire burden of convergence falls on W:

Theorem 4.2 (Convergence of the belief hierarchy). Because ρ(K) = 1 always (row-stochasticity), the recurrence B(k+1) = KB(k)WT + R converges for every B(0) if and only if ρ(W) < 1 — i.e. convergence of the belief hierarchy reduces entirely to a spectral condition on the learned natural-parameter transform W, independent of how many agent types N there are or how the interaction matrix K is structured. The general statement ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1 is stated for the case where K is not exactly row-stochastic (e.g. under a soft/temperature-scaled interaction matrix, or during training before the softmax has saturated), in which case ρ(K) can differ from 1 and both factors matter.

When the condition holds, taking k → ∞ in the closed form of Section 4.2 gives the fixed point directly, since KkB(0)(WT)k → 0 and the geometric-type sum ∑j=0∞ KjR(WT)j converges absolutely:

vec(B*) = (INs − K ⊗ W)−1 vec(R)

which is well-defined precisely because ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1 guarantees 1 is not an eigenvalue of K ⊗ W, so INs − K ⊗ W is invertible. Equivalently, B* solves the discrete Lyapunov/Stein equation B* = KB*WT + R — the algebraic equation whose iterative solution is exactly the recurrence of Section 4.

Economic reading. ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1 means beliefs are contractive: each additional level of "what does θ think θ' thinks…" carries strictly less weight than the level before it. This is the formal statement of bounded strategic depth. When ρ ≥ 1, the geometric sum diverges, there is no fixed point, and the recurrence is an unstable belief cascade — the mathematical signature of a reflexivity crisis (crash or bubble dynamics; Theorem 10.2, Section 10).

6. Multi-Scale Structure: How Belief Fields at Different Timescales Interact

Every object defined so far — K, W, R, and hence B itself — is implicitly indexed by the log-timescale s at which the reasoning is being carried out: K(s), W(s), B(θ, t, s). This is not a bookkeeping convenience; it reflects a real structural fact about markets: an HFT market maker's belief hierarchy over the next 50 milliseconds is a different mathematical object — different agent weightings, different effective interaction structure — from a discretionary macro fund's belief hierarchy over the next two quarters, even when both are reasoning about the same underlying instrument.

6.1 Coupling across scales

The belief fields at different timescales are not independent; they are coupled through two channels:

  • Shared fundamentals. B(·, t, s) at every s is initialized from the same underlying observation zt (Section 8), so a genuine change in fundamentals shows up, with different lag and different weighting, in belief fields across the entire timescale axis.
  • Cross-scale interaction weighting. The interaction matrix K(s) itself is timescale-dependent: at short s (milliseconds), K(s) is dominated by rows/columns for HFTs and market makers — the types whose beliefs are actually being revised at that cadence — while CTA and value-investor rows are close to a slowly varying constant (their beliefs don't meaningfully update within a millisecond window, so they act as an almost-fixed boundary condition on the fast-timescale recurrence). At long s (quarters), the roles invert: HFT beliefs average out to a stationary microstructure prior, while CTA and macro-fund rows carry the active reasoning.

Formally, this is implemented by letting the agent-type embeddings themselves be modulated by s through a learned timescale-conditioning map g: ℝ → ℝp, ei(s) = ei + g(s, θi), so that K(s)ij = softmaxj(ei(s)TWKej(s) / √p) becomes continuously deformable in s without introducing a separate parameter block per timescale bucket — a single shared WK, one lightweight conditioning function g.

6.2 What the multi-scale structure buys, concretely

Because K(s) ⊗ W(s) is evaluated per timescale, the spectral-radius stability condition of Theorem 4.2 is also evaluated per timescale, and it need not hold or fail uniformly. A market can be in a stable regime at short timescales (microstructure noise damps out normally, market makers' beliefs converge quickly to a consensus quote) while simultaneously approaching instability at long timescales (macro positioning is coiling toward a regime change that hasn't yet been priced into second-by-second flow) — or the reverse, a short-timescale liquidity air-pocket with no long-horizon narrative behind it. Comparing ρ(K(s) ⊗ W(s)) across the s axis is therefore a direct, quantitative decomposition of "where in horizon-space is the market's belief structure fragile right now" — not a single global stability number, but a curve.

This is the same structural relationship the Influence Kernel (Invention 1) uses when comparing K*(sfast) to K*(sslow): a divergence between what fast-timescale participants' propagation structure implies and what slow-timescale participants' propagation structure implies identifies exactly where the market's short-horizon story and long-horizon story are being told by structurally different kernels — the belief field is the richer, distributional object underlying that comparison; the Influence Kernel is the leaner shock-propagation operator built on top of it.

7. The Retraction Problem, Depth Truncation, and the Neural Forward Pass

7.1 Keeping the natural parameter valid

Every step of the recurrence must keep η inside Hnat; for the Gaussian family this means the precision block η2 = Σ−1 must stay positive definite. Three retractions are available:

  • Cholesky parameterization. Write η2 = LLT with L lower-triangular, diagonal passed through softplus to force positivity. Cheap, but the recurrence's linear update on η must be applied in Cholesky-factor space, which breaks the clean linear-algebra form of Section 4 unless handled carefully.
  • Matrix exponential. η2 = expm(S) for unconstrained symmetric S; differentiable via the Fréchet derivative of the matrix exponential. Always valid, but expm and its gradient cost O(m3) per call, which is non-trivial at the sizes used per agent type per recurrence step.
  • Sufficient-statistics parameterization (recommended). Parameterize the mean-parameter pair directly: η1 = 𝔼[X] = μ (unconstrained), η2 = 𝔼[XXT] = Σ + μμT, with η2 = softplus-diag(L)LT + η1η1T. This guarantees Σ = η2 − μμT is positive definite by construction and keeps the recurrence's linear structure intact in the mean-parameter (rather than natural-parameter) coordinates.

None of the three is uniformly best; the design choice trades computational cost against optimization friction and is left as an open implementation decision per deployment (see Known Gaps).

7.2 Adaptive depth via Adaptive Computation Time

Not every agent type reasons to the same depth: a retail investor doesn't model what hedge funds think about what market makers think; a top quant fund does. Rather than fix depth Kmax globally, REN learns a per-type halting distribution (Graves 2016, adapted):

h(k)(θi) = σ(whTη(k)(θi) + ch)

p0(θi) = h(0)(θi),   pk(θi) = h(k)(θi) ∏j=0k−1(1 − h(j)(θi))

η*(θi) = ∑k=0Kmax pk(θi)η(k)(θi),   depth(θi) = ∑k k·pk(θi)

This is fully differentiable end-to-end; a ponder loss λdepth∑idepth(θi) penalizes unnecessary depth so the network only pays the computational cost of reasoning a given agent type actually needs.

7.3 Forward pass, initialization to output

INPUT: z_t ∈ R^d_z (raw market observation: prices, volumes, order flow, news embeddings) Step 1 — Initialize zero-order beliefs from data, via agent embeddings: B_t^(0) = (E W_E) z_t W_z^T + E W_b [E ∈ R^{N×p} agent embedding matrix] Step 2 — Compute (possibly time-varying, timescale-conditioned) interaction matrix: K_t(s) = softmax( (E + f(z_t) + g(s)) W_K (E + f(z_t) + g(s))^T / sqrt(p) ) Step 3 — Run the belief hierarchy recurrence with adaptive halting: for k = 0 .. K_max: B_t^(k+1) = retract( K_t(s) · B_t^(k) · W_recur^T + R_t ) h^(k) = sigma(B_t^(k) w_h + c_h) accumulate B_t^(k+1) weighted by p_k Step 4 — Output effective belief field: B_t* = sum_k p_k B_t^(k) ∈ R^{N×s} Step 5 — Decode to market prediction (Section 9, market clearing): y_t = Decode(B_t*)

7.4 Multi-head belief attention

Generalizing the single interaction matrix to H heads lets different agent types attend to different aspects of one another's beliefs simultaneously — e.g. one head tracking beliefs about fundamentals, another tracking beliefs about positioning/crowding:

Kth = softmax(EWKhET / √(p/H)),   Bt(k+1) = (1/H)∑h KthBt(k)(WVh)T + Rt

8. Computational Complexity and Tractability

Per recurrence step, forming KB costs O(N2s) (an N×N matrix times an N×s matrix), and forming (·)WT costs O(Ns2) (an N×s matrix times an s×s matrix), for a total per-step cost of O(Ns(N+s)). Over a depth-Kmax hierarchy, total cost is O(Ns(N+s)Kmax).

ConfigurationPer-step costFull hierarchy (K_max=8)
N=16, s=64∼65K multiply-adds∼520K multiply-adds
Reference: transformer self-attention, 512 tokens, d=256—∼67M multiply-adds

The belief hierarchy is over 100× cheaper than a single transformer self-attention layer, because N (agent types) is orders of magnitude smaller than a typical sequence length and s (sufficient statistics) is orders of magnitude smaller than a typical model dimension d. This is the property that makes it feasible to maintain belief fields per instrument, per timescale, continuously updated in a live trading loop, rather than as an offline research artifact computed overnight.

Two further tractability levers, both used in production:

  • Implicit differentiation instead of storing the unrolled graph. When the recurrence is run to its fixed point (Section 5) as a Deep-Equilibrium-style implicit layer, the backward pass uses the implicit function theorem rather than backpropagating through every unrolled step: solve (I − dF/dB)Tv = dL/dB* by conjugate gradient (Bai et al. 2019, Jacobian-free method), then dL/dθ = vTdF/dθ. Memory cost is O(Ns), constant in depth, versus O(Ns·Kmax) for naive unrolled backprop.
  • Adaptive depth truncation (Theorem 10.4). An agent type with effective depth K(θ) can be ε-approximated by a depth-1 agent iff ||Bprivate(k)(θ)|| ≤ C·|λ2|k with C|λ2|/(1−|λ2|) < ε, where λ2 is the spectral gap of K (Section 6 of the underlying theory, common-knowledge decomposition). In coordinated markets (small λ2) most agent types can be truncated cheaply; only in fragmented markets (λ2 close to 1) does depth genuinely matter, and the ACT mechanism of Section 7.2 spends compute there automatically.

9. Concrete Numerical Example

Take N = 4 agent types — HFT market makers (MM), CTA trend followers (CTA), discretionary macro funds (MACRO), value-oriented long-only equity (VAL) — and a single fundamental (log price of the S&P 500 E-mini), so m = 1 and s = m + m(m+1)/2 = 2 (natural parameters η1 = μ/σ², η2 = 1/σ²).

Interaction matrix K (rows = "who I think is in the market"), at a short timescale s ≈ seconds:

KMMCTAMACROVAL
MM0.550.300.100.05
CTA0.250.500.150.10
MACRO0.100.200.450.25
VAL0.050.150.200.60

Each row sums to 1 (row-stochastic). Note the asymmetry: MM assigns CTA a 0.30 weight, but CTA only assigns MM a 0.25 weight — market makers think trend-followers dominate flow slightly more than trend-followers think market makers do, a plausible microstructure fact (HFTs watch for CTA-sized clips; CTAs mostly watch price, not who is quoting).

Natural-parameter transform W = 0.6·I2 (a simple contraction, chosen for this worked example so ρ(W) = 0.6). Then ρ(K ⊗ W) = ρ(K)·ρ(W) = 1 × 0.6 = 0.6 < 1: the hierarchy converges, geometrically, at rate 0.6 per depth level.

Zero-order beliefs B(0), expressed as (μ, σ) for readability (index price at 4,800, in percent return space so μ is bps/day):

Agentμ₀ (bps/day)σ₀ (bps/day)Reading
MM060no directional view, prices two-sided around fair value
CTA+3590trend-following, currently long, wide realized-vol estimate
MACRO−1575modestly bearish on a growth-slowdown thesis
VAL+1050mildly constructive on valuation, low vol estimate (long horizon)

Applying one step of the recurrence η(1)(MM) = W∑jKMM,jη(0)(θj) + r(MM) — ignoring the residual for illustration and working in μ directly for intuition — MM's first-order belief about "what the market believes" is the K-weighted average of the others' μ₀, contracted by W:

μMM(1) ≈ 0.6 × [0.55(0) + 0.30(35) + 0.10(−15) + 0.05(10)] = 0.6 × [10.5 − 1.5 + 0.5] = 0.6 × 9.5 ≈ 5.7 bps/day

i.e. even though MM's own zero-order view is flat (μ₀=0), MM's first-order belief — "what does the market as a whole believe" — is mildly bullish, pulled upward by MM's model of CTA positioning, which MM weights heavily (0.30). This is exactly the kind of quantity a market maker's inventory-skew logic needs and that a model without an explicit belief hierarchy cannot produce: it is not MM's own view, and it is not a simple average of everyone's view — it is MM's model of the consensus, correctly weighted by MM's own (learned) sense of who matters.

Common-knowledge decomposition (Section 5 of the underlying framework, spectral). K's second eigenvalue for this matrix is λ2 ≈ 0.34 (row-stochastic matrices this close to diagonal-dominant typically have a moderate spectral gap 1−λ2 ≈ 0.66). A moderate gap means private beliefs decay reasonably fast (∼0.34k) — by depth 3, private components are down to ∼4% of their initial magnitude, so most of the belief hierarchy's content is captured by depth 2–3 for this population, consistent with real markets where 3–4 levels of "I think you think" reasoning captures the overwhelming majority of strategic depth outside of genuinely fragmented or crisis regimes.

10. RKHS Embedding & Resolvent: Connection to the Influence Kernel

The Belief Field recurrence and the Influence Kernel of Invention 1 are two views of the identical resolvent structure. The Influence Kernel is defined as K*(s) = (I − Γ·A(s))−1A(s), the fixed point of iterating a single best-response operator A(s) damped by a strategic-depth discount Γ. The belief field's fixed point vec(B*) = (INs − K ⊗ W)−1vec(R) is the same Neumann-series resolvent, at higher fidelity: where the Influence Kernel propagates a single belief-shock vector through a single best-response operator, the belief field carries the entire distributional content of every agent type's belief (the full natural parameter, not just a shock direction) and factors the propagation operator into two learned pieces — K (who influences whom) and W (how a natural parameter transforms per level of reasoning) — rather than one undifferentiated operator A(s).

Concretely: K*(s) answers "if I shock agent type i's belief right now, how does that shock propagate to every other type's belief, at this horizon" in one matrix-vector product against a shock vector. The belief field answers the broader question "what does every agent type currently believe, about the world and about every other type's beliefs, to whatever depth matters" and is the object K*(s) is applied to (or derived as an approximation of, in the special case where you only care about propagation of a single shock rather than the full hierarchy). The RKHS embedding of Section 3 is what makes it possible to carry that fuller distributional object at the same asymptotic cost as the leaner shock-propagation operator: both reduce to an O(N2)-to-O((Ns)2)-sized linear-algebra problem rather than an intractable object growing with reasoning depth.

The shared diagnostic follows directly: ρ(K ⊗ W) crossing 1 and ρ(ΓA(s)) crossing 1 are the same phase-transition signature (Theorem 10.2), read off two different resolvents built from the same underlying reflexive-reasoning process. In practice both are monitored together: a divergence between where the two spectral radii sit (e.g. the belief-field resolvent showing more contraction margin than the leaner Influence-Kernel resolvent at the same timescale) is itself informative — it says the fuller distributional structure of beliefs is more stable than the single-shock propagation channel, which can happen when disagreement is concentrated in a narrow subspace of the belief space that the Influence Kernel's coarser operator does not resolve.

11. The "Belief PDE" Naming Issue — Addressed Directly

Elsewhere in this specification, the timescale-indexed belief-evolution machinery is referred to as the "Multi-Scale Belief PDE." That name is not accurate for the object actually defined here, and the imprecision is worth resolving explicitly rather than leaving it to a reader's charitable interpretation.

What is actually specified, in this document and in the companion component, is a discrete recurrence: B(k+1) = KB(k)WT + R, indexed by a discrete depth k (belief-hierarchy order) and evaluated at discrete points s along the log-timescale axis. No partial differential operator appears anywhere in the derivation — there is no ∂B/∂t, no ∂B/∂s, no spatial Laplacian or drift-diffusion term of the kind that would justify the name "PDE." The genuine PDE framework for this class of problem is mean-field games (Lasry & Lions 2007), which write a coupled Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman / Fokker–Planck system in continuous time and continuous population-density state, and that is a substantively different (and substantively harder to make tractable) mathematical object than what is specified here.

Two honest paths forward, neither of which is "leave the name as-is":

PathWhat it requiresAssessment
A: Derive the genuine continuum limitLet the depth index k and/or timescale index s become continuous. For the depth axis: define B(τ) via B(k+1) − B(k) = (K − I)B(k)WT + (K−I)R-type corrections as Δτ → 0, which formally yields an ODE dB/dτ = (K−I)BWT + R in depth — a linear matrix ODE, not yet a PDE. Getting an actual PDE additionally requires treating the timescale axis s as a continuous spatial-like variable with an explicit coupling term between adjacent s, which is not currently specified anywhere — Section 6 above defines coupling through shared initialization and a smoothly-varying K(s), not through a differential operator in s. This path is well-posedness work that has not been done: function spaces, existence/uniqueness, and a rigorously derived coupling term in s would all need to be stated and proven.Substantial, currently-unstarted mathematical work; would make the name accurate but is not a small fix.
B: RenameCall the component what it is: "Multi-Scale Belief Recurrence" (matching the actual object: a discrete linear recurrence, evaluated across a discrete or densely-sampled grid of timescales s).Costs nothing mathematically, immediately accurate, and loses no capability described anywhere in this document — every claim above (convergence, common knowledge, complexity, the numerical example) is stated for the recurrence as defined, not for a PDE.
This document does not adopt path A. Everything derived above — the Sylvester recurrence, its closed form, the ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1 convergence theorem, the multi-scale coupling of Section 6 — is stated and proven for the discrete recurrence, which is the object that is actually implementable and actually implemented. Referring to it as a "PDE" anywhere in investor- or researcher-facing material is a precision error that should be corrected to "Multi-Scale Belief Recurrence" (path B) unless and until the continuum-limit derivation of path A is carried out and independently checked.

12. Prior Art: Type Spaces and Harsanyi's Framework

The belief field is not a new object in the sense of solving a problem game theory hadn't already posed — Harsanyi (1967–68) introduced type spaces precisely to make incomplete-information games with infinite belief hierarchies tractable, by positing a common prior over types and letting each type's beliefs about others be derived from that prior via Bayesian updating, rather than specified as an independent infinite regress. The belief field's contribution is representational: it is a specific, finite-dimensional, differentiable, and learned instantiation of a Harsanyi type space, suitable for use as a layer inside a neural network trained end-to-end on market data.

Theorem 10.1 (Representation universality). For any Harsanyi type space (Θ, T, p) with finite types and beliefs restricted to the exponential family, there exists a belief field B ∈ ℝN×s and interaction matrix K ∈ ℝN×N such that the recurrent hierarchy B(k) = KB(k−1)WT + R exactly represents the k-th order beliefs of the type space, for every k. Sketch: set Kij to the common-prior conditional probability that type j is present given type i's information (Harsanyi's own construction gives this directly), set the rows of B(0) to each type's zero-order belief natural parameters, and take W = Is (no additional distortion beyond the mixing implied by K); the resulting recurrence reproduces exactly the iterated-expectation construction Harsanyi's framework defines by hand at each order. Belief Fields generalize this by learning K and W from data rather than assuming a known common prior, and by folding in a differentiable, adaptive-depth mechanism (Section 7.2) that Harsanyi's original formulation has no analogue for.

PropertyHarsanyi type spacesTransformer embeddingSSM hidden stateBelief Field
ObjectType space + belief hierarchy (abstract)Vector in ℝdVector in ℝnMatrix in ℝN×s
Higher-order beliefsDefined, but representation is exponential in depth without the common-prior shortcutNone (flat)Implicit (time only)Explicit, collapsed to linear recurrence via RKHS
Common priorAssumed, fixed a prioriN/AN/ANot assumed — K is learned per-episode, can be asymmetric across agent types
GeometryNot specifiedEuclideanEuclideanFisher-Rao (Riemannian, information-geometric)
Multi-agent structureNative but staticVia attention over tokens, not agentsNoneNative, learned interaction matrix K (attention over agent types)
Common knowledgeDefined axiomatically (Aumann 1976)NoneNoneComputed via spectral decomposition of K
EquilibriumStatic (Bayesian Nash)NoneNoneDynamic fixed point (DEQ-style, reflexive: prices feed back into beliefs)
Trainable end-to-end on dataNoYesYesYes

Belief Fields are, in this precise sense, not a departure from the classical game-theoretic object but a representation of it that a neural network can actually carry, update, and learn in real time — with an explicit information-geometric structure (Fisher-Rao metric on the natural parameters, natural-gradient updates, Bregman-divergence KL computation, geodesics on the Gaussian manifold) that neither the abstract Harsanyi formulation nor the standard transformer/SSM representations provide.

13. Why This Matters for Trading

  • Volume as a supervised target, not a nuisance variable. Under the market-clearing model (mean-variance demand, precision-weighted price aggregation), trading volume is proportional to belief dispersion: Volume ∼ ||B − BCK||F2, the Frobenius norm of the private (disagreement) component of the belief field. This is a second, independently observable supervision signal beyond price: a model whose belief dispersion doesn't predict observed volume is wrong in a checkable way, not just a way that shows up eventually in P&L.
  • Prices as precision-weighted belief aggregation, and therefore invertible. The equilibrium price under mean-variance demand is p* = [∑i(wi/γi)Σi−1]−1[∑i(wi/γi)Σi−1μi] — the decode function from belief field to tradeable prediction. Because it is differentiable in B, observed prices can be used to infer a belief field via an initialization loss solved by implicit differentiation through the clearing equation, closing the loop between market data and the belief representation.
  • Reflexivity as a first-class fixed point. Prices don't just result from beliefs; they feed back into them: Bt+1 = F(Bt, zt, p*t(Bt)), computed as a Deep Equilibrium Model with O(Ns) memory regardless of reasoning depth — a self-consistent belief-price loop running at production cost, not a stylized assumption made once at model-design time.
  • Graded common knowledge maps directly onto tradeable information categories. The λ=1 spectral component is common knowledge (e.g. the Fed funds rate, already fully arbitraged). Components near λ ≈ 0 are highly private (e.g. a specific fund's positioning, not yet reflected in price). Components in between are "almost common knowledge" (e.g. a macro-consensus shift most, but not all, participants have priced in). Which regime a piece of information sits in tells you directly whether it still has propagation left to run.
  • Multi-scale disagreement as a term-structure trade. Comparing the private-component decay rate λ2(s) across timescales s (Section 6) identifies whether disagreement is concentrated at short horizons (likely to resolve quickly, favors a mean-reversion or liquidity-provision posture) or persistent at long horizons (a genuine structural divide in market participants' worldviews, favors carrying a directional or dispersion position through the horizon over which it resolves).
  • Cheap enough to run continuously. At N=16, s=64, depth 8: ∼520K multiply-adds per full hierarchy pass, over 100× cheaper than a single transformer self-attention layer — making it feasible to maintain belief fields per instrument, per timescale, updated continuously in a live trading loop.
What is genuinely new here, stated precisely. Not the idea of a type space (Harsanyi, 1967) and not the idea of a kernel mean embedding (Sriperumbudur et al., 2010) — both pre-date this work by decades. What is new is the specific composition: restricting Harsanyi-style belief hierarchies to the exponential family, embedding them via kernel mean embeddings to prove the hierarchy collapses to a finite linear recurrence, learning (rather than assuming) both the interaction structure K and the natural-parameter transform W as attention-style differentiable functions of agent-type embeddings, indexing the entire structure by a continuous log-timescale s so a single object serves every trading horizon, and wiring the whole thing into a Deep-Equilibrium-style reflexive fixed point so that prices and beliefs are mutually consistent at inference time rather than assumed consistent at design time.
Known Gaps
  • Exponential-family restriction. The tractable recurrence depends on beliefs being restricted to an exponential family (Gaussian, in practice). This is a real restriction on the shapes of beliefs the model can represent — multimodal or fat-tailed belief distributions (e.g. genuine bimodal bull/bear disagreement within a single agent type) must be approximated, not represented exactly, without extending to mixture-of-exponential-family beliefs, which is not currently specified.
  • The retraction problem has no clearly best answer. The three proposed retractions (Cholesky, matrix exponential, sufficient-statistics parameterization) each add either computational cost or optimization friction; none is obviously best across regimes, and the choice has not been validated empirically against real market data at the time of writing.
  • K and W are learned, not derived from first principles. The interaction matrix and the natural-parameter transform are fit to data. A poorly identified K can produce a spectral gap λ2 that misrepresents true market fragmentation, with no independent ground truth to check it against beyond the volume-prediction supervision signal of Section 13.
  • Convergence is conditional, not guaranteed. The fixed point exists and the recurrence (or its DEQ forward pass) converges only when ρ(K ⊗ W) < 1. Near that boundary, both the forward iteration and the implicit-differentiation backward pass become numerically fragile — exactly the regime (a reflexivity crisis) where getting the answer right matters most.
  • The multi-scale coupling of Section 6 is currently ad hoc. The timescale-conditioning function g(s, θ) is a learned map with no derived functional form; nothing currently guarantees that K(s) varies smoothly or consistently across s beyond what the training objective happens to induce. This is the same gap that motivates Section 11's discussion of whether a genuine continuum-limit (PDE) formulation should be derived.
  • The "Belief PDE" naming issue (Section 11) is unresolved in the broader specification. As documented above, no PDE currently exists anywhere in this framework; the object is a discrete recurrence. This should be corrected by rename ("Multi-Scale Belief Recurrence") unless a rigorous continuum-limit derivation is carried out.
  • No interventional validation yet exists. Theorem 10.1's representation-universality result is a statement about expressiveness, not about whether the learned B, K, and W correspond to real agents' real reasoning processes versus a well-fit correlational surface. This is the same open interventional-benchmark gap noted for the Influence Kernel (Invention 1) and is a known gap across the broader endogenous-worldmodel field, not specific to this component.

14. Implementation Notes

  • Numerical stability near ρ ≈ 1. Compute ρ(K ⊗ W) as a monitored quantity at every training step (via power iteration on the vectorized operator, O(Ns) per iteration, not a full eigendecomposition), and apply a soft penalty or hard spectral-normalization projection on W to keep training away from the singular boundary, since gradients through the resolvent blow up as ρ → 1.
  • Agent-type count N as a hyperparameter, not a design constant. Validate N empirically per instrument class: too few types under-resolves genuinely distinct behavioral clusters (merging HFTs and CTAs, say, loses the asymmetric-interaction structure that matters most for adverse-selection modeling); too many types over-parameterizes K relative to available data and produces unstable, high-variance interaction-matrix estimates.
  • Warm-starting the recurrence from the previous timestep's fixed point. Because B*t and B*t−1 are typically close (markets don't fully re-equilibrate belief structure tick to tick), initializing the forward iteration from the previous solution rather than from B(0) cold dramatically reduces the number of iterations needed to reach tolerance, analogous to the neural-warm-start technique used in the Equilibrium Engine (Invention 3).
  • Testing the sufficient-statistics retraction (Section 7.1, Option C) end-to-end before committing to production. It has the best theoretical properties (guarantees positive-definiteness by construction, preserves linear structure in mean-parameter coordinates) but has not been benchmarked against the Cholesky and matrix-exponential alternatives on live market data; this benchmarking is a concrete, scoped, currently-open implementation task.
  • Volume-prediction auxiliary loss (Section 13) as a training-time sanity check, not just an inference-time signal. Because it is a second, independently observable supervision target, wiring it in during training (not only monitoring it post hoc) directly constrains K and the private/common-knowledge decomposition to be consistent with an observable outside of price alone, which meaningfully narrows the identification problem noted in Known Gaps above.

REN Invention 3 · August 2026 · Expanded Technical Reference

The Equilibrium Computation Engine: ATLAS + HYDRA + SEISMOGRAPH

A damped fixed-point solver that finds every self-consistent belief a market can hold, tracks how those beliefs move as the market moves, and watches the space between them for the moment a regime breaks. This is the computational core of REN: the object it computes — the reflexive equilibrium — is the model's output, not an internal detail hidden behind it.

0. The Central Object

REN's belief update map is Φ(b; x, θ) : 𝔹 → 𝔹, where b ∈ 𝔹 ⊆ ℝd is the belief vector, x is the observable market state (prices, order flow, fundamentals), and θ are learnable parameters. A reflexive equilibrium is a fixed point b* satisfying:

Φ(b*; x, θ) = b*

Equivalently, defining the residual g(b) = Φ(b; x, θ) − b, a reflexive equilibrium is a zero of g. Solving for b* is not a subroutine bolted onto a forecasting model — it is the entire forward pass of REN, and everything downstream (dispersion pricing, regime alerts, position sizing) reads off the equilibrium set the three engines below compute.

The reflexive factorization. Φ decomposes into three economically meaningful stages, and this factorization is not cosmetic — it is the computational lever every algorithm in this document exploits:

Φ(b; x, θ) = Uθ ° Pθ ° Aθ(b, x)
  1. Aθ(b, x) → a: given beliefs b and observables x, agents choose actions a (portfolio allocations, trade sizes, hedging ratios).
  2. Pθ(a, x) → p: the aggregate of all actions determines new prices p through a market-clearing mechanism.
  3. Uθ(p, x) → b′: given observed prices and fundamentals, agents form updated beliefs.

The Jacobian inherits the same factored structure:

DΦ = ∂U/∂p · ∂P/∂a · ∂A/∂b
   (price sensitivity) × (price impact) × (belief elasticity)

Each factor is a d×d matrix with distinct spectral properties. ATLAS uses this factorization to build its market-structure preconditioner (Section 1.3); SEISMOGRAPH uses it to read stability economically rather than as an opaque matrix (Section 3.1). Belief dimension d runs 64 (single-asset, compressed beliefs) to 512 (multi-asset, full cross-sectional beliefs) in practice; every algorithm below is designed and benchmarked for that range.

1. ATLAS: The Core Fixed-Point Solver

Adaptive Trajectory-Lifted Acceleration for Self-consistent Solutions. ATLAS combines three components: (i) a neural warm-start that predicts approximate equilibria, (ii) a market-structure-aware Anderson acceleration that converges to exact solutions, and (iii) an adaptive damping scheme that guarantees convergence even when Φ is not a contraction.

1.1 Neural Warm-Start Module

A feedforward network ψθ : ℝdx → ℝd maps the observable market state x directly to an approximate equilibrium:

b0 = ψθ(x)

Architecture. 3-layer MLP with [512, 256, d] hidden units, GELU activations, LayerNorm. ~400K parameters at d=256.

Training target. For each training sample (xi, bi*) where bi* is the converged equilibrium found by full iteration, minimize:

ℒwarm = ‖b0 − b*‖2 + λr‖g(ψθ(x))‖2

The second term penalizes the residual at the warm-start point directly, encouraging predictions that are already near-fixed-points even if the exact fixed point drifts during training. With a good warm-start, the number of Anderson iterations drops from 30–50 (cold start) to 3–8. At d=256 and CΦ ≈ 0.2ms per evaluation, this saves 5–10ms per inference — the difference between usable and unusable at trading speed.

1.2 Market-Structure Preconditioned Anderson Acceleration

Standard Anderson acceleration solves:

α* = argminα : ∑α=1 ‖Gkα‖22

where Gk = [gk−m+1, …, gk] collects the last m residuals. The iterate is then bk+1 = Bkα* + βGkα*, where Bk collects the last m iterates and β ∈ (0, 1] is a mixing/damping parameter. Intuitively: rather than taking the raw Picard step bk+1 = Φ(bk), ATLAS finds the affine combination of the last m iterates whose residual has minimum norm, then mixes it with the residual direction itself — extrapolation, not bisection.

The market-structure preconditioner. Financial beliefs have economic structure: beliefs about correlated assets should update together; no-arbitrage constraints link beliefs across maturities; cross-sectional factor structure concentrates belief updates in a low-dimensional subspace. Plain Anderson acceleration treats all d coordinates of the residual as equally informative, which wastes acceleration capacity on directions the belief map barely moves in. We precondition with a learned metric M ∈ ℝd×d:

α* = argminα : ∑α=1 ‖M1/2Gkα‖22

M is not a fixed matrix. It is updated every q iterations using the empirical covariance of residuals — the adaptive Mahalanobis preconditioner:

Mk = (1/m GkGkT + εI)−1

This learns which directions in belief space have large residuals and concentrates the acceleration along those directions, rather than treating co-moving assets or maturity-linked beliefs as independent unknowns.

Computational cost. The preconditioned solve requires a Cholesky factorization of GkTMkGk ∈ ℝm×m. Since m (the Anderson window) is typically 5–10, this is O(m3) ≈ O(1000) flops — negligible relative to a Φ evaluation. The preconditioner update itself is O(md2) but only runs every q ≈ 5 iterations, so its amortized cost per step is O(md2/q).

We fix memory depth m = 5 as the production default (the design sweep tested m ∈ {3, 5, 8, 12}; m=5 was the knee of the convergence-vs-cost curve — larger windows reduce iteration count only marginally past that point while the O(m3) and O(md2) terms keep growing). The history buffer holds the last 5 iterates and residuals; each new accepted step evicts the oldest pair (FIFO), and a fresh Anderson solve is re-run from a smaller effective window whenever a backtracking event (Section 1.4) forces a restart, since old history computed under a rejected step direction is no longer trustworthy.

1.3 Adaptive Damping via Safeguarded Line Search

When Φ is not a contraction (spectral radius ρ(DΦ) ≥ 1), Anderson acceleration can diverge. Financial belief maps are often non-contractive near bifurcation points — precisely when accurate computation matters most, and precisely where a solver that silently diverges is the most dangerous failure mode to ship.

Algorithm: ATLAS Damped Step
Input: candidate iterate bk+1AA from Anderson acceleration,
    current best iterate bk, current residual norm ‖g(bk)‖

1.  Set β = 1.0  (full Anderson step)
2.  btrial = (1−β)·bk + β·bk+1AA
3.  Compute ‖g(btrial)‖
4.  While ‖g(btrial)‖ > (1 − αβ)·‖g(bk)‖:  // Armijo condition
    β ← ρ·β   // ρ = 0.5, backtrack
    btrial = (1−β)·bk + β·bk+1AA
    recompute ‖g(btrial)‖
5.  If β < βmin:  // βmin = 0.01
    fall back to plain Picard: bk+1 = bk + βmin·g(bk)
6.  Return btrial, β

The Armijo parameter α = 10−4 and backtracking ratio ρ = 0.5 are standard choices. The key design decision is the fallback to Picard iteration: when Anderson acceleration fails entirely (the optimization landscape is too curved for the extrapolation to help), a small step in the raw residual direction is guaranteed to make progress whenever g is non-degenerate at that point — it converts a hard failure into a slow-but-monotone one.

1.4 Convergence Guarantees

Theorem (Convergence of ATLAS). Let Φ : 𝔹 → 𝔹 be continuously differentiable with bounded Jacobian ‖DΦ‖ ≤ L. Suppose the warm-start b0 = ψθ(x) satisfies ‖g(b0)‖ ≤ ε0. Then:

(a) If ρ(DΦ(b*)) < 1 at the target fixed point (stable equilibrium), ATLAS converges superlinearly with rate O(ε02k/(2k−1)) for window m and iteration k.

(b) If ρ(DΦ(b*)) ≥ 1 (unstable equilibrium), the safeguarded line search guarantees ‖g(bk)‖ is monotonically non-increasing, and ATLAS converges linearly with rate at most 1 − αβmin.

(c) Total Φ-evaluations to reach ‖g(bk)‖ < ε:

K ≤ Kwarm + log(ε0/ε) / log(1/(1−αβmin))

where Kwarm ≈ 5–8 is the typical accelerated-iteration count, and dominates whenever convergence is superlinear.

Proof sketch. Part (a) follows from Toth–Kelley (2015) on Anderson acceleration convergence for contractive maps: the preconditioning by Mk is a similarity transform on the residual space and does not change the order of convergence, only the constant. Part (b) follows directly from the Armijo line search's sufficient-decrease guarantee: ‖g(bk+1)‖2 ≤ (1 − 2αβk)‖g(bk)‖2 at every accepted step, and since βk ≥ βmin whenever the fallback does not trigger, the worst-case per-step contraction factor is bounded below. Part (c) is the telescoping sum of (a) and (b): superlinear convergence dominates the iteration budget in the common case (stable target), and the linear bound is the floor guarantee that never gets worse than plain damped fixed-point iteration.

1.5 Comparison to Vanilla Picard Iteration and Newton's Method

Three baselines are worth naming explicitly, because ATLAS is a composition of ideas from all three rather than a wholesale replacement of any one of them:

MethodPer-step costConvergence orderHandles unstable fixed points?Failure mode
Picard iteration (bk+1=Φ(bk))CΦLinear, rate ρ(DΦ)No — diverges when ρ≥1Silent divergence near bifurcation, the worst possible time
Newton's method (on g)CΦ + O(d3) per Jacobian solveQuadratic locallyYes, in principleFull d×d Jacobian solve every step is too slow at d=256 for tick-rate use; global convergence is not guaranteed without its own line search
Plain Anderson accelerationCΦ + O(m3)Superlinear (contractive regime)No — iterates Φ directly, so it inherits Picard's divergence outside the contraction regimeSame as Picard near/at bifurcation, just with a faster crash
ATLAS (warm-start + preconditioned Anderson + safeguarded line search)CΦ + O(m3+m2d) typicalSuperlinear when stable, linear-with-floor otherwiseYes — the line search minimizes ‖g‖2 rather than iterating Φ, so it converges to any zero, stable or notDegrades gracefully to Picard at βmin rather than diverging

The Newton comparison matters because it is the natural alternative a numerical analyst would reach for first: full quadratic convergence, well-understood theory. It is rejected here specifically because the O(d3) Jacobian factorization at d=256 costs roughly 16.7M flops per step before any line search, versus O(m3) ≈ 125 flops for the Anderson solve at m=5 — a five-order-of-magnitude gap that is the entire reason ATLAS exists rather than "just run Newton." The trade is real: ATLAS gives up Newton's quadratic local rate for superlinear, in exchange for a per-step cost that is dominated by CΦ rather than a dense matrix factorization.

1.6 Complexity Summary and the 1.4ms Benchmark

OperationCostFrequency
Warm-start ψθ(x)O(d·512)Once
Φ evaluationO(CΦ), CΦ ≈ 0.2msK times
Anderson solve (m×m linear system)O(m3+m2d)K times
Preconditioner updateO(md2)K/q times
Line search (backtracking)O(nbt·CΦ)Rare (only near bifurcation)
The 1.4ms figure. For a single equilibrium at d=256, m=8, K=6 accelerated iterations: 0.1ms (warm-start) + 6×0.2ms (Φ evaluations) + 0.05ms (Anderson overhead, no backtracking) ≈ 1.4ms. This number carries three conditions that matter for how it should and should not be cited: (1) it assumes the warm-start lands close enough that K=6 iterations suffice — a cold start with no warm-start module runs 30–50 iterations, or 5–10× slower; (2) it assumes Φ's spectral radius is comfortably below 1 at the target equilibrium, so the safeguarded line search never has to backtrack — near a bifurcation, backtracking adds nbt extra Φ evaluations per step and the effective cost rises; (3) it is the cost of finding one equilibrium, not the full multi-equilibrium forward pass — see Section 2.5 and 7.3 for the honest full-pipeline latency, which is materially higher.

2. HYDRA: Finding All Equilibria

Homotopy-Yielded Discovery with Recursive Avoidance. A single market state x may support multiple self-consistent belief equilibria — an optimistic equilibrium (agents believe prices will rise, so they buy, prices rise, beliefs confirmed) and a pessimistic equilibrium (mirror image, equally self-consistent). Finding one and stopping is a modeling error: it silently averages away a structural bimodality the market actually contains.

2.1 Deflation: Repelling from Known Solutions

After finding b1* via ATLAS, define the deflated residual:

g̃(b; {b1*}) = Mdef(b; b1*) · g(b)

where the deflation operator, for known solutions b1*, …, bk*, is:

Mdef = ∏i=1k (1/‖b−bi*‖p + 1) · I  +  σ ∑i=1k (b−bi*)(b−bi*)T / ‖b−bi*‖p+2

The first term (scalar deflation, from Farrell–Birkisson–Funke 2015) inflates the residual near known solutions, preventing re-convergence to a point already found. The second term (directional deflation, novel to REN) additionally curves the landscape away from known solutions along the approach direction — without it, a solver approaching tangentially can still slip past the scalar barrier. We use p = 2 and σ = 0.1.

Key property. g̃(b) = 0 if and only if g(b) = 0 and b ∉ {b1*, …, bk*}. The deflated map preserves every other zero of g exactly — deflation removes known equilibria from the solution set without distorting where the remaining ones are.

Algorithm: HYDRA-Deflate
Input: market state x, parameters θ, max_equilibria Kmax, failure_limit Nfail
Output: equilibria {b*1, …, b*K} with stability labels

1.  found ← [ ], failures ← 0
2.  while |found| < Kmax and failures < Nfail:
    a. generate initial guess b0:
        if |found| == 0: use warm-start ψθ(x)
        else: sample b0 ~ Uniform(𝔹), or perturb a known equilibrium along the homotopy tangent (Sec 2.2)
    b. run ATLAS on the deflated map g̃(b; found) from b0
    c. if converged to b* with ‖g(b*)‖ < ε:
        if b* not within δ of any member of found: found.append(b*); failures ← 0
        else: failures += 1  // re-discovered a known equilibrium
    d. else: failures += 1  // did not converge
3.  return found

2.2 Smart Initialization via Homotopy Continuation

Random restarts inside HYDRA-Deflate are wasteful in high dimension. Instead, HYDRA continues a parameterized family of maps from a trivial known solution to the real problem:

H(b, λ) = (1−λ) · gsimple(b)  +  λ · g(b)

where gsimple(b) = b − bref has a single known zero at bref (e.g. the mean of the belief space). At λ=0, H has exactly one zero. As λ increases to 1, that zero moves continuously toward a zero of g — but new zeros can also appear through bifurcation events along the homotopy path itself, and pseudo-arclength continuation is what lets HYDRA catch them as they're born rather than only finding whatever the single tracked branch lands on.

Algorithm: Homotopy Path Tracker
Input: start (bref, λ=0), target λ=1, step size ds

1.  Tangent computation: solve for the null vector [db, dλ] of [DbH | DλH] at the current point; normalize ‖(db, dλ)‖ = 1
2.  Predictor step: (bpred, λpred) = (bcurr, λcurr) + ds·(db, dλ)
3.  Corrector step (Newton on the augmented system):
    solve [DbH, DλH; dbT, dλ] · [δb; δλ] = [−H(bpred,λpred); 0]
    update (bpred, λpred) += (δb, δλ); repeat to convergence
4.  Bifurcation detection: if det(DbH) changes sign between consecutive points:
    a new branch has emerged — locate the branch point by bisection,
    initialize a new path tracker on the new branch, continue both branches

The power of homotopy over random restart: it automatically discovers new equilibria as they bifurcate into existence along the path, rather than hoping a random initial guess happens to land in a new basin of attraction.

2.3 Tracking Multiple Equilibria Simultaneously

HYDRA does not run its deflation loop and homotopy tracker as two independent, sequential procedures. In production the two are interleaved: the homotopy path tracker maintains a set of active branches, one per equilibrium discovered so far, and advances all of them together as λ (or, once at λ=1, as the live market state x) evolves. Each active branch carries its own local Jacobian estimate, its own deflation-adjusted residual (deflated against every other active branch, not just fully-converged ones), and its own convergence status. When a branch's determinant sign-flip signals a new bifurcation point, a new branch is spawned and added to the active set; when a branch's ATLAS solve fails to converge within the failure budget, that branch is retired and logged as a fold event rather than silently dropped. This is what lets HYDRA report "3 equilibria, one newly destabilizing" as a single coherent snapshot rather than three independent single-equilibrium solves that happen to have run in the same tick.

2.4 Equilibrium Probability Assignment

Given K equilibria {b1*, …, bK*}, weights {w1, …, wK} representing "how likely is the market to coordinate on each" are assigned by three methods, used at different cadences:

Method 1 — Basin volume. wi ∝ Vol({b ∈ 𝔹 : Φ(∞)(b) = bi*}), estimated via Monte Carlo: sample Nmc random initial beliefs, run ATLAS from each, count convergence targets. At Nmc=500 and ~1ms per ATLAS run, this costs ~500ms — far too slow for real time, so basin maps are precomputed and cached rather than run per-tick.

Method 2 — Boltzmann weighting by stability. Define stability energy Ei = log ρ(DΦ(bi*)), then wi = exp(−Ei/T) / ∑j exp(−Ej/T). Temperature T is a learnable parameter: at T→0, all weight concentrates on the most stable equilibrium; at T→∞, uniform. This is O(K) cost and is what runs in real time.

Method 3 — Stochastic stability (novel). Inject noise into the belief dynamics: bk+1 = Φ(bk) + σξk, ξk ~ 𝒩(0, I). The invariant measure μσ of this stochastic process concentrates on the stochastically stable equilibria: as σ→0, it concentrates on equilibria with the largest basins under noise, which can differ from the largest basins without noise when one basin is large but fragile (easily perturbed out of) versus small but robust-boundaried. Computed by a long ergodic trajectory and histogram — expensive, run only in overnight calibration.

In production: Method 2 for real-time inference, Method 3 for overnight recalibration of the Boltzmann temperature and as a cross-check on Method 2's rankings.

2.5 Complexity, and the Honest Latency Picture

OperationCost
First equilibrium (ATLAS)~1.4ms
Each additional equilibrium (deflated ATLAS)~2–3ms (deflation term adds overhead to every Φ evaluation)
All K equilibria~1.4 + 2.5(K−1) ms
Stability analysis (spectral radius)O(d2) per equilibrium via power iteration
Basin volume (Monte Carlo, cached)500ms (precomputed, not on the hot path)
The <15ms-for-5-equilibria claim, precisely stated. Plugging K=5 into the formula above gives 1.4 + 2.5×4 = 11.4ms, comfortably under 15ms — and that number is correct as a complexity-model extrapolation. But it describes the bifurcation-regime case: a market state where five genuinely distinct, well-separated equilibria coexist and all need to be found and deflated against one another. That is not the common operating point. In the typical single-asset setting, HYDRA finds 1–3 equilibria (Section 8.2's genericity theorem predicts an odd count, and 3 is the standard case: stable bull, stable bear, unstable tipping point between them). Reaching 5 simultaneously-tracked equilibria means the market is near a higher-order singularity (a cusp or swallowtail in the catastrophe-theoretic sense — see the CONTINUATOR discussion in the source design doc), which is intrinsically rarer and also intrinsically slower to resolve cleanly, because deflated ATLAS solves near a near-degenerate Jacobian converge more slowly per Section 1.4(b). Citing "<15ms for 5 equilibria" as if it were the typical forward-pass latency overstates throughput by roughly 4–6× relative to the common case below.

Forward-pass latency, stated honestly: the common case — warm-start, ATLAS to one equilibrium, HYDRA finding 1–2 more, SEISMOGRAPH and CONTINUATOR bookkeeping — runs at ~7ms (see Section 7.3's full budget). The bifurcation regime — 4–5 simultaneously tracked equilibria, deflated ATLAS solves each paying backtracking overhead because the underlying Φ is close to non-contractive by definition near a higher-order bifurcation — runs at ~20–25ms. Both numbers matter for capacity planning: 7ms sustains roughly 140 updates/second, which is the number to budget against for steady-state operation; 20–25ms sustains roughly 40–50 updates/second, which is the number to budget against for the handful of names, at the handful of moments, when the market is actually deciding between multiple self-consistent futures — which is also exactly when the output matters most and slower service is a defensible trade.

3. SEISMOGRAPH: Bifurcation Detection and Distance Measurement

Spectral Early Identification of Structural Metamorphosis via Operator Gradient Resonance Analysis, Phase Heuristics. A bifurcation occurs when an equilibrium appears, disappears, changes stability, or splits — the mathematical signature of regime change. SEISMOGRAPH detects this in real time, continuously, at every tracked equilibrium.

3.1 The Spectral Monitor

At each converged equilibrium b*, compute the Jacobian J = DΦ(b*) and monitor its spectrum. Bifurcation occurs when an eigenvalue crosses the unit circle |λ| = 1.

Bifurcation typeEigenvalue behaviorFinancial interpretation
Saddle-node (fold)Real λ→1−, then disappearsEquilibrium ceases to exist. The regime that "made sense" no longer does. Crash or forced repricing.
TranscriticalReal λ crosses through 1Two equilibria exchange stability. Gradual regime rotation, "new normal" replacing the old.
PitchforkReal λ→1−, splits into two branchesOne equilibrium splits into two. Bull/bear polarization, dispersion spike.
Period-doubling (flip)Real λ→−1Oscillatory instability. Choppy, trend-reversing regime, increasing amplitude.
Neimark–Sacker (discrete Hopf)Complex pair |λ|→1Equilibrium becomes a limit cycle. Persistent oscillation, characteristic-frequency vol regime.

3.2 Efficient Eigenvalue Tracking

Full eigendecomposition of J ∈ ℝd×d costs O(d3) — too expensive at d=256 to pay every tick. SEISMOGRAPH tracks only the dangerous eigenvalues: those nearest the unit circle. Between timesteps, J changes by a small perturbation ΔJ, and the eigenvalue nearest 1 shifts by approximately:

Δλ ≈ vT(ΔJ)u / vTu

where u, v are the right and left eigenvectors of J for eigenvalue λ. Maintaining u, v from the previous timestep and applying this incremental Rayleigh-quotient update costs only O(d) per tracked eigenvalue — three orders of magnitude cheaper than recomputation. SEISMOGRAPH tracks the top ncrit = 3 eigenvalues nearest the unit circle by default (one slot for each bifurcation family: real positive, real negative, complex pair), giving O(ncrit·d) = O(d) per timestep, with a full Arnoldi-iteration recomputation every Trefresh = 100 steps at cost O(d2·ncrit) to correct any drift the incremental update has accumulated.

3.3 Distance to Bifurcation

δbif(b*) = minλ ∈ σ(DΦ) | |λ| − 1 |

This is the distance of the nearest eigenvalue to the unit circle. When δbif→0, a bifurcation is imminent. The normalized bifurcation distance accounts for the rate of approach, not just the current gap:

δ̂bif(t) = δbif(t) / (|δ̇bif(t)| + ε)

This has units of time: an estimated countdown to bifurcation, assuming the current rate of approach continues. When δ̂bif < τwarn (calibrated to ~50 timesteps, i.e. 5–10 seconds of warning at a 100ms update rate), SEISMOGRAPH emits a bifurcation warning. This is a linear extrapolation, not a guarantee — the actual approach can accelerate, decelerate, or reverse, which is precisely why it is stated as an estimated countdown and paired with the confidence-degradation machinery of Section 3.6, not treated as a deterministic clock.

3.4 Critical Slowing Down (Scheffer 2009)

Near a bifurcation, a dynamical system's return-to-equilibrium after perturbation slows down — a well-documented early-warning signal in ecology and climate science (Scheffer et al., Nature 2009, "Early-warning signals for critical transitions"). SEISMOGRAPH exploits the same phenomenon inside the solver itself, without needing an explicit eigendecomposition: monitor the observed ATLAS convergence factor ρconv = ‖gk+1‖/‖gk‖. In normal operation ρconv ≈ 0.1–0.3 (superlinear convergence from Anderson acceleration). Near a bifurcation, ρconv→1 — convergence slows to linear or stalls entirely, because the map is losing contractivity in exactly the direction the solver needs to move. A running average of ρconv exceeding 0.8 for nstall consecutive solves is flagged as "critical slowing down" — a second, independent early-warning channel to the direct spectral monitor, cheap enough (it's a byproduct of ATLAS's own bookkeeping) to run on every solve at zero marginal cost.

3.5 The Triple Correspondence

The Triple Correspondence. Three quantities that arise from entirely different literatures turn out to be the same signal, read through three different lenses:
ρ(DΦ) → 1Spectral radius of the belief-update Jacobian (this document, Section 3.1–3.2)
ρconv → 1ATLAS's own convergence-factor stall (Section 3.4)
ε < γ/βPerdomo et al. 2020, Theorem 3.5 — the performative-stability threshold on the sensitivity of the outcome distribution to model deployment, violated as the ratio approaches unity
Scheffer indicatorCritical slowing down in the ecology/climate early-warning literature (Scheffer et al. 2009), the same "return-to-equilibrium speed collapses near a tipping point" phenomenon

All four are statements about the same underlying fact: the map governing the system's return to equilibrium is losing its contraction property. REN's contribution is not discovering that this correspondence exists in the abstract — Perdomo's performative-stability condition and Scheffer's critical-slowing-down indicator are each well established independently in their own fields — but wiring all three into a single real-time monitor with a shared numerical representation (the spectral radius of DΦ), so that a fold warning, a performative-instability warning, and a critical-slowing-down warning are not three separate systems that might disagree, but three readings of one number.

3.6 The Neural Bifurcation Predictor (Novel)

Spectral monitoring has a fundamental blind spot: it only detects bifurcations of the equilibrium it is already tracking. It cannot see the birth of a brand-new equilibrium appearing from nowhere (the other half of a saddle-node pair). A small network 𝒮φ is trained to predict bifurcations from the trajectory of fixed-point iterations, not just the converged Jacobian:

pbif = 𝒮φ(g0, g1, …, gK, Japprox)

where gk are the residuals from the most recent ATLAS solve and Japprox is a low-rank approximation of the Jacobian (top-r singular values/vectors, r=16). Architecture: 1D temporal convolution over the residual sequence (captures convergence-rate patterns), concatenated with the flattened singular-value spectrum, 2-layer MLP head. Output: 4-dimensional (pfold, ppitch, pflip, phopf) — probability of each bifurcation type within the next H timesteps. Trained on trajectories generated by sweeping parameters θ through known bifurcation points; the model learns precursor signatures directly: pre-fold convergence stalling, pre-pitchfork oscillation between two attractors before settling, pre-Hopf spiraling with growing amplitude. ~50K parameters, ~0.01ms inference — negligible overhead layered on top of the spectral monitor.

3.7 The Bifurcation Event Report

BifurcationEvent {
  type: FOLD | PITCHFORK | FLIP | HOPF | UNKNOWN
  confidence: float in [0,1]
  distance: float  // estimated timesteps to bifurcation, δ̂bif
  affected_equilibrium: index into current equilibrium set
  eigenvalue_trajectory: last 100 values of the critical eigenvalue

  // For FOLD: which equilibrium will disappear?
  disappearing_equilibrium: index
  surviving_equilibrium: index (if any)

  // For PITCHFORK: what are the nascent branches?
  branch_directions: two unit vectors in belief space

  // Trading implications
  regime_change_probability: float
  expected_volatility_multiplier: float
  recommended_action: HEDGE | REDUCE | MONITOR
}

3.8 Real-Time Monitoring Architecture

SEISMOGRAPH runs as a persistent process attached to every currently-tracked equilibrium in the CONTINUATOR's active-branch set (Section 6 of the source design doc), not as a one-shot check triggered by a trading decision. Each tick: (1) the incremental Rayleigh-quotient update refreshes the ncrit tracked eigenvalues per branch at O(d) cost; (2) the critical-slowing-down check reads ρconv off ATLAS's own last solve at zero marginal cost; (3) the neural bifurcation predictor runs on the residual trajectory of the last solve at ~0.01ms; (4) every 100 ticks, a full Arnoldi refresh corrects drift in the tracked eigenvalues at O(d2ncrit). Outputs from all four channels are fused into a single δ̂bif and confidence score per branch, following the same explicit-uncertainty design principle used elsewhere in RecWM's monitoring stack: state the countdown and its confidence, do not silently collapse disagreement between channels into a single number without surfacing that it happened.

3.9 Complexity

OperationCostFrequency
Incremental eigenvalue updateO(ncrit·d) = O(d)Every timestep
Full Arnoldi recomputationO(d2·ncrit)Every 100 steps
Neural bifurcation predictorO(K·d)Every timestep
Critical slowing down checkO(1)Every timestep

At d=256: < 0.05ms per timestep for continuous monitoring of one branch, plus ~0.5ms every 100th step for the Arnoldi refresh — SEISMOGRAPH is never the bottleneck in the combined forward pass.

4. The Self-Impact Layer Inside the Same Machinery

A structurally identical fixed-point problem arises one level up from the market-belief equilibrium: the model's own prediction, once acted on, becomes part of the state it predicted. This is performative prediction (Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, Hardt 2020) specialized into an implicit layer:

p* = T(p*; s, θ)

where T is the transition/impact operator: given a candidate prediction p, state s, and parameters θ, it returns the prediction the model would actually make after accounting for the market's reaction to a prediction of that magnitude. A self-consistent p* survives its own impact. This is solved with the exact same ATLAS machinery described in Section 1 — same Anderson acceleration, same safeguarded damping, same PHANTOM-style implicit differentiation for training (Section 5 of the full REN design doc) — applied to T instead of Φ. It is deliberately not a separate solver stack: sharing infrastructure means a spectral-radius reading of DpT at p* is directly comparable, and directly corroborating, with a SEISMOGRAPH reading of DΦ at the underlying belief equilibrium — two engines flagging instability together is a stronger signal than either alone. Deep treatment of this layer (confidence degradation, multiplicity of self-consistent predictions, the crowding and execution-footprint caveats that make it necessary despite RecWM's small-fund "pure reader" assumption) lives in Invention 4; it is noted here because Sections 1–3 are its entire computational substrate.

5. Integration: The Full Forward Pass

FUNCTION REN_Forward(x, θ):
  // Step 1: warm start, ~0.1ms
  b_0 = WarmStart(x, θ)

  // Step 2: first equilibrium via ATLAS, ~1.4ms
  b1_star, converged, iterations = ATLAS(
    Phi = λ b: Φ(b, x, θ), b_0 = b_0,
    tol = 1e-6, max_iter = 50, anderson_window = 5
  )

  // Step 3: chaos check (Lyapunov Sentinel, full REN doc §5)
  lambda_max = LyapunovSentinel.estimate(iterations)
  if lambda_max > 0.1: return ChaosOutput(analyze_attractor(Φ, b_0))

  // Step 4: additional equilibria via HYDRA, ~2–3ms each
  all_equilibria = HYDRA_Deflate(Φ, x, θ, known=[b1_star], max_equilibria=5, failure_limit=10)

  // Step 5: probability weights, ~0.1ms
  weights = BoltzmannWeights(all_equilibria, Φ, θ, temperature=T_learned)

  // Step 6: SEISMOGRAPH bifurcation monitoring, ~0.15ms for 3 equilibria
  for i, b_star in enumerate(all_equilibria):
    stability[i] = SEISMOGRAPH.monitor(b_star, Φ, θ)
  bifurcation_distance = min(s.delta_bif for s in stability)
  bifurcation_type = stability[argmin(...)].predicted_type

  // Step 7: branch-tracking update (CONTINUATOR), ~0.1ms
  landscape = CONTINUATOR.update(all_equilibria, weights, stability)

  return EquilibriumOutput(equilibria=all_equilibria, weights=weights,
    stability=stability, bifurcation_distance=bifurcation_distance,
    bifurcation_type=bifurcation_type, chaos_flag=(lambda_max > 0), landscape=landscape)

5.1 Latency Budget

ComponentLatencyNotes
Warm-start0.1ms3-layer MLP
ATLAS (first equilibrium)1.4ms6 iterations average, stable target
HYDRA (find 2 more)5.0msDeflation + re-solve, common case
Weight assignment0.1msBoltzmann formula
SEISMOGRAPH (3 equilibria)0.15msIncremental eigenvalue tracking
CONTINUATOR update0.1msPredictor-corrector
Lyapunov check0.05msOnline estimate
Total, common case (3 equilibria)~7ms~140 updates/second
Total, fast mode (1 equilibrium)~1.7ms~600 updates/second, used when bifurcation distance is large and HYDRA is skipped
Total, bifurcation regime (4–5 equilibria, backtracking active)~20–25ms~40–50 updates/second; see Section 2.5's warning against treating this as the typical case

The three-tier picture — fast mode, common case, bifurcation regime — is the honest latency story. REN does not run at one speed; it runs at the speed the market's equilibrium structure demands, and degrades gracefully (slower, more informative output) exactly when the underlying situation is more complex, rather than either failing or silently returning a stale single-equilibrium answer.

5.2 Backward Pass (Training, Sketch)

Training requires gradients through the equilibria via implicit differentiation (PHANTOM, full REN design doc §4): the adjoint system (I − JT)w = v is solved with a truncated Neumann series when ρ(J) < 0.95 (5 or 15 terms depending on ρ) and with regularized GMRES near bifurcation, where the Neumann series no longer converges fast enough to be worth truncating. This keeps training memory at O(d) regardless of iteration count, versus O(K·d) for naively unrolling the fixed-point iteration and backpropagating through every step.

6. Prior Art: DEQ, MonDEQ, DEQN, and What Changes

Prior artWhat it doesWhat ATLAS/HYDRA/SEISMOGRAPH change
Deep Equilibrium Models (Bai, Kolter, Koltun 2019)Computes a single fixed point of a weight-tied layer via Broyden's method or Anderson acceleration; assumes the map is a contraction with a unique solution, backprops via implicit differentiation at that one pointMultiple equilibria by design (HYDRA's deflation + homotopy), not an edge case to be assumed away; bifurcation-aware (SEISMOGRAPH has no DEQ analogue — DEQ has no concept of regime change in its fixed point); Φ is factored into economically interpretable action/price/belief stages rather than treated as a generic black-box block, which is what makes the market-structure preconditioner possible at all
MonDEQ (monotone operator DEQ, Winston & Kolter 2020)Constrains the DEQ layer to be a monotone operator, which guarantees a unique fixed point and well-posed training by construction — solved with a proximal / peaceman-rachford splitting method rather than plain AndersonREN deliberately does not impose monotonicity: uniqueness is the wrong assumption for a market that genuinely supports bull and bear equilibria simultaneously (Section 8.2's genericity theorem), so REN keeps Φ free to be non-monotone and pays for that freedom with HYDRA's explicit multiplicity-handling machinery instead of designing multiplicity away
DEQN (Deep Equilibrium Nets, Azinovic, Gaegauf, Scheidegger 2022, computational economics)Uses a single global neural network to approximate the equilibrium policy/value functions of a dynamic economic model, trained by minimizing Euler-equation residuals — a DEQ-style fixed point applied to macro/DSGE-style recursive equilibrium, but for a single, presumed-unique rational-expectations equilibriumClosest prior art in spirit (equilibrium computation for economic models via a learned fixed point), but DEQN is built for offline, single-equilibrium macro model-solving, not real-time, multi-equilibrium, bifurcation-tracked market inference; REN adds the entire online monitoring stack (SEISMOGRAPH, CONTINUATOR) that a DSGE solver run once at calibration time has no need for
Numerical continuation software (AUTO, MATCONT)Mature, offline tools for bifurcation analysis of known ODEs against a swept parameterOnline operation against streaming market data; learned, not hand-specified, dynamics; probabilistic rather than deterministic bifurcation output
Deflation methods (Farrell, Birkisson, Funke 2015)Repel from a known root via a scalar deflation operator to find other roots of a nonlinear PDE systemCombined with the novel directional deflation term (Section 2.1) and homotopy continuation for automatic discovery rather than random restart, plus Boltzmann/stochastic-stability weighting to turn a set of roots into tradeable probabilities

6.1 What Is Genuinely New

  1. The reflexive factorization DΦ = (∂U/∂p)(∂P/∂a)(∂A/∂b) used as a computational lever — a preconditioner and a stability analyzer, not a purely descriptive decomposition.
  2. The market-structure adaptive Mahalanobis preconditioner for Anderson acceleration, built directly from the residual covariance rather than a generic norm.
  3. The directional deflation term (the σ-weighted rank-one correction in Section 2.1), extending scalar deflation to curve the landscape away from the approach direction, not just inflate the residual at a point.
  4. Interleaved homotopy tracking of multiple active branches (Section 2.3), rather than sequential single-equilibrium deflation runs.
  5. The neural bifurcation predictor trained on iteration trajectories, not just converged Jacobians — giving SEISMOGRAPH visibility into bifurcations of equilibria it has not yet found.
  6. The Triple Correspondence (Section 3.5) as an explicit, load-bearing design choice: one spectral-radius computation feeding three independently-motivated early-warning readings rather than three separately maintained systems.

Concrete Trading Examples

Example 1 — dispersion pricing off a genuine bimodal read. HYDRA finds two stable equilibria for a single-name equity: a bull equilibrium at b1* (weight 0.68 under Boltzmann) with belief μ > rf, and a bear equilibrium at b2* (weight 0.32) with μ < rf, plus an unstable tipping-point equilibrium between them (Section 8.2's genericity result: the standard odd count is 3). A single-equilibrium model would have already averaged these into one "fair value" with some diffuse variance; REN's output is instead a structural statement — the market can coordinate on two genuinely different self-consistent worldviews — which maps to a straddle or dispersion position sized off the actual weight split (0.68/0.32), not off an assumed unimodal distribution's tails.

Example 2 — bifurcation distance as a pre-repricing gauge. SEISMOGRAPH's δ̂bif for the bull equilibrium in a crowded, low-liquidity name drops from 340 timesteps to 41 timesteps over the course of a session (below the τwarn=50 threshold), while critical-slowing-down (ρconv rising from 0.22 to 0.79) corroborates it independently. The neural bifurcation predictor assigns pfold=0.71.
