Regime Transition Engine (this invention)Detects transitions in generating structure (fragment coherence, correlation stability, vol-of-vol) ahead of price; models cascade propagation with a self-sustaining eigenvalue threshold; classifies transition speed and matches historical/novel regime templates; learns continuously from every transition and near-miss—

Why This Matters for Trading

Days of lead time that price-based models cannot give you. In the SVB worked example, RecWM's fragment coherence score would have flagged the regional banking sector 45 days before the FDIC seizure, and crossed the formal pre-transition threshold (Ptrans = 0.48) 14 days before — while KRE and SIVB equity were still trading near recent levels. A model watching price alone had nothing to see until the final week.

Knowing whether a shock is contained or self-sustaining. The cascade eigenvalue λmax is a single number that answers the question every PM actually needs answered during a live event: is this going to keep feeding on itself, or is it going to die out? λmax = 1.12 during the SVB event told the story before FDIC seizure headlines did.

Distinguishing a true transition from a near-miss in real time. September 2019's repo spike and the post-SVB containment both crossed the alert threshold and then reversed because of policy intervention. A model that only learns from completed disasters cannot tell these apart from a genuine cascade while it is happening; RecWM's near-miss catalog gives it a basis for estimating policy-response probability as the event unfolds, not just after the fact.

Known Gaps

The 8-stage cascade sequence (Liquidity → Credit → Volatility → … → Structure) is an empirical regularity drawn from a small number of major historical transitions, not a law — individual episodes can and do skip stages, reorder them, or start from an unusual node (e.g. a purely narrative-driven shock), and the engine's confidence in the canonical ordering is itself only as good as the ~20+ transitions needed before learned feature weights dominate hand-crafted ones (Section 8.2).

Coherence threshold (~0.7), CSI threshold (0.3–0.5), and cascade eigenvalue thresholds (0.5 / 0.8 / 1.0) are calibrated empirically per regime and are stated as design targets in this document; they have not been validated out-of-sample across a large enough population of true transitions and near-misses to rule out threshold instability across future, structurally different market regimes.

The contagion network's edge weights depend heavily on regulatory filings (which lag reality by the filing cadence) blended with real-time market-implied proxies (options-implied correlation, CDS-equity co-movement) that are faster but noisier; the current blending methodology is not yet formally validated against held-out crisis episodes beyond the ones cataloged here (2008, 2020, 2023).

Novel-regime detection (Section 5.2) can correctly flag "this doesn't match anything," but by construction has no playbook to offer once it does — the PM guidance defaults to generic maximum risk reduction rather than a regime-specific strategy, which is the right conservative default but also the least actionable output the engine produces.

Near-miss labeling requires a judgment call — "this was reversed by policy intervention" vs. "this was never going to complete" — that is not always cleanly separable after the fact, introducing label noise directly into the calibration signal the whole learning loop (Section 8) depends on.

Latency budgets in Section 9.2 assume clean, continuously available data streams across all seven fragments; degraded or delayed inputs from any single high-weight fragment (Liquidity and Credit carry the earliest signal in the cascade) can silently widen the engine's true detection lag well past the stated targets without any explicit fallback or staleness alert currently specified.

REN Invention 6 · August 2026

Scenario Branching Engine

RecWM does not predict the future. It maps the topology of possible futures so that no category of event arrives without a pre-computed response — a chess engine's exhaustive line-evaluation applied to fragment regime transitions, running continuously, re-branching, pruning, and maintaining a live Contingency Matrix that ties every high-impact scenario to a costed portfolio response.

0. Design Philosophy

The operating metaphor is not a crystal ball but a chess engine. AlphaZero does not know what move its opponent will play, but it has evaluated every plausible line deeply enough to respond instantly to any of them. The Scenario Branching Engine (SBE) is the same object applied to a portfolio: it consumes every fragment state update from the RecWM World Model, re-branches the scenario tree, prunes dead lines, and maintains a live Contingency Matrix that maps every high-impact scenario to a pre-computed portfolio response.

The PM never sees the tree. The PM sees five objects: the scenarios that matter most right now, ranked by expected impact multiplied by probability; what to do in each case; what it costs to hedge; and — the object every other system omits — the scenario the portfolio is not hedged for. Most scenario-analysis tooling stops at the first three. The SBE treats the fourth as the primary deliverable, because the scenarios a PM already knows about are, definitionally, not the ones that cause blowups.

Core contribution. A continuously-maintained, adaptively-pruned scenario tree over fragment regime transitions (not price levels), evaluated by a six-dimensional impact function, compressed into pre-computed, cost-and-feasibility-checked response playbooks, cross-validated against a persistent Scenario Memory that recalibrates the tree's own generation and pruning rules from realized outcomes. No single piece is novel in isolation; the closed loop — generate → prune → evaluate → pre-hedge → observe → recalibrate — running on a fixed GPU budget in production, is.

1. The Scenario Tree Structure

1.1 Defining "Moves" in the Financial Game Tree

In chess, moves are discrete and well-defined. In markets, the "move space" is continuous and high-dimensional. The SBE discretizes the move space into Fragment Regime Transitions (FRTs) — the atomic unit of scenario branching. A Fragment Regime Transition is a change in the regime state of any RecWM World Model fragment. The canonical fragment set:

FragmentRegime StatesTransition Triggers
LiquidityAbundant / Normal / Tight / CrisisFed balance sheet changes, repo rate spikes, dealer inventory shifts, money market stress
CreditExpansionary / Stable / Tightening / DistressSpread widening, default rate changes, rating agency actions, covenant violations
VolatilitySuppressed / Normal / Elevated / DislocationVIX regime shifts, realized vs. implied divergence, correlation breakdown, gamma exposure imbalance
RatesEasing / Stable / Hiking / Inversion-StressCentral bank actions, inflation data, term premium shifts, yield curve shape changes
SentimentRisk-On / Neutral / Risk-Off / PanicFlow data, positioning extremes, narrative shifts, contagion signals
Macro-GrowthAcceleration / Trend / Deceleration / ContractionGDP nowcasts, PMI shifts, employment data, earnings revision breadth
GeopoliticalStable / Elevated / Acute / SystemicConflict escalation, sanctions, trade policy shifts, election outcomes, commodity supply disruption

Each fragment maintains a transition probability matrix updated in real time by the World Model. A "move" in the game tree is one or more fragments transitioning simultaneously — which is precisely why the tree is not a chessboard: chess moves are mutually exclusive, but fragment transitions co-occur, interact, and amplify each other, which is the entire justification for the N-2 contingency analysis in Section 5.

1.2 Scenario Parameterization

Scenarios are not parameterized as simple directional moves ("stocks go down 10%"). They are parameterized as fragment regime vectors with associated dynamics:

S = (Fregime, Thorizon, Ppath, ΔC)

where:
  Fregime  = [Liquidity: Tight, Credit: Tightening, Vol: Elevated, Rates: Hiking, Sentiment: Risk-Off, Growth: Deceleration, Geo: Stable]
  Thorizon = time horizon over which the transition completes (1d, 1w, 1m, 1q)
  Ppath   = transition path type (gradual, sudden, oscillating)
  ΔC    = correlation regime shift matrix (how cross-asset correlations change under this scenario)

This parameterization captures what simple stress tests miss: the path matters. A gradual credit tightening over three months is a fundamentally different scenario from a sudden credit dislocation over three days, even when the endpoint regime is identical — because margin calls, forced selling, and the availability of counterparty capacity are all functions of the rate of transition, not just its destination. A stress test that only checks endpoints is blind to exactly the mechanism (Section 3.1's Max Drawdown Path) that turns a survivable scenario into a forced-liquidation event.

1.3 Tree Depth (Time Horizons)

Layer 0 (NOW)      : Current fragment state. Single node. Full precision evaluation.
Layer 1 (1 day)    : 12-20 branches. High precision. Updated every 5 minutes.
Layer 2 (1 week)   : 8-15 branches per Layer 1 node. Medium precision. Updated hourly.
Layer 3 (1 month)  : 5-10 branches per Layer 2 node. Lower precision. Updated every 4 hours.
Layer 4 (1 quarter): 3-5 branches per Layer 3 node. Directional precision. Updated daily.

Total theoretical tree size at full expansion: ~20 × 15 × 10 × 5 = 15,000 leaf scenarios at quarterly horizon. After pruning (Section 2), the live tree maintains 200–500 active leaf scenarios at any time — a 30–75x reduction that is the entire point of the pruning machinery: the raw tree is computationally intractable to evaluate at production latency, and most of its mass is either irrelevant to the current portfolio, effectively zero-probability, or a near-duplicate of an already-evaluated neighbor.

1.4 Tree Width (Branching Factor)

The branching factor is adaptive, not fixed. It depends on the current state of each fragment:

  • Near transition boundary: higher branching factor. When the Liquidity fragment sits near the Normal/Tight boundary, the engine explores more Liquidity branches.
  • Deep in regime: lower branching factor. When Liquidity is firmly Abundant, fewer Liquidity branches are needed.
  • High uncertainty: higher branching factor. When the World Model's confidence in a fragment's state is low, explore more.
  • Event-driven: spike branching around known catalysts — on FOMC day, the Rates fragment gets 3x its normal branching factor.
for each fragment F:
    base_branches(F) = 2  # minimum: stay or transition

    boundary_proximity = distance_to_nearest_transition(F)
    if boundary_proximity < threshold:
        branch_bonus += 3 * (1 - boundary_proximity / threshold)

    uncertainty_bonus = world_model_entropy(F) * 2

    catalyst_bonus = upcoming_catalyst_weight(F, horizon) * 4

    total_branches(F) = min(base_branches + branch_bonus + uncertainty_bonus
                            + catalyst_bonus, MAX_BRANCHES_PER_FRAGMENT)

The effect is a tree that is dense exactly where the World Model is least certain and sparse exactly where it is most certain — the inverse of a naive uniform grid, and the reason the SBE can afford full-precision Layer-1 evaluation on a fixed GPU budget (Section 9) rather than spreading compute uniformly across a search space that is, for most of the current state space, not worth exploring.

2. Pruning Heuristics

The raw tree is computationally intractable. Pruning is the core intellectual contribution of the SBE — it determines what the system thinks about and what it ignores, which is a judgment call with real consequences: prune too aggressively and the system misses the next SVB; prune too little and the system drowns in noise and cannot deliver an answer inside the PM's decision window. Four pruning strategies operate simultaneously, and three of the four are asymmetric by design.

2.1 Portfolio-Relevance Pruning

Principle: only explore scenarios that materially affect this portfolio. A scenario where emerging market currencies collapse is irrelevant to a portfolio with zero EM exposure — unless second-order effects (risk-off contagion, dollar strength) propagate into it.

def portfolio_relevance_score(scenario, portfolio):
    # First-order: direct exposure
    direct_impact = sum(
        position.notional * fragment_beta(position, scenario.fragment_changes)
        for position in portfolio.positions
    )

    # Second-order: contagion and correlation
    contagion_impact = estimate_contagion(
        scenario.fragment_changes,
        portfolio.correlation_matrix,
        scenario.delta_correlation
    )

    # Third-order: liquidity-adjusted impact
    # In a crisis, you can't just mark positions -- you have to exit them
    liquidity_penalty = sum(
        position.notional * liquidity_haircut(position, scenario)
        for position in portfolio.positions
        if position.days_to_exit(scenario) > position.days_to_exit(current_state) * 2
    )

    relevance = abs(direct_impact) + abs(contagion_impact) + liquidity_penalty
    return relevance

# Prune if relevance < 0.5% of portfolio NAV
PRUNE if portfolio_relevance_score(scenario) < 0.005 * portfolio.nav

Critical subtlety: the pruning threshold is asymmetric. Negative-impact scenarios are pruned at a higher bar (0.5% NAV) than positive-impact scenarios (2% NAV). The PM cares more about downside surprises than upside surprises, and the pruning function encodes that preference structurally rather than leaving it to a dashboard filter the PM has to remember to apply.

2.2 Probability Pruning

Principle: don't waste computation on scenarios with negligible probability — but never prune a scenario just because it hasn't happened before.

PRUNE if:
    scenario.probability < base_threshold
    AND scenario.max_impact < catastrophic_threshold

Where:
    base_threshold = 0.1% for Layer 1 (1-day scenarios)
    base_threshold = 0.5% for Layer 2 (1-week)
    base_threshold = 1.0% for Layer 3 (1-month)
    base_threshold = 2.0% for Layer 4 (1-quarter)

    catastrophic_threshold = 10% of NAV (never prune a scenario
                             that could lose 10%+ of NAV regardless
                             of probability)

The catastrophic override is essential. A 0.01% probability scenario that wipes out 50% of NAV must always remain in the tree. This is the lesson of every financial crisis: the "impossible" scenario is the one that matters most. A pruning rule that only looked at probability would have discarded 2008's tail exactly because it was, by construction, a low-frequency event in the historical sample used to estimate its probability.

2.3 Novelty Pruning (Inverse)

Principle: spend more computation on unprecedented scenarios. This is the opposite of chess engines, which prune unusual positions because they are likely bad. In finance, unprecedented scenarios are likely the most dangerous, because the portfolio is least prepared for them — no historical hedge exists, no playbook covers it, and no one else's positioning has adjusted for it either.

def novelty_score(scenario):
    # How similar is this scenario to any historical episode?
    min_distance = min(
        scenario_distance(scenario, historical_episode)
        for historical_episode in scenario_memory.episodes
    )

    # How similar is this to scenarios we've explored recently?
    exploration_recency = max(
        exploration_decay(scenario, explored)
        for explored in recently_evaluated_scenarios
    )

    # High novelty = high distance from history + low recent exploration
    return min_distance * (1 - exploration_recency)

# BOOST computation (anti-prune) for high-novelty scenarios
computation_allocation(scenario) *= (1 + novelty_score(scenario) * NOVELTY_WEIGHT)

This creates a natural exploration-exploitation balance: familiar scenarios are evaluated efficiently using cached historical analogs, while novel scenarios receive disproportionate computational attention. It is also the direct engineering response to Section 8.3's Rule 1 (Miss Incorporation) — every historical miss becomes, going forward, a permanent downward adjustment to how aggressively that scenario class gets pruned.

2.4 Sensitivity Pruning

Principle: focus on scenarios where small changes in assumptions produce large changes in outcomes — "phase transition" scenarios, where being slightly wrong about the world leads to dramatically wrong portfolio positioning.

def sensitivity_score(scenario):
    base_evaluation = evaluate_portfolio(scenario)

    perturbations = generate_perturbations(scenario, epsilon=0.05)
    perturbed_evaluations = [evaluate_portfolio(p) for p in perturbations]

    # Gradient magnitude: how much does the outcome change
    # per unit change in assumptions?
    gradient = max(
        abs(perturbed - base_evaluation) / epsilon
        for perturbed in perturbed_evaluations
    )

    return gradient

# NEVER prune high-sensitivity scenarios
PRESERVE if sensitivity_score(scenario) > SENSITIVITY_THRESHOLD

High-sensitivity scenarios are where the portfolio is most exposed to model error — the "knife edge" where the difference between a good outcome and a bad outcome depends on getting the scenario exactly right, which is precisely what you cannot do. Preserving these scenarios regardless of probability or relevance score is a deliberate override on the other three heuristics: sensitivity trumps everything else, because it identifies where the SBE's own confidence is least trustworthy.

Why four heuristics and not one composite score. Portfolio-relevance answers "does this matter to me." Probability answers "how likely is this." Novelty answers "how prepared am I." Sensitivity answers "how wrong could I be." Collapsing these into a single weighted score would let a scenario that is highly relevant but well-understood (low novelty, low sensitivity) crowd out compute from a scenario that is barely relevant today but catastrophically under-prepared-for (high novelty) — exactly the failure mode the system exists to prevent. Running all four as independent, non-substitutable gates is what keeps the tree honest.

3. The Scenario Evaluation Function

Each scenario leaf that survives pruning is evaluated by a multi-objective evaluation function producing a Scenario Impact Profile (SIP).

3.1 The Six Evaluation Dimensions

SIP = {
  pnl_impact:        float,   // Expected P&L change (dollars)
  max_drawdown_path: float,   // Worst peak-to-trough on the path to this scenario
  liquidity_score:   float,   // 0–1, can you actually exit positions?
  risk_limit_status: dict,    // Which risk limits are breached?
  margin_call_prob:  float,   // Probability of margin call from prime broker
  opportunity_cost:  float    // What alpha opportunities open up in this scenario?
}

P&L Impact is not a simple linear calculation. It uses the full RecWM fragment model to propagate scenario regime changes through to asset prices, accounting for non-linear payoffs (options), cross-asset correlations under the scenario's correlation regime, and funding costs:

def compute_pnl_impact(scenario, portfolio):
    # Step 1: Map fragment regime changes to asset price distributions
    asset_distributions = fragment_to_asset_model.propagate(
        scenario.fragment_vector,
        scenario.delta_correlation
    )

    # Step 2: Evaluate each position under the distribution
    position_pnls = []
    for position in portfolio.positions:
        if position.is_linear:
            pnl = position.delta * asset_distributions[position.asset].expected_move
        elif position.is_option:
            pnl = reprice_option(
                position,
                asset_distributions[position.underlying],
                scenario.implied_vol_surface
            ) - position.current_value
        elif position.is_structured:
            pnl = monte_carlo_reprice(position, asset_distributions, n_paths=1000)
        position_pnls.append(pnl)

    # Step 3: Aggregate with funding cost adjustment
    gross_pnl = sum(position_pnls)
    funding_adjustment = compute_funding_cost(scenario.rates_regime, portfolio)

    return gross_pnl - funding_adjustment

Maximum Drawdown Path exists because the terminal P&L might be acceptable while the path is catastrophic. A scenario where the portfolio drops 30% before recovering to −5% will trigger margin calls and forced selling that prevent the recovery from ever happening in practice. The MDP evaluator simulates the intra-scenario path rather than trusting the endpoint:

def compute_max_drawdown_path(scenario, portfolio):
    # Simulate 100 intra-scenario paths
    paths = generate_intra_scenario_paths(scenario, n=100)

    max_drawdowns = []
    for path in paths:
        cumulative_pnl = [evaluate_portfolio_at_time(portfolio, path, t)
                          for t in path.timestamps]
        running_max = accumulate_max(cumulative_pnl)
        drawdowns = [running_max[i] - cumulative_pnl[i] for i in range(len(path))]
        max_drawdowns.append(max(drawdowns))

    return percentile(max_drawdowns, 95)  # 95th percentile worst drawdown

Liquidity Score measures whether you can actually trade in a given scenario, using the Liquidity fragment's regime-dependent market depth model:

def compute_liquidity_score(scenario, portfolio):
    total_exit_cost = 0
    total_notional = 0

    for position in portfolio.positions:
        market_depth = liquidity_model.depth(
            position.asset,
            scenario.liquidity_regime,
            scenario.volatility_regime
        )

        # How many days to exit at <2% market impact?
        days_to_exit = position.notional / (market_depth.daily_capacity * 0.02)

        # Slippage cost over exit period
        exit_cost = estimate_slippage(position, days_to_exit, market_depth)

        total_exit_cost += exit_cost
        total_notional += abs(position.notional)

    # Score: 1.0 = fully liquid, 0.0 = completely trapped
    return max(0, 1 - total_exit_cost / (total_notional * 0.05))

Risk Limit Status maps each scenario to the portfolio's risk limits and identifies breaches directly, rather than leaving the PM to infer them from a raw P&L number:

def check_risk_limits(scenario, portfolio, risk_limits):
    breaches = {}

    scenario_risk = compute_risk_metrics(scenario, portfolio)

    for limit in risk_limits:
        if limit.type == 'VAR':
            if scenario_risk.var_99 > limit.threshold:
                breaches[limit.name] = {
                    'current': scenario_risk.var_99,
                    'limit': limit.threshold,
                    'overage_pct': (scenario_risk.var_99 - limit.threshold) / limit.threshold
                }
        elif limit.type == 'GROSS_EXPOSURE':
            if scenario_risk.gross > limit.threshold:
                breaches[limit.name] = {...}
        elif limit.type == 'CONCENTRATION':
            for sector, exposure in scenario_risk.sector_exposures.items():
                if exposure > limit.threshold:
                    breaches[f'{limit.name}_{sector}'] = {...}

    return breaches

Margin Call Probability and Opportunity Cost complete the six dimensions: the former from the prime broker's margin methodology applied to the scenario's simulated path (not just the endpoint), the latter from the same evaluation machinery run on the scenario's upside tail — what alpha becomes available if this scenario occurs, which is what prevents the system from treating every scenario as purely defensive.

3.2 Composite Scoring

The six dimensions combine into a single Scenario Urgency Score (SUS) that determines how prominently the scenario is surfaced to the PM:

SUS = w1·norm(pnl_impact) + w2·norm(max_drawdown_path) + w3·(1−liquidity_score) + w4·count(risk_limit_breaches) + w5·margin_call_prob − w6·norm(opportunity_cost)

Default weights: w1=0.25, w2=0.25, w3=0.20, w4=0.15, w5=0.10, w6=0.05

The weights are PM-configurable. A PM running a market-neutral book might weight liquidity higher; a PM running a directional book might weight P&L impact higher. The default weighting itself encodes the same asymmetric-attention principle as Section 2's pruning thresholds: 85% of the weight (w1–w5) sits on downside dimensions, and only w6 works in the opposite direction, subtracting urgency for scenarios that are actually favorable.

4. Pre-Computed Responses

Every scenario with SUS above the alert threshold has an associated Response Playbook computed and maintained in real time — not generated on demand when the scenario starts to unfold, when there is no time left to think.

4.1 Response Playbook Structure

ResponsePlaybook = {

Three features of this structure are load-bearing. First, do_not_actions is a first-class field, not an afterthought — the most valuable line in a crisis playbook is often the one that stops the PM from doing the instinctively obvious thing that turns out to remove a natural hedge. Second, cost_to_pre_hedge makes explicit the decision the system is not making on the PM's behalf: whether to pay the insurance premium now or hold the playbook in reserve. Third, execution_feasibility is checked against real counterparty capacity and operational dependencies (ISDA masters, market hours) — a playbook that is optimal on paper but unexecutable at 2am because the required ISDA is only in place with one counterparty is not a playbook, it is a wish.

4.2 Response Optimization Algorithm

For each high-SUS scenario, the engine solves a constrained optimization:

minimize:  portfolio_loss(scenario, current_portfolio + hedge_adjustments)
subject to:
  hedge_cost < max_acceptable_cost
  execution_time < scenario_onset_window
  liquidity_consumed < available_market_depth × 0.25  // Don't move the market
  risk_limit_compliance(adjusted_portfolio) = True

// Feasibility constraints
  for each adjustment in hedge_adjustments:
    adjustment.instrument must be tradeable in scenario conditions
    adjustment.size must be executable given market depth

The optimizer runs a two-stage process. Stage 1 — Candidate Generation: enumerate candidate hedge instruments from a pre-defined universe (index options, single-name CDS, rate swaps, FX forwards, futures), scoring each by hedge effectiveness per unit cost. Stage 2 — Portfolio Optimization: solve the constrained optimization using sequential quadratic programming, with the non-linear constraints (liquidity, feasibility) handled via penalty functions.

4.3 Response Ordering

When a scenario involves multiple actions, ordering matters. The engine ranks actions by a priority function:

priority(action) = impact_per_dollar(action) × urgency_decay(action) × liquidity_window(action)

where:
  impact_per_dollar  = reduction in scenario loss per dollar of hedge cost
  urgency_decay       = exponential decay based on how quickly the hedge becomes unavailable
  liquidity_window   = estimated time window in which the action is executable

Actions with the shortest liquidity windows execute first. This prevents the common crisis failure mode where a desk executes the easy hedges first and finds the critical ones are no longer available — the classic pattern of using up scarce dealer capacity on a convenient trade before realizing, an hour too late, that the trade that actually mattered has gone illiquid.

5. The Contingency Matrix

The Contingency Matrix is the financial equivalent of power-grid N-1/N-2 analysis, run continuously rather than as an annual stress-test exercise.

5.1 N-1 Fragment Contingency

For each of the seven fragments, evaluate the portfolio impact if that single fragment transitions to its stress regime while all others remain unchanged. Illustrative output, updated every 15 minutes:

5.2 N-2 Fragment Contingency

For the top three most impactful N-1 scenarios, evaluate all pairwise combinations. There are C(7,2) = 21 pairs, but the engine only evaluates the dangerous combinations identified by the N-1 analysis — full pairwise evaluation of all 21 at production frequency is not worth the compute when the N-1 ranking already tells you which fragments are worth pairing.

Fragments StressedP&L ImpactMax DDLiqMargin
Credit + Liquidity−$52.3M−$68.1M0.1872%

Worst N-2: Credit + Liquidity (−$52.3M, 72% margin call probability). This is the 2008 pattern; Playbook CL-2008 activates automatically when both fragments cross their stress thresholds simultaneously.

N-2 impacts are not additive. Credit + Liquidity produces −$52.3M, not −$28.7M + −$12.4M = −$41.1M. The excess −$11.2M is the correlation breakdown premium — the non-linear interaction when multiple fragments stress simultaneously. A risk system that evaluates fragments independently and sums the results will systematically underestimate joint-stress scenarios by exactly this premium, which is why the Contingency Matrix computes joint scenarios directly rather than composing single-fragment results.

The playbook's value is stated in the same units as the risk it addresses: roughly a 40–50% reduction in realized loss versus an unhedged full-stress path, purely from having the sequence of actions decided and costed before the scenario begins rather than improvised inside it.

Not all stress is negative. The matrix also evaluates positive contingencies daily, on the same infrastructure — the opportunity side is not a separate afterthought system:

6. Red Team / Adversarial Analysis

6.1 The Adversarial Module

The Red Team module asks: "If a sophisticated, well-capitalized adversary knew our exact portfolio, what would they do to maximize our losses?" This is modeled as a minimax game:

maxadversary minportfolio Loss(portfolio, adversary_action)

where adversary_action is drawn from the set of feasible market actions:
  – large directional trades that move prices against our positions
  – withdrawal of liquidity in our key markets
  – information release that triggers regime transitions
  – coordinated action with other large participants

The adversary is constrained to be realistic: it cannot violate market mechanics or regulations, but it can exploit knowledge of our positions — the "crowded trade" scenario, which is the mechanism that actually hurts real portfolios far more often than illegal manipulation does.

6.2 Adversarial Scenario Generation

Four attack vectors are enumerated systematically against the current portfolio:

def generate_adversarial_scenarios(portfolio):
    scenarios = []

    # Attack vector 1: Position crowding
    # Find positions where we (and likely others) are concentrated
    for position in portfolio.positions:
        if position.size > market_depth(position.asset).daily_volume * 0.1:
            scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario(
                type="CROWDED_EXIT",
                target=position,
                mechanism="Large holder exits, triggering stop-losses and margin calls",
                our_vulnerability=position.size / market_depth(position.asset).daily_volume,
                estimated_impact=compute_crowded_exit_impact(position, portfolio)
            ))

    # Attack vector 2: Correlation exploitation
    # Find hidden correlations that would hurt us
    stress_correlations = compute_stress_correlation_matrix(portfolio)
    normal_correlations = compute_normal_correlation_matrix(portfolio)

    correlation_surprises = find_largest_divergences(
        stress_correlations, normal_correlations
    )

    for surprise in correlation_surprises:
        scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario(
            type="CORRELATION_BREAKDOWN",
            assets=surprise.asset_pair,
            mechanism=f"Correlation shifts from {surprise.normal_corr:.2f} "
                      f"to {surprise.stress_corr:.2f}",
            estimated_impact=compute_correlation_impact(surprise, portfolio)
        ))

    # Attack vector 3: Liquidity trap
    # Find positions that become illiquid under stress
    for position in portfolio.positions:
        stress_liquidity = liquidity_model.stress_depth(position.asset)
        if position.days_to_exit(stress_liquidity) > 10:
            scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario(
                type="LIQUIDITY_TRAP",
                target=position,
                mechanism="Market depth evaporates; position becomes untradeable",
                days_trapped=position.days_to_exit(stress_liquidity),
                estimated_impact=compute_trapped_position_impact(position, portfolio)
            ))

    # Attack vector 4: Basis risk
    # Find hedges that fail under stress
    for hedge_pair in portfolio.identified_hedges:
        basis_risk = compute_basis_risk_under_stress(hedge_pair)
        if basis_risk.hedge_effectiveness < 0.5:
            scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario(
                type="HEDGE_FAILURE",
                hedge=hedge_pair,
                mechanism=f"Hedge effectiveness drops from "
                          f"{hedge_pair.normal_effectiveness:.0%} to "
                          f"{basis_risk.hedge_effectiveness:.0%}",
                estimated_impact=basis_risk.unhedged_exposure
            ))

    return sorted(scenarios, key=lambda s: s.estimated_impact, reverse=True)

The fourth vector — hedge failure — is the one most systems skip entirely, because it requires the module to be adversarial about its own risk-reduction trades, not just its raw exposures. A hedge that looks effective under the normal-regime correlation is exactly the kind of thing a sophisticated adversary (or simply a regime shift) can quietly neutralize before the PM notices the basis has moved.

6.3 The "Unhedged Nightmare" Report

The most important output of the adversarial module: what is the single most dangerous scenario the portfolio is currently not hedged for?

UNHEDGED NIGHTMARE REPORT (updated every 4 hours)
Scenario: Simultaneous Credit + Liquidity stress with basis blow-out in CDX vs. single-name CDS

Current hedge coverage: 12% (effectively unhedged)
Estimated impact: −$38.4M
Probability: 3.2% over next quarter
Expected loss contribution: −$1.23M (probability × impact)

Recommended hedge:
  – Buy CDX IG protection, 3-month, $100M notional
  – Cost: $340K premium
  – Hedge effectiveness: raises coverage from 12% to 67%
  – Cost-benefit ratio: $340K cost vs. $1.23M expected loss reduction

PM DECISION REQUIRED: accept unhedged exposure or execute hedge?

The report ends in a decision, not a recommendation the system executes unilaterally — consistent with the axiomatic principle in Section 10.8: the SBE never trades, it prepares.

7. Monte Carlo Simulation Layer

7.1 Path Generation Architecture

The Monte Carlo layer generates 10,000 forward paths per simulation cycle. Paths are not simple geometric Brownian motion. They incorporate four mechanisms simultaneously:

  • Regime-switching dynamics: each path draws from the fragment transition probability matrix; at every time step the path may undergo a regime transition with probability given by the World Model.
  • Fat tails: return distributions use a mixture model — normal returns 85% of the time, drawn from a Student-t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom 12% of the time, and drawn from a jump-diffusion process 3% of the time.
  • Correlation regime-switching: cross-asset correlations are drawn from the correlation regime associated with the current fragment state; in stress regimes correlations rise — the well-documented "correlations go to 1 in a crisis" phenomenon.
  • Reflexivity: paths incorporate feedback loops — a large drawdown triggers margin calls, which trigger forced selling, which triggers further drawdown. The simulation models these cascading effects directly rather than treating them as an out-of-model tail adjustment.
def generate_path(portfolio, horizon, dt=1/252):
    path = [current_state()]
    t = 0

    while t < horizon:
        current = path[-1]

        # Step 1: Check for regime transitions
        for fragment in fragments:
            transition_prob = world_model.transition_probability(
                fragment, current.regime[fragment], dt
            )
            if random.random() < transition_prob:
                current.regime[fragment] = sample_new_regime(
                    fragment, current.regime[fragment]
                )
                # Regime transition triggers correlation update
                current.correlation_matrix = get_regime_correlation(
                    current.regime
                )

        # Step 2: Generate returns
        # Draw from regime-appropriate distribution
        dist_type = sample_distribution_type()  # normal / fat-tail / jump

        if dist_type == 'normal':
            returns = multivariate_normal(
                current.expected_returns,
                current.correlation_matrix * current.vol_vector
            )
        elif dist_type == 'fat_tail':
            returns = multivariate_t(
                current.expected_returns,
                current.correlation_matrix * current.vol_vector,
                df=4
            )
        elif dist_type == 'jump':
            returns = multivariate_normal(...) + jump_component(current.regime)

        # Step 3: Apply reflexivity
        portfolio_pnl = compute_portfolio_pnl(portfolio, returns)
        if portfolio_pnl < -margin_buffer * 0.5:
            # Margin pressure -> forced selling -> additional market impact
            forced_selling_impact = compute_forced_selling(
                portfolio, portfolio_pnl, current.market_depth
            )
            returns += forced_selling_impact  # Feedback loop

        # Step 4: Update state
        new_state = apply_returns(current, returns)
        path.append(new_state)
        t += dt

    return path

7.2 Simulation Frequency and Triggers

The Monte Carlo runs on two schedules. Scheduled runs: a full 10,000-path simulation every 15 minutes during market hours, every hour outside market hours. Triggered runs: an immediate re-simulation fires when any fragment transitions to a new regime, when portfolio composition changes (new trade, position closed), when a scheduled macro data release occurs (NFP, CPI, FOMC), when VIX moves more than 2 points in any 30-minute window, or when any position approaches a risk limit.

7.3 Presenting 10,000 Outcomes to a PM

Raw Monte Carlo output is useless to a PM. The presentation layer compresses 10,000 paths into two actionable objects.

Distribution Summary:

FORWARD SIMULATION SUMMARY (10,000 paths, 1-month horizon)
Expected P&L:        +$2.3M  (median: +$1.8M)
5th percentile:     −$18.4M
1st percentile:     −$31.2M
95th percentile:    +$14.7M
Probability of loss:  38%
Probability of >5% DD: 12%
Probability of margin: 4%

Scenario Clustering: the 10,000 paths are clustered into 5–8 archetypal scenarios using k-means on path features (terminal P&L, max drawdown, regime at terminal date). Each cluster is presented as a narrative rather than a statistic:

ARCHETYPAL SCENARIOS (from 10,000 path clustering)

Cluster 1 (42% of paths): "Grind higher"
  – Fragments stable, gradual P&L accumulation
  – Terminal P&L: +$3M to +$8M

Cluster 2 (23% of paths): "Sideways chop"
  – No clear direction, increased vol
  – Terminal P&L: −$3M to +$3M

Cluster 3 (18% of paths): "Rate surprise"
  – Rates fragment transitions, credit follows
  – Terminal P&L: −$5M to −$15M

Cluster 4 (11% of paths): "Risk-off episode"
  – Sentiment shifts, broad de-risking
  – Terminal P&L: −$10M to −$25M

Cluster 5 (6% of paths): "Tail event"
  – Multiple fragment stress, liquidity crisis
  – Terminal P&L: −$25M to −$50M+
  – PLAYBOOK ACTIVATED: see Contingency Matrix (Section 5)

Cluster 5 is where the Monte Carlo layer and the Contingency Matrix meet: a cluster of simulated paths that resembles a cataloged contingency scenario is linked directly to that scenario's pre-computed playbook, so the PM sees not just "6% of paths end badly" but "6% of paths end badly, and here is exactly what we do if we're in one of them."

8. Scenario Memory

8.1 The Scenario Ledger

Every scenario that reaches evaluation (survives pruning) is logged in a persistent Scenario Ledger with full metadata, including fields that only get filled in after the fact:

ScenarioLedgerEntry = {
    scenario_id:            uuid,
    created_at:             timestamp,
    fragment_vector:        dict,
    probability_at_creation: float,
    sus_score:              float,
    pre_computed_response:  PlaybookRef,

    # Tracking fields (updated as reality unfolds)
    did_occur:              bool,
    occurrence_date:        timestamp | null,
    actual_impact:          float | null,
    predicted_impact:       float | null,
    prediction_error:       float | null,  # actual - predicted
    response_executed:      bool,
    response_effectiveness: float | null,

    # Meta-learning fields
    was_novel:              bool,     # No historical analog existed
    was_pruned_initially:   bool,     # Was this pruned and later restored?
    surprise_factor:        float,    # How surprised was the system?
}

The meta-learning fields are what turn the ledger from an audit log into a training signal: was_pruned_initially is the direct feedback loop for Rule 4 in Section 8.3, and surprise_factor is the direct feedback loop for the novelty-pruning boost in Section 2.3.

8.2 Accuracy Tracking and Calibration

The Scenario Memory system tracks prediction accuracy across three dimensions, each with an explicit numeric target rather than a qualitative aspiration.

Impact accuracy: when scenario X occurred, did the predicted P&L impact match reality?

impact_accuracy = 1 − median( |actual_impact − predicted_impact| / |actual_impact| ) over occurred scenarios

Target: impact_accuracy > 0.70 (within 30% of actual impact)

Probability calibration: of the scenarios assigned 10% probability, did roughly 10% occur?

For each probability bucket [0–5%, 5–15%, 15–25%, …]:
  assigned_count = count(scenarios in bucket)
  occurred_count = count(scenarios in bucket that occurred)
  calibration_error = |occurred_count/assigned_count − bucket_midpoint|

Target: calibration_error < 5% for each bucket

Coverage tracking: what fraction of actual significant events were pre-explored in the scenario tree?

coverage = count(significant_events matched to a pre-explored scenario) / count(all significant_events)

Target: coverage > 0.85 (at most 15% of significant events should be surprises)

These three targets are the system's own scorecard, tracked continuously rather than audited annually — a scenario engine that cannot state its own calibration error is not meaningfully different from a PM's gut feeling with better production values.

8.3 Scenario Evolution Rules

Based on the Scenario Memory, the engine evolves its scenario generation over time through four explicit rules.

Rule 1 — Miss Incorporation: when a significant event occurs that was not in the scenario tree, the engine permanently adds that event class to its generation rules.

Example: March 2023 — SVB failure was not in the scenario tree.
Action: added "Regional bank failure cascade" as a permanent scenario class.
Sub-scenarios: single bank failure, regional contagion, systemic bank stress.
These are now evaluated in every N-1 and N-2 contingency cycle.

Rule 2 — Probability Recalibration: when calibration tracking shows systematic over- or under-estimation of probabilities for certain scenario types, the transition probability matrices are adjusted.

Example: the system consistently assigned 2% probability to credit spread blowouts, but they occurred 5% of the time.
Action: multiplicative recalibration of credit stress transition probabilities by factor 2.5.

Rule 3 — Impact Model Correction: when impact predictions are systematically biased (typically underestimating), the evaluation function itself is recalibrated.

Example: liquidity stress impacts were underestimated by 40% on average.
Diagnosis: the liquidity model used normal-regime market depth estimates even in stress scenarios.
Fix: added regime-conditional market depth to the liquidity scoring model.
Result: impact accuracy improved from 0.55 to 0.78.

Rule 4 — Pruning Audit: a quarterly review of pruned scenarios that subsequently occurred. Any pattern of dangerous pruning triggers a modification to the pruning heuristics themselves.

Example: three scenarios were pruned as "low probability" that subsequently occurred within the same quarter.
Analysis: all three involved the Geopolitical fragment, which had been assigned overly stable transition probabilities.
Fix: reduced the probability pruning threshold for Geopolitical scenarios from 0.5% to 0.1%.
Why this matters more than any single accuracy number. Rules 1–4 mean the SBE's own generation and pruning logic is itself under continuous revision from realized outcomes — a static scenario library, however comprehensive at inception, degrades as the world's structure shifts (new participant types, new instruments, new fragility patterns). The Scenario Memory is what keeps the tree from calcifying into "the last crisis, refought."

9. System Architecture and Compute Budget

9.1 Compute Allocation

The SBE operates within a fixed compute budget, allocated dynamically across its five subsystems:

Total GPU-hours per day: 48 (2 GPUs dedicated)

Allocation:
  Scenario tree maintenance & pruning:  20%  (9.6 GPU-hours)
  Scenario evaluation (SIP computation): 35%  (16.8 GPU-hours)
  Monte Carlo simulation:           25%  (12.0 GPU-hours)
  Adversarial analysis:              10%  (4.8 GPU-hours)
  Scenario memory & recalibration:   5%  (2.4 GPU-hours)
  Buffer for triggered re-simulations: 5%  (2.4 GPU-hours)

The 5% buffer is deliberate slack, not rounding error: without a reserved allocation for triggered re-simulations, a VIX spike that fires every trigger in Section 7.2 simultaneously would either queue behind scheduled work or starve the scheduled cadence — and a scenario engine that becomes slow exactly when the world becomes dangerous has failed at its one job.

The Recalibration Loop closing back into the Generator is the architectural feature that separates this from a conventional scenario-analysis pipeline: every other production stress-testing system this maps against is a straight line from data to dashboard, with human analysts as the (slow, quarterly) feedback mechanism. Here the feedback is a first-class, weekly-cadence subsystem.

10. Design Principles (Axiomatic)

  1. Asymmetric attention. The system spends 80% of its compute on downside scenarios and 20% on upside. Survival comes first; opportunity comes second.
  2. Never prune the catastrophic. Any scenario that can lose more than 10% of NAV stays in the tree regardless of probability. The PM may choose to ignore it; the system may not.
  3. Pre-compute, don't predict. The system does not claim to know which scenario will occur. It claims to have a good response ready for whichever one does.
  4. Path over destination. A scenario that ends at −5% but passes through −30% is more dangerous than one that ends at −10% smoothly. Drawdown paths matter because they trigger margin calls, forced selling, and behavioral errors.
  5. Reflexivity is real. The system models the fact that its own actions (and those of similar portfolios) affect market outcomes. A hedge that "everyone" is putting on is not actually a hedge — it is a crowded trade that will unwind violently.
  6. Novelty is danger. The most dangerous scenario is the one that has never happened before, because no one is positioned for it, no hedges exist for it, and no playbook covers it. The system deliberately over-invests in exploring novel scenarios.
  7. Memory makes it smarter. Every scenario that actually occurs — whether predicted or missed — improves the system. The feedback loop from Scenario Memory to Scenario Generation is the primary learning mechanism.
  8. The PM decides, the system prepares. The SBE never executes trades. It presents options, costs, and tradeoffs. The PM retains full agency. The system's job is to ensure the PM is never in a position where they have to make a critical decision without having thought about it before.

Why This Matters for Trading

The 34% margin-call scenario stops being a surprise. Section 5.1's N-1 table shows Credit → Distress carrying a 34% margin call probability before it happens — not diagnosed after the desk is already scrambling for collateral. A PM who reviews the Contingency Matrix each morning has, by construction, already seen every single-fragment stress the World Model considers plausible and knows which one is closest to firing.

The correlation breakdown premium is priced, not discovered live. Section 5.2's finding that Credit + Liquidity costs −$11.2M more than the sum of its parts is exactly the kind of non-linearity that a linear VaR model misses and a crisis reveals at the worst possible moment. Having it in the Contingency Matrix ahead of time turns a live discovery into a known cost.

The Unhedged Nightmare Report answers the question every risk committee actually wants answered. Not "what is our VaR," which is a number, but "what is the specific scenario we are most exposed to right now, and what does closing that gap cost." Section 6.3's worked example — 12% coverage, $340K to raise it to 67%, against a $1.23M expected loss — is a decision a PM can make in the time it takes to read it.

Prior Art & What's New

ApproachWhat It DoesWhat It Misses
Regulatory stress tests (CCAR, EBA)A small number of prescribed macro scenarios applied annually or semi-annuallyFixed, low-frequency, endpoint-only (no path dynamics), not portfolio-specific, no pre-computed response, no adversarial or novelty component
Traditional VaR / Expected ShortfallDistributional risk summary from historical or parametric returnsA single number, not a scenario tree; no causal structure (fragment regimes), no playbooks, systematically underweights correlation-breakdown non-linearity
Ad hoc desk-level scenario spreadsheetsAnalyst-built "what if" stress cases, usually a handful, updated manuallyNot systematic, not continuously maintained, no formal pruning (coverage is whatever the analyst thought of), no adversarial red-teaming, no memory/recalibration loop
Game-tree search (chess/Go engines)Exhaustive, depth-adaptive branching and pruning over a well-defined, discrete move spaceAssumes a fixed, known rule set and a single opponent; no analogue of catastrophic-tail override, no notion of portfolio-specific relevance or liquidity-adjusted impact
Power-grid N-1/N-2 contingency analysisSystematic single- and double-failure analysis against a known topologyTopology (the grid) is fixed and fully observed; financial fragments are latent, regime-conditional, and estimated, and the "failure modes" interact non-additively in ways grid components mostly don't
Scenario Branching Engine (this invention)Continuous, adaptively-pruned tree over fragment regime transitions; six-dimensional path-aware evaluation; N-1/N-2/full-stress/asymmetric contingency; adversarial red-teaming with an explicit "unhedged nightmare" output; pre-costed, feasibility-checked response playbooks; closed-loop Scenario Memory that recalibrates generation and pruning from realized outcomes—
Known Gaps

Fragment transition probabilities and correlation regime shifts are estimated substantially from historical co-stress episodes, which are rare by definition — the tail scenarios the catastrophic-override rule (Section 2.2) is specifically designed to preserve are also the ones with the thinnest calibration data. The system's own accuracy targets (Section 8.2) are explicit about this: a 0.70 impact-accuracy target concedes up to 30% error even on the scenarios that do occur, and that error is almost certainly worse, not better, in the tail.

The N-2 contingency analysis evaluates only the pairwise combinations flagged by the top-3 N-1 results (Section 5.2), not the full C(7,2)=21 pairs, on compute-budget grounds. This is a deliberate trade-off, but it means a dangerous pairwise interaction between two fragments that individually rank outside the top 3 in N-1 impact could be missed until it shows up as a Rule-4 pruning-audit finding after the fact.

The adversarial module (Section 6) models a single rational, capital-constrained adversary via minimax. It does not model coordinated multi-adversary dynamics, nor does it model an adversary with better information than the market-implied signals the SBE itself observes — if a real adversary has genuine private information about the portfolio beyond what public positioning and flow data reveal, the Red Team's estimate of "our vulnerability" is a lower bound, not a true worst case.

The cost-to-pre-hedge recommendation in every Response Playbook (Section 4.1) is a point estimate of breakeven frequency built on the scenario's probability_at_creation. Because probability estimates for novel or geopolitical scenarios have historically required 2–5x recalibration after the fact (Section 8.3, Rule 2), the "DO NOT pre-hedge" recommendation is itself only as reliable as the probability estimate underneath it — a scenario that looks like poor value to pre-hedge today can become good value to pre-hedge after a single Rule 2 recalibration event, and the playbook does not currently flag this sensitivity to the PM explicitly.

Response Playbooks assume the execution feasibility constraints captured at computation time (counterparty capacity, ISDA coverage, market hours) remain valid until the scenario fires. In a genuinely systemic event, counterparty capacity and dealer balance sheet willingness are themselves regime-dependent and can shrink exactly when the playbook needs them most — the playbook's execution_feasibility field is a snapshot, not a live guarantee, and is not currently re-validated at execution time against real-time dealer capacity.

RecWM Invention · August 2026

Fragment Composition Algebra: Fα ⊗ Fβ

A typed, non-associative algebra for composing seven heterogeneous streams of financial reality — liquidity, momentum, risk, credit, structure, sentiment, policy — into a single coherent world state. The mathematical heart of RecWM.

0. Motivation

A knight on d5 is strong not because of any intrinsic property of the square, but because of relationships: the supporting pawn on c3, the absent challenging bishop, the weakness it creates on e7. AlphaZero evaluates positions compositionally — the value of each piece is a function of every other piece.

RecWM applies the same insight to financial reality. A credit spread of 150bp is not inherently alarming. But 150bp when liquidity is withdrawing, momentum is reversing, and policy is tightening — that is the opening movement of a crisis. The information lives not in any fragment, but in the composition of fragments.

Core thesis. The Fragment Composition Algebra (FCA) is a typed algebraic framework formalizing how seven distinct aspects of financial reality compose into a coherent world state — not by concatenation, but by an operator engineered to surface exactly the information that exists only in the interaction, not in either fragment alone.

1. Fragment Type System

1.1 The Fragment Universe

FragType ::= Liq | Mom | Rsk | Crd | Str | Sen | Pol

T = {Liq, Mom, Rsk, Crd, Str, Sen, Pol}, |T| = 7 — each capturing an irreducible aspect of financial reality.

1.2 Fragment Type Signature

Each fragment is a parameterized dependent type over asset universe A and time t:

Fragment(τ, A, t) := { state : StateSpace(τ, A), traj : Trajectory(τ, A, [t - w(τ), t]), conf : [0, 1], stale : ℝ≥0, provenance : Source × Method }

StateSpace is the type-specific state manifold; Trajectory is a path through state space over lookback window w(τ); conf reflects measurement quality; stale is time-since-update in the fragment's natural timescale; provenance records source and method.

1.3 Type-Specific State Spaces

Each type has a distinct geometric state space — deliberately. Liquidity does not live in the same kind of space as Risk, and flattening them to interchangeable feature vectors erases the geometry that makes composition meaningful.

Liquidity Liq:

StateSpace(Liq, A) := { depth: A→ℝ≥0×ℝ≥0, spread: A→ℝ≥0, resilience: A→ℝ, cross_venue: A→Simplex(V), funding: ℝ^k }

L ≅ ℝ4|A|+k, non-negative depth/spread ⇒ L is an open cone in ℝn.

Momentum Mom:

StateSpace(Mom, A) := { returns: A→ℝ^m, trend: A→S¹, acceleration: A→ℝ, breadth: ℝ, dispersion: ℝ≥0 }

M ≅ (ℝm×S¹×ℝ)|A|×ℝ×ℝ≥0. The S¹ component (trend direction as angle) makes M a fiber bundle over ℝn — direction wraps around; there is no meaningful "greater than" between 359° and 1°.

Risk Rsk:

StateSpace(Rsk, A) := { vol: A→ℝ≥0, corr: Sym+(|A|), tail: A→ℝ, contagion: Graph(A,ℝ≥0), regime: Simplex(R) }

Part of the state lives on Sym+(n), the positive-definite matrix manifold — a Riemannian symmetric space. Distance between correlation regimes must use the affine-invariant metric, not Euclidean norm: naive Euclidean differencing of correlation matrices doesn't respect positive-definiteness and misjudges how "far apart" two regimes really are.

Credit Crd:

StateSpace(Crd, A) := { spread: A→ℝ≥0, hazard: A→ℝ≥0, recovery: A→[0,1], basis: A→ℝ, systemic: ℝ≥0 }

Structure Str:

StateSpace(Str, A) := { flows: A→ℝ, positioning: A→ℝ, leverage: ℝ≥0, concentration: ℝ≥0, gamma: A→ℝ }

Sentiment Sen:

StateSpace(Sen, A) := { tone: A→[-1,1], attention: A→ℝ≥0, consensus: A→[0,1], narrative: Simplex(N), velocity: A→ℝ }

Policy Pol:

StateSpace(Pol, A) := { stance: ℝ, rate_path: ℝ^h, fiscal: ℝ, regulatory: Simplex(RegRegime), credibility: [0,1] }

1.4 Trajectory Type

A fragment is never just a snapshot — it carries recent history and rate of change:

Trajectory(τ, A, [t₀, t]) := { path: [t₀,t]→StateSpace(τ,A), speed: ℝ≥0, curvature: ℝ, direction: TangentSpace(StateSpace(τ,A)) }

The trajectory lives in path space P(StateSpace(τ, A)), an infinite-dimensional manifold; in practice we approximate with a finite basis of path features (speed, curvature, direction).

1.5 The Effective Fragment

For computation, a fragment projects to an effective fragment:

eff : Fragment(τ, A, t) → ℝd(τ) × [0, 1] × ℝ≥0

where d(τ) is effective dimensionality; the last two components are confidence and staleness. This preserves what composition needs while discarding reconstruction detail — it is the interface the composition operator actually consumes.

2. The Composition Operator ⊗

2.1 Design Principles

  • Emergence. F1 ⊗ F2 must contain information absent from both individually — a concatenation operator fails this trivially.
  • Degradation awareness. Composition with a stale or low-confidence fragment must reflect that uncertainty, not silently propagate false precision.
  • Type safety. Defined for all fragment-type pairs, with type-specific interaction logic — Liq⊗Crd and Sen⊗Pol are not the same functional form.
  • Geometric naturality. Respects the geometry of underlying state spaces (the cone L, the Riemannian Sym+, the fiber-bundled trend circle).

2.2 Formal Definition

Let Fα : Fragment(α, A, t), Fβ : Fragment(β, A, t), α, β ∈ T.

⊗ : Fragment(α, A, t) × Fragment(β, A, t) → ComposedFragment({α, β}, A, t)

ComposedFragment(S ⊆ T, A, t) := { individual : ∏τ∈S eff(Fragment(τ, A, t)), interaction : InteractionSpace(S), coherence : [0, 1], composed_conf : [0, 1], effective_stale : ℝ≥0 }
InteractionSpace({α, β}) := { coupling: ℝ^{d(α)×d(β)}→ℝ^{d_int}, residual: ℝ^{d_res}, surprise: ℝ≥0 }

Definition 2.1 (Pairwise Composition)

Fα ⊗ Fβ := ( individual = (eff(Fα), eff(Fβ)), interaction = I(α,β;xα,xβ), coherence = κ(xα,xβ;Hαβ), composed_conf = min(confα,confβ)·κ(xα,xβ;Hαβ), effective_stale = max(staleα/τα, staleβ/τβ)·(τα+τβ)/2 )

τα, τβ are natural timescales; Hαβ is the learned historical coupling matrix.

Interaction Function:

I(α, β; xα, xβ) := φαβ(xα ⊗T xβ) − ψα(xα) − ψβ(xβ)

xα⊗Txβ is the tensor product (a d(α)×d(β) matrix); φαβ is a learned type-pair-specific projection to ℝd_int; ψτ are marginal projections.

Subtracting the marginals is the essential move. I(α,β) captures only information that exists in the interaction — what you know from seeing both fragments together that neither alone reveals. This is the information-theoretic analog of mutual information, computed in state space rather than probability space. It is what separates the FCA from feature-concatenation: concatenation keeps redundant marginal information; I(α,β) keeps only the residual the marginals cannot explain.

Surprise Component:

surprise(α,β) := ‖I(α,β) − 𝔼[I(α,β)|regime]‖² / Var[I(α,β)|regime]

A chi-squared-type statistic on the interaction residual, normalized by regime-conditional variance. High surprise signals potential regime transition.

2.3 Algebraic Properties

Theorem 2.1 (Non-Commutativity)

⊗ is non-commutative in representation but commutative in information content.

Proof sketch. I(α,β;xα,xβ) = I(β,α;xβ,xα) since xα⊗Txβ and xβ⊗Txα are transposes and φαβ is transpose-equivariant: φαβ(M) = φβα(MT). But (eff(Fα),eff(Fβ)) ≠ (eff(Fβ),eff(Fα)) as ordered tuples. Define ~ ignoring individual-component ordering; under ~, Fα⊗Fβ ~ Fβ⊗Fα for all α,β∈T. Thus ⊗ is commutative up to canonical isomorphism. ∎

Theorem 2.2 (Non-Associativity, by Design)

(FL ⊗ FC) ⊗ FR ≠ FL ⊗ (FC ⊗ FR)  in general

Proof. (Liq⊗Crd)⊗Rsk first produces "liquidity-adjusted credit" I(Liq,Crd), then interacts that composite with Risk — three-way effects filtered through the Liq–Crd lens. Liq⊗(Crd⊗Rsk) instead filters through the Crd–Rsk lens. Formally, I((α⊗β),γ) = φ(αβ)γ([eff(Fα),eff(Fβ),I(α,β)] ⊗T xγ) − …, which depends non-linearly on I(α,β); since φ is non-linear, order matters. ∎

Non-associativity is a feature. "Liquidity-adjusted credit risk" is a different concept from "credit-risk-adjusted liquidity." The order of composition reflects the analyst's causal model — RecWM exposes that order as a modeling choice, not a hidden implementation detail.

Theorem 2.3 (Identity Element)

A neutral fragment e exists with e⊗Fα ~ Fα for all α. Construction: e := Fragment(⊥,A,t), state=0∈ℝ⁰, traj=const 0, conf=1, stale=0. Then I(⊥,α;0,xα)=0, coherence=1, and the composed fragment reduces to a trivially-wrapped Fα. ∎

Corollary

(Fragments / ~, ⊗, e) is a unital magma: a set with a binary operation and identity, but neither associativity nor commutativity in general. Not a monoid, not a group, not a ring.

This is the correct structure, not a compromise. Financial reality has no reason to respect associativity: composition order encodes a causal hypothesis, and forcing associativity would silently discard it. Any framework that composes multi-modal financial signals via a commutative, associative operator (plain averaging, concatenation-then-linear-layer) implicitly claims an order-independence financial causation does not have.

2.4 Confidence-Weighted Composition

Ieff(α,β) := I(α,β;xα,xβ) · w(confα,confβ,staleα,staleβ)

w(cα,cβ,sα,sβ) := (cα·cβ) · exp(−λαsα/τα) · exp(−λβsβ/τβ)

Three consequences: low-confidence fragments attenuate their interactions (cross-signals from noisy data aren't trusted); staleness decays exponentially at each fragment's own natural timescale (stale sentiment decays fast, stale policy decays slowly); and cα·cβ means either fragment being unreliable tanks the interaction — the weakest-link principle. A composition cannot be more trustworthy than its least trustworthy input.

3. Interaction Signatures

The ten most critical pairwise interaction signatures, each with mathematical form and financial interpretation.

1 · Liq ⊗ Rsk → "Liquidity-Conditioned Volatility"

I(Liq,Rsk) := vol · (1 + α·depth⁻¹ + β·spread) · resilience⁻¹

Raw volatility is meaningless without liquidity context. VIX 25 with SPY spread 1 cent and 50M on the bid: manageable. VIX 25 with spread 5 cents and 2M on the bid: crisis in progress. Same print, opposite implication — this produces the effective volatility that matters for execution.

2 · Crd ⊗ Pol → "Policy-Conditioned Credit Stress"

I(Crd,Pol) := spread · (1 − credibility · σ(stance_alignment))

200bp when the Fed is easing and has pledged to backstop credit is fundamentally different from 200bp when the Fed is tightening and on record that markets must clear on their own — same spread, vastly different forward distribution depending on the policy put.

3 · Sen ⊗ Str → "Narrative-Flow Coupling"

I(Sen,Str) := |corr(tone_velocity, flow_acceleration)| · attention · leverage

When narrative sentiment shifts with mechanical fund flows, attention is high, and leverage is elevated, the move amplifies: stories attract flows, flows validate stories. This coupling's magnitude predicts the convexity of the next 48 hours.

4 · Liq ⊗ Str → "Flow Absorption Capacity"

I(Liq,Str) := flows / (depth · resilience)  [≅ Kyle's lambda]

Large flows into deep, resilient markets: no problem. Modest flows into thin, fragile markets: significant displacement. The market's "digestive capacity."

5 · Mom ⊗ Rsk → "Risk-Adjusted Trend Conviction"

I(Mom,Rsk) := trend_strength · breadth / (vol · tail_risk) · (1 − corr_instability)

corr_instability := ‖Σt−Σt−1‖F/‖Σt‖F. A strong trend with stable correlations and low tail risk is a trend to ride; unstable correlations and elevated tail risk mean a trend about to break — this tells you whether momentum signals are trustworthy.

6 · Crd ⊗ Liq → "Funding Stress Index"

I(Crd,Liq) := spread · funding_rate · (1 + |basis|) / depth_credit_markets

When spreads widen AND funding rates spike AND CDS-bond basis blows out AND credit depth drops, that's a funding crisis — distinct from either credit stress or liquidity stress alone.

7 · Pol ⊗ Mom → "Policy Inflection Momentum"

I(Pol,Mom) := Δstance · trend_reversal_probability · rate_path_surprise

Policy shifting direction AND momentum rolling over AND rate-path surprise together mark a macro inflection point — the signature of regime change.

8 · Sen ⊗ Crd → "Narrative Credit Coupling"

I(Sen,Crd) := consensus · |Δtone| · spread_velocity · (1 − recovery)

Rapidly shifting, high-consensus negative sentiment plus moving spreads plus dropping recovery expectations: a credit narrative crystallizing — the phase transition from "under pressure" to "uninvestable."

9 · Rsk ⊗ Str → "Structural Fragility"

I(Rsk,Str) := gamma_exposure · vol · leverage · concentration

Dealers short gamma, rising vol, high leverage, concentrated positioning: the market structure is fragile — small shocks produce large non-linear moves. Individual components concerning; their product catastrophic.

10 · Liq ⊗ Sen → "Liquidity Sentiment Divergence"

I(Liq,Sen) := sign(tone) · sign(Δdepth) · |tone − normalized_depth_change|

Bullish sentiment with quietly withdrawing liquidity (or vice versa): smart money contradicting the crowd. Historically the most profitable single interaction — it detects informed disagreement via actual liquidity provision, not stated opinion.

3.2 Interaction Signature Taxonomy

CategorySignaturesPredicts
Amplification3, 7, 9Alignment produces non-linear amplification — magnitude of future moves.
Conditioning1, 2, 5One fragment recontextualizes another — corrects interpretation.
Divergence4, 6, 8, 10Fragments tell contradictory stories — predicts directional change.

4. Higher-Order Compositions

4.1 Multi-Way Composition

For S ⊆ T, the simultaneous composition operator:

⊗S({F_τ}τ∈S) := { individual : {eff(F_τ)}τ∈S, pairwise : {I(α, β)}α,β∈S, α≠β, higher_order : {I_k(S_k)}S_k⊆S, |S_k|=k, k≥3, coherence : κ_S({x_τ}τ∈S), gestalt : G_S({x_τ}τ∈S) }

Ik(Sk) := φSk(⊗τ∈Sk xτ) − ∑S'⊂Sk (−1)|Sk|−|S'| I|S'|(S')

Inclusion–exclusion for interaction information — the k-way term is what remains after subtracting all lower-order interactions, mirroring the Möbius function on the subset lattice: every higher-order term is defined relative to what's already explained at lower order, so nothing is double-counted.

The gestalt GS : ∏τ∈S ℝd(τ) → ℝd_G is a low-dimensional "what is the overall situation?" projection. For S=T (all seven), GT maps state to a point in the world state space W ≅ ℝd_G.

4.2 Resonance Patterns

Definition 4.1

Resonance(S)  ⇔  I_k(S) > μIk + z·σIk

Three empirically-observed patterns:

Crisis Resonance  R_crisis := Liq⊗Crd⊗Rsk⊗Str

I4 = depth⁻¹ · spread · vol · leverage · gamma · concentration

The multiplicative fragility index. Historical calibration: every major crisis since 1998 was preceded by I4 > μ+3σ at least 48 hours before the acute phase.

Inflection Resonance  R_inflect := Mom⊗Pol⊗Sen

I3 = |Δtrend| · |Δstance| · |Δtone| · sign_alignment

Marks macro regime transitions — "risk-on" to "risk-off" or vice versa.

Dislocation Resonance  R_disloc := Liq⊗Str⊗Sen

I3 = flow_magnitude · depth⁻¹ · tone_consensus · attention

Detects dislocations: mechanical flows overwhelming market structure, amplified by narrative consensus — the largest short-term alpha opportunities.

4.3 The Full Composition

W(t) := ⊗T({F_τ(t)}τ∈T)

ComponentCountApprox. dimension
Individual fragments77×d̄ ≈ 70

Total effective dimensionality: ≈400 parameters, of which perhaps 50 are significantly non-zero at any time — far more compact than raw data (millions of points) but far richer than a single-number summary ("VIX at 20").

5. Consistency Checking

5.1 Coherence Metric

Definition 5.1

κ_S := 1 − D_conflict(S) / D_max(S)

D_conflict(S) := ∑α,β∈S wαβ · d_conflict(α,β;xα,xβ)

d_conflict(α,β) := ‖πα(xα) − πβ(xβ)‖²

πα, πβ project each fragment's state onto the shared implication space — predictions both types make about common observables.

Example. Both Liquidity and Credit imply corporate bond market conditions. If liquidity says "credit markets are calm" but credit spreads say "stress is building," the conflict distance is large.

5.2 Contradiction Detection

Definition 5.2

A contradiction exists when κS < κthreshold AND at least one pairwise conflict exceeds its historical p=0.01 quantile:

ContradictionReport := { conflicting_pairs : List((α, β, d_conflict, direction)), implied_resolution : List(Hypothesis), historical_precedent : List(PastEpisode), expected_resolution_time : ℝ≥0 }

Every contradiction must resolve: one fragment is wrong (measurement error, staleness) or reality is in a transient state that cannot persist. implied_resolution generates hypotheses about which fragment moves to restore coherence — often the most profitable signal in the system.

5.3 Coherence Potential

V_κ(w) := −log(κ(w))

Low potential (high coherence) = stable state; high potential (low coherence) = unstable, must resolve. −∇Vκ predicts likely world-state evolution — the system "falls" toward coherence, like a ball rolling downhill.

6. The World State Manifold

6.1 Topology

W is a fiber bundle W→B: base B ≅ Simplex(R) is regime space (probability over bull, bear, crisis, transition, …); fiber over regime r is Wr ≅ ℝd_W. W is not globally Euclidean — moving between regimes is a topological transition, not a smooth deformation, which is why regime changes cannot be modeled as continuous interpolation of state.

6.2 Basins and Ridgelines

Definition 6.1 (Basin)

Connected region Br⊂W where ∇²Vκ(w)≻0 (positive-definite Hessian) — locally stable states the system returns to after small perturbations: "normal bull market," "orderly correction," "flight to quality."

Definition 6.2 (Ridgeline)

Codimension-1 surface Γ⊂W where det(∇²Vκ(w))=0 and ∃v: vT∇²Vκv<0 — unstable boundaries between basins, where any perturbation pushes into one basin or another. Where regime transitions happen.

6.3 Distance Metric

A Fisher-Rao type metric accounting for different scales and uncertainties:

ds² = ∑τ∈T (1/σ²τ)‖dxτ‖² + ∑α<β (1/σ²αβ)‖dI(α,β)‖² + (1/σ²G)‖dG‖²

σ² terms are natural variances from the historical distribution. "How different is today from yesterday?" = geodesic distance; "how far from a crisis state?" = distance to nearest crisis-basin boundary.

Proposition 6.1

Under this metric W has finite diameter within each regime but potentially infinite distance between regimes, since regime transitions involve discrete jumps in the base space.

6.4 The Landscape Function

L(w) := V_κ(w) − S(w) + R(w)

Vκ: contradiction pressure; S(w): stability (basin depth); R(w): resonance (active patterns).

Landscape readingPortfolio implication
L < 0, decreasingStable regime, trends reliable, carry strategies work
L ≈ 0Neutral, no strong signal
L > 0, increasingInstability rising, contradictions building, reduce risk
L > L_criticalRegime transition imminent/in progress, maximum defensiveness

The landscape function is the master signal — every FCA quantity (fragments, interactions, resonances, coherence) rolls up into this single scalar trajectory.

7. Temporal Composition

7.1 The Multi-Timescale Problem

FragmentTimescale τUpdate Frequency
SentimentMinutes–hoursContinuous
LiquidityHours–daysIntraday
MomentumDays–weeksDaily
RiskDays–weeksDaily
StructureWeeksWeekly
CreditWeeks–monthsDaily/Weekly
PolicyMonths–quartersEvent-driven

Naively treating all seven as synchronous snapshots forces sentiment to update at policy's glacial pace, or forces policy to re-estimate every sentiment tick — neither correct.

7.2 The Temporal Fiber Bundle

F_τ(t + dt) = Φ_τ(dt) · F_τ(t) + η_τ(dt)

Φτ(dt) is the type-specific evolution operator, ητ the innovation. Key insight: fast fragments evolve conditioned on slow fragments — sentiment evolves differently depending on policy regime: ΦSen(dt|Pol) ≠ ΦSen(dt).

7.3 Adiabatic Approximation

For well-separated timescales (τfast«τslow), borrowing from quantum mechanics:

F_fast(t) ≈ F*_fast(F_slow(t)) + δ_fast(t)

The deviation δfast is the signal: when the fast fragment hasn't adjusted to the slow fragment's state, there is temporal arbitrage. Example: Policy shifts dovish→hawkish (slow); sentiment hasn't adjusted (fast deviation). δSen measures how much re-pricing remains.

7.4 The Multi-Resolution World State

W(t) := {W^(k)(t)}k=1K,   W^(k)(t) := ⊗_T({F̄^(k)_τ(t)}τ∈T)

F̄^(k)_τ(t) := ∫_{−∞}^{t} K_k(t − s) · F_τ(s) ds

Kk is a kernel of characteristic width τk, producing a stack of world states: intraday (k=1) captures fast dynamics, weekly (k=4) medium-term trends, quarterly (k=6) macro regimes.

7.5 Cross-Scale Interaction

I_cross(k₁, k₂) := W^(k₁)(t) − π_{k₁}(W^(k₂)(t))

Example. Quarterly world state says "bull regime." Daily world state says "emerging stress." This cross-scale divergence signals a regime transition in progress — the fast world leading the slow world. The faster the divergence grows, the more imminent the regime change.

8. Implementation: From Algebra to Algorithm

8.1 The Composition Pipeline

Raw Data → Extraction → Fragment Formation → Pairwise Composition → Higher-Order Composition → Coherence Check → World State → Landscape Evaluation → Portfolio Signal
  1. Extraction. Type-specific pipelines extract state, trajectory, confidence, staleness from raw streams.
  2. Formation. Fragment(τ,A,t) objects instantiated with type-checked fields.
  3. Pairwise. All C(7,2)=21 interactions computed in parallel.
  4. Higher-order. Three-/four-way interactions computed only for the ~10 significant resonance patterns, not exhaustively.
  5. Coherence. κT evaluated; contradictions trigger alerts.
  6. World state. Composed state projected to gestalt dimensions.
  7. Landscape. L(w) evaluated — the master signal.

Closest in spirit to interaction information / co-information (McGill 1954; Williams & Beer 2010's partial information decomposition), and to how physicists define connected correlation functions by subtracting disconnected pieces. The novelty is packaging that principle as a typed algebra over seven financially-meaningful, geometrically-distinct state spaces, with explicit non-associative composition order, confidence-weighted decay, and a coherence-potential dynamical reading of the resulting manifold.

10. Formal Summary

FCA := (F, T, ⊗, ⊗_S, I, κ, W, L, ds², Φ)

Fthe set of all possible fragments across all types
Tthe set of seven fragment types
⊗pairwise composition operator (non-associative, commutative up to isomorphism)
⊗Ssimultaneous multi-way composition operator
